# Light on the Tantras
<note>original: "Tantrāloka"</note>

->Composed by the most eminent teacher of the Great Lord’s path, the venerable Abhinavagupta.<-
->Accompanied by the commentary named *Discernment* <note>original: "Viveka"</note> composed by the eminent teacher Jayaratha.<-

<image-desc>decorative horizontal divider with scrollwork and a central diamond-shaped ornament</image-desc>

## The First Lesson
<note>original: "Prathamam Āhnikam"</note>

<image-desc>decorative horizontal divider featuring a central diamond and flanking line-and-dot patterns</image-desc>

From whom all diverse movements arise, from whom the foundations of bliss and consciousness emerge;
Whose very splendor of power is all this, and who is of such a nature:
May that radiance—the non-dual essence of the <term>Trika|The "Threefold" system of Kashmiri Shaivism, focusing on the triad of the individual, the divine power, and the Supreme Lord</term> reality, which shines with the fullness of sovereign freedom—
Destroy the veil covering the secret of the Shaiva scriptures <note>original: "Śiva-śāsana-āgama"</note> within 
->my heart. ||1||<-

---

<note>The following are textual variants found in different manuscript copies used by the editors.</note>
Line 1, Manuscript B: "From whom the diverse movements [arise] which are appropriate, those various manifestations of the world..."
Manuscript C: "...which are appropriate, those various powers of manifestation. May that radiance—the non-dual essence of the Threefold Reality, which has arisen from the delusion of Maya. That which never assumes such a form, or rather, which is of such a form: May it entirely dispel the darkness residing in the dwelling of my heart."
This is the reading.

<meta>This page continues the introductory verses (maṅgala) of the Tantrāloka. # Light on the Tantras
<note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note>

->Even while in this body, I am truly liberated. I take refuge in my heart in that True Teacher <note>original: "sadguru"</note>, who is a venerable ocean of welfare <note>original: "Śrīmat-Kalyāṇa-vāridhi"; a double-meaning referring to his father and teacher, Kalyanaraja</note>, by whose mere droplets of compassion [I have attained this state]. ||2||<-

->Whose command, like a crest-jewel worn by all kings upon their heads, has swiftly taken refuge in my heart, even though it was hardened by the heavy burdens of worldly existence. ||3||<-

->I have not set out here to win the status of an author, nor to display an unprecedented skill in speech. Rather, my desire is that through the deep study of this work's meaning, the seeker might gain a **refinement of thought-constructs** <term>vikalpa-saṃskāra|The process of purifying or 'polishing' the mind's conceptual frameworks so they no longer obscure the non-dual truth</term>. ||4||<-

---

Line 1: Manuscript G reads: "...I am [liberated] because of the glance of even a small portion of his grace. **I bow to the venerable Kalyanaraja, my father and teacher.**"

Line 2: Manuscript B reads "shriye" <note>implying 'for the sake of splendor'</note>. After this verse, Manuscript G shows two additional verses as follows:

> By those teachers, experts in the secret of the Shaiva scriptures <note>original: "Śiva-śāsana-āgama"</note>, with deep hearts and rising mercy, glances were cast upon me by those friends of the wretched with unerring speech, eyes reddened by compassion. 

> Thus, the secret essence of all things spoken by Shiva took refuge in my mind through the cultivation of that inner state, quickly finding a home even though my heart was hardened. <note>These two verses are linked as a pair (yugmam).</note>

Line 3: Manuscript A reads "mūrdhni taṃsa iva"; Manuscript B uses the neuter form "uttaṃsam."
Line 5: Manuscript G reads "māptumnāstapurvam."
Line 6: Manuscript G reads: "The wise have set out to spread their own skill."
Line 8: Manuscript G reads: "My desire" <note>instead of "Our desire"</note>.

<summary>Abhinavagupta honors his father and teacher, Kalyanaraja, and explains that the Tantrāloka is intended not for his own fame, but to help seekers refine their consciousness through "vikalpa-saṃskāra."</summary>
<keywords>Kalyanaraja, spiritual teacher, liberation in life, vikalpa-saṃskāra, thought-purification, Shaiva scriptures, humility, manuscript variants</keywords>

# Chapter One: The Daily Lesson
<note>original: "Prathamāhnikam"</note>

->Some come and go, while others stay; some are ignorant, and others are envious.<-
->Some are full of doubt. What can I say of those listeners who have not even arrived? ||5||<-

->Because the deep meaning—sweet with the skill of my own heart—is not heard [properly] by others, my mind wavers, even though this work is filled with profound intent. ||6||<-

->Whatever unconstrained power shines forth here, though it exceeds my own share of strength, it is but the expansion of the **Great Bliss** <term>mahānanda|The supreme state of aesthetic and spiritual rapture in Kashmir Shaivism</term> of the Venerable Supreme Lord. ||7||<-

Now, indeed, at the very beginning of this treatise, the author contemplates the appropriate **Chosen Deity** <term>iṣṭadevatā|A personal or preferred deity invoked for the success of a task</term> through an extraordinary blessing. This blessing encapsulates the essence of the **Six-and-a-half-fold Scripture** <note>original: "ṣaḍardha-śāstra"; a traditional name for the Trika system of Tantra</note> that is about to be explained:

->The Mother is the great support of pure arts and fresh creation,<-
->And the Father, whose body is full, has his radiance hidden within five faces.<-
->May my heart—which is the **Lineage of the Nectar of the Unsurpassable**<-
-><term>anuttarāmṛta-kula|A technical term for the supreme reality that is both 'beyond' (anuttara) and 'embodied' or 'familial' (kula)</term>—<-
->consisting of the creative emission of reality flashing from the union of those two, shine forth!<-
->||1||<-

---

<margin>Line 2: In manuscript 'Kha', the reading is "he should say" <note>original: "brūyāt"</note> instead of "should I say."</margin>

<vocab>First Daily Lesson, Six-and-a-half-fold Scripture, Chosen Deity, Support of Pure Arts, Lineage of the Nectar of the Unsurpassable, Great Bliss, At the beginning of the treatise</vocab>

<summary>Abhinavagupta expresses the difficulty of finding fit disciples before transitioning into the formal invocation of the Tantrāloka. The first verse of the work proper uses wordplay to simultaneously honor his physical parents (Vimalā and Narasiṃhagupta) and the cosmic union of Śakti and Śiva.</summary>
<keywords>Abhinavagupta, Trika, Mahānanda, Anuttara, Visarga, creative emission, spiritual lineage, divine union, Vimalā, Narasiṃhagupta</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka, specifically explaining the phrase "May my heart flash forth." It defines the "heart" not as a physical organ, but as the supreme state of Universal Bliss (Jagadānanda) and the union of Shiva and Shakti.</meta>

### The Venerable Tantrāloka

The word **"My"** <note>original: 'mama'</note> refers to the Self. The **"Heart"** <note>original: 'hṛdayam'</note> is the true reality, which is also called **Universal Bliss** <term>jagadānanda|The seventh and highest state of spiritual rapture where the entire universe is perceived as the vibration of one's own consciousness</term>. This heart should **"flash forth"** <note>original: 'sphuratāt'</note>—meaning it should expand or blossom—as something that is not limited by the three divisions of time (past, present, and future). This occurs through the radiance of the state of **Immersive Absorption** <term>samāveśa|A profound state of mystical union where the practitioner's individual identity dissolves into the Divine</term>, which is preceded by the casting aside of the habitual tendencies of the limited perceiver, such as identifying with the physical body or the vital breath.

What is the nature of this "Heart"? It is described as **"both of them"** <note>original: 'tadubhaya'</note>. "That" refers to what will be explained in the first half of the verse, and "both" refers to the **Twin-Union** <term>yāmala|The dyadic, inseparable state of the Absolute as both masculine and feminine</term>. As it will be stated later in this work:

> "That union of the two is known as the **Creative Encounter** <term>saṃghaṭṭa|The dynamic 'rubbing together' or meeting of Shiva and Shakti that generates the universe</term>."

From that encounter comes the **"flashing state of being,"** which possesses a reality that shines forth by its own power, independent of anything else. It is this very state that is described:

> "For this very reason, this **Creative Emission** <term>visarga|The 'outpouring' or 'discharge' of divine energy that manifests as the world</term> is of the nature of the unmanifested 'Ha' sound <note>The 'Ha' sound represents the Shakti/Power that completes the alphabet and initiates creation</note>."

---

### Notes

<note>Footnotes from the original text</note>

1. **Universal Bliss** <note>original: Jagadānanda</note> is the single, constant witness of the six levels of bliss <note>The six lower blisses are: Nijānanda, Nirānanda, Parānanda, Brahmānanda, Mahānanda, and Cidānanda</note>. It is free from rising or setting (beginning or ending) and its ultimate purpose is the state of resting within the Self. The author himself will state later in this text:

->Where there is no division of any kind, which flashes forth from all sides;<-
->Which is nourished by the supreme nectar of 'unstruck' awareness;<-
->Where practices such as meditation have no primary relevance;<-
->That is the Universal Bliss which Lord Shiva described to us.<-

---

<margin>Line 6: In the Ga-manuscript, the reading is "of the nature of the identity of taste" <note>original: sāmarasya-rūpaḥ</note> instead of "the identity of the Twin-Union."</margin>

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the "Heart" of the practitioner, identifying it as the state of Universal Bliss (Jagadānanda). It explains that this state arises from the union (Yamala) of Shiva and Shakti, which transcends the limitations of time and the physical body.</summary>
<keywords>Jagadānanda, Samāveśa, Yāmala, Saṃghaṭṭa, Visarga, Universal Bliss, Creative Emission, Abhinavagupta, Kashmir Shaivism</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the detailed commentary on the first verse of Abhinavagupta’s Tantrāloka. Having previously established the 'Heart' as the union of Shiva and Shakti, the text now moves to define the specific qualities of this union, focusing on the concepts of the Supreme (Anuttara) and the Creative Outpouring (Visarga) that generates the universe.</meta>

५

-> Verse 1 ] Chapter One <-

By saying this, the **Emission** <term>visarga|Literally 'letting go' or 'outpouring'; in Tantric thought, it is the divine urge of consciousness to manifest the universe</term> consists of the dual brilliance of the manifest and the unmanifest <note>original: "kulākula-ubhaya-chaṭā"</note>. It takes the form of a fraction of the letter 'ha' <note>The letter 'ha' represents the totality of the universe; its internal divisions symbolize the subtle stages through which pure consciousness begins to externalize itself</note> and its very nature is the desire to shine forth externally. This Emission is the source from which everything originates. Because of this, the author says: "**The Family of the Supreme Nectar**" <note>original: 'anuttarāmṛtakulam'</note>. 

The **Supreme** <term>anuttara|The 'unsurpassed' or 'ultimate' reality which has nothing above it; also identifies the first letter 'A' of the Sanskrit alphabet</term> is called so because it is superior to other forms of "nectar" or states of immortality which only last for a limited time. It is superior because:

> "Where there is no fear at all, nor old age, nor even diseases; 
> where there are no obstacles, no death, and where Time does not exert its power."

Because it is not reckoned by Time, it is that state where "death" <note>original: 'mṛta'</note> is non-existent. The "**Family**" <note>original: 'kula'</note> refers to the "body" or the totality of manifestation. Thus, the phrase means: the nature of the digit known as **Amā** <term>amā-kalā|The seventeenth, 'stainless' digit of the moon that remains constant and provides nectar to the other sixteen phases; it represents the unchanging aspect of the Divine</term>. 

As it has been stated elsewhere:

> "That seventeenth digit is the one whose very form is Nectar."

Furthermore, what is meant by "both of them"? The text says: "**The Mother and the Father**." 

What is the nature of the Mother? She is the one who "**rests in the stainless digit**" <note>original: 'vimalakalāśrayā'</note>. "Stains" <note>original: 'mala'</note> refer to the limiting conditions of the individual soul; the Mother is she from whom these limitations have departed. The "**Digit**" <note>original: 'kalā'</note> is the power of agency—the ability to act—which is characterized solely by Supreme Awareness. That digit is the "**Rest**" <note>original: 'āśraya'</note>, meaning it is her very foundation and essence. This signifies that she is the **Power of Pure Sovereignty** <term>svātantrya-śakti|The absolute, independent freedom of God to create, sustain, and withdraw the universe purely by will</term>.

---

<margin>Line 1: The manuscript marked 'ka' reads 'half-form of the letter ha' instead of 'half-of-the-half-form'.</margin>
<margin>Line 2: The manuscript marked 'ka' reads 'where that is' instead of 'is that where'.</margin>

<summary>This page explains the metaphysical components of the 'Heart' of reality, identifying it as the union of the Mother (the Power of Sovereignty) and the Father (the Supreme), whose creative outpouring (Visarga) generates the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Visarga, Anuttara, Nectar of Immortality, Amā Digit, Mother and Father, Sovereignty, Pure Awareness, Tantraloka</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka. Having defined the "Family of the Supreme Nectar," the text now explains how the world's diversity arises solely from the Absolute Freedom (Svātantrya) of the Divine, rather than through external causes like ignorance or karma.</meta>

६

# The Light of the Tantras
-> (Śrī Tantrāloka) <-

Therefore, it is said that in the "fresh"—meaning the first—"creation," which occurs in the **Pure Way** <term>shuddhādhva|The 'Pure Path' or 'Pure Way'; the higher levels of manifestation where the divine will acts directly without the obscuration of limited individuality</term>:

> "In the Pure Way, Shiva is the Agent..." <note>original: 'śuddhedhvani śivaḥ kartā...'</note>

According to this principle, because Shiva himself is directly perceived there, it is said: "She whose **radiance** <note>original: 'mahaḥ'</note> is the expansion of light characterized by absolute fullness." 

In this **Non-dual Tradition** <term>advaya-naya|The school of thought (specifically Trika Shaivism) which holds that there is no ultimate difference between the individual, the world, and God</term>, the Lord himself—by the greatness of his own **Absolute Freedom** <term>svātantrya|The sovereign, self-dependent power of consciousness to act and create without external causes</term>—makes the world appear as if it were separate, even though it is not actually separate from him. The world's essence is "mere appearance." Thus, it is stated that this Absolute Freedom, which depends on nothing else, is the sole cause of the world’s diversity. 

It is unreasonable to claim that **ignorance** <note>original: 'avidyā'</note> or **karmic impressions** <note>original: 'vāsanā'</note> are the causes of the world's diversity. This is because those concepts are undermined by the logical contradictions of "difference" and "non-difference" <note>In this system, if ignorance is different from God, it creates a dualism; if it is the same as God, it cannot be 'ignorance.' Therefore, only God's free Will can be the cause</note>. Therefore, although the Lord possesses infinite powers such as **Consciousness** <note>original: 'cit'</note> and the rest, they are all merely his own **vibration** <term>sphuraṇa|The rhythmic pulsation or 'sparking' of divine consciousness</term>. Because Absolute Freedom is the most predominant of these powers, it is specifically mentioned here. As will be stated later:

> "Therefore, He is joined with the power of Absolute Freedom; this is the direct rule." <note>original: 'tena svātantryaśaktyaiva yukta ityāñjaso vidhiḥ'</note>

And what is the nature of the Progenitor <note>Shiva</note>? It is said: he is "**of full body**" <note>original: 'bharita-tanuḥ'</note>. "Full" means characterized by total completeness, resulting from the cessation of all desires.

<summary>This page argues that the diversity of the universe is not caused by ignorance (avidyā) but by Shiva's Absolute Freedom (Svātantrya), which manifests the world as an internal reflection of his own fullness.</summary>

<keywords>Shiva, Shuddhādhva, Svātantrya, Absolute Freedom, Non-dualism, Advaya, Creation, Sphuraṇa</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka. Having established that the Absolute Freedom of consciousness is the cause of the world, Jayaratha now explains the "body" and "faces" of the Divine mentioned in the root verse, identifying them with the five fundamental powers and the five cosmic acts.</meta>

७

# The Light of the Tantras
-> (Verse 1 | Chapter 1) <-

His **body** <note>original: 'tanuḥ'</note> is "filled," meaning his very nature is full. He is **independent** <term>svatantra|The sovereign power of the Absolute to act without external influence</term> because he does not look toward anything other than himself—this is the point. Precisely because of this, he is filled by **five faces** <note>original: 'pañcabhiḥ mukhaiḥ'</note> consisting of the powers of Consciousness, Bliss, Will, Knowledge, and Action. 

As it is said:

> "The Power of Shiva <note>Śakti</note> is here called the 'Face'."

By this statement, we see that his **desire** <note>original: 'ruchiḥ'</note>—which is his "interest" or "shining forth"—is **protected** <note>original: 'guptā'</note> or fully pervaded by these powers. Since no specific object is mentioned, this desire refers to the **Five-fold Cosmic Act** <term>kṛtya-pañcakam|The five operations of the Divine: creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace</term>. The meaning is that he is the one who eternally performs these five acts.

As it has been stated:

> "The Lord who is the creator of both **emission** <note>sṛṣṭi/creation</note> and **withdrawal** <note>saṃhāra/destruction</note>, who causes **concealment** <note>vilaya</note> and **maintenance** <note>sthiti</note>, the God who bestows **grace** <note>anugraha</note> and destroys the suffering of those who bow to Him."

Thus, by the nature of the expansion of **emission** <term>visarga|The 'outpouring' or 'overflow' of divine consciousness that results in the manifestation of the universe</term>, that which is the "unnameable" reality has been invoked here to destroy the host of obstacles. This reality is the seed of the world’s diversity, known as the **Supreme Triad** <term>Para-trika|The 'Highest Three'; the core doctrine of this school involving the union of the Subject, the Object, and the means of Knowledge (or Shiva, Shakti, and the Individual)</term>, which is the union of Shiva and Shakti.

As it is said:

> "Even there, the Great Lord, full of His own Self, when He attains union <note>saṅghaṭṭa</note> with His Power <note>Śakti</note>, enters the supreme state of mystical immersion."

***

<margin>Line 7: Manuscript K reads "the specific five-fold act" <note>original: 'pañcaka-viśeṣa'</note>.</margin>
<margin>Line 15: Manuscript K reads: "even there, the Great Lord, through the power of his own Self, is free from the mortal realm." Manuscript Kh shows an original reading: "even there, devoid of Power."</margin>

<summary>This page explains that the "body" of the Divine is pure freedom, expressing itself through five "faces" or powers (Consciousness, Bliss, Will, Knowledge, Action) to perform the five cosmic acts of creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.</summary>
<keywords>Five Acts (kṛtya-pañcakam), Five Powers (Shaktis), Emission (visarga), Union (sanghatta), Supreme Triad (Para-trika), Maheshvara</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka. The previous page discussed the "Five Faces" of the Divine as the five powers (Consciousness, Bliss, Will, Knowledge, and Action). This page specifically identifies the "Supreme Face" with the "Heart" and the Goddess Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī, further defining the key Trika concept of the "Absolute" (Anuttara).</meta>

८

# The Holy Tantrāloka

As it is said:

> "Then His supreme **Face** <note>original: 'vaktra'</note> is the seat for the expansion of **Emission** <term>visarga|The creative 'outpouring' or 'overflow' of divine consciousness that results in the manifestation of the universe</term>. It is beautiful with the **Bliss of the World** <note>original: 'jagad-ānanda'</note> that arises from the unfolding of the **Absolute** <term>anuttara|The 'unsurpassed' or the Ultimate Reality beyond which nothing exists</term>. It remains as the **Seed** of everything, held in a state where the future 'faces' <note>the various powers of manifestation</note> are not yet divided. It is considered the first wave of the supreme essence arising from the **Vibration of the Heart** <term>hṛd-spanda|The subtle, eternal 'throb' or 'resonance' of consciousness</term>. This is the supreme, subtle **Triad** <term>Trika|The philosophical system centered on the trinity of Shiva, Shakti, and the Individual; or the three goddesses Parā, Parāparā, and Aparā</term>, where all powers exist without division."

And also, regarding the word **"Heart"**—

-> "The Heart is the thread of Power..." <-

By this and similar statements, [the Heart] is the abode of the venerable **Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī** <note>The supreme form of the Goddess in the Krama system, whose name means 'She who draws in Time'</note>. This abode manifests in a shimmering form by "threading together" the entire wheel of powers, beginning with the venerable **Sṛṣṭikālī** <note>The aspect of the Goddess Kali who presides over the 'emission' or creation of the world</note>. The phrase **"May it shine forth"** <note>original: 'saṃsphuratāt'</note> signifies: "May I become one with that abode through absolute identity." 

What is the nature of this abode? It is described as the **"Family of the Nectar of the Absolute"** <note>original: 'anuttarāmṛtakulam'</note>. Because the acts of creation and the rest dissolve into this very place, there is no "beyond" <note>uttara</note> or higher reality than it; for this reason, it is the **Absolute** <note>anuttara</note>. Precisely because of this, it is **Nectar** <note>amṛta</note>, for its ultimate reality is nothing but the "wonder" <note>camatkāra</note> of one's own Self. For this very reason, it is the **Family** <term>kula|In this context, the 'totality' of divine power or the 'embodiment' of consciousness</term>...

---

Line 2: Another manuscript reads: "the world which is a ray of the unfolding of the Absolute."
Line 3: Another manuscript reads: "by the division of the faces."
Line 4: Another manuscript reads: "The vibration of the heart is the form of the supreme essence of vision, composed of that [Absolute] without any sense of 'mine'."
Line 6: Another manuscript reads: "by the threading together of the wheel of all powers starting with the time of creation."
Line 11: Another manuscript reads: "one through that identity."

<summary>Jayaratha explains the "Heart" as the supreme face of the Divine, identifying it with the Goddess Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī and the "Absolute" (Anuttara). He defines the Absolute as the state where all creative powers exist in an undivided, blissful "seed" form before manifestation.</summary>
<keywords>Anuttara, Heart, Kalasankarshani, Srishtikali, Visarga, Spanda, Kula, Bliss of the World, Trika philosophy</keywords>

Having established the "Heart" as the seat of the Goddess Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī, Abhinavagupta (via the commentator Jayaratha) now defines the nature of the "Unnameable" state and the mystical fusion of creation and destruction.</meta>

# First Daily Portion <note>original: 'āhnika'</note>
### Verse 1

"...Kula is known by the name of the Lotus..."

This refers to the **Unnameable** <term>anākhya|The 'nameless' or 'ineffable' fourth state in Krama philosophy that transcends and permeates creation, maintenance, and dissolution</term> form—this is the meaning. What else is it like? He says, "of both of these." "Both" refers to the cycles of **Creation** and **Dissolution** <note>original: 'sṛṣṭi-saṃhāra'</note> that are about to be explained. Their **Union** <term>yāmala|Literally 'twin' or 'couple'; the non-dual state where Shiva and Shakti, or any two opposites, exist in perfect equilibrium</term> is a state of **Fusion** <term>lolī-bhāva|A mystical state of 'liquefaction' or 'melting together' where the distinction between subject and object, or creation and destruction, is dissolved</term>. Thus:

> "The Supreme State shines within the two wheels <note>the 'wheels' of creation and dissolution</note>, having become **Fused**."

And likewise:

> "From the **Fusion** between emergence and disappearance, the sequence known as **Descent** <note>original: 'avatāra'; here referring to the movement of consciousness into manifestation</note> occurs."

By this logic, the diverse **Manifestation** <note>original: 'sarga'</note>, whose essence is **Maintenance** <note>original: 'sthiti'</note> and which possesses a shimmering existence, is composed of that union. The intention is this: it is the supreme, **Unnameable** venerable **Consciousness** <term>saṃvit|The foundational, self-aware light of reality</term> who, through her own **Absolute Freedom** <term>svātantrya|The sovereign power of the Divine to manifest anything without external instruments or causes</term>, makes creation and the rest appear within her own Self and dissolves <note>original: 'vilāyayati'</note> them—this is the point. As it has been said:

> "Whose single radiance is eternally risen, destroying the passage of **Time**; She shines in the void of the sky that blooms within the **Heart-Lotus**. She, who takes the form of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, delights in their withdrawal."

---

<margin>Line 10, Manuscript Kh: "Dissolves" <note>original: 'vilāpayati'</note> is the reading.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka. The previous page discussed the fusion of creation and dissolution within the "Heart" of the Absolute. Now, the commentator Jayaratha explains the specific terms "Mother" and "Father" as metaphors for the dual aspects of the Supreme Consciousness—the powers of manifestation and withdrawal.</meta>

१०

# The Venerable Tantrāloka <note>original: 'Śrītantrāloka'</note>

In this way, the author explains both realities referred to by the word "that": "**The Mother and the Father**" <note>original: 'jananī janakaśca'</note>. She is the "**Mother**" because she generates the universe. She is the Supreme Goddess of the Great Lord, the beginning of the wheel of creation and the other cycles. <margin>Note on line 3: Some manuscripts read "the wheel of creation of the Supreme Goddess."</margin> Because she is of the nature of pure consciousness alone, she is called "**Pure**" <note>original: 'vimalā'</note>. She is the primordial lunar "**Digit**" <term>kalā|A 'digit' or 'phase' of the moon; in this context, it refers to the 16th or 17th lunar phase which represents the unchanging, nectar-filled essence of the Goddess</term> who is the "**Abode**" <note>original: 'āśrayaḥ'</note>—meaning she is the support and the movement. The sense is that she consists of the supreme nectar that nourishes the entire world. As it has been said:

> "Creation, which is the form of supreme bliss, sits above, raining down a shower of nectar; she is the supreme phase belonging to the **Bindu** <term>bindu|The 'point' or 'seed' of condensed consciousness from which all manifestation radiates</term>."

And likewise:

> "The peaceful lunar digit stands above, the Goddess who consists of the essence of the bliss of full nectar."

Therefore, within the "**Ever-new**" <note>original: 'abhinavāyām'</note>—following the principle that she exists "forever for the sake of the play of creation"—she is that "**Radiance**" <note>original: 'mahaḥ'</note> whose defining characteristic is **Absolute Freedom** <term>svātantrya|The sovereign power of Consciousness to manifest and perceive all things according to its own will, without external necessity</term>. This radiance is always shining within the outward form of **Creation** <note>original: 'sṛṣṭi'</note>. <margin>Note on line 14: Various manuscripts read "always for the sake of illumination" or "eternal."</margin> Conversely, he who generates the dissolution of all existing things is the "**Father**" <note>original: 'janakaḥ'</note>, the Beautiful One...

<summary>This page explains the first verse's reference to the "Mother" and "Father," identifying the Mother as the lunar, nectar-filled power of creation (Vimalā Kalā) and the Father as the power of dissolution.</summary>
<keywords>Mother (Jananī), Father (Janaka), Pure (Vimalā), Lunar Digit (Kalā), Nectar (Amṛta), Creation (Sṛṣṭi), Absolute Freedom (Svātantrya)</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka. The previous page defined the "Mother" as the Goddess Vimalā and began describing the "Father" as the Supreme Subject. This page elaborates on how this Supreme Subject, the "Father," interacts with the world through his sensory powers and maintains his fullness by "swallowing" all objective reality.</meta>

<column-break/>

### Verse 1 | First Daily Lesson | 11

The Supreme Subject <note>original: 'parah pramātā'</note>, through the **"mouths"**—which are the gateways in the form of the activities of the senses like the eyes—of the **"five"** powers of conveyance <margin>Line 1: Manuscript 'Kh' reads "powers of conveyance" (vāhanaśakti) instead of "powers of Vāmeśī."</margin> led by the Goddess Vāmeśī <term>vāmēśī|The 'Goddess of the Left' or the 'Emitting Goddess' who governs the flow of sensory experience and the wheel of powers</term>, acts according to the following principle:

> "By whichever sensory path a particular object shines forth, the yogi, by the power of his own self-support, should reach that object and become one with it."

Following this logic, his **"Radiance"** <note>original: 'ruciḥ'</note>—meaning his inner light—is **"Protected"** <note>original: 'guptā'</note> or preserved by the power of his self-support through the seizing of various objects. The meaning is that his state as the Supreme Subject is fully ignited because he is the "swallower" of all objective states of being. For this very reason, he is **"Replete of body"** <note>original: 'bharitatnuḥ'</note>. This means he is "full" because he rests in his own Self alone; this fullness arises from a state of total desirelessness produced by the "shrinking" <note>the withdrawal of external diversity back into the unity of the self</note> of all those various objective states.

Thus, it should be said that here the author has contemplated the Supreme Divine Consciousness <note>original: 'pāramēśvarī saṃvit'</note>. She is known as the "Unnameable" <note>original: 'anākhyā'</note>. Even as she manifests the appearance of the three-fold sequence of creation, sustenance, and dissolution <term>kramatraya|The three-fold process of the universe; here, the author suggests a fourth state that transcends and includes them</term>, she shines by transcending them. Her nature is both the sequence and the non-sequential. As has been said by my great-grand-teacher <note>original: 'parameṣṭhiguru'; Manuscript 'Ka' reads "by our teacher."</note>:

> "I place in my heart that Goddess, the Supreme Consciousness, who shines intensely; she who constantly crosses the three sequences by the very act of resting upon them. She radiates as one whose form is the sequence itself, yet whose essential nature is non-sequence."

Line 13: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "by our teacher."

## ...Thus.

And furthermore, **"the heart"** <note>original: 'hṛdayam'</note>—which is the reality characterized by the raising up of one's own power—should, because no specific limitation is mentioned, **"manifest"** <note>original: 'sphuratāt'</note> or blossom for everyone through the perfect ascent of both the known and the named. This is the meaning.

And of what nature is this heart? He says, **"of that pair"** <note>original: 'tadubhaya'</note>. That which is to be explained in the first half of the verse is the **"pair"** <note>original: 'yamalam'</note> consisting of the Mother and the Father <term>yāmala|the 'dyad' or 'twin' union of Shiva and Shakti representing the state of non-dual consciousness</term>. In that primary union, there is a **"vibrant state"** <note>original: 'bhāvaḥ'</note>, a specific inner disposition full of joy, which is **"vibrating"** <note>original: 'sphuritaḥ'</note> due to the interplay of their mutual orientation and the degrees of their aesthetic wonder <note>original: 'camatkāra'</note>.

By that state, there is an **"emission"** <note>original: 'visargaḥ'</note>—a projection or flow of the specific substances known as *kunda* and *gola* <term>kunda and gola|esoteric ritual substances representing the male and female creative essences</term>. That emission is its very nature. For this reason, in the **"Supreme"** <note>original: 'anuttare'</note>—which is the **"nectar"** <note>original: 'amṛte'</note> or essence that is superior to the semen and blood of animals because of the contemplation of the deities of white and red light—there is a **"totality"** <note>original: 'kulam'</note> or form. As it is said:

-> "...Kula is the sphere of origin." <-

The author asks, "What is that pair?" and answers, **"The Mother and the Father"** <note>original: 'jananī janakaśca'</note>. Of what nature is she...

### First Daily Lesson
<meta>Verse 1 (continued)</meta>

And who is the **Mother**? She is **"supported by the pure digits"** <note>original: 'vimalakalāśrayā'</note>. "Pure" refers to the digits or creative arts of the phonemes <term>varṇakalā|the mystical powers associated with the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet</term>; she whose **"support"** <note>original: 'ālambanam'</note> or basis consists of these is she who is named Vimalakalā <note>Abhinavagupta’s mother’s name was Vimalā or Vimalakalā</note>—this is the meaning.

Furthermore, she is **"the greatness of the new creation"** <note>original: 'abhinavasṛṣṭimahā'</note>. The **"creation"** <note>original: 'sṛṣṭiḥ'</note> of **"Abhinava"**—that is, the illustrious Abhinavagupta—is his very birth. As it is said:

> "His fathers rejoice and his grandfathers rejoice:
> Today a devotee of the Great Lord Shiva <note>original: 'māheśvara'</note> is born; he will carry us across the ocean of worldly existence."

Based on such sayings, because of the birth of a noble son, she has fulfilled her life’s purpose <note>original: 'kṛtakṛtyatayā'</note>. Thus, by producing an extraordinary state of aesthetic and spiritual wonder <note>original: 'camatkāra'</note>, she is one for whom there is a **"festival"** <note>original: 'mahaḥ'</note> or great celebration.

And likewise, of what nature is the **Father**? He is **"one whose brilliance is protected by the Five-Faced One"** <note>original: 'pañcamukhaguptaruciḥ'</note>. The **"Five-Faced One"** refers to a lion <note>original: 'siṃha'</note>. He whose **"brilliance"** <note>original: 'ruciḥ'</note> or fame is spread everywhere under the name Siṃhagupta <note>literally "Protected by the Lion"</note> is he. As the verse says:

> "His son is known among the people as Chukhulaka,
> Narasiṃhagupta, whose intellect is as bright and pure as the moon."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verse of the Tantrāloka, specifically explaining the dual identity of the author's parents as both physical human beings and as embodiments of the divine Shiva and Shakti. It explains why the father is referred to by both "Siṃhagupta" and "Narasiṃhagupta."</meta>

१४
->**The Illustrious Tantrāloka**<-

This means that he is famous by the name Narasiṃhagupta <note>original: 'narasiṃhagupta-saṃjñayā'</note>, as will be explained later. According to the teachers <note>original: 'guravaḥ'</note>, the parents of this author are the illustrious Narasiṃhagupta and Vimalā.

->'Indeed, there are those who use only a part of a word to stand for the whole.'<-

Following this linguistic rule, just as "Bhīma" is used for "Bhīmasena," here too the names Narasiṃhagupta and Siṃhagupta are used interchangeably. Regarding the phrase **"filled with the body"** <note>original: 'bharitatnuḥ'</note>:

> "One should contemplate the mutual form of Shiva and Shakti.
> One should not view them with a merely human intellect, joined with passion and delusion.
> Everything should be performed by the best of practitioners through the contemplation of spiritual knowledge."

Following this logic, since it is intended to describe both parents as being filled with the immersion <term>samāveśa|a state of being possessed by or absorbed into the divine</term> of Shiva and Shakti, the description should be applied through the **"Logic of the Crow’s Eye"** <term>kākākṣinyāya|the ancient Indian poetic rule where a single word is placed between two sentences or concepts and applies to both, like the single eye of a crow which was believed to move between two sockets</term>. Therefore, because he was born from the union <note>original: 'melaka'</note> of such parents, who were essentially perfected Yoginis:

> "He whose body is formed in the womb 
> from the bud of such a ritual union, 
> is called 'Born of a Yoginī.' 
> He is naturally a devotee and a vessel for knowledge."

It defines him as a 'Yoginībhū,' one born of a spiritually consecrated union who possesses innate divine knowledge.</summary>

The previous page established that the author, Abhinavagupta, is a "Born of a Yoginī" (yoginībhū), a spiritually perfected being born from the ritual union of his parents, who are viewed as human incarnations of Shiva and Shakti. This page transitions into justifying his authority to write this comprehensive work on the Trika system.</meta>

१५
# Verse 1] First Chapter

By stating in this way his own suitability for the **unexcelled state of non-dual knowledge** <note>original: 'niruttara-padādvaya-jñāna'</note>, the author indicates his authority <term>adhikāra|the traditional qualification or right to compose or study a sacred text</term> to compose this work, which is a **compendium of the essence of all the Trika scriptures** <term>ṣaḍardha-śāstra|literally 'the six-and-a-half scriptures,' a technical name for the Trika school of Shaivism</term>. Even though other interpretations are possible here, they have not been provided for fear of making the text too bulky and because they are not useful for the current subject. The incorrectness of certain other interpretations, although very likely, has not been exposed. For indeed:

> "...and one should not perform the cause <gloss>2</gloss> for that."

This refers to the state to be described later, which suggests a seed of criticism <gloss>3</gloss> toward the Great Teachers <note>referring to Abhinavagupta’s lineage</note> in one's own self, which would bring about a **violation of the spiritual tradition** <term>samayalopa|a breach of the sacred bonds or vows that maintain a lineage</term>.—

---

2 The "cause" means an objection or criticism.
3 "Bringing about a violation of the spiritual tradition" means producing a fall from proper conduct. Regarding the "seed of criticism for the Great Teachers," certain individuals of limited understanding <note>original: 'mandadhiyaḥ'</note> argue the following: "Pure Digit" <note>original: 'vimalakalā'</note> refers to the sixteenth lunar digit from which all stains of impurity have departed—namely, the New Moon <term>amāvāsyā|the night of the new moon, often considered a time of great occult power</term>. This is the "New Creation" <note>original: 'abhinava-sṛṣṭi'</note>, which is the creation of the fifteen lunar digits; at that time, she <note>the Goddess/Mother</note> is engaged in effort and her body is thus filled. Regarding "hiding the brilliance of the five faces": assuming a day consists of five watches and the night of three, the "five faces" refer to the day, in which his brilliance is hidden—meaning his desire is seen at the beginning of the New Moon day. 

This is called a "seed of criticism" because it is based on the perspective of the skeptical science of astrology, rather than from the **Unexcelled perspective** <term>anuttara-dṛṣṭi|the highest non-dual realization where such distinctions are transcended</term>. In that higher state, since the beginnings of the New Moon day must be protected/honored, this is actually righteous conduct. In this matter, only the "true-hearted" <term>sahṛdaya|a person of refined aesthetic and spiritual sensitivity</term> are the authority.

---

Line 8: In the manuscript marked 'kha', there is an additional word: "the cause of that itself."

१६
### The Light of the Tantras

...so it might be. Who, indeed, when beginning a **peaceful ritual** <term>śāntikarma|a ritual intended to pacify negative influences or bring harmony</term>, would go about **raising a ghoul** <note>original: 'vetālottḥāpanam' - a metaphor for creating a terrifying or unnecessary complication just as one is trying to achieve peace</note>? Moreover, since we have promised here only to select the essence of the explanation of those scriptures, that is exactly what is being done. Therefore, let those who are wise discern for themselves the lack of essence everywhere else in those lengthy details. Enough, then, with this talk; let us declare the matter at hand.

In this way, having contemplated the **Supreme Triad** <term>Param Trika|the highest level of the Trika system, referring to the union of Shiva, Shakti, and the individual</term>, the author now begins to contemplate the **Supreme-Non-Supreme** <term>Parāparā|the intermediate goddess or energy that bridges the gap between absolute unity and worldly diversity</term>. First, he contemplates the **Supreme Goddess**:

->I bow to the Goddess who is the **Light of Consciousness**,<-
->the Supreme **Bhairava-Yogini**,<-
->who has made her seat upon the **lotus-trident**<-
->composed of the parts of the **knower**, the **means of knowledge**, and the **object of knowledge**. // 2 //<-

"**Supreme**" <note>original: 'parām'</note> means "Full" or "Perfect." For this very reason, She protects the world—even though it appears diverse—within her own self in a form of **non-difference** <note>original: 'abheda'</note>. And because she is not oriented toward anything other than the Self, she is "Excellent."

As it is said in such passages as:

> "That which is the **inherent Power** of the Creator of the universe..."

By this and other statements, she is called "**Bhairava-Yogini**" because she is eternally inseparable from the **Supreme Knower** <note>original: 'para-pramātṛ', referring to Shiva</note> and is essentially of his nature. For this reason...

### Verse 3 ] The First Daily Lesson

->“O Goddess, she becomes the state of Will for Him as He desires to create.”<-
<note>original: "icchatvaṃ tasya sā devi sisṛkṣoḥ pratipadhyate"</note>

By such statements, it is shown that this **Intuition** <term>Pratibhā|the creative flash of divine insight</term> is composed of consciousness. I bow to that Goddess who, in her nature as the "original emergence" <note>original: 'ādyocchalattā'—the first vibration of divine consciousness toward manifestation</note>, possesses a natural desire to shimmer outward. She is called a "Goddess" because She shines as the very form of cognition, serving as the "place of rest" even for the individual subject. 

Therefore, even in the external world, the **knower**, the **means of knowledge**, and the **object of knowledge** are the "spokes" or components of Her **Trident** <term>śūla|the three-pronged power of Shiva: Will, Knowledge, and Action</term>. She has "made her seat" upon the **lotuses of the trans-mental state** <term>aunmanasa|the highest state of consciousness, 'unmanā', which is beyond the reach of the ordinary mind</term>, appearing even as She transcends them. "I bow" <note>original: 'naumi'</note> means: "I enter into Her true nature" by subordinating the limited identity of the body, the breath, and other worldly attributes. // 2 //

Having spoken thus of the nature of the Supreme Goddess, the author does not yet describe the nature of the Immanent <term>Aparā|the goddess in her manifest, 'lower' form</term>. Because it is difficult to express the nature of the "Supreme-Immanent" <term>Parāparā|the intermediate goddess who bridges unity and diversity</term> which consists of both, the author skips the Supreme-Immanent Goddess for now and first turns his attention to the Immanent Goddess:

## **I bow to the Goddess dwelling in the body of the dancing Bhairava,**
## **shining like a streak of lightning in the sky thick with the clouds of the monsoon. // 3 //**

१८
### Of the “Dancing” One

->“The Self is the dancer.” (Shiva Sūtras 3.9)<-

From the perspective of the *Shiva Sūtras*, [the Goddess] resides within the body of the **Supreme Self** <term>Paramātman|the ultimate reality or universal consciousness</term>, whose form is **Bhairava** <term>Bhairava|the "frightful" or "vast" aspect of Shiva representing the totality of consciousness</term>. He reveals the unfolding theater of the world's various diversities while remaining anchored in his own hidden, essential nature. 

> “When the desire arises, ‘Let this object be thus,’ and She immediately brings that object into being—that is called the **Power of Action** <term>Kriyā|the divine capacity to manifest and do</term>.”

By such statements, it is shown that She is seated within the very nature of the Self, for She creates the endless and wondrous appearances of the knower (the subject) and the known (the object). I bow <note>original: 'naumi'</note> to that **Goddess** who performs the play of bringing the universe into joyful expression as the "Lower" or "Immanent" power <term>Aparā|the goddess in her manifest state, accessible to the senses</term>. Therefore, even though She shines externally as the soul of the universe, She is described as being "dark and tawny" because She rests within the Supreme Knower. As the verse says: “Shining like a streak of lightning in a sky filled with dense monsoon clouds.” 

> “Because She swallows the fragments of light belonging to **Maya** <term>Māyā|the power that creates the illusion of separation and duality</term>—which cause the feeling of difference—She is called the **Dark One** <note>original: 'Kṛṣṇā'</note>, appearing in the form of darkness because She is the destroyer of all duality.”

This is why Her form is described as both dark and lightning-bright. // 3 //

### Verse 4 | First Chapter. 19

Now, he contemplates the Goddess **Parāparā** <term>Parāparā|The "Supreme-Non-Supreme," the intermediate energy of consciousness that bridges absolute unity and the world of many forms</term>, whose nature consists of both the Supreme and the Non-Supreme.

**May the throbbing Trident of Wisdom shine forth,**
**Consuming the triple bond of duality with its blazing streaks of light;**
**It is capable of cutting through both the "proponent's view" and the "opponent's view." || 4 ||**

Regarding the word "Wisdom" <note>original: 'jñāna'</note>:

->“‘This object is exactly thus and not otherwise’—this is determined with certainty.<-
->Making this known in this world is what is called the **Power of Knowledge**.”<-

Even though the nature of the Power of Knowledge <term>Jñāna-śakti|the divine capacity for discernment and awareness</term> is stated in this way, it also contains within it the hidden threads of the powers of Will <note>original: 'Icchā'</note> and Action <note>original: 'Kriyā'</note>. For this reason, she is designated by the name **Parāparā**. Because of this, as will be explained in the following principles:

->“Because the three powers have become fused together, they form the **Trident**.”<-

It is thus called the “Trident” <term>Triśūla|the three-pronged spear of Shiva, here symbolizing the union of the powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action</term>. Furthermore, it is described as having “blazing”—meaning unobstructed—and “streaks of light” which take the form of the activities of the various senses. As it will be stated:

->“Wherever the rays [of the senses] meet,<-
->there the All-pervasive Lord expands.”<-

By this principle, and according to the nature that will be described, it is the cause of "singeing" <note>original: 'ploṣa'</note> or burning away the **Triple Bond**, which consists of the three impurities <term>Mala|The three spiritual "stains" (Āṇava, Māyīya, and Kārma) that limit the soul's power and produce the illusion of separation</term>...

# The Auspicious Tantrāloka

...the Trident. For this very reason, it is "throbbing" <note>original: 'sphurat'</note>, meaning its essence is a pulsation of pure, singular consciousness. Consequently, the "true position" <note>original: 'san pakṣo'</note> is **Universal Bliss** <term>Jagadānanda|The highest state of enlightenment where the entire universe is experienced as one's own blissful self</term>. 

The "opposing positions" <note>original: 'vipakṣāḥ'</note> to that state are the various other forms of bliss, such as Innate Bliss and the others, which appear as incomplete expansions of the self. These include both those that are considered "blissful" and those "not blissful" <margin>The six stages of bliss that precede the ultimate state are: Innate Bliss (*Nijānanda*), the Bliss of the Void (*Nirānanda*), Supreme Bliss (*Parānanda*), the Bliss of Totality (*Brahmānanda*), Great Bliss (*Mahānanda*), and the Bliss of Consciousness (*Cidānanda*).</margin>. To "sever" <note>original: 'utkartanaṃ'</note> them means to dissolve or consume them into the perfect, full expansion of consciousness. The sentence concludes by saying the Trident is "capable" <note>original: 'kṣamaṃ'</note> of this task.

As it has been said:

> **"Victorious are the moonbeams of knowledge arising from the face of the Supreme Lord, which are capable of dissolving all positions opposed to the Bliss of the Universe."**

|| 4 ||

***

Now, he speaks in order to contemplate another Triad <term>Trika|The 'Trinity' of goddesses or powers—Supreme (Parā), Intermediate (Parāparā), and Lower (Aparā)—central to this philosophical system</term>:

->**The power of Freedom, the desire to create sequence,**<-
->**And the nature of sequence itself—these are the Lord’s glory.**<-
->**May that same triad of goddesses remain within me,**<-
->**Manifesting the Unsurpassable nature.** || 5 ||<-

"The power in the form of Freedom" <note>original: 'svātantrya-śakti'</note> belongs to the Lord Shiva, the All-Pervasive One who possesses infinite powers. "Sequence" <note>original: 'krama'</note> <insert>meaning the orderly flow of time and manifestation</insert>...

# [Verse 5] First Chapter

> **"Through the variety of forms, He makes the spatial sequence appear; and through the appearance of the variety of actions, the Lord makes the temporal sequence appear as well."** <note>original: 'mūrtivaicitryato...' from the Īśvarapratyabhijñā-kārikā 2.1.5</note>

Following the logic stated in this and other verses, regarding the creation of the universal variety consisting of space and time, the **Desire to Create** <term>sisṛkṣā|The divine impulse or "will to emit" that precedes the act of manifestation</term> is the Supreme Lord's power in the form of Will. The **nature of sequence** is explained as:

-> "Sequence relies on difference; and difference itself arises from the appearance of presence and absence." <note>original: 'kramo bhedāśrayo...' from the Īśvarapratyabhijñā-kārikā 2.1.4</note> <-

According to this principle, **Finitude** <term>naratvam|The state of being a "Nara" or limited individual soul</term> is characterized primarily by "difference" and is interspersed with an infinity of distinct appearances. Thus, this triad consisting of the **Individual, Power, and the Divine** <term>Nara-Śakti-Śiva|The fundamental triad of Kashmiri Shaivism representing the human, the energy, and the Godhead</term> is the **Glory** <term>vibhūti|The sovereign power and unfolding of the divine essence</term> of the **All-pervasive** <note>original: 'vibhoḥ'</note> Lord—who is the Supreme, Absolute Light. 

Because this glory is essentially the flashing forth of that Light, it is **"that very"** previously mentioned **Triad of Goddesses** <note>The three powers: Parā (Supreme), Parāparā (Intermediate), and Aparā (Lower)</note>. Because they are essentially the Supreme Light, they are **Absolute** <note>original: 'anuttaraṃ'</note>. They **"make manifest"** His **"own"** **"form"**—a form that is unique to Him because He is the agent of all actions. Even while these various differences appear, His nature remains unhidden. The text concludes: **"may it abide within"** me—meaning, may it shine forth as identical with my own self. This is the meaning. || 5 ||

After thus contemplating the deities appropriate to his own philosophical system <note>The Trika school</note>, he now simultaneously approaches **Gaṇeśa** and **Baṭuka** <note>The elephant-headed remover of obstacles and the youthful form of Bhairava/Shiva, traditionally worshipped at the start of a rite</note> by entering into that very essence of the self.

***

# The Tantrāloka of Śrī Abhinavagupta

## [Verse 6]
## He alone stands as the Sovereign of the Wheel of the Great Rays,
## which arise from the glory of those very deities.
## May that Gaṇapati, the son of the Goddess,
## shimmering with the luster of the moon, 
## cause the ocean of my consciousness to perfectly swell. 6

The phrase **"He alone"** <note>original: 'eka eva'</note> signifies that he is without aid or companion, due to his absolute independence from anything else. The term **"of the host"** <note>original: 'gaṇasya'</note> refers to the "cycle of the instruments" <term>karaṇa-cakra|The collective group of sensory and mental organs through which an individual experiences the world</term>.

-> "Salutations to him who, like the sun, bears the lordship over the host of categories beginning with the Great Principle." <note>original: 'dinakarasama-mahadādika...'</note> <-

According to this perspective, the **"Lord"** <note>original: 'patiḥ'</note> is the Master in the form of the **I-sense** <term>ahaṅkāra|The 'ego' or 'I-maker'; in this context, the central unifying principle of self-awareness that coordinates all sensations</term>. Therefore, by the **"glory"**—meaning the expansion of the nature of the Supreme Light—of **"those"** deities just mentioned:

-> "That which does not rest within that Light is like a flower in the sky." <note>original: 'yat tatra na hi viśrāntam...'—a 'flower in the sky' is a traditional Sanskrit idiom for something that is impossible or non-existent.</note> <-

Following the logic that will be explained later, the **"Great Rays"** <note>original: 'mahā-marīcayaḥ'</note> are the deities of the various senses. They possess the nature of "becoming" and shine forth as being identical with the Light. He who acts like a Lord within the **"Wheel"** <term>cakra|A configuration or circle of energies or deities</term> of those rays, and whose own state is such, is the one being invoked. 

Because it is unfathomable, the **"Ocean"** <note>original: 'abdhiḥ'</note> is the **"Consciousness"** <term>saṃvid|Pure, foundational awareness</term> of **"mine"** (the author's own self). **"Perfectly"** <note>original: 'samyak'</note> means from all sides and in every way, achieved by dissolving the turbidness caused by attachment to external objects...

<margin>Line 14: In manuscript 'ga', the reading is "his own state" (accusative case: nijasthitim).</margin>

<summary>In this verse and commentary, Abhinavagupta invokes Gaṇapati as a symbol of the spiritualized "I-sense" (Ahaṅkāra) that governs the sensory powers (the "Great Rays"). He prays for this divine principle to stir his consciousness into a vast, clear ocean of awareness.</summary>

# The Tantrāloka of Śrī Abhinavagupta

<header>First Daily Lesson</header>

<margin>Verse 6</margin>
By means of the doorway of consciousness flowing out through those various sensory organs, "may he cause to swell" <note>original: 'ucchalayatāt'</note>—meaning, may he cause it to expand and produce a state of oneness with that [Supreme]. Because it is appropriate for an ocean to swell [under the influence of the moon], the phrase **"shimmering with the luster of the moon"** <note>original: 'sphuradindukāntiḥ'</note> is used. In a literal sense, this is an instruction regarding how he possesses the **pervasion of the downward breath** <term>apāna-vyāpti|The movement of the vital energy associated with inhalation and the lunar, cooling aspect of the breath</term>.

Furthermore, the **"son of the Goddess"** <note>original: 'devīsuto'</note> known as **Vaṭuka** <term>Vaṭuka|A youthful, fierce form of Bhairava (Śiva) often worshipped as a protector in Tantric traditions</term> is also of this nature; however, he is described as **"shimmering with the luster of the moon"** due to the pure whiteness of his physical body. The Gurus <note>venerated teachers</note> instruct that he possesses the **pervasion of the life-breath** <term>prāṇa-vyāpti|The movement of vital energy associated with exhalation and the solar, heating aspect of the breath</term>. The designation **"Son of the Goddess"** is appropriate for both of them according to the **Kula scriptures** <term>Kula-śāstra|The body of sacred texts belonging to the Kula tradition, a major school of Tantric Shaivism focusing on the power of Śakti</term>. As it has been said:

-> "Here, Vaṭuka is the son of the Goddess, surrounded by his own circle of powers." <note>original: 'devīputro'tra vaṭukaḥ...'</note> <-

And also:

-> "This Ganesha, the remover of obstacles, is the son of the Goddess..." <note>original: 'gaṇeśo vighnahartāsau...'</note> <-

### Now, at the beginning of the scripture

> "...the division of the currents <note>the different lineages or 'streams' of revelation</note> and the enumeration itself. One should set in motion [the mention of] one's own Guru, for one would become a thief by failing to proclaim them."

---

Line 2: The G. manuscript reads "producing" <note>original: 'utpādayatām'</note>.
Line 5: The K. manuscript reads "Therefore, the Goddess..." <note>original: 'ata eva devī'</note>.
Line 7: The Kh. manuscript lacks the phrase "thus they instruct," reading only "is the pervasion of the breath, according to the Gurus."

<summary>This page explains the lunar imagery of Gaṇapati as a metaphor for the expansion of consciousness and the downward breath (apāna), while also identifying Vaṭuka Bhairava as a secondary 'Son of the Goddess' associated with the life-breath (prāṇa). It concludes by emphasizing the necessity of honoring one's lineage and Guru at the start of a sacred work.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening verses of the Tantrāloka. Having previously identified the "Son of the Goddess" as the unified state of consciousness, Abhinavagupta now moves toward the formal necessity of honoring the lineage of teachers (guru-paramparā) who brought these teachings into the human realm, specifically focusing on the superiority of the Kula path.</meta>

# The Tantrāloka of Śrī Abhinavagupta

->### The Auspicious Tantrāloka ###<-

In view of what has been stated above, the authors of sacred scriptures must necessarily praise their own Teachers and predecessors. Consequently, although the scripture about to be explained follows a twofold methodology—consisting of both **Kula** <term>Kula|A major school of Tantric Shaivism focusing on the 'Family' of energies and the non-dual power of the Goddess</term> and **Tantra** <term>Tantra|Here refers to the broader ritualistic and dualistic traditions of Shaivism</term>—the methodology of the **Kula** is prioritized over all others, as it is said:

> "Just as the stars in the sky do not shine when the sun has risen, so the **Siddhānta Tantras** <term>Siddhānta-tantra|The dualistic school of Shaivism that emphasizes ritual, external purity, and the distinction between the soul and God</term> do not shine once the **Kula tradition** <term>Kulāgama</term> has appeared. Therefore, there is no other means for salvation from the cycle of rebirth than that which is derived from the **Kula**."

Because the **Kula methodology** <note>original: 'kulaprakriyā'</note> is superior to other methodologies, the author first praises **Turyanātha** <term>Turyanātha|Meaning 'Lord of the Fourth State,' a semi-mythical founding teacher of the Kula lineage who represents the state of pure consciousness</term>, who brought this teaching down to our world. This is in accordance with the succession of the lineage described in the following verses:

> "From **Bhairava** <term>Bhairava|The supreme, terrifying aspect of Śiva representing absolute reality</term>, the **Yoga** <note>original: 'yogam'</note> was received by **Bhairavī** <term>Bhairavī|The Goddess as the supreme power of consciousness</term>, pervading all; from her, O fair-faced one, it was obtained by the **perfected master** <note>original: 'siddhena'</note> known as **Mīna**. In the great sacred center of **Kāmarūpa** <term>Kāmarūpa|A legendary site in Assam, India, considered the primary 'seat' or power-center for Tantric traditions</term>, it was revealed by the great-souled **Macchanda**."

Through the status established by such verses, he first glorifies the one who brought the teachings down.

---

**Variant Readings from Manuscripts:**

Line 9: Manuscript Kh. reads "pervading the Yoga, then..." <note>original: 'yogam vyāpi tataḥ'</note>.
Line 11: Manuscript K. reads "Kāmapīṭha" instead of "Kāmarūpa."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the opening of the Tantrāloka. After establishing the Kula lineage's superiority in the previous section, Abhinavagupta now offers a specific praise of Macchanda (Matsyendranātha), the legendary human founder of the Kula tradition, interpreting his name and his role in liberating the soul from the "net" of worldly illusion.</meta>

[Page 25]

### Verse 7: The First Chapter ###

->**May that all-pervasive Lord Macchanda be pleased with me—**<-
->**He who cast aside onto the external path**<-
->**The net reddened by passion and tangled with knots,**<-
->**Which operates through its weaving and spreading,**<-
->**And is tossed about by the waves of the world.**<-

The word "He" <note>original: 'sa'</note> refers to the one who is famous for bringing down all the **Kula scriptures** <term>Kula-śāstra|The body of sacred texts belonging to the Kula school of Tantra</term> to humanity. 
As it is said:
> "The 'Maccchas' <note>original: 'macchāḥ'</note> are traditionally explained as the snares, the flickering and unstable movements of the mind. Since these were cut by him, he is celebrated as **Macchanda** <term>Macchanda|Also known as Matsyendranātha, the 10th-century sage regarded as the founder of the Kaula path. His name literally means 'Lord of the Fish,' but here it is interpreted as the 'Lord who cuts the snares of the mind'</term>."

By this explanation, Macchanda’s very nature is the "breaking of bonds." Because he possesses a complete immersion into the Supreme Lord, may he—the "All-pervasive Lord" <note>original: 'vibhuḥ'</note>—be "pleased" with me. This means: may he reveal my fitness to partake in the vision of the Self.

He is the one who made the "net" <note>original: 'jālam'</note>—which refers to both a literal fishing net and the Great Illusion <term>Māyā|The cosmic power that creates the appearance of duality and hides the true nature of reality</term> that acts like a magician's trick—into an "external path" (that is, he cast it away).
As it is said:
> "The eight great-souled **Perfected Beings** <term>Siddhas|Enlightened masters who have attained liberation and supernatural powers</term> are those who have the net behind them and possess great radiance."

The meaning is that by remaining established in the nature of the **Fourth State** <term>Turīya|The state of pure, non-dual consciousness that underlies and transcends waking, dreaming, and deep sleep</term>, he cast aside all "contraction" <note>original: 'saṃkoca'</note> and reduced it to something negligible. 

Furthermore, that net was "reddened" <note>original: 'aruṇām'</note> by "dye" <note>original: 'rāgeṇa'</note>—which refers both to physical substances like red chalk and to the **Element of Passion** <term>Rāga-tattva|In this philosophy, the cosmic limitation that produces specific desires and emotional attachment in the individual soul</term>.

<margin>Line 11, Manuscript Ka: "the net of the senses" <note>original: 'indriyajāla'</note> instead of "the net of magic."</margin>
<margin>Line 14, Manuscript Kha: provides a variant reading for the phrase "by the stated method."</margin>
<margin>Line 15, Manuscript Kha: reads "the state of being attentive" instead of "the state of being negligible."</margin>

<summary>This page features a salutation to Macchanda (Matsyendranātha), interpreting his name as "the Lord who cuts the bonds of the mind." Abhinavagupta explains the metaphor of the "net" as the illusion of the material world which the master casts aside through the power of pure consciousness.</summary>
<keywords>Macchanda, Matsyendranatha, Kula, Maya, Turiya, Raga-tattva, liberation, snares of the mind, Siddha</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and etymological analysis of Verse 7 from Chapter 1. Abhinavagupta is explaining the metaphorical "net" (jāla) of the world, which was mentioned on the previous page as something the sage Macchanda (Matsyendranātha) cast aside. The text then transitions into the legendary history of how the various schools of the Shaiva tradition descended to earth by divine command.</meta>

[Page 26]

# The Splendor of the Tantras #
## Chapter One (Continued) ##

The word "performed" <note>original: 'kṛtam'</note> follows the meaning of "it moves" or "it goes" <note>original: 'iyarti'</note>, signifying that the net is a form that spreads through various states of differentiation. Similarly, it is described as being filled with "knots" <note>original: 'granthibhiḥ'</note>, which are the bonds of worldly existence, and "holes" <note>original: 'bilaiḥ'</note>, which are the outlets through which the water [of consciousness] flows out. Within the "knot"—which refers to the second division of **Māyā** <term>Māyā|The cosmic power of illusion that creates the appearance of duality and limitation</term>—these "holes" are the hollow openings known as the "sources of pleasure" <note>original: 'bhaga'</note>, the various realms of worldly enjoyment. 

Furthermore, the phrase "weaving and spreading" <note>original: 'ātāna-vitāna-vṛtti'</note> refers to its longitudinal and lateral expansion; because the net takes the form of the entire universe, it is a form that spreads out in every direction. Finally, it is "woven" <note>original: 'umbhitam'</note> by **Kalā** <term>Kalā|The principle of limited agency; the power that allows a soul to act, but only in a restricted way</term>—meaning it is constructed by the specific limitation of the "Kalā-tattva," which initiates the manifestation of the world down to the element of Earth. 

As it has been said:

> "The seeker of the **Kula** <term>Kula|The 'Family' or totality of divine powers; the highest school of Tantra</term> should perceive the Net as having the nature of **Māyā**. This Great Net has the form of the entire universe and is bound together by the threads of the **nāḍīs** <term>Nāḍī|The subtle channels through which the life-force or Prāṇa flows in the body</term>. It is equipped with the 'axles' of the various worlds and made firm by the knots of the **tattvas** <term>Tattva|The fundamental principles or building blocks of reality, from Earth to Pure Consciousness</term>. It is also imbued with **Kalā** (limited power) and **Rāga** (limited desire)..."

And so on. // 7 //

<margin>Note in Manuscript K: The text reads "should hold the net at the hip" <note>original: 'dhārayetkubja'</note> instead of "should perceive."</margin>

***

> "By the command of the illustrious Lord **Śrīkaṇṭha** <term>Śrīkaṇṭha|An auspicious form of Shiva regarded as the original teacher of the Tantras</term>, the Siddhas <note>The 'Perfected Masters' who attained liberation and descended to teach</note> came down to earth. Known as **Tryambaka**, **Āmardaka**, and **Śrīnātha**, they were masters of the Non-dual, the Dual, and the Dual-Non-dual doctrines respectively within the teachings of Shiva. From the first (Tryambaka) a lineage arose; a second lineage came through the sequence of a daughter. That is the lineage well-established as the 'Half-Tryambaka.' Thus, there are three and a half monastic centers <note>original: 'maṭhikā'</note> here in the order of transmission."

# The Illustrious Tantraloka

->“Having extracted the essential nectar from the streams of the auspicious lineages,<-

# Now

> “An instructor <term>Upadhyaya|A teacher who teaches a portion of the Vedas for a livelihood</term> is surpassed by ten teachers <term>Acharya|A spiritual preceptor who initiates a student and teaches the entire scripture</term>, but a father is worth a hundred such teachers.”

Based on such traditional sayings which record the father's superior weight of authority even over a teacher, the author now addresses his own father with a blessing:

-> May the illustrious Chukhulaka, <-
-> who has mastered the meaning of all scriptures and rests in perfect bliss, <-
-> grant me my heart’s desire; he is my supreme Guru. [12] <-

“Chukhulaka” is another name for him, well-known in common parlance. The reason for calling him “Supreme Guru” is the aforementioned memory of the father’s superior status. Therefore, it is said elsewhere:

> “The father named Chukhula is even weightier than one's teachers.”

***

Thus, after turning toward the gurus who are close to the methodology of the Tantras <term>Tantra-prakriya|The path of the Shaiva Tantras which often emphasizes ritual and external structures</term>, he now exalts the teacher of the methodology of the Kula <term>Kula-prakriya|The 'Family' or 'Totality' tradition, a more esoteric and internalized path focusing on the power of the Goddess and the heart</term>, as his ultimate place of rest:

-> Victorious is the singular Shambhunatha, <-
-> together with the Goddess <note>Refers to the teacher's consort or the divine feminine energy</note>, who is capable of uplifting the world. <-
-> By the rays of his spoken teachings, <-
-> this scriptural path—though dense—has been made clear to me. [13] <-

***

### Verse 16 ] First Chapter ###
### Page 33 ###

Many various manuals <term>Paddhatis|Step-by-step ritual guidebooks or procedural manuals</term> exist within the numerous streams of revelation. However, in the sequence of the "Highest Three" <term>Anuttara-shadardha|A technical name for the Trika system, referring to the "Highest" (Anuttara) and the "Three" (Shadardha, literally 'half of six') goddesses</term>, not even a single one is to be found. || 14 ||

And it could not be otherwise in this matter—thus, proclaiming his own authority <note>original: 'aptatvam'</note>, he demonstrates his capacity to undertake this vow as follows:

Thus, having been requested many times by the virtuous—my own disciples and fellow students—I shall compose this manual of ritual procedure <term>Prakriya|A systematic exposition or manual that explains the practical application of scriptural theory</term> clearly and with complete meaning. || 15 ||

From the lotus-like feet of the illustrious Bhattasvamin <note>Literally 'Lord of Scholars'; Abhinavagupta's teacher of the Kula tradition</note> as well as from the pair of feet of the illustrious Bhattarika <note>The teacher's consort, essential in the Kula lineage</note>, there arises the lineage of teachers. Abhinavagupta—who is radiant with the realization <note>original: 'bodha'</note> arising from the contemplative worship of that lineage, which destroys the poison of the bond of "otherness" <note>The dualistic delusion that anything exists separate from universal consciousness</note>—composes this work. || 16 ||

The "contemplative worship" <note>original: 'upasanam'</note> of that knowledge which has descended through the lineage of teachers means the repeated settling of that knowledge within the mind. From that arises "realization" <note>original: 'bodhah'</note>, which is the direct experience of the subject matter to be taught. By that realization, he is "radiant," meaning he is one who has thoroughly understood the essential nature of reality. Being such, he creates "this"—referring to the definition of the procedure for the meaning of the "Highest Three" <note>original: 'anuttara-trika-artha-prakriya'</note>, which he has mastered through the teacher’s instruction, free from all doubt and error—

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 16 of the first chapter. Having identified himself as the author, Abhinavagupta now justifies his authority to teach and defines the key components of the spiritual lineage (the Guru and his consort) that empowered him to write this manual.</meta>

# The Illustrious Tantrāloka #

## Page 34 ##

With the desire to make the truth known to others, he "makes" [this work], which is to say, he instructs. By mentioning the name "Abhinavagupta," which is famous throughout the world, his status as a reliable authority <term>Apta|A trustworthy person whose words are authoritative because they have direct experience of the truth they describe</term> is further reinforced. For it is said:

> One who has realized the truth <note>original: 'sākṣātkṛta-dharmā'</note> and is prompted by the desire to communicate the matter exactly as it was perceived is an authoritative teacher.

The commentary now explains the meaning of the word "that" [from the verse]: "that lineage of teachers." The "lineage of teachers" <term>Guru-santati|The unbroken succession of masters and the spiritual knowledge transmitted through them</term> refers to the knowledge taught by them, remaining in an unbroken tradition. And what is the nature of that lineage? It is said to be: "that which destroys the poison of the bond of otherness from pure awareness." As will be stated later:

> Whatever is perceived as different from the Supreme Shiva—who is described as beautiful through the absolute freedom of supreme non-dual consciousness—that is called a "bond" <term>Pāśa|A fetter or bond that ties the soul to worldly existence by creating a false sense of separation from the Divine</term>.

According to this and other passages, "other than awareness" refers to the manifestation of duality <note>original: 'bheda-prathā'</note>, which consists of the non-recognition of the Supreme Shiva. That very duality is the "bond." Because it causes delusion, it is like "poison." That lineage is the one that removes it. Likewise, the "Illustrious Master" <note>original: 'Śrī-Bhaṭṭanātha'</note> refers to the Illustrious Shambhunatha. The "Illustrious Lady" <note>original: 'Śrī-Bhaṭṭārikā'</note> refers to the Goddess who is his consort <term>Duti|Literally 'messenger,' referring to the female spiritual partner or counterpart of the master in the ritual tradition</term>. As has been stated by Abhinavagupta himself:

> I salute Shambhu, the Great Guru, who is the beginning and the end, known by many names: the Master, the Lord of the Lady, Shrikantha, the Joyful Bhairava, the one endowed with the glory of the power of manifestation, the Lion-Man, and the fierce Hero.

# The Illustrious Tantrāloka #

## Page 35 ##

**Thus.**

> "The wise man should deposit the teaching in the mouth of a woman; he should cause others to receive it again from the mouth of a woman."

**Because of such statements, in the Kula tradition <term>Kula-prakriyā|The 'Family' tradition of Tantra which emphasizes the union of consciousness and its power</term>, the tradition of imparting knowledge to the disciple is specifically through the 'mouth of the consort' <term>Dūtī-mukha|Literally 'mouth of the messenger'; the spiritual transmission occurring through a ritual partner</term>. Therefore, here the Guru and his consort are mentioned as being of equal status <note>original: 'samaskandhatayā' — literally 'having equal shoulders'</note> in the act of transmission. || 16 ||**

<margin>Line 6, Manuscript Ka: the reading is "generally" <note>original: 'sāmānyena'</note>.</margin>
**Now, an objection may be raised: having promised to establish the ritual process of the Trika philosophy <term>Trika-darśana|The 'Threefold' system of non-dual Shaivism</term> in a general sense, and given that there exists a vast body of scriptures explaining that very topic, why is it that only the *Shrī Mālinīvijayottara Tantra* is taken as the primary authority to fulfill this task? Anticipating this doubt, he says:**

**There is nothing here that has not been specified in the *Shrī Mālinīvijayottara* by the God of gods, either in express words or through symbolic signs <note>original: 'liṅgataḥ'</note>. || 17 ||**

**Regarding the name "*Shrī Mālinīvijayottara*": through the "victory" <note>original: 'vijayena'</note>—meaning the supreme excellence—of the *Mālinī* <term>Mālinī|The Goddess of the alphabet in a specific non-sequential arrangement</term> who is composed of letters from *Na* to *Pha* <term>Nādi-phāntā|The specific 'Mālinī' arrangement of the Sanskrit alphabet where 'Na' is the first letter and 'Pha' is the last</term>, this scripture "surpasses" <note>original: 'uttarati'</note> or floats above all other streams of revelation because it is the very essence of all sacred texts. || 17 ||**

->He explains this very point:<-

**Of the ten, eighteen, and eight-fold divisions <note>referring to the 10 Shaiva, 18 Raudra, and 64 (8x8) Bhairava Tantras</note> of the Lord's teaching, the Trika scripture is indeed the essence; and the essence of that Trika is the *Mālinī* doctrine. || 18 ||**
