<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Tantrāloka. Having previously established the authority of the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra, the author now explains how the divine Word (Vāc) descends from pure consciousness through various levels of speech to become the manifested scriptures (Śāstras).</meta>

# The Illustrious Tantrāloka #

## Page 36 ##

In this context, the Supreme Speech <term>Parā Vāc|The highest level of language, identified with the vibration of pure consciousness</term> is the essence of supreme self-reflection <note>original: 'para-parāmarśa'</note>. Because it is filled with the fullness of all existence, all scripture <term>Śāstra|Sacred teaching or authoritative text</term> expands solely as a form of supreme consciousness.

In the "visionary" stage <term>Paśyantī|The second level of speech, where the word and its meaning are still a unified "vision" within consciousness</term>, it arises internally as the essence of the "I-reflection" <note>original: 'aham-pratyavamarśa'</note>. In this state, there is no distinction between the word and its meaning. Therefore, when the perceiving subject <note>original: 'pramātṛ'</note> reflects upon the meaning of what is to be expressed, that meaning shines forth as if entirely enveloped by "I-ness" <note>original: 'ahantā'</note>.

Following this, in the "intermediate" stage <term>Madhyamā|The third level of speech, which exists as internal mental discourse or thought</term>, language shines forth as a distinct relationship between the word and its meaning. This occurs internally through the emergence of the expansion of the "known" and the "knower."

In that state, the Supreme Lord <term>Parameśvara|The ultimate reality or God</term>—who consists of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action—acts through the thread of his five "faces" <note>original: 'vaktra-pañcaka'</note>. Occupying the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara <note>High metaphysical levels where the universe begins to take shape</note>, he brings down the entire body of scripture by weaving together those five faces. This scripture flows in five streams, categorized by the carving out of the stages of non-duality <note>original: 'abheda'</note>, non-duality-in-duality <note>original: 'bhedābheda'</note>, and duality <note>original: 'bheda'</note>, appearing in all its various forms and sub-divisions.

This reaches full clarity in the stage of "articulated speech" <term>Vaikharī|The fourth and final level of language, the spoken word as heard by the ear</term>.

To explain further: first, through the faces named Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, and Sadyojāta <note>Three of the five traditional "faces" or aspects of Shiva</note>, a threefold division of duality was manifested as each face desired to emerge. Because they were manifested, there are six individual divisions. When these three are combined, one more division is manifested. From the combination of Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna and Sadyojāta...

Through the union of **Sadyojāta** and **Tatpuruṣa** acting as a dual nature <term>Dvyātmaka|A combination of two divine aspects or "faces"</term>, these three have manifested a triad of distinctions. Thus, these are the ten divisions of Shiva <term>Śivabheda|The ten dualistic scriptures or Āgamas of the Shaiva tradition</term> where differentiation predominates. It has been said:

> "Through **Īśāna**, **Tatpuruṣa**, and **Sadyojāta**—which have arisen and are about to arise—the state of the ten Shiva-divisions was established by means of six individual ones, one triad, and three dual-natured ones." <note>This verse explains the combinatorial logic used to categorize the 10 dualistic Shaiva scriptures based on which "faces" of Shiva revealed them.</note>

By the mixing of these same faces with **Vāmadeva** and **Aghora**, the eighteen divisions of Rudra <term>Rudrabheda|The eighteen scriptures of the Raudra tradition, which are considered 'dual-non-dual'</term> come into being. In that context, through each individual division consisting of Vāmadeva and Aghora, there are only two divisions. This is because, even though there is a five-fold nature, the triad of faces beginning with Īśāna has already been described within the Shiva-divisions. To repeat what has already been said would be logically inconsistent.

Likewise, the three dual-natured divisions and the three triple-natured <term>Tryātmaka|A combination of three divine aspects</term> divisions among the five faces have already been mentioned in the context of the Shiva-divisions. As for **Tatpuruṣa** and **Sadyojāta**, because they do not possess this specific nature, and because there is no connection with them, there is an absence of a four-fold division. From **Īśāna**... <note>The text continues on the next page regarding the specific emanations from the Īśāna face.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical combinatorial analysis of Shiva's five "faces" (Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and Aghora) and how their interactions produce the specific number of scriptures in the Shaiva canon. The previous page established that the 18 Rudra-scriptures (the dual-non-dual Āgamas) are formed through combinations involving the faces of Vāmadeva and Aghora.</meta>

# The Honorable Tantrāloka #

### Page 34 ###

-> **The First Lesson** <-

The combinations of **Vāmadeva**, **Īśāna-Aghora**, and **Aghora-Vāmadeva**—these three dual-natured <term>Dvyātmaka|A combination where two divine aspects or "faces" of Shiva work in unison</term> forms are all that remain; thus, there are three dual-distinct divisions <term>Dvikabheda|Scriptural categories based on the union of two divine aspects</term>.

Likewise, when all five faces—**Īśāna**, **Tatpuruṣa**, **Sadyojāta**, **Vāmadeva**, and **Aghora**—are blended into triple-natured forms <term>Tryātmaka|A combination of three divine aspects</term>, there are ten possible variations. Specifically, in the sequential mixing of **Īśāna** with the other faces, there are six combinations; for **Tatpuruṣa**, there are three; and for **Sadyojāta**, with the remaining face-blends, there is only one. 

However, even though there are ten such variations, only eight triple-natured divisions actually remain as distinct categories. This is because the first triad—consisting of **Īśāna**, **Tatpuruṣa**, and **Sadyojāta**—has already been accounted for within the Shiva-divisions <term>Śivabheda|The ten dualistic scriptures described on the previous page</term>. Furthermore, the remaining triad of **Īśāna**, **Vāmadeva**, and **Aghora** is intended to be employed for a different ritual or functional purpose <note>The author is explaining why the mathematical total of 10 combinations is reduced to 8 when categorizing the 18 Rudra-scriptures, to avoid double-counting scriptures already classified as "Shiva-type" or those reserved for other categories</note>. Therefore, there are exactly eight triad-divisions <term>Trikabheda|Scriptural categories based on the union of three divine aspects</term>.

For this reason, one should not claim that the individual enumeration of these faces is questionable. Regarding **Tatpuruṣa**, **Sadyojāta**, **Vāmadeva**, and **Aghora**, a prohibition against certain combinations is intended when they generate knowledge in either a dual or quadruple nature. If such a prohibition were to apply to the triple-natured state as well, it would result in the exclusion of many scriptural divisions. Therefore, the explanation of the seven-fold division <note>A further technical sub-classification of the scriptures</note> is also logical and correct.

### [Verse 18] First Chapter ###

->**Page 41**<-

When the other four faces, which consist of sixteen divisions, are simultaneously dissolved within, then through their mutual combination, there arise the **sixty-four** <term>Bhairavabheda|The sixty-four non-dual divisions of the Bhairava scriptures</term> where non-duality is primary. As it has been said:

> “That which is at the end, the **Right Face** <note>original: "dakṣiṇaṃ" - In this tradition, the South face of Shiva is also the "Right" face, associated with the fierce form of Bhairava and the heart center</note>, relating to the heart, is considered the phallus of the supreme heart.
> Even that is overflowing with the entire creation drawn within it.
> Because it performs the dissolution of everything, it is **black** <note>original: "kṛṣṇaṃ" - The color black signifies the absorption of all colors and the dissolution of the objective world</note>, wearing the form of darkness.
> It consists of swallowing the luminous portions of the Maya-born world <term>Māyīya|Relating to Maya, the power that creates the illusion of separation or duality</term> that cause the sense of difference.
> Into that [South Face], the other four faces become dissolved:
> those desiring to manifest, those already manifested, those desiring to conceal, and those already concealed.
> In this way, simultaneously, these sixteen divisions
> enter the Right, the creative, the heartfelt, the independent, and the auspicious [Face of Shiva].
> That scripture is simultaneously named after **Bhairava**, consisting of **eight times eight** <note>original: "aṣṭāṣṭaka" - 64</note> parts.”

### The Radiance of the Scripture ###

Thus [the division is established]. By these [categories], the scriptures are of many kinds, characterized by the diversity of divisions and sub-divisions.

And so on. Likewise:

> "Hear now of that other [tradition] which was born from **Vamadeva** <term>Vāmadeva|The northern face of Shiva, associated with the power of preservation and feminine energy</term>..."

Regarding the diversity of other divisions and sub-divisions mentioned [in those texts], it is understood that because each individual face of the Lord is itself composed of five faces <note>This refers to the fractal nature of the deity; while Shiva has five primary faces, each of those faces contains the essence of all five, leading to a geometric expansion of teachings</note>, these are simply sub-divisions born of the primary ones already discussed. Therefore, they are included within this collection and no separate effort is made to list them here.

As it has been said:

> "Because each single face is praised as being five-faced, the divisions of the ten and eighteen <note>Referring to the 10 Shiva-tantras and 18 Rudra-tantras</note> become countless in their further sub-divisions."

### The Threefold Division of Scripture ###

Thus [it is established]. Therefore, it is a settled tenet that this scripture has emerged in three ways, known as **Shiva** <term>Śiva|In this context, referring to the ten dualistic scriptures</term>, **Rudra** <term>Rudra|Referring to the eighteen scriptures that teach a mix of dualism and non-dualism</term>, and **Bhairava** <term>Bhairava|Referring to the sixty-four scriptures of pure non-dualism</term>, which respectively expound dualism, dualism-cum-non-dualism, and non-dualism.

Regarding this, it has been said:

> "This **Tantra** <term>Tantra|A body of esoteric teachings and rituals</term> was born threefold, known as Rudra, Shiva, and Bhairava. For in reality, the existence of knowledge manifests in precisely three ways:
> 
> Through dualism <note>original: "bhedena"; the perspective that the individual soul and God are eternally separate</note>, through dualism-cum-non-dualism, and likewise through that which partakes in non-dualism."

In this way, although this scripture consists of these [three] divisions, it should be made to overflow with the nectar of supreme non-duality. This is achieved by embracing the "Sixth Triad" <note>This refers to a specific grouping of the five faces of Shiva plus a sixth, representing the heart of the Trika system</note> which consists of the aspects of **Parameshwara** <term>Parameśvara|The Supreme Lord</term>, **Isha**, **Vama**, and **Aghora**, and by finding its resting place in the triad of the three Goddesses—**Para** and the others <note>Para, Parapara, and Apara; the three primary energies of the Trika tradition</note>. 

As it is stated:

> "As fragrance exists within the flower, as oil is in the sesame seed, as the soul is in the body, and as flavor is in water;
> 
> Just so, the **Kula** <term>Kula|The 'Family' or 'Heart' of the tradition; the internal, non-dual essence that gives life to external rituals</term> is established within all the scriptures."

By such statements, [the teacher] should infuse the teachings with the nectar of non-duality; otherwise, these scriptures would not serve as the means for attaining the Supreme State. Thus it is said—

Our response is: This is not so. Indeed, **Agama** is defined as that which is an undisputed and well-known tradition. As it has been stated:

### Verse 18 ] First Lesson ###

> ‘Public tradition is considered scripture in this world, whether it is supported by logic or otherwise. In the realm of both higher knowledge and ignorance, it serves as proof because it is undisputed.
> For tradition that is uncontradicted is considered the true **Voice of the Lord** <note>original: "vāgaishvarī"; some manuscripts read "vāgīśvarī," meaning the Goddess of Speech or Sarasvati</note>. Therefore, whatever is established in a particular way should be accepted by those who are free from doubt.’

Thus [it is said]. And that [tradition] indeed exists here, through the uncontradicted testimony of the great-souled **Great Teachers** <term>Mahāguru|The foundational preceptors of this spiritual lineage</term>. Therefore, what is the point of searching for other means of proof? 

And if a **Revelation** <term>Śruti|Sacred scripture "heard" by ancient seers; typically refers to the Vedas, but used here for foundational Tantric texts</term> of this kind has not reached the ears of short-sighted people like you, it cannot be said on that basis alone that this [teaching] is impossible. For the absence of a **means of proof** <term>Pramāṇa|A valid source of knowledge</term> does not result in the absence of the **object of knowledge** <term>Prameya|The reality or truth being sought</term>. <note>This is a standard logical argument: just because you cannot see or prove a thing right now does not mean the thing itself does not exist.</note>

Nor are these [teachers] deceivers who would teach something falsely; for we see the practical application of the meaning of all the **Shaiva scriptures** <gloss>the Tantric revelations of Shiva</gloss> based solely on their instruction. 

Therefore, just as in the **Tradition of Manu** <term>Manvādi-smṛti|The ethical and legal codes of Hindu tradition, such as the Laws of Manu</term>, a foundational Revelation is inferred for rituals like the **Ashtaka sacrifices** <note>A series of rites traditionally performed on the eighth day of the dark lunar fortnight</note> because the original scriptural branches they belong to are now lost, the same should be understood here. For those who have realized the true essence of all Shaiva scriptures would not speak in such a way without having seen such a Revelation—

->**The Light of the Tantras** <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note><-

...would they teach falsely? Enough with this bad habit of cross-examining the instructions of the **Great Teachers** <term>Mahāguru|The foundational preceptors of the Tantric lineage</term>. 

But, regarding the scriptures, an objection is raised:

> ‘Since all [revelations] originate from **Shiva** <note>The supreme consciousness</note> and bestow the fruit of Shiva’s own abode...’

By such statements, there is a unity established because the regulating cause [Shiva] and the result [the state of Shiva] are one. If so, what is the reason for the diversity of these scriptures mentioned here? 

It is true—however, their diversity is projected based on the differing capacities and **dispositions of the seekers** <note>original: "anugrāhya-āśaya-bheda"</note> who are to be graced. As it has been said:

> ‘All this [diversity] is intended to prompt action, according to the differences among the listeners. This distinction in meaning is merely a metaphorical construction. One should not imagine a difference in the ultimate result; or if one does, it must be understood appropriately to the context.’

But if that is the case, then consider the statement:

> ‘Higher than the **Vedas** <term>Veda|The ancient, orthodox scriptures of India</term> and others is the **Shaiva** <term>Śaiva|Scriptures focused on the deity Shiva</term>; higher than Shaiva are the **Left** <term>Vāma|The "Left-hand" path of Tantra, often involving unconventional practices</term> and the **Right** <term>Dakṣiṇa|The "Right-hand" path of Tantra</term> currents. Higher than the Right is the **Kaula** <term>Kaula|The supreme "Family" or "Totality" tradition, considered the heart of the teaching</term>, and there is nothing higher than the Kaula.’

If all results are the same, then the hierarchy of superiority described here would not be logical, would it?

Not at all—because the relationship between these paths is described as being like a "door" and "the one who enters through the door." They relate to one another as the **means** <term>Upāya|A method or technique for spiritual realization</term> and the **goal** <term>Upeya|The ultimate objective or reality being sought</term>. Therefore, [the scriptures] are established as teaching the supreme **Non-Duality** <term>Advaya|The state of oneness where the self and the universe are not separate</term>...

<meta>This page transitions from the general hierarchy of scriptures to Abhinavagupta’s specific purpose in writing the Tantrāloka. Having established the Trika system as the supreme synthesis of all spiritual paths, he now explains his authority to reveal its hidden meanings, derived from both his lineage and divine grace.</meta>

### The Holy Tantrāloka

And therefore, because this system encompasses everything, and because it is fitting that the fulfillment of the initial promise of this work be carried out through the authority of the Trika alone, the author says:

->Therefore, everything contained herein, which remains unseen<-
->by those scholars who have abandoned the living tradition,<-
->we now reveal by the command of our Lord Guru. [19]<-

The word "**Therefore**" <note>original: "ataḥ"</note> refers to the preeminence of this specific scripture based on the reasoning already established. "**We reveal**" means we do so by creating this systematic exposition <term>prakriyā|A technical, structured manual that explains the practical application of tantric theory</term>. Thus, the underlying sentiment is: "**Effort expended on the principal subject is what truly yields fruit.**" 

"**By the command of our Lord Guru**"—the sense here is that without the guru's command, one would not even have the authority <note>original: "adhikāra"</note> to engage with this subject matter. [19]

Furthermore, to show that the cause for revealing what has not been seen by others is nothing other than the **grace of the Lord** <note>original: "bhagavat-prasāda"</note> within his own soul, he says:

->This is the work of Abhinavagupta;<-
->this is the name given to him by his teachers,<-
->he who attained fame through meditating<-

To show that this is indeed a comprehensive statement, he says, "The Initial Statement."

In this context, even though we do not accept any motive for engaging in the study of this scripture other than the **descent of power** <term>śaktipāta|The touch of divine grace that initiates a person's spiritual journey</term> from the Supreme Lord, it is nonetheless the established style of the great authors to compose an "Initial Statement" as a gateway for the student. This serves to explain the **subject matter** <note>original: "abhidheya"</note>, the **purpose** <note>original: "prayojana"</note>, and other such factors as the formal reasons for beginning the work.

Furthermore, the five verses beginning with "Śrī Bhattunātha" <note>A reference to a specific teacher in the lineage</note> were composed to demonstrate the excellence of this work through the skill of describing its author and by declaring this **Root Scripture** <note>original: "maulāgama"</note> to be the foremost among all scriptures. This tradition has been passed down through a continuous **lineage of teachers** <term>guruparamparā|The uninterrupted chain of transmission from teacher to student that ensures the purity of the teachings</term>.

As it is said:

-> "Therefore, they point to the Supreme Shiva,<-
->which has come down through the sequence of gurus."<-

Following this logic, the work becomes effective for fulfilling one's own spiritual goal. To demonstrate this lineage as an essential component of the teaching, the verse dedicated to the praise of the gurus—

### Verse 21 ] The First Daily Lesson

The **heptad** <note>original: "saptakam"; referring to the first seven verses of the work which lay the foundation</note> has been clearly marked out. Consequently, the **purpose** <note>original: "prayojana"</note> of this work is the granting of **liberation while living** <term>jīvanmukti|The state of spiritual freedom achieved while still inhabiting a physical body</term>. This is achieved through the **recognition** <term>pratyabhijñā|The central doctrine of this school, asserting that liberation is simply 're-cognizing' one's true nature as identical to God</term> of one's own Self by following the sequence of spiritual means that will be described later. While this purpose is hinted at in various verses, it is stated directly in the verse beginning with the words "Shri Shambhunatha" <note>Abhinavagupta’s primary teacher in the Trika system, credited with showing him the true essence of the path</note>. 

With this goal in view, who indeed—if they are conscious and purified by the **descent of divine power** <term>śaktipāta|The touch of grace or spiritual energy from the Divine that prompts a person to seek higher truth</term> from the Supreme Lord—would not proceed to study this? This serves as the "motive for engagement." 

However, even for one who has begun, obstacles can arise in the attainment of this knowledge. As it is said in the scriptures: 

> "The **Obstruction-makers** <note>original: "vināyakāḥ"; a class of spirits or energies that distract practitioners</note> yoke the seeker to fleeting enjoyments." 

To dispel such interference, the author has included the praise of Ganesha and Batuka <note>Forms of the deity who protect the practitioner and remove hurdles</note>. Furthermore, the title of the work, **The Light of the Tantras** <note>original: "Tantrāloka"</note>, is given based on the upcoming declaration: 

> "Therefore, this 'Light of the Tantras' is being composed by me regarding other scriptures," 

following the earlier promise, "I compose this as requested." 

In this way, the **connection** <note>original: "sambandha"</note>—defined by the relationship between the expression and the expressed, and between the subject matter and the goal (the means and the end)—is established by implication. The **condensed meaning** <note>original: "piṇḍārtha"</note> is this: these multiple sentences, when combined, form a single "Initial Statement" that acts as the primary cause for the student to engage with the text. ||21||

<meta>This page continues from the introductory verses of Chapter 1, shifting from the general praise of the lineage and the goal of the work (liberation) to a technical investigation of why liberation is necessary. It marks the transition into the "Examination of Bondage and Liberation," setting the stage for Abhinavagupta’s critique of other philosophical schools.</meta>

<page-num>54</page-num>

### Shri Tantrāloka: The Light on the Tantras

In this context, it is undisputed among all philosophical proponents that **liberation** <term>mokṣa|The final release from the cycle of birth and death</term> is the only thing truly worth attaining, while its opposite, **worldly existence** <term>saṃsāra|The continuous cycle of suffering, rebirth, and limitation</term>, is to be abandoned. It is also agreed that **false knowledge** <note>original: "mithyājñāna"</note> is the cause of this worldly existence, and its antidote is the **knowledge of reality** <term>tattvajñāna|Direct, experiential understanding of the ultimate nature of existence</term>. Thus, by the direct realization of reality, ignorance is removed and liberation is achieved—this much is common ground. 

Nevertheless, these other theorists have not truly understood the specific, essential nature of knowledge and ignorance. As it has been said:

->'Illusion indeed deludes them with the desire for liberation in that which is not truly liberation.'<-
<note>original: "bhramayatyeva tān māyā hyamokṣe mokṣalipsayā"</note>

To demonstrate that the "liberation" accepted by other schools is not true liberation at all, and to highlight the primary importance of this investigation—which is distinguished from other scriptures and will be explained in detail later—the author begins by outlining the "Examination of Bondage and Liberation" right at the start of the work.

> **Verse 22**
> Here, in all the sacred scriptures, it is loudly proclaimed: 
> **Ignorance** is the cause of worldly existence, 
> and **Knowledge** is the sole cause of liberation.

The author further explains that this is not merely his own original invention <note>original: "svopajñam"; an idea one has discovered or authored oneself without prior tradition</note>:

> **Verse 23**
> They consider **Impurity** to be **Ignorance**, 
> the cause of the sprout of worldly existence. 
> This has been stated in the venerable **Mālinīvijayottara Tantra**.
> <note>The Mālinīvijayottara is the primary scriptural authority for the Trika system; Abhinavagupta considers it the most important of all Tantras.</note>

<note>The term used here for impurity is **Mala**. In this system, it refers to a spiritual "stain" or limitation that masks the soul's natural divinity, making it feel small, finite, and separate from the Divine.</note>

<summary>This page introduces the fundamental premise of the Tantrāloka: that while everyone seeks liberation, most do not understand what ignorance and knowledge actually are. It establishes "Impurity" (Mala) as the root of spiritual ignorance, citing the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra as authority.</summary>

<keywords>liberation, worldly existence, ignorance, knowledge, Mālinīvijayottara Tantra, impurity, Mala, delusion, reality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of Verse 22 and concludes the commentary on Verse 23 of the first chapter. It transitions from the general definition of ignorance to a technical classification of the "impurities" (mala) that bind the soul, specifically focusing on how "spiritual ignorance" serves as the root cause of worldly suffering.</meta>

<page-num>५५</page-num>
<header>Verse 23 ] First Chapter . 55</header>

'**Ignorance**' <note>original: "ajñānaṃ"</note> is a darkness whose essence is the concealment of one’s own true nature, brought about solely by the play of the Supreme Lord’s **sovereignty** <term>svātantrya|The absolute, independent creative freedom of Universal Consciousness</term>. It is characterized by the false identification of the Self with what is not the Self, and the non-Self with the Self; it is "incomplete knowledge." This very thing is the **impurity** <term>mala|Spiritual dross or limitation that clouds the soul's natural state</term> of the "atomic" or individual soul <note>original: "āṇava mala"</note>. It is not, however, a physical substance-like entity, a view that will be refuted in the ninth chapter and elsewhere. As it has been said:

->'The loss of the sovereignty of consciousness, and the lack of awareness of that sovereignty;<-
->this "atomic" impurity is twofold, arising from the loss of one's true nature.'<-

**Thus** it is described. And what is the nature of this ignorance? The author explains with the words: "of worldly existence." For **worldly existence** <note>original: "saṃsārasya"</note>—

->'The appearance of distinct objects of knowledge right here is called the impurity of Illusion...'<-

—as well as the other described characteristics of the **impurity of illusion** <term>māyīya mala|The limitation that creates the sense of difference and duality</term>. 

->'Action is the cause of worldly existence; it is called the sprout of worldly existence.'<-

According to the logic that will be explained later, the '**sprout**' or cause is the **impurity of action** <term>kārma mala|The limitation arising from motivated actions that lead to future rebirth</term>, and [spiritual ignorance] is the **cause** of that. This is stated in the **Venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra**:

->'Impurity is the cause of action, while that which follows is its effect.'<-

This present work proceeds specifically under the authority of that scripture, which strengthens the argument. ||23||

Even though ignorance is twofold, being both **spiritual** <term>pauruṣa|Pertaining to the innate limitation of the individual soul (puruṣa)</term> and **intellectual** <term>bauddha|Pertaining to the misconceptions held in the intellect (buddhi)</term>, in this context, only the spiritual kind is intended and no other. Thus, the author says:

<margin>Line 1: Manuscript 'Kha' reads "ignorance-darkness" as a single compound. Manuscript 'Ka' reads "brought about" and "nature" as separate words.</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines ignorance not as a total lack of knowledge, but as "incomplete knowledge" and identifies it as the root 'atomic impurity' (āṇava mala) that triggers the further impurities of illusion and action. He emphasizes that this teaching is rooted in the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra and distinguishes between spiritual and intellectual ignorance.</summary>

<keywords>ignorance, sovereignty, mala, impurities, āṇava mala, māyīya mala, kārma mala, Mālinīvijayottara Tantra, spiritual vs intellectual ignorance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the distinction between innate spiritual ignorance (anava mala) and intellectual ignorance (bauddha ajnana). The previous page established that the primary "impurity" is a limitation of the soul's sovereignty, while this page clarifies the secondary role of the intellect in the cycle of worldly existence.</meta>

<page-num>५६</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Tantraloka</header>

**By means of the qualification [placed upon] that which is situated in the intellect and which occurs after worldly existence, [the author] has negated the possibility [of it being the primary cause of bondage] and stated that liberation occurs in its absence. || 24 ||**

"By means of the qualification" refers to the phrase "the cause of the sprout of worldly existence" <note>This refers back to the description of karma in Verse 23</note>. Intellectual ignorance, which takes the form of faulty judgment, is not the actual cause of **action** <term>karma|The law of cause and effect driven by past deeds</term>. Rather, intellectual ignorance is the result of that action <gloss>5: "That" refers to action; "its" refers to intellectual ignorance; "this" refers to intellectual ignorance.</gloss>. 

How then can this qualification be appropriate? Such intellectual ignorance is possible only when there is a body produced by past actions, because the body consists of the collection of various organs, and the **intellect** <term>buddhi|The higher mental faculty of discernment and judgment</term> is included within that group of organs. For this very reason, it was said that it "occurs after worldly existence." 

As it is said in other scriptures:

->'The structure of the body and the world is proclaimed to be a product of **Illusion** <term>māyā|The power that creates the appearance of duality and material form</term>.'<-

Following this logic, "after worldly existence" means following the formation of the body. 

What is achieved by negating this possibility? The author explains: "[he] stated that liberation occurs in its absence." Liberation would not occur simply through the cessation of intellectual ignorance alone. This is because when that ignorance ceases, "intellectual knowledge" arises; even if that knowledge is of the nature of **pure conceptualization** <term>śuddha-vikalpa|Mental constructs that align with reality, such as "I am the Self," which help dismantle bondange</term>, according to the principle:

->'All conceptual thought is worldly existence...'<-

It would still lead to the manifestation of worldly existence. How then could liberation happen even in the absence of intellectual ignorance? This is the point intended even by those outside this tradition...

---

<gloss>5: "That" refers to action; "its" refers to intellectual ignorance; "this" refers to intellectual ignorance.</gloss>
<note>Line 5, Manuscript K: Reads "How is this of his..." instead of "How does this..."</note>

<summary>Abhinavagupta distinguishes between innate spiritual ignorance and the secondary ignorance of the intellect. He argues that since the intellect is part of the physical body produced by past actions, intellectual ignorance cannot be the root cause of bondage, but rather a symptom of it.</summary>

This page clarifies that true liberation depends on the removal of "spiritual" or "innate" ignorance (pauruṣa-ajñāna), while intellectual knowledge (bauddha-jñāna) serves to confirm that liberation in the practitioner's lived experience.</meta>

<page-num>५७</page-num>
<header>Verse 24 ] The First Daily Lesson</header>

> 'The wise person should not become attached even to thoughts regarding the Supreme Reality. For what difference is there in a thought, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious?' <note>original: "paramārtha-vikalpe'pi..." This quote suggests that at the highest level of realization, even "holy" conceptual thoughts are still limitations.</note>

As stated in the passage above, when **spiritual ignorance** <term>pauruṣa-ajñāna|The innate limitation of the soul that obscures its divine nature</term> is removed by means of **initiation** <term>dīkṣā|A ritual of spiritual transmission that severs the bonds of ignorance</term> and similar means, if **intellectual knowledge** <term>bauddha-jñāna|Correct conceptual understanding of reality within the intellect</term> should then arise, it could—according to the principles to be explained later—become a cause for **liberation while living** <term>jīvanmukti|The state of being spiritually liberated while still inhabiting a physical body</term>. However, it has already been stated that by intellectual knowledge alone, nothing will be accomplished. Spiritual knowledge, on the other hand, once it has arisen, is the cause of liberation without depending on anything else. As it is said:

> 'The bonds pertaining to the person are to be purified during initiation, not those situated in the intellect. Therefore, even if the intellect is faulty, initiation is not fruitless.' <note>original: "pāśāśca pauruṣāḥ śodhyā..." This confirms that the primary goal of initiation is the soul's innate bondage, not the mind's mistakes.</note>

This spiritual knowledge is essentially pure awareness. Indeed, the absence of **non-recognition** <term>akhyāti|The failure to recognize one's true divine nature; a lack of self-awareness</term> is itself "Full Recognition." And that recognition is the true, essential nature of the Self, which is a dense mass of Light and Bliss. The manifestation of that nature is liberation itself. Thus, it was rightly said: "[the author] has stated that liberation occurs in its absence" <note>Referring to the absence of the "sprout of worldly existence" or the limitation of ignorance.</note>. || 24 ||

Why should it not simply mean the "absence of knowledge"? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

## Ignorance is not the mere absence of knowledge, for that would lead to an absurd conclusion.
## Such an absence of knowledge exists even in a clod of earth or a stone, yet those objects do not undergo the cycle of rebirth.
->॥ २५ ॥<-

->He explains what this "absurd conclusion" <note>original: "atiprasaṅga"</note> is with the words: 'Such an absence...' and so on.<-

It is therefore rightly stated that the meaning of the word **ignorance** <term>ajñāna|In this system, ignorance is not a void, but a "partial" view that mistakes a piece of reality for the whole</term> is "incomplete knowledge." || 25 ||

->He says this:<-

## Therefore, that knowledge which consists of the incomplete manifestation of the reality to be known in its totality
## is what is called "ignorance" in the **Shiva Sutras**.
## || 26 ||

"Therefore" refers to the reason just stated. Regarding the "reality to be known"—such as the perception of the color blue or feelings of pleasure—its nature will be described later as:
->"The supreme reality of everything to be known is Shiva, who is the nature of pure Light."<-
Because this "reality" is without distinction everywhere, existing as a single, solid mass of consciousness, "incomplete manifestation" refers to the fragmented experience of duality—such as thinking "this is blue" or "this is pleasure." This **incomplete knowledge** <term>apūrṇa-jñāna|Knowledge that perceives limits and boundaries where there are none</term> is itself what is meant by **ignorance**. It is not merely a total absence of knowledge. This is what is meant by the word "stated" <note>original: "bhāṣitam"</note> in the **Shiva Sutras** <note>The Shiva Sutras are the foundational aphorisms of Kashmiri Shaivism, said to have been discovered by the sage Vasugupta carved into a rock.</note>. || 26 ||

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of ignorance as incomplete knowledge. Abhinavagupta is now applying this definition to the foundational Shiva Sutras, explaining how a grammatical play on the words "knowledge" and "ignorance" reveals that limited perception is the true source of spiritual bondage.</meta>

<page-num>५९</page-num>
<header>Verse 30 ] [ First Chapter </header>

## In the two sutras "The Self is Consciousness" and "Knowledge is Bondage," this meaning has been demonstrated
## through both the union and the separation of the letter "a."
## || 27 ||

The phrase "through union and its opposite" <note>original: "saṃśleṣetarayogābhyām"</note> refers to the rules of grammatical combination <note>original: "saṃhitayā"</note>. In other words, by either joining or splitting the vowel "a" <note>This refers to a clever reading of the Shiva Sutras 1.1 and 1.2. By taking the "a" from the end of "atma" in the first sutra and applying it to "jnanam" in the second, "Knowledge is bondage" becomes "Ignorance is bondage."</note>, the meaning produced is both "**knowledge** is bondage" and "**ignorance** is bondage." This serves to define the word "ignorance" as "incomplete knowledge." || 27 ||

->He explains this further:<-

## The word "Consciousness" <term>caitanya|The abstract state of being conscious, derived from 'cetana' (the conscious being)</term> ends with a suffix denoting a state of being; it signifies absolute freedom alone.
## In that ancient sutra <note>referring to Shiva Sutra 1.1: "caitanyam ātmā"</note>, it is described as being without any perceived distinctions.
## || 28 ||

## However, by the second sutra, which speaks of knowledge as either an "action" or an "instrument,"
## duality is predicated of that which is essentially pure consciousness.
## || 29 ||

## This manifestation of duality is "ignorance." Because of its worthlessness, it is called "bondage."
## For that very reason, it must be completely eradicated; this is established through the repetition of the teaching.
## || 30 ||

In this context, nothing exists that is not perceived; therefore, the "act of consciousness" <term>citi-kriyā|The dynamic, creative movement of awareness that brings the world into being</term> is the universal form of all things. One who perceives is "conscious"—possessing full power of knowledge and action. The state of such a being is "Consciousness" <note>original: "caitanyam"</note>, which is the fullness of knowledge and action...

---

<note>Line 16 in the manuscript (labeled 'kha') reads: "possessing full knowledge."</note>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that the Shiva Sutras define bondage as limited knowledge (duality) and liberation as the absolute freedom of universal consciousness. He uses a grammatical pun to show that "knowledge" of specific things is actually a form of "ignorance" of the whole.</summary>

<page-num>६०</page-num>
<header>The Holy Tantraloka</header>

[The state] of being; and that very thing is called Absolute Freedom <term>svatantrya|The inherent power of the Divine to act and will without external constraint</term>, which is the nature of supreme sovereignty.

As it was said: "Absolute freedom alone." This means absolute freedom by itself. For this very reason, he says it is "without severed distinctions" <note>original: anācchinna-viśeṣam</note>. "Unsevered" refers to the fact that even though qualities such as eternity and pervasiveness are its constant companions, they do not create "distinctions" or divisions within it. For a word ending in a suffix denoting a state of being <note>original: bhāva-pratyaya; in Sanskrit grammar, suffixes like -tva or -ta function like '-ness' or '-hood' in English</note> expresses the exclusion of other accompanying qualities. This is precisely the distinction of such a word from one that denotes a substance. As they say:

> "The exclusion or non-exclusion of other qualities [belongs] to those two [types of words].
> Having understood the place of the conventional sign through the requirement of clarity,
> this indeed is the difference everywhere between words denoting a substance and those denoting a state."

Regarding the "second" [sutra]—namely the word "Knowledge" found in the second sutra—it refers to the act of knowing or the means of knowing. Through the etymological derivations of "knowledge is the act of knowing" and "knowledge is that by which one knows," it denotes primarily "action" and "instrument." Therefore, of "that"—the Self whose nature was described as "Consciousness"—it is said that "duality is predicated." This is because the Self is the "Conscious One" <term>cit|The pure subject or 'perceiver'</term>, the agent in the act of consciousness; yet [in the second sutra] its "form" is [restricted] to that [limited action] alone.

---

<margin>Line 7, Manuscript K: The reading is "Therefore, the word denoting..."</margin>
<margin>Line 10, Manuscript K: The reading for "distinction" is of this [different] sort.</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta uses Sanskrit grammatical theory to show how the word "Consciousness" represents absolute freedom, while the word "Knowledge" introduces duality by treating the Self as a mere instrument or a limited action.</summary>
<keywords>Svatantrya, Absolute Freedom, Caitanya, Consciousness, Jnana, Duality, Sanskrit Grammar, Shiva Sutras, Abhinavagupta</keywords>

--- Page 71 ---
<meta>This page continues Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the first chapter of the Tantraloka. Having established that absolute "Consciousness" is freedom, he now explains how "Knowledge"—when it is limited and fragmented—becomes the source of bondage and dualism.</meta>

<page-num>61</page-num>
<header>Verse 30 ] The First Daily Lesson</header>

Because of the introduction of distinct limiting factors—specifically the two types of action, as well as the roles of the agent, the object, and the act itself—the framework of dualistic manifestation is established. This means that [this state] does not reveal its full, perfect nature.

"That"—meaning, because of the failure to reveal the full nature of the perfect, non-dual Self of Consciousness—is why "dualistic manifestation" itself is called "Ignorance" <note>original: ajñāna</note>. This is incomplete knowledge. Because of its incompleteness, it takes the form of various types of contracted knowledge—such as the false belief in one's own insufficiency, the latent impressions of "good" and "bad" actions, and the identification with the physical body and the external world. Constituting the "three impurities" <term>malatraya|The three stains of spiritual limitation: Āṇavamala (the sense of being a limited individual), Māyīyamala (the perception of things as separate from oneself), and Kārmamala (bondage to the results of one’s actions)</term>, it is called "Bondage." Since it is the nature of bondage, this ignorance must be "completely eradicated."

As it has been stated:

> ->"Impurity, action, and that which is called 'the product of Maya'—<-
> ->all of this is declared to be something that must be discarded..."<-

By this quote, the meaning is that it is "to be abandoned" <note>original: heyam</note>. Now, one might ask: how is it known that "Ignorance" is simply incomplete knowledge characterized by dualistic manifestation? Anticipating this doubt, the author states: "established by repetition." "By repetition" means that by returning once more to the term "Ignorance" as it appears in the sequence of the scriptures, its deeper meaning is revealed.

28, 29, 30.

He concludes that because this ignorance causes bondage, it must be discarded to realize the full nature of Consciousness.</summary>

<meta>On the previous page, Abhinavagupta explained how "Ignorance" is not a total absence of knowledge, but rather fragmented or "incomplete knowledge." This incompleteness creates the "three impurities" that bind the soul. Now, he addresses the logical follow-up: if bondage is just a state of awareness, what then is the formal definition of Liberation?</meta>

<page-num>62</page-num>
<header>The Sri Tantraloka</header>

### Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, let the definition of Liberation be stated," he says:

->Other than the Independent Self,<-
->whether something non-existent or real,<-
->nothing called "Liberation" exists.<-
->Indeed, not even a separate name is accepted. || 31 ||<-

"There is nothing else" is the implied completion of the sentence. If Liberation were "non-existent" <note>original: tuccha; referring to a void or a mere absence</note>, then based on the logic mentioned previously, it would simply be another form of Bondage. If it were "real" <note>original: atuccha</note>, then because it possesses absolute reality, it cannot be distinct from the Independent Self. As the author will state later:

> "Liberation is truly nothing else; it is the unfolding of one’s own true nature. And the true nature of the Self is Consciousness..." <term>saṃvit|Pure, non-dual consciousness that is the foundation of all experience</term>

And so on. What is being expressed here? In this system, it is undisputed that "Knowledge of the Self is Liberation." Therefore, whatever defines the Self also defines Liberation. Since the two are inseparable <note>original: tannāntarīyakatvāt; a logical term for two things that cannot exist without each other</note>, the definition of Liberation is already established by defining the Self; thus, a separate definition has not been provided. This is why the author uses the word "even" in the phrase "not even a name"—to suggest: "if even a separate name is not accepted, what need is there to speak of a separate definition?" || 31 ||

---

<margin>Line 7, Manuscript Kh: "Because if non-existent..."</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines Liberation (Moksha) not as a new state to be reached, but as the "unfolding" of one's own inherent, independent Consciousness. He argues that because Liberation is identical to the Self, it requires no separate definition or even a distinct name from the Self itself.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 62, where Abhinavagupta argued that Liberation is not a separate thing but the realization of the Self's own nature. Having established the Trika view, he now begins to explain how "knowledge" and "liberation" are viewed in other systems of thought to highlight the difference.</meta>

<page-num>63</page-num>
<header>Verse 32 ] Chapter One</header>

Even so, in order to highlight the unique distinction of this system, he begins to describe the nature of Liberation as it is taught in other philosophical systems:

**But that knowledge which consists of the "complete-incomplete" manifestation**
**of the true nature of the objects of knowledge,**
**that progressive knowledge brings peace to each respective cycle of worldly existence. || 32 ||**

The word "That" <note>original: *yat*</note> refers to the "objects of knowledge" <note>original: *jñeya*</note>, which comprise the "Path" <term>adhvan|The cosmic map or hierarchy of levels through which the soul journeys toward the Absolute</term> consisting of the ritual divisions, the categories of existence, and the world-planes <term>kalā-tattva-bhuvana|Three of the six levels of the objective universe in Tantric cosmology</term>. 

The "true nature" <note>original: *satattvam*</note> of this path refers to how these elements are situated, both in their vertical hierarchy and in their mutual distinction from one another. 

"Progressive" <note>original: *uttarottaram*</note> means moving higher and higher, in a sequence of transcending each specific world-plane. By following this order, the limitations of those specific levels are removed. Depending on the level reached, this knowledge consists of a perception of duality; yet, even though it remains "contracted" <note>original: *saṃkucita*</note>, it is described as **"knowledge consisting of complete-incomplete manifestation."** This knowledge arises because the seeker has transcended the web of lower categories.

As it is said in the scriptures:

> "The circle of worldly existence which is said to be of fourteen types <gloss>6</gloss>."

From this and similar passages, the phrase "bringing peace to each respective" refers to the fourteen types of births; it means that such knowledge acts as the "bringer of peace," or the deliverer, from that specific cycle of existence.

---

<gloss>6</gloss> The fourteen-fold nature of worldly existence is described thus:
> "The divine is of eight varieties; the animal and bird kingdom is fivefold; the human is of one kind. This, in brief, is the material creation."
<note>This is a traditional classification from the Samkhya system: 8 types of gods, 5 types of animals/plants, and 1 type of human, totaling 14.</note>

<summary>Abhinavagupta describes a "progressive" or "incomplete" type of knowledge found in other traditions, which allows a soul to transcend specific levels of the fourteen-fold material world, contrasting this partial liberation with the absolute realization of the Self.</summary>

--- Page 74 ---
<meta>Continuing from page 63, where Abhinavagupta discussed how knowledge of the various levels of the objective universe (the "Path") allows a seeker to gradually transcend limitations. He is now explaining that while "knowledge" is generally defined as that which liberates, different philosophical schools define the scope of that liberation differently based on their specific understanding of the self.</meta>

<page-num>64</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras (Sri Tantraloka)</header>

For the essential function of knowledge is liberation itself; specifically, it is the process of that which is **contracted** <note>original: *saṃkucita*; referring to limited, individual awareness</note> becoming **uncontracted** <note>original: *asaṃkucitatvam*; expanding into universal consciousness</note>. || 32 ||

He demonstrates this very point:

->**I am internally untainted by passion and the like;**<-
->**I am the Void, devoid of agency.**<-
->**In this way, through both synthesis and analysis,**<-
->**Knowledge liberates to that respective extent. || 33 ||**<-

The word "In this way" <note>original: *ittham*</note> refers to the nature defined in the first half of the verse. The grammatical connection is that "Knowledge" <note>original: *jñānam*</note> liberates the seeker "to that extent" <note>original: *tāvataḥ*</note>—meaning from a specific, limited state of bondage. This refers to the systems of the **Buddhists** <term>Bauddha|Followers of the Buddhist philosophical traditions</term> and others. 

Within that context, the realization "I am untainted by passion and the like" is the knowledge held by the **Yogacara** <term>Yogācāra|A major school of Mahayana Buddhism that emphasizes that reality is 'Mind-Only' and that liberation is the purification of consciousness</term> school. As they say:

> "The mind tainted by passion and other defilements is the cycle of suffering <term>saṃsāra|The continuous round of birth, death, and rebirth driven by karma</term>; liberation is being free from that. In brief, liberation has been described by the Victors <note>original: *jinaiḥ*; a title for the Buddhas as 'conquerors' of delusion</note> who have discarded all veils."

And likewise:

> "This mind <term>citta|The individual consciousness or psyche</term> is luminous by nature; the impurities are merely accidental arrivals. When they are removed, that light shines as the imperishable reality of all things."

<page-num>65</page-num>
<header>Verse 33 ] Chapter 1</header>

...and so on. Here is the meaning: Even though the **mind** <term>citta|Individual consciousness or mental faculty</term> is inherently radiant by nature, it becomes covered by accidental impurities like passion due to beginningless ignorance <term>avidyā|Spiritual ignorance that obscures the true nature of reality</term>. This leads to the appearance of the cycle of suffering <term>saṃsāra</term>. However, through the power of practicing the path consisting of **meditative cultivation** <term>bhāvanā|The process of repeated contemplation or habituation of a realization</term>, those accidental impurities are abandoned. Through the "revolution of the substrate" <note>original: *āśraya-parāvṛtti*; a technical term in Yogacara Buddhism for the fundamental transformation where the mind stops projecting external objects and realizes its pure, non-dual nature</note>, the manifestation of one's own nature as an imperishable form of light is liberation.

This is their position—but it is not logical. You claim that meditative cultivation is the cause here, but that cultivation cannot produce a specific excellence or change in **momentary mental events** <term>citta-kṣaṇa|The Buddhist doctrine that the mind is not a continuous entity, but a stream of discrete, fleeting flashes of consciousness</term> that perish instantly. This is because the ability to impart such an excellence requires a stable, single substrate upon which the cultivation can act. 

To illustrate: permanent objects like sesame seeds are scented by flowers that are also permanent; this is how a new quality is imparted. This should be the case here as well. Therefore, since mental moments arise as something entirely new every instant and perish without leaving a trace—similar to the repeated practice of jumping <note>original: *laṅghana-abhyāsa*; a standard logical example meaning that practice cannot accumulate if the performer doesn't persist</note>—meditative cultivation would not be able to produce a radiant mental moment from a previous mental moment that has not yet attained any excellence. Thus, what is the point of this practice?

Furthermore, defiled mental moments, due to their inherent power to produce like effects, are only capable of producing other defiled mental moments like themselves—not dissimilar, radiant ones. Thus, because of the momentary nature of mental events, meditative cultivation would not be effective even for the abandonment of impurities.

<page-num>66</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Light of the Tantras</header>

Thus, what talk can there be of a "revolution of the substrate" <note>original: *āśraya-parāvṛtti*</note>? Enough with this talk of liberation for those who advocate the **doctrine of momentariness** <term>kṣaṇikavāda|The Buddhist theory that all things, including consciousness, exist for only a single infinitesimal moment before vanishing</term>. 

Bondage and liberation are only logical in a position that accepts a single, stable entity. Indeed, it is a bound person who strives for **liberation** <term>mokṣa|Freedom from the cycle of suffering and rebirth</term>, and having attained it, becomes one whose striving has ceased. Furthermore, a "stream of consciousness" <note>original: *santāna*</note> cannot be considered a single entity, because that concept is destroyed by the logical dilemma of whether the stream is different or non-different from the individual moments that compose it.

Even within the nature of **pure consciousness** <term>saṃvid|The foundational, self-aware light of reality</term>, the followers of the **Middle Way** <term>mādhyamika|The Buddhist school founded by Nāgārjuna which emphasizes the "emptiness" of all things</term> hold the realization: "I am empty." They indeed advocate that all things lack an inherent nature. By asserting that consciousness itself lacks an inherent nature and is therefore false, they would describe liberation as occurring only within that **emptiness** <term>śūnyatā|The ultimate void or lack of essence in all phenomena</term>. As it has been said:

> "This universe is but mind alone"—this teaching of the Sage <note>original: *muneḥ*; referring to the Buddha</note> 
> was to remove the fear of the childish <note>original: *bālānām*; meaning those spiritually immature or beginners on the path</note>; it is not the ultimate truth.
> Even that establishment of "Mind-Only"
> was demolished by the Great-Souled ones <note>The Mādhyamika philosophers who critiqued the Yogācāra "Mind-Only" school</note>.

However, that too is incorrect. If consciousness is "false" and its independent nature is set aside, then in that falseness, existence itself would not be possible. This is because consciousness does not possess a "dependent form" in the way that objects like "blue" do. In the case of objects like "blue," even when their independent nature is set aside due to their being false, they still [subsist] as the nature of consciousness—

---

<summary>This page critiques the Buddhist Mādhyamika view of emptiness, arguing that liberation requires a stable subject and that consciousness cannot be dismissed as "false" or "empty" because it is the very basis of existence.</summary>

<page-num>67</page-num>
<header>Verse 33 ] First Chapter</header>

If there is [no stable] state, and if **consciousness** <term>saṃvid|The foundational, self-aware light of reality</term>—which is essentially nothing but **vibrant manifestation** <term>sphurattā|The pulsating, self-luminous flash of consciousness that makes things appear</term>—were non-existent due to being "false," then nothing at all would manifest. This would result in a state of **utter stupor** <note>original: *mūrcchā*; a state of total unconsciousness or "blackout"</note>. Furthermore, it is impossible to deny consciousness, as its very essence is that vibrant manifestation. Therefore, this argument [of the Nihilists] is of no consequence.

Now, [the opponent might argue]:

> "It is empty of all objects of perception, empty of all living beings without exception, and empty of all latent traces of affliction; yet it is not empty from the perspective of the **ultimate reality** <term>paramārtha|The highest level of truth or existence</term>."

By this reasoning, if you say that consciousness is empty only in its imagined form—such as the **subject-object relationship** <note>original: *grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva*</note>—but not empty in its own nature as consciousness, then you have simply accepted the position of the **Consciousness-Only School** <term>vijñānavāda|A Buddhist school (Yogācāra) asserting that only consciousness is real, while the external world is an illusion</term>. For that school also accepts that consciousness is empty of the "imagined" and "dependent" forms, as it is said:

> "This world is but the vibrant play of the **inner instrument** <term>antaḥkaraṇa|The internal mental faculty, comprising the intellect, ego, and mind</term> alone, which appears as a variety of forms when its true nature is not realized."

Thus, they have accepted **pure cognition** <note>original: *vijñapti*</note> alone as being ultimately real.

<meta>Continuing from page 67, Abhinavagupta (the author) and Jayaratha (the commentator) move from a critique of Buddhist Nihilism and Idealism to a critique of the Sāṃkhya school of philosophy. <page-num>68</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Light of the Tantras <note>original: *Śrī-Tantrāloka*</note></header>

Nothing new has been conceived by my long-lived friend <note>A polite but firm way of addressing an opponent in classical Indian debate</note>. The flaw in that position has already been stated: the knowledge that **"I am a non-doer"** <note>original: *akartāhaṃ bhavāmi*</note> is the view of the **Sāṃkhyas** <term>Sāṃkhya|One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, which posits a dualism between consciousness (Puruṣa) and matter (Prakṛti)</term>. They indeed accepted the **Self** <term>Ātman|The true, eternal essence of the individual</term> as being entirely inactive; for they believe that otherwise, it could not possess **consciousness** <term>caitanya|The quality of being sentient or aware</term>—since activity is observed only in non-conscious things like milk and so on <note>Referring to the traditional Sāṃkhya example of milk flowing "unconsciously" from a cow to nourish a calf, used to explain how nature acts without a soul</note>.

This view is incorrect. Indeed, if the **Spirit** <term>Puruṣa|The passive, conscious observer in Sāṃkhya philosophy</term> were a non-doer, there would be **no liberation** <term>anirmokṣa|The state of being unable to achieve final release from the cycle of rebirth</term>. For if the Spirit were truly "doing nothing," then even after **discriminative insight** <term>viveka-darśana|The realization of the absolute difference between the conscious Spirit and unconscious Nature</term> <margin>Manuscript K: "even when the discrimination between Nature and Spirit has arisen"</margin> has arisen, there would be no stable abiding in its own nature. This is because it is impossible for **Nature** <term>Prakṛti|The material world and its unconscious energy</term>, whose very essence is activity, to become indifferent; the possibility of her acting for that Spirit’s sake would remain.

Furthermore, Nature cannot reflect:

> "I have been seen by him,"

or

> "I shall not act for his sake again,"

because she is unconscious—she lacks the capacity for **deliberate foresight** <note>original: *prekṣā-kāritva*; the ability of an agent to act with a conscious purpose or plan</note>. Thus, just as she acts again to provide the experience of sound and other senses even after they have been experienced once, she would likewise act for him again even after **discriminative knowledge** <term>viveka-khyāti|A synonym for discriminative insight</term> has been achieved—because her inherent nature remains unchanged. In this way, what has been done does not become undone <margin>Manuscript K: "becomes undone"</margin>—and thus, even this restricted [view]...

<meta>Continuing from page 68, the text persists in its comparative analysis of different philosophical schools. Having critiqued the Sāṃkhya view of the passive "non-doer," the author now contrasts the Buddhist goal (attainment of the Intellect or Buddhi) with the Sāṃkhya goal (attainment of the Spirit or Puruṣa), arguing that each school's liberation is limited to the specific "level" of reality they recognize.</meta>

<page-num>69</page-num>
### [Verse 33] Chapter One | 69

Knowledge for the **Buddhists** and others should perform its own appropriate **purposeful action** <term>arthakriyā|The capacity of a thing to produce an effect or perform a function; in Indian philosophy, this is often the test for whether something is "real"</term>. For instance, the **Buddhists** say:

-> "We perceive this single **form of consciousness** <note>original: *saṃvid-rūpa*</note> appearing as various forms such as joy, grief, and so on." <-

By such reasoning, they have accepted that reality is **knowledge** <term>jñāna|Specifically referring here to cognitive states</term> consisting of the fluctuations of the **Intellect** <term>buddhi-vṛtti|The active "waves" or modifications of the mind's higher reasoning faculty</term>. Therefore, for them, liberation is nothing more than the attainment of the **level of the Intellect** <term>buddhi-tattva|In the hierarchy of cosmic principles, this is the level of individual and cosmic intelligence, which is still considered part of 'matter' in many systems</term>. As it has been said:

-> "Brahma resides in that **level of Intellect** as the sovereign ruler; and that very state, which they call 'all-knowing,' is the supreme goal of the **Buddhists**." <-

It is for this reason that for them, there is a cessation of the **worldly cycle** <term>saṃsāra|The cycle of suffering and rebirth</term> that exists below the level of the Intellect. Thus, it is rightly said: **"Knowledge liberates to that extent."** <note>This implies that while knowledge helps, it only liberates the seeker up to the highest level of reality they can conceive of</note>.

The **Sāṃkhyas**, on the other hand, accept that reality is the **Spirit** <term>Puruṣa|The eternal, pure conscious observer who is distinct from the physical and mental world</term> abiding in its own nature through its separation from **Nature** <term>Prakṛti|The primordial material cause of the world, which includes thoughts and emotions</term>, which consists of pleasure, pain, and so on. Thus, for them, liberation is the attainment of the **level of the Spirit** <note>original: *puṃ-tattva*</note>. As it has been said:

-> "The state of the **Spirit** <note>original: *pauruṣa*</note> for the **Sāṃkhyas** is devoid of pleasure, pain, and the rest." <-

Because the **view of the Self** <note>The Sāṃkhya belief in a permanent individual soul</note> is superior to the **view of No-Self** <note>The Buddhist doctrine of *anātman* or *nairātmya*, which denies a permanent soul</note>, the knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas is considered a more **complete manifestation** <note>original: *pūrṇa-prathā*</note> of knowledge than that of the Buddhists. Therefore, their attainment is of the **level of the Spirit**, which exists above the level of the Intellect. And thus, this complete manifestation—

### [Verse 33 Continued] Chapter One | 70

...higher and higher knowledge. In this way, the point promised in the previous verse has been fulfilled. Thus, although the **Sāṃkhya** and **Patañjala** <note>The Yoga school of Patañjali</note> systems are similar in their knowledge of the **Spirit** <term>Puruṣa|The pure, conscious individual soul</term> as being distinct from **Primordial Matter** <term>Prakṛti|The unconscious material cause of the universe</term>, the followers of **Patañjali** are superior to the **Sāṃkhyas** because of their **devotion to the Lord** <term>Īśvara-praṇidhāna|The practice of surrendering to a supreme God, which Yoga includes but Sāṃkhya traditionally does not</term>. Because of this, it is said that they attain the **Level of Destiny** <term>Niyati-tattva|The cosmic principle of necessity, order, and spatial/temporal restriction; in this system, it sits just above the individual soul</term>, which exists above the level of the Spirit. As it is said:

-> "The twenty-sixth principle, O Goddess, is the supreme state in the **Yoga scripture**." <-
<note>original: *ṣaḍviṃśakaṃ tu deveśi yogaśāstre paraṃ padam*</note>

Similarly, for the **Mauśula**, **Pāśupata**, and other sects, the attainment of higher and higher cosmic levels constitutes their "supreme state" according to the excellence of their specific knowledge. As it has been stated:

-> "In the **Mauśula** and **Kāruka** schools, the **Level of Illusion** <term>Māyā-tattva|The principle of obscuration and diversity that marks the boundary between the pure and impure worlds</term> is proclaimed as the goal." <-

And likewise:

-> "In the **Pāśupata** vow, the **Level of Sovereignty** <term>Aiśvara-pada|The state associated with Īśvara, where the sense of 'I' and 'This' are balanced</term> is said to be the supreme state." <-

In this context, knowledge serves as a liberator in varying degrees: for the **Buddhists** and others, it removes parts of the **Impurity of Illusion** <term>Māyīya-mala|The stain of perceiving difference where there is unity</term>; for the **Mauśulas**, it also addresses the **Impurity of Action** <term>Kārma-mala|The stain of past deeds and their consequences</term>; and for the **Pāśupatas**, it even liberates from the **Impurity of Individuality** <term>Āṇava-mala|The primal stain of feeling limited or 'small,' arising from the false belief that the Self is something other than the Infinite</term>. All of this has been stated "both concisely and in detail." **[33]**

<meta>Catchword/Verse reference: Verse 34</meta>

<margin>Verse 34</margin>

Now, an objection is raised: "If the bond is dissolved according to the propriety of one's own philosophical system, why is such a person not considered truly liberated?" To answer this, he says:

### Therefore, though one may be liberated from one limitation, 
### because of the presence of another limitation, 
### one remains unliberated. The truly liberated one, 
### however, is free from all limitations. || 34 ||

Based on the statement:

> "...the **Cosmic Path** <term>Adhvan|The structured hierarchy of the universe consisting of various levels, sounds, and principles</term> is the cause of bondage,"

it follows that the Path acts as a binder. In this context, the **Buddhists** and others—because of the dissolution of the bonds up to the **Level of the Intellect** <term>Buddhi-tattva|The psychological and cosmic principle of discernment, which some schools mistake for the ultimate Self</term>—are indeed liberated from that specific level. However, because they still reside within the **limitations** <term>Avaccheda|A boundary, restriction, or defining limit</term> of another part of the Path situated above that level, they are actually still unliberated. 

For this very reason, at the beginning of a new cycle of creation, they are created again, and thus the **cycle of worldly existence** <term>Saṃsāra|The continuous flow of birth, death, and rebirth</term> reappears for them, because the cause of bondage has not been completely and utterly destroyed. As the author will say later:

> "Those who have attained perfection through **Sāṃkhya**, the **Vedas**, and other such paths are created again by **Srikantha** <note>A name for the deity (a form of Rudra/Shiva) who presides over the lower regions of the pure universe</note> at the dawn of his 'day.' Therefore, such liberation is not complete."
<note>original: *sāṃkhyavedādisaṃsiddhān śrīkaṇṭhastadaharmukhe | sṛjatyeva punastena na samyaṅmuktirīdṛśī ||*</note>

This is also stated in the **Venerable Svacchanda Scripture**... <note>The *Svacchanda Tantra*, a fundamental text for this tradition</note>

<vocab>
**Mukta**: Liberated; one who has achieved freedom from bondage.
**Bandha**: Bondage; the restriction of the soul's natural power.
**Avaccheda**: Limitation or boundary; that which defines or restricts a state of being.
**Adhvan**: The Path; the entire range of cosmic levels that a soul must traverse.
**Bauddhādayaḥ**: The Buddhists and other similar schools.
**Sāṃkhya**: One of the six classical schools of Indian philosophy, focusing on the dualism of spirit and matter.
**Vedādi**: The Vedas and other related scriptures.
**Śrīkaṇṭha**: The regent of the lower pure worlds who manages the souls who have not reached ultimate liberation.
**Svacchanda-śāstra**: The *Svacchanda Tantra*, an important scripture of the Kashmir Shaiva tradition.
**Saṃsāra-āvirbhāva**: The reappearance or manifestation of the cycle of rebirth.
</vocab>

<summary>This page explains that liberation is not an all-or-nothing state; many schools (like Buddhism or Sāṃkhya) achieve a partial liberation from lower cosmic levels but remain "unliberated" because they are still limited by higher levels of the cosmic path. True liberation is defined as the removal of every possible limitation (avaccheda), ensuring one is not pulled back into the cycle of rebirth during a new creation.</summary>

> "For worldly beings, there is creation again and then destruction again;
> mounted upon the **wheel of worldly existence** <term>Saṃsāra|The repetitive cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</term>, they are like a **water-wheel** <note>original: 'ghaṭa-yantra' — an ancient irrigation device with buckets that rise and fall, symbolizing the repetitive ascent and descent of souls</note>."

### Having stated this in a general way,

> "Even one who is liberated from a specific restriction is bound again by the Lord.
> Bondage within the world persists again until one discovers **God** <note>original: 'devam'. Some manuscript variants read 'deham' (the body), implying bondage lasts until the body is transcended</note>."

This was said specifically to illustrate the intermediate philosophical systems, such as **Buddhism** <note>The 'intermediate' systems are those that recognize some level of transcendence but do not reach the ultimate non-dual source</note> and others, as examples of the principles mentioned. On the other hand, the one whose bondage to the entire **Cosmic Path** <term>Adhvan|The structured hierarchy of the universe encompassing all sound, matter, and consciousness</term> has been completely and utterly extinguished is the only one who is truly and directly liberated. As the text says: "The liberated one is devoid of all **limitations** <term>Avaccheda|Defining boundaries or restrictions of the finite self</term>."

As it has been stated:

> "The Supreme Abode of the **Shaivas** <note>Followers of the non-dual path of Shiva</note> is that which has moved beyond the entire Path."

And likewise:

> "The **Shaiva Adept** <term>Siddha|A perfected being who has realized their identity with the Divine</term> shines at the head of all these; once liberated, he does not descend back down during a new creation." || 34 ||

In this context, only this kind of **Full Knowledge** <term>Pūrṇa-jñāna|The complete, unconditioned awareness of reality</term> is the cause of such liberation. Thus, he says:

# That knowledge of the reality of the known, 
# which is entirely free from all 
# limitations—nowhere is that considered ignorance; 
# it alone grants true liberation. || 35 ||

"By **limitations** <term>Avaccheda|Defining boundaries or restrictions of the finite self</term>," which cause a contraction of consciousness and create the perception of "this-ness" <note>original: 'idantā-parāmarśaiḥ' — the tendency to view reality as an external 'this' rather than as the internal 'I'</note>. ### The Division of Knowledge and Ignorance

Now he distinguishes the nature of the two—knowledge and ignorance—which were previously mentioned:

> **The nature of knowledge and ignorance which has been stated, each of these is said to be twofold in the Teachings of Shiva, distinguished as Personal and Intellectual.** || 36 ||

"In the **Teachings of Shiva**" <note>original: 'Śiva-śāsane'</note> refers to the philosophy of the Supreme Lord, which takes the form of the **Five Streams** <note>original: 'pañca-srota' — the five channels of Tantric revelation through which the scriptures were revealed</note>. This has indeed been stated everywhere without exception. || 36 ||

He defines these categories:

> **Among these, the ignorance of the Person is called "Stain"; even though it is born of that, it consists of the obscuration of Shiva-nature, which is the very form of full Consciousness and Action.** || 37 ||
> **It takes the form of contracted Consciousness and Action; for the bound soul, this ignorance is non-conceptual.**

# Sri Tantraloka
### The First Daily Lesson
->74<-

The word **"now"** <note>original: 'atha-śabda'</note> indicates a sequence; the idea is that after the "naming" of the subjects, the opportunity arises for their "definition" and "examination." <margin>7. Naming a thing by its name alone is **Mention** <term>Uddeśa</term>; the cause that describes the unique characteristics of a thing, distinguishing it from those of its own kind or other kinds, is the **Definition** <term>Lakṣaṇa</term>; and the discrimination between what is logical and illogical is **Examination** <term>Parīkṣā</term>.</margin>

"Among those" <note>original: 'tatra'</note>—meaning, from between the two types of knowledge and ignorance—

> **"...emerging supreme for the person."**

This refers to the "impurity" <term>Mala|The primordial stain or limitation that obscures the soul's true nature</term> whose nature was just described. It is characterized by limited knowledge and action, which are not common to the soul’s true state. It is "born" or "manifested"—meaning it has emerged—from **Shiva** alone, who is the Supreme Knowing Subject. 

For the Supreme Lord himself, through his own **Absolute Freedom** <term>Svātantrya|The sovereign, unimpeded power of Shiva to manifest and withdraw the universe</term>, veils his own self. He does this by setting aside his full omniscience and agency through the appearance of **Primordial Impurity** <term>Āṇava-mala|The innate limitation of being an 'individual' rather than the 'whole'</term>, which is essentially a lack of self-awareness. It has been said:

> **"That supreme freedom of the Great Lord, which accomplishes even the impossible, is the Goddess Maya-shakti; this is the veiling of Shiva’s own self."** <note>Paramārthasāra, verse 15</note>
> 
> **"By accepting the influence of Maya, consciousness becomes stained, and the person becomes a 'bound soul'."** <note>original: 'paśu' — literally 'cattle' or 'animal', referring to the soul tethered by the bonds of ignorance; Paramārthasāra, verse 16</note>

And he will say further:
