### Verse 38 ] The First Daily Lesson

"Therefore, the manifestation of impurity is merely an expression of the absolute freedom of one’s own nature." <note>original: 'tena svarūpa-svātantrya-mātram mala-vijṛmbhitam'</note>

This very same knowledge belongs to the **bound soul** <term>Paśu|Literally 'tethered one', an individual soul limited by ignorance</term>. Even though he is joined with the three types of impurity—Primordial, Illusion-based, and Action-based—his knowledge is restricted by factors such as space and time. It consists of a limited "vision" and "action," appearing as a specific type of observation. Indeed, it is the **Supreme Lord** <term>Parameśvara</term> himself who, by setting aside his omniscience and other divine powers, has reduced his own self to the state of an **atom** <term>Aṇu|The limited individual subject</term>. He then brings about a connection with **Limited Agency** <term>Kalā</term> and the other sheaths, which endows the individual with a restricted capacity for knowing and acting. As it has been said:

> "She <note>Referring to the power of Maya, the creative matrix</note> brought forth the element of **Limited Agency** <term>Kalā-tattva</term>; by joining with this, the spirit becomes a **'person'** <term>Pumān|The individual egoic subject</term> <margin>Line 8: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "became again" instead of "became a person."</margin>. Then, she created **Limited Knowledge** <term>Vidyā</term> and **Attachment** <term>Rāga</term>, which grant the capacity for knowing and acting <margin>Line 9: Manuscript 'Kha' confirms "the capacity for knowing and acting."</margin>.
> **Limited Knowledge** distinguishes for him the nature of an action and its cause and effect <margin>Line 10: Manuscript 'Kha' reads "makes known" instead of "distinguishes."</margin>. **Attachment** colors his experience, drawing him even toward enjoyments that are impure.
> **Necessity** <term>Niyati|The law of karma and cosmic order</term> binds this individual soul <term>Pudgala</term> to his specific duties. **Time** <term>Kāla</term> also governs him, existing through divisions such as the smallest blink of an eye <note>original: 'truṭi'</note>."

Thus, although the primary goal is to define the nature of **Knowledge**, the nature of **Ignorance** is defined at the outset to demonstrate that it is something that must inevitably be eradicated <margin>Line 14: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "the state of being limited" instead of "to be eradicated."</margin>.

Thus, the former is indeed the cause; for a resident of the **Coconut Island** <note>original: 'nārikela-dvīpa' — an ancient Indian trope for a remote tropical island where inhabitants have never seen fire</note> would not even have a desire for the conceptualization of fire, [since they have no prior experience of it]. || 40 ||

->**Having thus described ignorance, he now speaks in order to describe two kinds of knowledge:**<-

When the **limited tendencies** <term>Paśu-saṃskāra|The habitual patterns and latent impressions of a bound soul</term> are destroyed, for the person who has attained the supreme state, that expanded consciousness is the **spiritual** [knowledge], which is **non-conceptual**. || 41 ||

The determination that arises in accordance with the expanded, non-conceptual knowledge is **intellectual** [knowledge]. That spiritual knowledge is, as before, both the **nourished and the nourisher**. || 42 ||

Because it is stated that even the mere traces of the **atomic impurity** <gloss>āṇava-mala</gloss> of the limited soul <note>original: 'paśu' — literally 'tethered cattle', referring to the bound individual</note> are destroyed, then by the logical maxim that **"when the cause is absent, the effect is also absent,"** <note>original: 'nimittābhāve naimittikasyāpy abhāvaḥ'</note> the impurities of **action** <gloss>kārma</gloss> and **illusion** <gloss>māyīya</gloss> are also destroyed. For the **"person"** <gloss>puṃsaḥ</gloss> who is released from all bonds and has therefore attained identity with the supreme consciousness, there is an **"expanded"** consciousness. This consists of the awareness of the **supreme I-ness** <term>Parāhantā-vimarśa|The ultimate, non-dual self-recognition of the Divine</term> and is **"non-conceptual,"** meaning it is free from the conceptual constructs of the artificial ego and its derivatives...

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines the two types of spiritual knowledge: Pauruṣa (spiritual/essential) and Bauddha (intellectual). # The Light of the Tantras
## Verse 43 | Chapter One

->८०<-

> 'The state of knowledge is bestowed, and the animalistic latencies are destroyed. Because it is joined with the acts of **giving** <gloss>dāna</gloss> and **destroying** <gloss>kṣapaṇa</gloss>, it is celebrated in this tradition as **initiation** <term>dīkṣā|The term is etymologically explained as dā (to give) + kṣi (to destroy)</term>.'

By an initiation of the nature described in the passage above, ignorance is certainly destroyed. **Nevertheless**, **that** self-knowledge—which is essentially the absence of ignorance—even though it is inclined toward manifesting, [does not fully flower immediately]. 

> '...one should not purify the single **karmic residue** <term>prārabdha|The portion of one's past karma that has already begun to bear fruit and is responsible for the current physical body</term>.'

As stated above, because of the continued presence of the **impurity of action** <term>kārma-mala|The binding force of past deeds that necessitates rebirth</term> which began this present body, it is said that **at the end** of this current body, knowledge **is clearly manifested**. 

> '...upon the falling of the body, one shall go to Shiva.' <note>original: 'dehapāte śivaṃ vrajet'</note>

The meaning of these statements is that [liberation] flashes forth as a direct, intuitive realization at the time of death. Furthermore, by the use of the word "etc." [in the original verse being commented upon], we include the "residual functioning" <note>the natural lifespan of the body</note>, but not the **very intense descent of power** <term>tīvratara-śaktipāta|A powerful influx of divine grace that can cause immediate liberation</term>. This is because that descent of power is the cause (or prerequisite) for the initiation itself; therefore, its inclusion is already established by the mention of initiation. In this system, there is no cause for liberation other than initiation. As it has been said:

> 'Therefore, from that extensive bond which blocks the supreme state, initiation alone liberates the soul upward and leads it to the **Abode of Shiva**.' <note>original: 'śaivaṃ dhāma' — the state of ultimate reality and peace</note>

# The Light of the Tantras
## Verse 44 | First Chapter

->८१<-

In cases such as the **most intense descent of power** <term>tīvratara-śaktipāta|A swift and powerful influx of divine grace that requires little to no human effort</term>, initiation might occur through the **process of "no-means"** <term>anupāya|The highest stage of realization in Trika philosophy where liberation is achieved almost instantly without ritual</term> and its related sequences. Through this, one achieves **liberation** <term>apavarga|The final release from the cycle of birth and death</term> at that very moment. As it has been said:

> ‘Through that connection, some are liberated in that very moment.’ <note>original: "tat-saṃbandhāt tataḥ kaścit tat-kṣaṇād apavṛjyate"</note>

One should not imagine that this [instant liberation] occurs without any regard for initiation at all; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the **scriptures** <note>original: "śruti-virodha"</note>. 

> ‘For him, even without initiation, through the **ripening of self-refinement** <gloss>ātma-saṃskāra-pariṇāmataḥ</gloss>, perfect knowledge established in all scriptures shall arise.’

In passages such as this, the negation [of initiation] is intended to refer specifically to **external ritual initiation** <term>bāhya-kriyā-dīkṣā|The formal ceremony involving physical tools, fire, or mantras</term>. Otherwise, how could the meaning of the phrase "self-refinement" even be coherent? But enough on this matter.

Now, an objection may be raised: "If liberation only occurs at the end of the physical body's life through initiation, how can it be said that ‘he is liberated while yet living’ and so on?" Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->But when, by **intellectual knowledge**,<-
->the expansion of **intellectual ignorance**<-
->is dissolved, then **liberation-while-living**<-
->is held in the palm of one's hand. ॥ ४४ ॥<-

# The Light of the Tantras
## Chapter 1, Commentary on Verse 44

->८२<-

“By **intellectual knowledge**” <term>bauddha-jñāna|Knowledge residing in the intellect (buddhi), gained through study and reasoning, rather than direct spiritual intuition</term> refers to that knowledge which arises from hearing the non-dual scriptures of the **Supreme Lord** <note>original: "parameśvara-advaya-śāstra"</note>. As it has been said:

> ‘When the oral tradition is revealed by the **Guru** <term>guru|A spiritual teacher who transmits wisdom and power</term> at the proper time, from that moment on, the seeker is liberated; the body remains merely like a mechanical frame.’ <note>original: "guruṇaiva yadā kāle sampradāyo nirūpitaḥ..."</note>

This should be understood as applying specifically to the eligibility of those who have been **initiated** <note>original: "dīkṣitādhikāreṇa"</note>. Indeed, for one who has not received initiation, there is no eligibility even for hearing the scriptures; how then could the manifestation of knowledge, which is caused by understanding those scriptures, even occur? As it has been stated:

> ‘One should not recite the **Path of Shiva** <term>Śiva-paddhati|A ritual or philosophical guidebook of the Shaiva tradition</term> in the presence of the uninitiated.’

Furthermore, it has already been stated that this intellectual knowledge accomplishes nothing for a person whose **innate spiritual ignorance** <term>pauruṣa-ajñāna|The deep-seated, "human" ignorance that binds the soul to the cycle of rebirth, which can only be removed by divine grace or initiation</term> has not been destroyed. If this were not the case, thinking people would have no reason to pursue initiation at all—since the goal of their efforts would lack a necessary cause. For this reason, one must not speak of initiation with a lack of conviction or indifference; it is the fundamental root cause of **liberation** <term>mukti|Release from the cycle of suffering and rebirth</term>.

Thus, although the **innate spiritual knowledge** <term>pauṃsna-jñāna|The realization of one's true nature as the Self, initiated by divine grace</term> prompted by initiation is moving toward expression, it does not grant liberation at that very moment—for it is stated that its full manifestation occurs only when the physical body ceases to exist. However, *this* [intellectual realization] occurs at that very moment; hence, its primary importance is highlighted here.

---

<summary>This page explains that while formal initiation (dīkṣā) is the essential root of liberation, intellectual knowledge gained from scriptures and a Guru is what allows a seeker to experience liberation even while still in a physical body. It maintains that spiritual study is only valid and effective for those who have first been initiated into the tradition.</summary>

# The Light of the Tantras
## Verse 45 | Chapter 1

->८३<-

It is not only for this reason that intellectual knowledge holds primacy; there is another reason as well, as the author states:

->**Even initiation is preceded by**<-
->**intellectual knowledge; truly, it is liberating.**<-
->**Therefore, even in that ritual, intellectual**<-
->**knowledge holds the position of primacy. (45)**<-

In this context, there is a traditional saying:

> ‘Even if he is devoid of all other outward signs, one who possesses knowledge is the best of **Gurus** <term>guru|A spiritual teacher who transmits wisdom and power</term>.’

Based on such statements, it is clear that only a Guru who has fully grasped the meaning of the **scriptures** <term>śāstra-artha|The profound philosophical and practical intent of the sacred texts</term> has the authority to perform **initiation** <term>dīkṣā|The ritual process of spiritual awakening and purification that removes the soul's primary ignorance</term>. For this very reason, the primary characteristic of a Guru is stated as follows:

> ‘He must be one who knows the ordinances of the **Shaiva Scriptures** <note>original: "śiva-śāstra-vidhāna-jña"</note> and is skilled in both spiritual knowledge and the objects of that knowledge.’

If it were otherwise, then:

> ‘Success shall not be attained through an initiation performed by one who is devoid of scriptural knowledge, O one worshipped by heroes!’

According to such statements, an initiation would not even be **liberating** <note>original: "vimocikā"</note> without that knowledge. Therefore, because intellectual knowledge is a necessary cause for the performance of initiation, the ritual itself could not be successfully completed without it. (45)

And this is not merely our own invention, as he says:

<note>Kheṭapāla was an early commentator on the Shaiva Siddhanta scriptures. Abhinavagupta cites him here to show that even in the dualist traditions, the primacy of knowledge was recognized.</note>

As it is stated in the **venerable *Svāyambhuva Tantra***:

> "Now, for the sake of liberation from the bonds known as **impurity** <term>mala|The innate spiritual "stain" or limitation that obscures the soul's true nature</term>, **illusion** <term>māyā|The material cause of the universe that provides the soul with a body and environment</term>, and **action** <term>karma|The chain of cause and effect resulting from past deeds</term>, and for the manifestation of **Shiva-nature** <note>original: "śivatvasya"</note>, the **Wisdom of Shiva** <note>original: "śiva-jñāna"</note> begins to operate."

**And further:**

> "Now, beginningless impurity is declared to be the **animal-hood** <term>paśutva|The state of being a 'pasu' or bound soul, lacking spiritual sovereignty</term> of souls. Due to the presence of that impurity, the **flood of bonds** <note>original: "pāśaugha"</note>—beginning with ignorance—is known to affect the individual. Therefore, one desiring undying liberation must understand this according to its true essence."

**Also in the venerable *Ruru Tantra*:**

> "Those who are skilled in the essence of **mantras** <term>mantra|Sacred sounds or formulas used in ritual and meditation</term>, whose doubts have been severed by an initiation permitted by the **tradition of the Guru** <note>original: "guru-tantra-ādi"</note>, perform worship through various sacrifices."

**And:**

> "Mantras are not to be debated or questioned by men of small intellect. Wise men should place their faith in them, accepting the **revealed scripture** <term>āgama|The authoritative sacred texts of the Shaiva tradition</term> as the standard of truth."

# The Light of the Tantras
## Verse 46–47 | Chapter 1

->८६<-

> "...[personal] knowledge, having properly arisen, makes a distinction between what is essential and what is not." <note>This quote concludes the citation from the previous page, likely from the Cillācakreśvarīmata</note>

**Initiation** <term>dīkṣā|The formal ritual process of spiritual awakening and the removal of karmic bonds</term> is not effective in manifesting **personal knowledge** <term>pauruṣa-jñāna|The innate, non-conceptual realization of one's own divinity</term> until the seeker has first acquired **intellectual knowledge** <term>bauddha-jñāna|The conceptual understanding of reality gained through study and reflection</term>. Because of this, intellectual knowledge is said to be even more primary than initiation itself. **|| 46 ||**

Furthermore, how could even this intellectual knowledge arise without the **scripture** <term>śāstra|Sacred texts, specifically the Shaiva Tantras, viewed as the breath or command of the Divine</term> of the Supreme Lord? Since scripture is the root cause, it is the primary factor here. As it is said:

->For the attainment of intellectual knowledge,<-
->characterized by that specific kind of resolve,<-
->scripture alone is primary,<-
->as it reveals the true nature of reality.<-
**|| 47 ||**

The word "attainment" means "in order to generate it." Because the "reality" of any "knowable" object—whether it be an external color like blue or an internal feeling like pleasure—is ultimately the **nature of Shiva** <note>original: "śiva-svabhāvatvaṃ"</note>, who is the essence of pure **Light** <term>prakāśa|The fundamental light of consciousness that allows all things to be known</term>. These objects could not exist or be perceived otherwise than as manifestations of this Light. 

The scripture is the "revealer" of this truth because it expresses and provides instruction on the **supreme non-duality** <note>original: "parādvaya"</note>. For this very reason, the text also hints at how these sacred teachings are distinct from other, lesser scriptures which fail to reveal this ultimate reality. **|| 47 ||**

# The Light of the Tantras
## Chapter 1: The Nature of Knowledge

->८७<-

One might ask: "Let it be as you say. But what is the reason that upon the removal of **personal ignorance** <term>pauruṣa-ajñāna|The deep, innate 'stain' or limitation on the soul that prevents it from experiencing its own infinite power</term>, liberation occurs only at the end of the physical body's life, whereas upon the removal of **intellectual ignorance** <term>bauddha-ajñāna|The conceptual errors and false beliefs held by the mind</term>, liberation is achieved immediately?" Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->Even when the internal, personal ignorance<-
->has been dissolved through initiation,<-
->because the ignorance residing in the intellect remains,<-
->dualistic thought-constructions may still occur.<-
**|| 48 ||**

The phrase "residing in the intellect" refers to ignorance. **Dualistic thought-construction** <term>vikalpa|The mental habit of categorizing reality into opposites, such as 'I' and 'Other'</term> consists of the manifestation of difference. It has been stated many times that this very thing is "ignorance," because it takes the form of **non-recognition** <term>akhyāti|The failure to perceive the true, non-dual nature of reality</term>. **|| 48 ||**

But one might then ask: "If intellectual ignorance is not removed, what impact does that have on the Self?" <note>The questioner is asking why a purified soul would still be affected by a messy mind.</note> In response, he says:

->Because the sense of self remains tied to the intellect<-
->for as long as the body exists,<-
->liberation would not [fully] manifest even at the end of the body<-
->merely through the destruction of personal ignorance.<-
**|| 49 ||**

While the previous page explained that dualistic thoughts (vikalpa) persist due to intellectual ignorance even after initiation, this page clarifies why liberation for most occurs only at death, and how "living liberation" (jīvanmukti) is possible for those who also clear their intellectual misconceptions.</meta>

# The Light of the Tantras
## Chapter 1: The Nature of Knowledge

->८८<-
->The Light of the Tantras<-

For even an initiated person <note>original: "dīkṣitasyāpi"</note>, there remains a persistent identification of the Self with the intellect for a set duration <note>specifically, the duration of the current body's lifespan</note>. Because of the lack of distinction between these two (the Self and the intellect), **intellectual ignorance** <term>bauddha-ajñāna|Conceptual errors and false beliefs held by the mind</term> can be said to accumulate upon the Self. This is the underlying meaning. 

Therefore, it is only at the end of the physical body's life—when the identification of the Self with the intellect finally ceases—that liberation occurs. Since **personal ignorance** <term>pauruṣa-ajñāna|The deep, innate limitation of the soul</term> was already destroyed previously through **initiation** <term>dīkṣā|The ritual process of spiritual awakening and purification</term> and other rites, the soul’s true nature is revealed. Thus it has been correctly stated: "At the end of that body, that knowledge is clearly manifested." **|| 49 ||**

In this context, **dualistic thought-construction** <term>vikalpa|The mental habit of perceiving reality in fragments or opposites</term> acts as an obstacle to immediate liberation. Thus, liberation does not occur at the same moment as initiation. However, when such dualistic thought is no longer possible, liberation is achieved even while the body remains. He states:

> ->But upon the cessation of intellectual ignorance,<-
> ->because dualistic thought is surely uprooted,<-
> ->liberation occurs at that very moment; thus it was<-
> ->said by the Creator in the glorious Nishatana.<- <note>original: "Niśāṭana", refers to the Niśāṭana Tantra, an authoritative scripture in the Trika tradition.</note> **|| 50 ||**

To show that this is not a baseless claim, he uses the phrase "thus it was said," indicating scriptural authority. **|| 50 ||**

> ->One whose mind is joined with dualistic thought<-
> ->attains the state of Shiva upon the fall of the body.<-
> ->The other attains it right then—this is the<-
> ->primary teaching of the scripture in this matter.<- **|| 51 ||**

---

<margin>Line 5, Manuscript 'Ka' reads: "Then at the end of the body."</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that while ritual initiation removes innate ignorance, conceptual ignorance in the mind often delays full liberation until death. However, if a seeker uproots dualistic thinking through intellectual clarity, they achieve "living liberation" (jīvanmukti) instantly.</summary>

### Verse 52 ] The First Chapter

"The other" refers to the **thought-free state** <term>nirvikalpa|A state of consciousness devoid of mental constructs or dualities</term>. "At that very time" means "while the physical body is still present." As it is stated in that same scripture:

> "One whose mind is joined with **dualistic thoughts** <term>vikalpa|The mental habit of perceiving reality in fragments or opposites</term> shall attain the state of Shiva only upon the falling of the body. But one whose mind is free of such thoughts, who perceives the Self as the eternal, unchanging Shiva through purity of being, is a **living-liberated soul** <term>jīvanmukta|One who has achieved spiritual liberation while still physically alive</term>, of this there is no doubt."

Now, he concludes the discussion on the primacy of the Scripture <note>original: "shastra"</note>, which was promised at the beginning, by saying "Thus," and so on. The word "Thus" <note>original: "iti"</note> should be applied according to the **Crow’s Eye Maxim** <note>original: "kākākṣi-nyāya"; a logical rule where a single word acts like a crow's eye, which was thought to shift between two sockets, looking at two things at once</note>. By this, it should be interpreted as referring both to the conclusion of the *Shri Nishatana* text and to the reason for what has been established. This was also mentioned earlier with the phrase "revealer of the reality to be known," and so on. **|| 51 ||**

Now, one might ask: "What exactly is the 'reality of the known' <note>original: "jñeyasya tattvam"</note> which, when shown, demonstrates the supreme importance of the Scripture?" Anticipating this, he says:

-> The supreme reality of all that is known <-
-> is Shiva, whose very nature is Light. <-
-> For that which lacks the nature of light <-
-> can have neither manifestation nor even existence. || 52 ||

### Page 90

->**Shri Tantraloka**<-

Regarding the "object of knowledge" <note>original: "jñeyasya"</note>—such as a blue object—its very "blueness," which is its state of being manifest, is not an inherent property of the object itself. If that were the case, it would be manifest to everyone at all times; it would not be the case that it appears only at certain times to certain people. If it were inherent, everyone would be omniscient. 

Therefore, when one thinks "this appears" or "this appears to me," that appearance is only logical if it is connected to the **Subject** <term>pramatṛ|The conscious observer or "knower"</term> whose very nature is **Light** <term>prakāśa|The fundamental radiance of consciousness that allows anything to be known</term>. Thus, objects like "blue" do not possess a self-contained nature that exists independently. **Shiva** alone is the Subject, the nature of Light itself. Anything other than Him is invalidated by the false dilemmas of **difference and non-difference** <term>bhedābheda-vikalpa|The logical struggle to define whether an object is the same as or different from its perception</term>. 

Consequently, because objects like "blue" are only known through their manifestation in consciousness, He alone is the ultimate reality. This is why it is said: "Shiva, the nature of Light, is the Supreme Reality."

Now, one might raise an objection: "Even if the object is not inherently made of light, perhaps it becomes so through a *connection* with Light?" Anticipating this, the author says, "Not indeed," and so on. Even if a blue object is manifest through a connection with Light, it can only shine if it is itself essentially of the nature of Light. It is impossible for something to be **devoid of light** <note>original: "aprakāśa-rūpa"</note> and yet still be manifest. A palace that is not white cannot appear white. <margin>A variant reading in manuscript 'ka' suggests 'blue, pleasure, etc.' instead of just 'blue' in the first line.</margin> Furthermore, without this nature of Light, the object would not even possess "thing-ness" or existence. No object is possible if it abandons the nature of Light. This is the intended meaning. **|| 52 ||**

<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation from Page 91. Having established that both existence and non-existence are forms of Shiva's consciousness, Abhinavagupta now addresses the epistemological question: how do we prove the existence of this universal "Light" of consciousness? He concludes that Light is self-evident and beyond the need for proof.</meta>

### Page 92

# The Radiance of the Tantras

### [First Daily Lesson]

->**That which is called Light** <term>prakāśa|The fundamental radiance of consciousness that makes all experience possible</term><-
->**shines everywhere and in all things.**<-
->**Because it can never be denied,**<-
->**what use is there for postulating proofs for it?** || 54 ||<-

A **means of knowledge** <term>pramāṇa|A valid method of proof, such as perception or inference</term> is generally understood to have as its object something that was previously unknown. As the authorities on logic have said:

> "A means of knowledge concerns an unapprehended subject, or it is the illumination of a previously unknown thing." <note>original: "anadhigata-viṣayaṃ pramāṇam ajñātārtha-prakāśo vā"</note>

In the case of **Light** <note>here meaning the Light of Consciousness</note>, it can never be "previously unknown" because it is perpetually manifest. Since it is **undeniable** <term>anapahnavanīya|That which cannot be hidden, concealed, or refuted</term>, any attempt to establish a proof for it is useless.

To explain further: Light could only be manifest as something "previously unknown" if it had first existed in a state of being unapprehended or not shining. Such a state [where consciousness does not shine] could only be confirmed if there were a **memory** <term>smṛti|The mental faculty of recalling past experiences</term> of a prior time that was devoid of that Light. 

However, a memory cannot arise without a corresponding **experience** <term>anubhava|Direct perception or lived experience</term>, because the nature of memory is the "retention of a previously experienced object." There is no such thing as an experience of a prior time that is devoid of Light, for the very nature of "experience" is Light itself. Indeed, it is that very Light that constitutes experience.

# The Holy Tantraloka

### Page 94

Indeed, if in its own self blue were yellow, or yellow were blue, what contradiction would not arise? If one were to argue: "Whatever shines is established in its own self exactly as it shines; therefore, blue is not yellow and yellow is not blue"—then, in that case, no distinct quality would be attributed to their own individual natures, other than the fact that they "shine." 

Thus, it is **Light** <term>prakāśa|The fundamental, self-luminous consciousness that illuminates all things</term> itself that constitutes their true form. Because this Light is the ground for the establishment of each object’s fixed identity, it "extends their life" <note>original: "jīvitaṃ vitanuyāt"</note>, enabling us to prove that "this is blue" and "this is yellow." 

Furthermore, when this Light takes on the specific coloring of an object like blue, it comes to be designated by the term **means of knowledge** <term>pramāṇa|A valid instrument of cognition or proof</term>. 

There is no need for anything else to establish the existence of this Light, because it is the very nature of Light to illuminate both itself and others. Even so, this Light—despite being as described—would not be the firm foundation for the manifestation of either the object or the self if it were devoid of **Reflective Awareness** <term>vimarśa|The dynamic, self-aware capacity of consciousness to recognize itself</term>. 

For "Light" alone <note>mere luminosity without self-recognition</note> cannot be that which establishes the existence of itself or others. If it could, then even a blue object would be self-established simply by being blue. Therefore, the capacity to illuminate self and others...

<margin>Line 5, Manuscript Kha: "but light" <note>original: "api tu prakāśa iti pāṭhaḥ"</note></margin>
<margin>Line 16, Manuscript Kha: "in the self-establishment of self-illumination" <note>original: "svaprakāśātmasiddhāviti pāṭhaḥ"</note></margin>

प्रथमाह्निकम् ।

For the establishment of even that [Light], **Reflective Awareness** <term>ahampāramarśa|The dynamic, self-recognizing "I-reflection" of consciousness</term> must be accepted as its soul and its very life-force—for it is by this awareness that everything is established. As it has been said:

-> "The resting of Light within its own self is indeed proclaimed as the **I-feeling**." <-
<note>original: "prakāśasyātma-viśrāntir-ahambhāvo hi kīrtitaḥ"</note>

And that very nature of the supreme Light is the Supreme Lord Shiva. As it was stated [previously]: "He is the supreme life-force even of those [individual subjects]; He is the Supreme Lord." (Verse 55)

Because the Lord is self-established in this and other ways, not only is a proving **means of knowledge** <term>pramāṇa|A formal proof or instrument of valid cognition</term> irrelevant, but even a refuting argument is ineffective. Thus he says:

-> Even for one whose nature is <-
-> the habit of denying everything, <-
-> the truth that "knowledge is for the sake of the self" <-
-> does not appear to me as "not so." <-
(Verse 56)

"Of all"—meaning subjects, the act of knowing, and objects—"denial" refers to their rejection or negation. One whose "habit" <note>original: "hevāka" | a persistent tendency or addiction</note> or "nature" is such a denial is the **Buddhist** <term>Bauddha|A follower of Buddhist philosophy, characterized here by the doctrine of "no-self"</term>. 

Among them, the **Madhyamikas** <term>Mādhyamika|The "Middle Way" school of Mahayana Buddhism, which uses dialectical negation to show the emptiness of all concepts</term> are those who argue for the non-existence of all three (knower, knowing, and known). The **Yogācāras** <term>Yogācāra|The "Mind-Only" school, which denies external objects but accepts the reality of consciousness</term> are those who argue for the non-existence of both the subject and the object. The **Vaibhāṣikas** <term>Vaibhāṣika|An early Buddhist school that accepts the existence of external objects but denies a permanent, underlying self</term> are those who argue for the non-existence of a [permanent] subject. 

Even such a person [the Buddhist], despite their habit of denial, finds that the statement "Knowledge is for the sake of the self" does not appear to me—the conscious subject—as... <meta>Note: This sentence continues on the next page.</meta>

"Of all things"—meaning those whose nature consists of the **knower, the act of knowing, and the object known** <note>original: "jñātṛ-jñāna-jñeya"</note>. --- Page 107 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from Page 96 regarding the self-evident nature of the conscious subject (the Knower). Abhinavagupta is explaining why formal logical proofs (pramāṇas) cannot be used to "prove" the existence of the subject, as the subject is the one who employs those very proofs.</meta>

### Page 97

[...and it is so.] Nor is such the nature of the **Knower** <term>pramātṛ|The conscious subject or the "I" who experiences</term> that he could be delimited by a **means of knowledge** <term>pramāṇa|A formal proof, like perception or inference</term>. For when he is engaged in the determination of objects and so forth, because he is **self-luminous** <term>svaprakāśa|Self-shining; that which is known by its own light without needing an external lamp</term> by nature, he is not separate from the Light of Consciousness. 

Nor can he be grasped through "this-ness" <note>original: "idantā"</note>—that is, as an external object—because his essence consists of the reflexive awareness of "I" <note>original: "ahaṁ-pratyavamarśa"</note>. If he were to be an object of a means of knowledge, then in that act of knowing, there would have to be another knower, and in that case yet another, resulting in an **infinite regress** <term>anavasthā|A logical fallacy where one explanation requires another ad infinitum, never reaching a foundation</term>. Therefore, there is no logical justification for the operation of a formal proof in this matter. 

As for certain spiritual instructions on meditation that say, "This Self, the Knower, is eternally manifest," where the Self is referred to with the word "This" <note>indicating an object</note>, that is not the literal reality. In those instances, the Self is not directly perceived as an object; rather, it is perceived through the mediation of "I-ness." Let us leave this for now, as this point will be expanded upon at every step of this work. The fact that formal proofs are inapplicable to the subject has already been established and shown just a moment ago; thus, it is not elaborated upon further. (Verse 58)

-> Not only is there logic for this, but Scripture says so as well: <-

## Therefore, in the Kamika Tantra, it is said 
## that [the Self] is beyond the reach of logical arguments.

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that the Knower (the subject) cannot be proven by external logic because he is the self-luminous foundation of all proof, and attempting to treat the "I" as a "this" leads to a logical infinite regress. ## The universe, the physical form, the light,

**The universe** <term>bhuvana|The various planes of existence or 'worlds' that make up the cosmos</term> refers to that which is to be presided over within those various worlds; it is the foundation for all experience.

->“Having the shape of a globe of Kadamba flowers,<-

**The void** <term>kha|Literally 'sky' or 'ether', used here for the spiritual Void</term> refers to the **Void** <term>śūnya</term>—which is characterized by the subtle levels of **Energy**, **Pervasiveness**, and **Equanimity** <note>original: "śakti, vyāpinī, samana," which are progressive stages of consciousness in the ascent toward the absolute</note>.

**Sound** <term>śabda</term> has the nature of the **Resonance** <term>nāda|The subtle, internal vibration or 'unstruck sound' that precedes physical sound</term>.

**Mantra** consists of the nature of the letters **A**, **U**, and **M** <note>the components of the sacred syllable 'Om'</note>. 

The qualifier for these is: **distinguished by the Point, the Resonance, and so forth.** As it has been said:

> “The practitioner should meditate on Shiva as the soul of these six substances—the Point, the Resonance, the Void, the Mantra, the Universe, and the Form—according to the different fruits they wish to achieve.”

# The Illustrious Tantraloka

The phrase **"established in [unconditionedness]"** and so on is explained as follows: **"In the dissolution of limitations"** refers to the dissolution of those factors—such as the various Worlds <term>bhuvana|The physical and subtle levels of existence</term>—which cause **Contraction** <term>saṃkoca|The process by which infinite consciousness limits itself to become an individual</term>. This signifies the state of **Transcendence** <term>viśvottīrṇatā|The aspect of the Divine that remains beyond and untouched by the created universe</term>.

The intention here is to show that even while the Lord possesses a **Universal Nature** <term>viśvamayatva|The state of being composed of the entire universe</term>, He does not fall away or deviate from His own essential nature. 

**[Objection:]** One might argue that if the Lord is understood to have a fixed nature in both these ways (as both the universe and beyond it), then He is still being defined by a **Limitation** <term>avaccheda|A boundary, definition, or conceptual limit</term>. 

To answer this doubt, the author says: **"established in the unconditioned state."** Because even though He is the universe, He is fundamentally rooted in a state of **Unconditionedness** <term>anavacchinnatā|The state of being without boundaries or limits</term> due to His transcendence. It is the one **Independent Awareness** <term>svatantra-bodha|The primal, self-governing consciousness that is the source of all things</term> that flashes forth in all these various forms. ||65||

### [ Verse 66 ] First Daily Lesson

...even though it appears as something distinct, it is **not separate from the mirror itself**. If it were otherwise, the mirror and the reflected object <note>original: "ghata" (pot); a standard example in Indian philosophy for any physical object</note> would be perceived as entirely separate and detached from one another. In the very same way, this entire universe—consisting of both moving and unmoving beings—is manifested by **Shiva**, whose nature is **Pure Light** <term>prakāśa|The fundamental, self-shining consciousness that allows all things to be known</term>. This manifestation occurs through His own **Will** <term>svatantrya-shakti|The absolute freedom of the Divine to act and create</term>, appearing as if it were outside His own nature. However, because it is pervaded by Him, and because its manifestation would be impossible under any other condition, the universe is embraced as being **inseparable from His own essential nature**. 

Therefore, even while He is **Identical with the Universe** <term>viśvamaya|The immanent aspect of God as the fabric of all things</term>, He is **Transcendent to the Universe** <term>viśvottīrṇa|The aspect of God that remains beyond all categories of time, space, and form</term>. And even in His transcendence, He remains identical with the universe. In this way, there is no logical flaw in either description. 

For this very reason, it has been said: **"He is all-formed, yet formless."**
*   **"All-formed"** means He is identical with the universe.
*   **"Formless"** means He is transcendent to the universe.

By repeating this truth, we see that even while He is the essence of all categories, He remains beyond them. Thus, it is this one Supreme Lord alone, whose nature is Light, who expands and unfolds in all directions. Therefore, the **Non-duality of the Lord** <term>īśvarādvaya|The philosophical realization that there is no division between the Creator, the creation, and the individual soul</term> is the only ultimate reality. || 66 ||

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the non-dual nature of Shiva. Having established that the universe is inseparable from the Divine Light (Prakāśa) in the previous section, the text now addresses a potential logical objection: if we describe God using various attributes like "omnipresence" or "eternity," does this not introduce a plurality that contradicts the core principle of oneness?</meta>

# The Auspicious Light of the Tantras

Let us let the matter stand that the Lord is essentially one, consisting of **Pure Light** <term>prakāśātmaka|A nature defined by self-shining consciousness</term>. 

However, a question arises regarding the group of attributes such as **Omnipresence** <term>vibhutva|The quality of being all-pervading</term> that have been predicated of Him. Given that the distinction between an attribute and the possessor of that attribute—as well as the distinctions between the attributes themselves—is undeniable, how can this manifested duality be avoided? How can the doctrine of **Non-Duality** <term>advaya-vāda|The philosophical position that reality is a single, undivided whole</term> be maintained if the Lord is seen as a collection of different qualities? 

To address this doubt, the author says:

->**Nor is His attribute, such as omnipresence,**<-
->**different from Him or from one another.**<-

This attribute of **Omnipresence** is not something distinct from His essential nature, nor is it some quality that adds an external excellence to Him. Rather, it is His very essence. 

To explain: **Omnipresence** is defined as "pervasiveness." Normally, pervasiveness would require something else to be pervaded <note>In standard logic, a pervader requires a space or an object to fill</note>. However, apart from the **Supreme Light**, nothing else—such as the directions or space—could possibly exist. Therefore, what exactly would He "pervade"? <note>The argument here is that since God is everything, He doesn't "fill" the universe like water fills a cup; rather, He IS the space and the substance itself.</note>

**Eternity** <term>nityatva|The state of being outside of or lasting through time</term> is also not an "attribute" of His in the conventional sense. Conventionally, eternity refers to a form that persists through the three divisions of time <note>Past, present, and future</note>. But the Lord is **untouched by time** <term>akāla-kalita|Beyond the measuring or dividing influence of temporal sequences</term>. # Verse 71 ] First Chapter #

Because [these powers] possess the nature of being essentially one, they are unable to split the nature of one another. # The Venerable Tantraloka #

### ->...In the mirror of the Subject, which is one's own consciousness,<- ###
### ->through Freedom in meditation and other practices. [73]<- ###

**Shiva** <note>The supreme consciousness in this tradition</note> is the established **Subject** <term>Pramātā: The conscious knower or perceiving self</term> who identifies with the intellect and other limited faculties. His defining characteristic is His own "contracted" consciousness. Because of His absolute clarity, He is capable of receiving reflections, and thus He is like a **mirror** <note>original: makura</note>. 

Within that mirror—through His own **Freedom** <term>Svātantrya: The absolute, independent power of the Divine Will</term> and through practices such as meditation or receiving spiritual instruction—He appears to have attained the state of an **Object** <term>Prameyatā: The condition of being an object of knowledge or perception</term>. This occurs through a constructed sense of difference, such as the distinction between the one who meditates and the deity being meditated upon. 

However, even when appearing as an object, He does not actually become something separate, because He remains essentially one with the Subject. As the text states, He is one **"whose glory is never lost"** <note>original: alupta-vibhava</note>, which means He never abandons His fundamental nature as the Knower. As it has been said:

> "Through His freedom, the Lord creates Himself as twofold. Through resolves such as the 'Will of the Ruler' and so forth, He manifests Himself in meditation and other practices for the sake of worldly interaction." <note>original: *Īśvarapratyabhijñā-kārikā* 1.5.16; a foundational text of the Recognition School</note>

[73]

**He now concludes this very point:**

### ->Therefore, through whichever aspect He appears,<- ###
### ->even though He is partless, He is experienced in that way.<- ###

# Verse 74 ] The First Chapter #

### ->Power is indeed the ultimate reality;<- ###
### ->the sequence between Power and its Possessor is clear. [74]<- ###

Therefore, because it is logical that both **Shiva** <note>The supreme consciousness</note> and **Shakti** <note>His divine energy or power</note> appear through a distinction that has been intentionally created, the following is true: 

Even though Shiva is partless—since His nature is solely **Pure Light** <term>Prakāśamātra: The fundamental, self-shining consciousness that requires no other source to be known</term>—He nonetheless appears in practices like **creative contemplation** <term>Bhāvanā: A refined state of meditation where the practitioner "becomes" the object of focus</term> through a "face" or an aspect. This aspect is characterized by specific parts, such as the various worlds and levels of existence. 

Regarding that "face," it has been stated in the scriptures:

> "...Shakti is said here to be the face of Shiva."

According to this and similar teachings, it is **Power** <note>original: Śakti</note> alone that serves as the **Means** <term>Upāya: The method or instrument used to reach a goal</term> for attaining Shiva. Indeed, in the process of realizing Him, no other means exists, nor is any other possible. 

Consequently, the "sequence"—which consists of the relationship between the **Means** <note>Shakti</note> and the **Goal** <term>Upeya: The final end or objective to be reached, here referring to Shaktiman/Shiva</term>—is perfectly clear and well-established. There is no room for doubt in this matter. This is the meaning of the verse. [74]

And so, this relationship of Means and Goal between these two is proclaimed throughout various **scriptures** <term>Āgama: The sacred revealed texts of the Tantric tradition</term>, as the author now explains:

# Verse 75 ] The First Chapter #

### ->And in the venerable *Kiraṇa Tantra*,<- ###
### ->following a sequence of questions and answers:<- ###
### ->"Direct experience is a mental construct;<- ###
### ->yet the mind does not exist in Shiva." [75]<- ###

### ->This serves as the answer to the question:<- ###
### ->"How can initiation occur without first knowing Shiva?"<- ###

The word "That" <note>Referring to the previous discussion</note> implies the conclusion of the sentence: that the Shaiva scriptures describe **Power** <term>Shakti: The dynamic, creative energy of the Divine</term> as the **Means** <term>Upāya: The method or instrument for spiritual realization</term>.

The author demonstrates this very point through the "meaning" aspect of the text—since scriptures operate in two ways, through both word and meaning—beginning with the phrase "Direct experience..." 

In that scripture, **Garuda** <note>In this context, Garuda is the disciple seeking wisdom from the Lord</note> asks:

> "How can the reality of Shiva be 'void'? If it is void, it is not within the range of the senses. Sensory perception is what we call direct knowledge; surely what lies beyond that is simply nothing."

Because it was asked whether the reality of Shiva is "nothing" due to it being beyond sensory perception, the Blessed Lord replied:

> "**Maya** <term>Māyā: Here referring to the limiting, material energy of the universe</term> is to be abandoned; Shiva is to be grasped; the 'grasper' or subject is known as the **Person** <term>Purusha: The individual soul or conscious subject</term>. Shiva is called 'void' only because He is empty of the attributes of Maya..."

Continuing with:

> "Even for a reality that is beyond the senses, is there not still a direct experience? # Verse 75 ] The First Chapter #

By the conclusion of the previous passage, it has been settled that although the **Reality of Shiva** <term>Shivatattva: The ultimate principle or essence of the Divine</term> is not perceptible by the external senses, it is an object of internal mental perception; therefore, it is indeed "something" <note>Meaning it is a positive existence rather than a "void" or "nothingness"</note> rather than nothing.

This point was raised again by **Garuda** <note>The disciple in this tantric dialogue</note> in the following way:

-> * <-

> "Experience arises from conceptual thought, and that thought is a function of the mind. That which is to be known is 'with-mind' <term>Samanaska: involving the activity of the mental faculties</term>, yet the Reality is 'beyond-mind' <term>Amanaska: a state of consciousness where the ordinary discursive mind is stilled</term>. 
>
> If the **Teacher** <term>Deshika: A spiritual guide or guru who points the way</term> does not know the Reality, how can he perform **Initiation** <term>Diksha: The ritual ceremony that bestows grace and removes spiritual bonds</term>? The object must be known in its entirety, yet He can never be fully known in that way."

This and other questions were asked. The author has condensed the meaning of these questions into his own words for the sake of brevity. Here is the meaning:

Just as hunger and other internal states are objects of mental perception <note>known as the "Analogy of Hunger" or *Bubhurksha-nyaya*</note>, the same has been said of the mental perception of Shiva. In that context, mental experience—

> "The mind here is the conceptualizer..."

***

<gloss>* "That" refers to mental conceptualization, which is "with-mind"; however, the Reality of Shiva is "beyond-mind." "The object" refers to the fact that initiation and other rituals proceed from this understanding.</gloss>

<margin>Line 10: Hunger and such, though not visible to the eyes or other external senses, come within the range of the mind; it is the same in this case.</margin>

# Sri Tantraloka #

According to this logic, because it is composed of formative intent <note>original: 'saṃkalpātmakatvāt'</note>, **conceptual thought** <term>Vikalpa: the discursive, labeling activity of the mind</term> has a nature that does not "touch" the actual object directly. Therefore, the mind is not a valid means of knowledge <term>Pramana: a reliable method or instrument of proof</term> regarding **Shiva**. 

Where no valid means of knowledge can function, that thing remains "unknown." If the **Reality of Shiva** <term>Shivatattva</term> remains unknown, how could **Initiation** <term>Diksha</term> occur? A **Teacher** <term>Daishika: one who points the way</term> must surely know the Supreme Reality in order to unite the candidate for initiation with that Reality. 

This is precisely why it is said: "Knowledge resides in the Guru." The word "thus" <note>iti</note> marks the end of the inquiry. In this context, "thus" refers to the question asked by **Garuda** <note>The student in this dialogue</note>. The "Answer" is the resolution provided by the **Lord** <note>Bhagavan, the divine source of the teaching</note>. [Verse 75]

He explains this very point:

-> The experience of hunger and such is certainly not <-
-> a mental conceptualization. [76] <-

The word "not" is placed out of its usual order in the verse; it should be applied to negate the premise of the question, as if saying, "This is not a valid question." The word "indeed" <note>hi</note> indicates the reason: because the mental experience of hunger and other such states is not merely a product of **conceptual thought** <term>Vikalpa</term>. For these states, there is first a non-conceptual mental perception...

...[it] is also an object of **perception** <term>Pratyaksha: direct immediate experience</term>; otherwise, the subsequent conceptual thought "I wish to eat" would never arise. There is no fault in these experiences being considered objects of **conceptual mental perception** <note>original: 'savikalpaka-manasa-pratyaksha'</note>, because such perception is accepted as a valid means of knowledge <term>Pramana</term> since it is grounded in an actual object. In this same way, **Shiva** also becomes an object of mental perception—however, the distinction is that this occurs through the gateway of **His Power** <term>Shakti</term>. As stated in the subsequent text of that very work:

->*<-

> "Where there is the experience of hunger and such, there **conceptual thought** <note>original: 'vikalpa'</note> does not exist. Even a conceptual thought based on a real object does not perceive that object as if it were a physical jar. This mental thought is subtle, having merged into the **power of the Void** <term>Shunya-shakti</term>. For the one who possesses that state, everything else is cut off; therefore, that state is free from the [ordinary] mind. Knowledge arises from the union of the Self and the senses; the Self is the actor, and the mind is the activity. **Shiva** is to be understood as the goal to be attained here—the All-pervading One who shares a single nature [with the seeker]."

Thus, as for the description of this state as "**the Void**" <term>Shunyatva</term>, it is used figuratively to describe the fading away of **Illusion** <term>Maya</term>. It is "Void" because it is empty of the characteristics of Illusion, such as the tendency to change or transform <note>original: 'parinamitva'</note>.

# Sri Tantraloka #

...as has been stated. By comparison to other [limited] things, it follows logically that this state is not "void" <note>original: 'ashunya'—meaning it is a full, positive reality rather than a vacuum</note> at all. Therefore, once the **spiritual teacher** <term>Daishika: the preceptor who provides direction</term> has known **Shiva** through the gateway of **His Power** <term>Shakti</term>, he unites the **initiate** <term>Dikshya</term> with that reality through **initiation** <term>Diksha</term>. Thus, there is no flaw in this argument. (76)

One might object: "An object is only truly 'known' when it is understood in its entirety, not just in part. However, **conceptual thought** <term>Vikalpa: the labeling mind</term> cannot know an object in its entirety because its nature is to focus only on specific, limited aspects. Therefore, even if Shiva is made an object of the mind through the gateway of His Power, He is still not truly known, because He cannot be fully grasped by that thought." Anticipating the rest of this question, the author says:

->Just as one knows a tree<-
->By its form, even without determining its taste;<-
->In that same way, conceptual thought knows Shiva<-
->Through the Primordial Sound and the Point. (77)<-

In this context, "conceptual thought" refers to the mental processing that follows an **immediate, non-conceptual awareness** <term>Nirvikalpaka: the raw, direct experience before words</term>. Through that <gloss>1. conceptual thought</gloss>, one perceives a tree—which is actually a composite of form, taste, and other qualities—only through its visual form and not through its taste, because that specific act of perception is restricted <gloss>3. to qualities like form or taste</gloss>. <note>Footnote 2 in the original clarifies that we know taste through the tongue and form through the eyes; we rarely experience every sense of an object simultaneously, yet we still say we "know" the object.</note>

### Verse 77 ] First Chapter ###

It is not reasonable to argue that because He is not grasped in His absolute totality, He is not grasped at all. Such a claim contradicts our direct experience. In the same way, the established doctrine is that **Shiva** is indeed known through the gateway of **Power** <term>Shakti</term>, which manifests as the **Primordial Sound** <term>Nada</term> and the **Point** <term>Bindu: the metaphysical drop or seed of creative energy</term>. This has been stated in that very same scripture:

> "Just as a tree is perceived through its visual form alone, even if its taste and other qualities are not grasped, so is the Lord, who is the **Power of Knowledge** <term>Jnana-shakti</term>. He is grasped in His essential reality <note>original: 'tattva-bhāvena'</note> by moving beyond the perception of Him as a mere physical object."

And also:

> "The **Point**, the **Sound**, and **Power** are conceptualized within the **Void** <note>original: 'shunyatve'—referring to the state of pure potentiality</note> for the purpose of providing a location for the mind to rest; once fixed there, the mind becomes eternally steady. Because of His extreme subtlety, He is beyond the reach of the senses. **Power** is subtle, and He resides within Her. She is regarded as the **Power of Knowledge**; through the knowledge of Her, He is truly known."

Thus, it is proven that **Power** alone is the supreme means for attaining the **Supreme Reality**. And as has already been stated, this Power manifests in infinite ways, such as in the form of the various worlds. (77)

Furthermore, whatever diversity exists in the universe—whether sentient or insentient—and whatever pertains to the cycles of creation or the states of consciousness <margin>Line 17, Manuscript K: the reading is 'the state of waking, etc.'</margin> such as waking, all of it is simply the **vibrant expansion of the Power** <term>Shakti-sphara</term> of the **Supreme Lord** <term>Parameshvara</term>. As the author says:

# The Light of the Tantras #
## Shri Tantraloka ##

A property of any object is of two kinds: that which provides its very life, and that which serves as the cause for its specific distinctions. The first is like "generality" <note>original: sāmānya</note>; for instance, without the quality of "cow-ness," a cow cannot truly be a cow. The second is like a "quality" <note>original: guṇa</note>; for example, a color such as white distinguishes an object that has already attained its existence. 

In this context, the **Self** [Atman] alone is the "life-giving" property of the entire assembly of principles <note>the 36 tattvas or levels of reality</note> because it constitutes their very nature. For this reason, it is said to be "undecaying" and "eternally inseparable." The word "for" <note>original: hi</note> in the text indicates the reason. If one asks what the proof for this is, it is stated: "This is the doctrine of the **Triśiromata**." (82)
<term>Triśiromata: "The Opinion of the Three-Headed," an important early Tantric scripture cited frequently by Abhinavagupta as an authority.</term>

The author now presents the text of that very scripture. Since the teaching proceeds in two ways—through the form of the word and the form of the meaning—he explains it in both ways:

->Located in the heart, located in all bodies,<-
->abiding in its own nature, and extremely subtle.<-
->The totality of the principles [tattvas]<-
->is proclaimed by the word "Village." (83)<-

"Totality" <note>original: sāmūhyam</note> simply means a collection. The word "**Village**" <note>original: grāma</note> functions here to signify a collection or group.

> "The nature of the entire village of principles which has been swallowed up..."

We see such usage in phrases like this. Furthermore, that [Self] is found everywhere—in the external world and in the body.

<header>Verse 86 ] Chapter One</header>

For one who is attentive <note>original: sāvadhāna</note>, a functional state arises in the Supreme Self, which is the ultimate goal, flooded with the nectar of Shiva. As it has been said:

> "In the knowledge of two objects, having recognized the middle, one should take refuge in it. By abandoning both simultaneously, the Reality shines forth in the center. When an object is abandoned and consciousness is restrained, it does not move toward another object; then, through that state of the 'middle,' the intense creative contemplation blossoms."

This "should be known" is to be applied according to the **Crow’s Eye Maxim** <term>kākākṣi-nyāya: a logic rule where a single word—like a crow's eye which was mythically thought to move between two sockets—serves two parts of a sentence</term>. By this, the "dwelling" or functional state should also be known as the state of the Seer, which takes the form of the direct realization of the ultimate reality. 

Furthermore, this state is **free from veiling** <term>vigata-āvṛtti</term>. "Free" means ceased or removed. "Veiling" refers to the external forms consisting of being, non-being, and so on. To put it simply: it is devoid of the limitations of external space and similar boundaries. Moreover, it is that whose "repetition" <note>original: āvṛtti; here playing on the word for veiling and the cycle of time</note>—which consists of the mental reckoning of time in its higher and lower forms—has vanished. It means **it is not grasped by Time** <term>akala-kalitam</term>. As it is said:

> "Time up to the sixteenth phase is 'lower'; the seventeenth is 'higher.' But that Time which is both higher and lower, O Beloved, is the eighteenth, the Lord. The Breath, having divided Time into these three parts, should then abandon it once more."

***

<insert>Line 1, Manuscript Ka: The reading is "having abandoned the object, in Supreme Shiva..."</insert>
<insert>Line 5, Manuscript Kha: The reading is "If, when the object is abandoned, consciousness is restrained..."</insert>

<summary>This page describes the "middle state" between thoughts where the nectar-filled Supreme Self is realized. It explains that this state is "free from veiling" because it transcends both external objects and the limitations of chronological time.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of "veiling" or "repetition" (āvṛtti) mentioned on the previous page. It specifically defines the "eleven steps" of the breath and sound that the practitioner must transcend to reach the state of unconditioned reality.</meta>

<page-num>128</page-num>

<header>Śrī Tantrāloka</header>

...and so on. Likewise, it is that whose **repetition consisting of the eleven steps** <term>pada-ekādaśaka-ātmikā āvṛtti: the sequence of eleven stages of sound and breath</term> has vanished. This means, in effect, that it is free from the specific forms of Brahma and the other deities <note>Each of the eleven stages of the breath is traditionally associated with a presiding deity (like Brahma, Vishnu, etc.); to transcend the stages is to move beyond these limited divine forms</note> who are restricted to those stages. As it has been said:

> "This 'eleven-stepped' sequence moves constantly in the breath: 
> The sound 'A', the sound 'U', the sound 'M', the **Point** <term>bindu</term>, 
> the **Half-moon** <term>ardhacandra</term>, the **Obstructor** <term>nirodhī</term>, 
> the **Resonance** <term>nāda</term>, the **End of Resonance** <term>nādānta</term>, 
> the **Power** <term>śakti</term>, the **Pervasive** <term>vyāpinī</term>, 
> and the **Leveling** <term>samanā</term> is remembered as the eleventh."

Because of this, the essential meaning <note>original: piṇḍārtha</note> is that this state becomes the direct realization of the ultimate reality. It takes the form of a Knower who is non-different from the **Beyond-Mind** <term>unmanā: the highest state of consciousness where mental movement ceases</term>. As it is said:

> "The state 'Beyond-Mind' transcends those [eleven]; what lies even beyond that is the Stainless Reality."

For this reason, there is that Reality <note>original: vastu</note> which is the supreme principle, characterized by **Great Being** <term>mahāsattā: universal existence or the 'Is-ness' of everything</term>. It is distinct from—and free from the limitations of—specific places, times, or forms. In that Reality, there is a pure consciousness consisting of the **Supreme I-Awareness** <term>parā-ahaṃ-parāmarśa: the absolute, non-egoic self-recognition of the Divine</term>, which is described consistently in all the sacred scriptures <term>āgamas</term>. One who becomes stainless through that awareness, and who has **shattered all bonds** <term>khilī-kṛta-nikhila-bandha</term> by attaining oneness with that Reality, [transcends] the inclinations of common worldly life:

> "Having attained the state of the Goddess <note>Bhairavī</note> from the God <note>Bhairava</note>..."

<header>Verse 85 ] Chapter One</header>

Because of such statements, our teacher has also said: "This is the statement of **Śrīkaṇṭha**" <note>Śrīkaṇṭha is an ancient name for Shiva, often referring here to a specific lost scripture or a revered lineage authority</note>. It is stated there as follows:

> "I shall now explain the fourth state, categorized by the distinction of the **Village-Law** <term>grāma-dharma: here used as a technical term for the soul's relationship with the components of the body</term>."

Beginning with that, the text continues:

> "That which resides in the heart, in the whole body, in one's own nature, and is extremely subtle—the **collective of the primary elements** <term>tattvas: the building blocks of reality</term> is what is meant by the word 'Village' <term>grāma</term>.
> The **Self** <term>ātman</term> is indeed what is called 'Law' <term>dharma</term>; thus the term 'Village-Law' <term>grāma-dharma</term> is proclaimed.
> It is **Knowledge** <term>jñāna</term> situated in the **Light of Consciousness** <term>prakāśa</term>, standing between being and non-being.
> Remaining in one's own place is known as 'abiding'; this abiding is called a **Function** <term>vṛtti</term>.
> This 'Function,' once one has known their own true state, is described as the **state of being the Seer** <term>draṣṭṛtva: the capacity to observe reality without being entangled by it</term>.
> One should recognize that state as fully Awakened, free from external coverings, released from the duality of 'higher and lower,' and **transcending the eleven steps** <note>original: ekādaśapadojjhitam; this refers back to the eleven stages of breath/sound mentioned on page 128</note>.
> That knowledge which exists within the Self, by the Self, is flooded with the **nectar of Shiva** <term>śivāmṛta</term>.
> It is stainless, characterized by pure consciousness, and described as the distinct Reality.
> This is called the 'Activity of the Village-Law,' and it is explained in every way in this Tantra."

And this very point is further stated:

> "Or rather, the practitioner who knows the supreme reality should desire Shiva..."

and

> "One should establish oneself in that reality, endowed with the radiance of the **Middle Power** <term>madhya-śakti: the central channel of energy, or Suṣumṇā</term>."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the "Village-Law" (grāmadharma), a practice of internalizing all sensory and elemental experiences into the Self. <page-num>130</page-num>

<header>The Light of the Sacred Tantras</header>

With the intention of incorporating the meaning of the previously cited text into a new work, the author connects it with his own words, stating: "Everything is accomplished for him." This means that for the practitioner of the **Village-Law** <term>grāmadharma-vṛtti: the practice of seeing the "village" of the body and world as the "law" of the Self</term>, everything—both external and internal—manifests intensely as identical with **Shiva** <note>The Supreme Reality or Pure Consciousness</note>. This is achieved by breaking the movement of the **incoming and outgoing breaths** <term>prāṇa and apāna</term> and entering the **Central Dwelling** <term>madhyadhāman: the suṣumṇā or central energetic channel of the body</term>, thereby attaining a state of "equal-tastedness" or union with the **Supreme Power** <term>para-śakti</term>. As it has been said:

> "When the mind is bound by the medicine of **contemplating Shiva** <term>śiva-bhāvanā</term> and then cast into the world of transmigration—even among objects like wood or walls—it turns them into the 'gold of Shiva,' just as base metals are turned to gold by an **elixir** <note>original: rasavat; referring to the alchemical process where mercury or a medicinal elixir transforms common metals into gold</note>."

|| 84 || 85 ||

->Therefore, he says:<-

->**Abandoning the upper, one should enter the lower,**<-
->**established in the sound *Rā*, abiding in the central region. || 86 ||**<-

Regarding the phrase **"the upper"**: because the **out-breath** <term>prāṇa</term> flows upward; **"the lower"**: because the **in-breath** <term>apāna</term> flows downward. **"Abandoning"** means breaking or halting their flow. In doing so, that practitioner of the "Village-Law" should essentially enter the **central channel** <term>madhyanāḍī</term>. And what is the nature of such a person? He is one **"abiding in the central region,"** meaning he stands in the very center of the central channel. There resides the **Power** <term>Śakti</term>, which has the delicate form of a **lotus fiber** <note>original: bisasūtrākārā śaktiḥ; a traditional metaphor for the extremely subtle, thread-like nature of the kundalini-energy within the central channel</note>.

<header>Verse 86 ] The First Daily Chapter [ 131</header>

**Space:** This refers to a specific region in the form of the **internal void** <term>antar-vyoma: the subtle, empty space within the heart or the central channel</term>. He "goes to it," which means he knows or realizes it.
**He who:** This refers to the practitioner who is "established in that," meaning they possess a state of one-pointed focus on that reality.
As it has been said:

->“By means of the Goddess, who takes the form of a **lotus fiber**<-
->residing in the **central channel** <term>madhya-nāḍī: the suṣumṇā</term>,<-
->and who is contemplated as the inner void, the God shines forth.”<-
<note>original: "madhya-nāḍī madhya-saṃstha-bisa-sūtrābha-rūpayā / dhyātāntar-vyomayā devyā tayā devaḥ prakāśate"</note>

For this reason, it is said that he is **established in Rā** <note>original: rāmasthaḥ; literally "standing in Rama," but here interpreted through the seed-syllable "Rā" and the root "ram" (to play)</note>.

->“...Alone, I do not take delight.”<-
<note>A reference to the Upanishadic motif where the Primordial Being desires a second for the sake of "play" or "delight" (ramaṇa)</note>

Based on such statements, the **Supreme Self** <term>paramātmā</term> is called **Rama** because He "delights" (*ramate*). That is, He plays by manifesting the vast diversity of the universe, consisting of both sentient and insentient beings. To be "established in Him" means to reside there, vibrating or manifesting as the very nature of that Reality. This is explained in the ***Tantra of the Three-Headed Bhairava*** <term>Triśiro-bhairava</term>:

->“One whose intellect is firmly rooted in the rising of the<-
->**incoming and outgoing breaths** <term>prāṇa and apāna</term>, serving both the lower and the upper—<-
->abandoning the upper, one should enter;<-
->therefore, one is 'established in Rama' here.”<-

In that same text, a **challenging question** <margin>1. *Āgūraṇa* means a challenge or objection.</margin> is posed by the Goddess:

->“O God, what is called 'Rama'?<-
->And who is it, O Lord, who is established here?<-
->What indeed is the nature of this practice?<-
->O Great Lord, tell me everything!”<-

<column-break/>

<note>original: "bisasūtrābhasūnnayā" — variant reading from Manuscript Kh in line 4.</note>
<note>original: "yatrasthaḥ sa ca kaḥ" — variant reading from Manuscript Ka in line 14.</note>

<header>The Light of the Tantras (Shritantraloka)</header>

When this was asked, the **Lord** <term>Bhagavan: usually referring to Shiva as the supreme teacher</term>, after making a promise in the following words:

|| 86 ||

Here, the author presents that very same concept through the meaning of the words:

->Movement and stability, dreaming and waking,<-
->opening and closing the eyes;<-
->running and jumping,<-
->as well as exertion and the experience of power;<-
|| 87 ||
->the various divisions of the intellect, the states of being,<-

->all this is Rama, the all-pervasive<-

**Dreaming** refers to **conceptual thought** <term>vikalpa: the mental activity of making distinctions</term>. 
**Waking** refers to **objective knowledge** <term>jñāna: here meaning ordinary awareness of the external world</term>. 
**Opening** <term>unmeṣaṇa: literally "un-winking," often referring to the emergence of the world</term> refers to the **state of Ishvara** <note>In this system, the "Ishvara" stage represents the divine outward gaze where the universe begins to appear as "This"</note>. 
**Closing** <term>nimeṣaṇa: the withdrawal of the world</term> refers to the **state of Sadashiva** <note>The stage where the universe is experienced as "I am this," leaning back into pure subjectivity</note>. 

**Exertion** <term>āyāsa</term>: The root *ay* means 'to go'. The sense of "going" here implies "knowing." Therefore, *aya* or *ayana* signifies **knowledge**. Its *āsa* refers to its "throwing away" or cessation. Thus, the word "exertion" here means **ignorance** <term>ajñāna</term>. 

The **eight** states [of the intellect] beginning with **virtue** <term>dharma</term>...
<note>This refers to the eight "dispositions" (bhavas) of the intellect in Samkhya and Shaiva philosophy: virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power, and their opposites.</note>

<summary>This page defines "Rama" not as a deity, but as the all-pervasive Shiva who encompasses every state of existence—from physical movement and intellect to the cosmic cycles of manifestation and withdrawal. It provides esoteric etymologies for common terms like "exertion" to link them to the concepts of knowledge and ignorance.</summary>

<header>Verse 89 ] Chapter One</header>

**Attributes of the intellect**, **names**—referring to arbitrary designations like *Dittha* and others <note>original: "ḍitthādayaḥ"; in Sanskrit linguistics, 'Dittha' is a standard example of an arbitrary name without intrinsic meaning, similar to "John Doe" or "Placeholder."</note>, and **actions**—meaning physical or mental activities. By these fourteen categories <note>The fourteen states mentioned across verses 87 and 88: movement, stability, dreaming, waking, opening eyes, closing eyes, running, jumping, exertion, power, intellect-attributes, states of being, names, and actions.</note> starting with "movement," the entire universe is encompassed. 

That which consists of "movement" and the rest is this **Rama**—the **Supreme Self** <term>Paramatma</term> and **Supreme Lord** <term>Parameshvara</term>, who is devoted to the play of manifesting the entire universe. Therefore, it was said in the verse, "*Shiva, the Supreme Cause, is all-pervasive here.*" "Here" refers to this entire world characterized by movement and the other activities. The underlying meaning is that this vast expansion <term>sphāra: the 'unfolding' or 'efflorescence' of divine consciousness</term>, which constitutes the whole universe, is indeed the work of Shiva alone. 

As it has been stated in the scriptures:

> “He resides in all objects and in all the objects of the senses; wherever one may look, nothing that is not Shiva <note>original: "nāśivaṃ"; a pun in Sanskrit meaning both 'nothing inauspicious' and 'nothing that is not the God Shiva'.</note> exists anywhere.”

|| 87 || 88 ||

He now explains how the state characterized by attaining oneness with Him occurs in this context:

->With a mind whose impurities are destroyed,<-
->and by the restraint of mere memory,<-
->one meditates on the Supreme Object of Meditation,<-
->abiding in the state of going and coming.<-
|| 89 ||

<header>The Splendor of the Tantras</header>

## Indeed, one attains the Supreme Shiva,
## known as Bhairava, even through recitation.

By him whose mind is such that its **impurity**—the darkness caused by the appearance of various dualities—has been diminished. The mind is called "mind" <term>manas</term> because it "thinks" or "mentally constructs" <note>original: "manute iti manaḥ"; a Sanskrit etymological explanation connecting the mind (manas) to the act of cognition or reflection (manana).</note>; thus, he possesses an awakening characterized by **self-reflective awareness** <term>vimarśa</term>. By him:

> "All conceptualization is memory..."

According to this logic, there is only **memory**—the mere memory of conceptualization consisting of physical forms like the body, face, hands, and so on. The **suppression** of that conceptualization—meaning its neutralization by becoming void of the delineation of such forms—is used as a support. Because there is an absence of **contraction** <term>saṃkoca: the limitation of infinite consciousness into finite forms</term> into those specific fixed shapes, the **Supreme Object of Meditation**, characterized as **Shiva**, the **Supreme Cause**, is meditated upon. That is, He is perceived as non-different from one's own self. 

As it has been stated:

> "Meditation is that steady intellect which is formless and without support; meditation is not the conceptualization of the body’s face, hands, and the like."

Such is the meditator. **Movement** <term>gama</term> means going or motion, and **non-movement** <term>agama</term> means the absence of motion or staying in place. In the state characterized by these two, immediately following—
