<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of the Tantraloka (The Splendor of the Tantras), picking up from the discussion on how a practitioner's consciousness moves toward the divine. It moves from the definition of meditation to the internal, esoteric definition of recitation (japa) as a state of pure, self-reflective awareness.</meta>

<page-num>135</page-num>
<header>Verse 90 ] Chapter One</header>

...located in the fourteen-fold support <note>original: "caturdaśavidhe āśraye"; referring to the various levels of the psychological and cosmic organs of the practitioner</note> already mentioned. For this reason, one attains **Shiva**, who is called **Bhairava**, the Supreme and the Full—this means one achieves immersion <term>samāveśa: the state of being possessed by or absorbed into the divine</term> in Him. It is stated that one attains Shiva not only through meditation, but also through recitation—indicated by the words "even from recitation" <note>referencing verse 86</note>.

In anticipation of the question, "What is this thing called recitation <term>japa</term>?" he says:

### Recitation is said to be His very nature, 
### fallen from the states of existence and non-existence. || 90 ||

"His" refers to Shiva. His nature is the essence of **Supreme Speech** <term>parāvāk: the highest level of language, which is identical to pure consciousness</term>, the very form of the Self. In other words, **recitation** <term>japa</term> is that which is reflected upon again and again. 

For this reason, it is "fallen from the states of existence and non-existence" <note>original: "bhāva-abhāva-pada-cyutaḥ"</note>. Following the logic previously explained, this means its essence is nothing but the reflection of **pure consciousness** <term>saṃvit</term> flashing in the interval between being and non-being. As it has been stated:

> "That contemplation which is repeatedly practiced within the Supreme State is indeed recitation. In this context, it is the spontaneous Sound <term>nāda: the subtle internal resonance of consciousness</term>, the soul of the mantra; such is the nature of what is to be recited."

This state of consciousness allows the practitioner to achieve full immersion into Shiva.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the first chapter of the Tantraloka, specifically elaborating on the esoteric definitions of meditation and recitation (japa). It cites the Trishirobhairava Tantra to support the idea that all human activities, when viewed through the lens of pure awareness, are forms of divine resting or support.</meta>

<page-num>136</page-num>
<header>The Splendor of the Tantras</header>

Thus, it would be said that even the activity of the sense organs <note>original: "grāmadharma-vṛttiḥ"; literally "the way of the village," referring to the collective functions of the senses</note> is situated within the "resting place" or "support" of consciousness <note>original: "rāmasthaḥ"</note>. This is stated in the sacred **Trishirobhairava** <note>One of the foundational scriptures of the Trika school, often quoted by Abhinavagupta</note>:

> "Walking, standing, sleeping, waking, opening the eyes, and closing them;
> 
> Running, jumping, and even physical exertion or the sensing of power;
> 
> The various distinctions of the intellect, as well as states of being, perceptions, and many kinds of actions—
> 
> These are proclaimed to be the fourteen-fold support <note>original: "rāma"; here referring to the fourteen 'supports' of the soul, including the five senses of perception, five organs of action, and the four internal organs: mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness</note>.
>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of spiritual means (upāyas) within the Trika system of Kashmir Shaivism. Building on the previous page's description of all activities as supports for consciousness, it now explains why different spiritual paths exist and how they are categorized based on their proximity to the ultimate goal, attributing this diversity to the absolute freedom of the Supreme Lord.</meta>

<header>Verse 92 ] First Chapter</header>
<sig>18</sig>

->Therefore, here too, by His own<-
->sovereign freedom, there is fashioned<-
->a distinction such as "far" or "near"—<-
->relative to the freedom of Consciousness. // 61 //<-

In this context, the Supreme Lord <term>Parameśvara</term> alone is the ultimate reality, for His nature is the Light of Freedom and His essence consists solely of the Supreme I-Reflection <note>original: "parāhaṃparāmarśa"; this refers to the primordial, non-conceptual self-awareness of God as the "I" that encompasses all of existence</note>. Therefore, regarding the attainment of Him, the diversity of spiritual means <term>upāya</term> is fashioned by Him alone through the variety of different teachings. Because of this, a spiritual means that shines forth with the predominance of the Freedom of Consciousness <note>original: "cit-svātantrya"</note> is called "near" <note>proximate or direct</note>; otherwise, if this freedom is less apparent, the means is called "far" <note>distant or indirect</note>. This is what is meant by the phrase "far [and near]." 

Even so, one should not mistakenly think that only that which is "near" to the goal can serve as a means. The relationship between the means <term>upāya</term> and the goal <term>upeya</term> will be explained later as a relationship between a gate and the one who passes through the gate <note>the "gatekeeper" or "dweller at the gate"</note>. // 61 //

The author now concludes this point:

->Thus, being full of Sovereign Freedom,<-
->and performing this most difficult task,<-
->in what form indeed<-
->does the Supreme Lord not shine? // 62 //<-

<header>The Blessed Tantraloka</header>

"...by His form" means by the nature of His various individual powers. // 62 //

Therefore, the author says:

-> He shines forth unveiled; <-
-> He shines with His own nature veiled; <-
-> He shines as the Unveiled among the veiled, <-
-> in many ways, due to the contact with differentiation. // 63 // <-
-> Thus, this triad of powers in the Lord— <-
-> which is but another name for His Freedom— <-
-> has been revealed by the Teachers <-
-> under the names of Will and the rest. // 64 // <-

"Unveiled" <note>original: "nirāvaraṇam"</note> refers to the state of consisting of Pure Light <term>Prakāśa</term>. "Veiled" <note>original: "āvṛta"</note> refers to the state where the turbidity of differentiation <note>original: "bheda-kāluṣya"; the mental state of seeing reality as divided rather than a unified whole</note> has arisen. "The Unveiled among the veiled" <note>original: "āvṛtānāmṛtaḥ"</note> refers to the state where, despite the presence of pure knowledge, there is no seepage or influence from the turbidity of differentiation.

Because of this, there exists the threefold condition of the Supreme, the Lower, and the Supreme-cum-Lower <note>original: "parā-apara-parāparatvam"; these are the three levels of reality in the Trika school: non-duality, duality, and the state that encompasses both</note>. The phrase "in many ways" refers to the diversity of the objects to be willed <note>original: "eṣaṇīya"</note> and so forth; it means that there are many different modes of manifestation. Indeed, even in the "unveiled" state, because differentiation is in the process of being negated, it still exists in the form of a mere latent impression <term>vāsanā</term>.

<header>Verse 95 ] The First Chapter</header>

The word "thus" <note>original: "iti"</note> acts as a reflection of the Lord's very own nature. By this means, the triad of powers—the "Supreme" <term>Parā</term> and the others—which manifest as the "unveiled" state and so forth, have been revealed by the Great Teachers who brought this scripture into our world. Though they have assigned names to these powers such as "Will" <term>Icchā</term> and so on when referring to the Supreme Lord, these are simply different designations for His Power of Freedom <term>Svātantrya-śakti</term>. Thus, the principle has been established: "Even His possession of many powers is nothing but His inseparability from that one Power of Freedom." // 63 // 64 //

Indeed, the "possession of many powers" is the very reason why these specific names are used. Thus, the author says:

-> For the Divine is taught through <-
-> words found in the scriptures that are meaningful; <-
-> this is the Great God Bhairava, <-
-> the Lord who is Supreme Shiva. // 95 // <-

"Meaningful" <note>original: "anvarthaiḥ"</note> means names that are etymologically derived or explained. "Found in the scriptures" <note>original: "śāstroktaiḥ"</note> means names that are established by the sacred tradition. // 95 //

The author explains that very point:

-> He bears the universe by filling and <-
-> sustaining it, and by that connection He is "borne" by it. <-
<note>This is a play on the etymological roots of the name Bhairava: *Bha* for "bearing/maintaining" (*bharana*), *ira* for "filling" (*pūraṇa*), and the sense of being the support of all things.</note>

<meta>This page continues the detailed etymological analysis of the name "Bhairava" from page 140. It focuses on the linguistic roots associated with supporting the universe, the cry for help from suffering souls, and the Lord’s mastery over Time.</meta>

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>Verse 100 ]        The First Daily Lesson</header>

He bears—meaning He supports and nourishes [the universe] by causing it to manifest through its being attached to the wall of His own Self <term>svātmabhitti; the concept that the universe is a reflection or mural painted upon the "wall" of pure consciousness</term>. By "that"—meaning by the universe—He is borne; that is, He is supported and nourished, because He shines everywhere precisely through His nature of being the universe itself. Because of His nature of "sounding" <note>original: rava</note>, and because of His acts of bearing <note>original: bharaṇa</note> and withdrawing <note>original: ravaṇa</note>, He is called **Bhairava**. This is the etymological explanation <term>nirukta</term>.

He is **Bhairava** because He acts for the benefit of those who are afraid <note>original: bhīru</note>. The cause of this fear is the cycle of worldly existence <term>saṃsāra; the repetitive cycle of birth, suffering, and death</term>. Thus, the meaning is that He is the giver of fearlessness to those caught in that cycle.

Fear <note>original: bhīḥ</note> is the terror of worldly existence. The "sound" <note>original: rava</note> produced by that fear is the cry for the Lord or the reflective awareness of Him. Since He is born from that [cry or reflection], He is called **Bhairava**. This means He shines in the heart—the ground of Ultimate Reality <term>paramārtha</term>—of those who cry out or practice such reflection.

Fear of existence is "bhī." Its "roar" <note>original: rava</note> is the act of discernment and reflective awareness <term>vimarśana</term>. He is the cause of this through the descent of power <term>śaktipāta; the touch of divine grace that initiates spiritual awakening</term>; hence He is **Bhairava**. The implication is that He alone is the cause for turning away from worldly existence.

The "lights" <note>original: bhāni</note> are the stars; He who impels or drives <note>original: īrayati</note> them is "Bhera," which is Time <note>original: kāla</note>. The essential nature of Time consists of units such as moments and other divisions. Of that [Time], He is the one who completely—

<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

Those who cause the withering and subjugation [of worldly existence] are said to "conquer Time" <note>original: kālam vāyanti</note>; they are the **Bhairavas**—meaning those Yogis whose focused attention is firmly established in the meditation of "swallowing Time" <term>kālagrāsa-samādhi; an advanced state of meditation where the practitioner transcends the limitations of past, present, and future</term>. Because the Lord is the Master who is manifest in His true essence within these Yogis, He is called **Bhairava**.

Furthermore, for the "fear" <note>original: bhī</note> of the "bound soul" <term>paśu; a person limited by the ego and the illusion of separation</term>—whose nature is contracted and who perceives only duality—there is terror regarding the arising of various pleasures, pains, and other worldly experiences. For such souls, there is "sounding" <note>original: ravaṇa</note>, which is the reflective awareness <term>vimarśa</term> of the powers of the alphabet <note>original: kādi-kalā; the creative energy inherent in the sounds of the Sanskrit language</note> arising from the Great Mass of Sounds. These sounds belong to the "Goddesses of one's own organs"—the powers of the senses.

Likewise, there is a fourfold group consisting of the "Moving Forces" <note>original: khecaryādiko gaṇaḥ</note> which constitute the internal and external world of the perceiver and the perceived. These are:
1. **Khecarī** <gloss>Moving in the void of consciousness; the power of the subject</gloss>
2. **Gocarī** <gloss>Moving in the inner senses; the power of the mind</gloss>
3. **Dikcarī** <gloss>Moving in the directions; the power of the external senses</gloss>
4. **Bhūcarī** <gloss>Moving on the earth; the power of external objects</gloss>

These forces are "terrifying" <note>original: bhīravāḥ</note> [to those caught in duality], and since He is their Master, He is called **Bhairava**. He is "Greatly Formidable" <note>original: mahābhīma</note>, and thus the name **Bhairava** is used here as a technical designation. This is the sense [of the preceding verses].

## The Master is praised in this Scripture
## as **Bhairava** through these meaningful etymologies. // Verse 100 //

<meta>Continuing from the etymological analysis of the word "Deva" (the Divine) based on the Sanskrit root 'div'. The previous page established that the Divine acts without external necessity, purely through play and sovereign will. This page further explores the specific meanings of 'div'—conquest, discourse, and illumination—as they relate to the nature of the Supreme Lord.</meta>

<page-num>145</page-num>
<header>Verse 103 ] The First Chapter</header>

The **Lord** <term>Īśvara; the Supreme Being as the sovereign agent</term> proceeds at the beginning of creation and other cosmic acts; for this very reason, the fact that He is a **Mass of His own Bliss** <note>original: "svānandaghanatvam"</note> is cited here as the cause. Because of this, His nature is one of absolute **Sovereignty** <term>Svātantrya; the self-dependent power of the Divine</term>. 

The **desire for victory** <note>original: "vijigīṣutā"</note> is the "desire to exist with supreme excellence." Indeed, for one who desires victory, the desire is essentially this: "How may I exist, having overcome all others?" 

The word "likewise" <note>original: "tathā-śabdaḥ"</note> serves to connect this with the previous definitions. Thus, He is called **Deva** <note>The root *div* means both "to play" and "to desire victory"</note> because "He plays" or "He desires to conquer." 

Furthermore, regarding the word **Deva**: even though His own Self is undifferentiated from everything, there is a manifestation of diversity such as "I know this." This **internal dialogue** <note>original: "saṃjalpaḥ"; the subtle inner speech of consciousness</note> is what is meant by **discourse** <note>original: "vyavaharaṇam"; literally 'usage' or 'worldly activity'</note>, which is a manifestation in a provisional, non-ultimate form. Therefore, He is called **Deva** because "He plays"—meaning He discourses or interacts. 

The manifestation of the entire universe—consisting of both **subjects** <term>pramātṛ; the conscious knowers</term> and **objects** <term>prameya; the known things</term>—within the totality of His being is **illumination** <note>original: "dyotanam"</note>. Thus, He is called **Deva** because "He plays"—meaning He shines or causes all to shine.

Since this entire world, from the moment it attains its own existence through to every duty to be performed, depends upon His activity, this constitutes His **praise**. For all beings—the state of **Shiva**, the **Lords of Mantras**, and the **Great Lords** <note>original: "śiva-mantra-maheśvarādayaḥ"; various levels of high spiritual beings in the Tantric hierarchy</note>—are indeed **bowed down** <note>original: "prahvāḥ"; suggests a state of orientation or leaning toward the source</note> in readiness, because their very existence is dependent on Him. This is the underlying sense. The word "of Him" <note>original: "asya"</note> functions here in the objective sense...

<header>The Splendor of the Tantras (Śrī Tantrāloka)</header>

The sixth [meaning of the root *div*] is to praise; thus, He who is praised or hymned is called **Deva**. He whose essential activity is complete and total, characterized by **reflective awareness** <term>vimarśa; the self-referential power of consciousness to know itself</term>, and whose qualities or powers consist of **vision and action** <note>original: "dṛk-kriye"</note>. Because He is of such a nature, His movement—lacking any specific limitation—is a spreading of knowledge everywhere. Thus, it is established that He is **Omniscient** and **All-pervasive**. Therefore, He is **Deva** because He shines, He knows, and He pervades. ||101||

102||103||

He summarizes this very point:

->Thus, through these etymological definitions, the **Deva**<-
->is recorded by the Teachers in the **Scriptures of the Body of Shiva**.<-

"By the Teachers" refers to the venerable **Bṛhaspatipāda** <note>An ancient authority in the Shaiva tradition</note>. The Lord is described [in his work] with phrases such as:

> “Thus is the 'Beautiful Lord' (*Vāmadeva*); He shines and plays, for He is the Sovereign.”

and ending with:

> “Because His movement is unimpeded, He is the Lord sung as **Sadāśiva** <term>The 'Ever-Beneficent' state of consciousness where being and doing are in perfect equilibrium</term>.”

The meaning is that the Lord has been fully described in this manner throughout that text.

With the word "governance" (*śāsana*), he now provides the etymological definitions of the words **Pati** <term>Master or Protector</term> and **Śiva** <term>The Auspicious One</term>.

<header>Verse 104 ] The First Daily Lesson (Prathamāhnikam)</header>

# Through governance, restraint, protection,
# and maturation, He assists everyone.
# Therefore, the Master is the essence of goodness;
# He is the Auspicious One, and in Him, nothing is inauspicious. ||104||

**Governance** (*śāsana*) refers to the awakening of those capable of being enlightened through scriptural instruction and other means. 

**Restraint** (*rodhana*) refers to keeping worldly souls in their current state of existence, as they are "scented" <note>Influenced or affected</note> by the **Power of Concealment** <term>vilaya-śakti; the divine energy that hides our true nature to allow for the experience of a separate world</term>. 

**Protection** (*pālana*) is the preservation of the **manifold diversity of the universe** <note>original: "viśva-vaicitryasya"</note> exactly as it is, through the established laws of nature and reality. 

**Maturation** (*pācana*) means bringing the actions (*karma*) of those who act to a state of readiness, so that they may produce their intended fruits or results.

As it has been said:

> “Even during the cosmic sleep, He remains, awakening those fit for awakening, binding those who must be restrained, and ripening the deeds of those who act; bringing into manifestation those suited for the power of **Illusion** <term>Māyā-śakti</term>, and seeing every object exactly as it is.”

The word “therefore” <note>original: "tena"</note> indicates that the term **Master** (*Pati*), although usually implying the act of protection, is used here because He is the performer of these functions like governance and the rest. Because of this—

<header>The Holy Tantrāloka</header>

He is called the **Master** (*Pati*) because He protects (*pāti*) and guards. He is **composed of the highest good** (*śreyomayaḥ*) because His essential nature is **Supreme Non-duality** <term>parādvaya; the state where there is no distinction between the observer, the observed, and the act of observation</term>. In contrast, **"Inauspiciousness"** (*aśivam*) refers to **dualism** <term>dvaita; the false perception of being separate from God or the universe</term>. ||104||

Now, one might ask: "Even if this is true, why is it necessary to add specific qualifiers to these names?" Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

-> A nature such as this might, <-
-> to some small degree, <-
-> shine forth in deities like Rudra or Upendra. <-
-> Therefore, to dispel any limitation, <-
-> the qualifier of the "Supreme Great State" has been employed. ||105||

The term **"such a nature"** (*īdr̥k*) refers to the meanings demonstrated through the etymology of names like **Bhairava** <note>A terrifying yet protective form of Shiva representing the vastness of pure consciousness</note>. 

The term **"some small degree"** (*kiyat*) means only partially, not in its entirety. This is because a portion of this divine nature can be found everywhere and in everyone to some extent. This is exactly why the qualifier characterized by the term **"Supreme Greatness"** (*parama-mahat-pada*) was used: to distinguish the Absolute from all others and to demonstrate His absolute superiority over everything. ||105||

<margin>Note on variants: Some manuscripts read "Supreme Non-dual nature" (paramādvaya) in line 1, and "with a specific qualifier" (viśeṣeṇa yogena) in line 3.</margin>

Now, it is said that **ignorance** (*ajñāna*) is the cause of **worldly existence** <term>saṃsāra; the cycle of birth, death, and suffering</term>, and **knowledge** (*jñāna*) is the cause of **liberation** (*mokṣa*). Ignorance is defined as the **non-recognition of one's own true nature** <note>original: "sva-svarūpa-akhyāti"</note>, while knowledge is the recognition of that nature...

It concludes by introducing the fundamental Tantric premise that spiritual ignorance is the root of worldly suffering.</summary>

# First Chapter
## Verse 106

The nature of the **Self** (*Atman*) is the **Supreme Light** <term>parah prakashah; the ultimate, self-shining consciousness that makes all experience possible</term>. It is He who, by His own **will** (*iccha*), conceals His true form and manifests Himself as the **totality of the universe** (*vishvarupa*). 

Even so, the means for attaining Him is His own **Power** (*Shakti*), through which the **recognition of one's own nature** (*svarupa-khyati*) occurs. This alone is what must be known; it is the central theme of all sacred scriptures and has been mostly addressed here already. One might then ask: "If it has been addressed, why continue?" Anticipating this, the author says:

-> Thus, the true essence of that which is known <-
-> is perceived by Shiva’s command, <-
-> by me, through my own self-awareness, right reasoning, <-
-> and the lineage of the Master’s scriptures. || 106 ||

This concludes the **"Introduction"** (*upodghata*). 

"Thus" (*iti*) refers to the manner described: the **true essence** (*satattva*) or ultimate reality of that which is to be known—such as **bondage and liberation**—which is discussed in other scriptures, has been briefly outlined here. That essence is now "perceived" by me—meaning it is being explained in detail—by relying on the **command of Shiva** and **self-awareness** (*svasamvit*). In this context, **Shiva** refers to the **Guru** <note>In this tradition, the Guru is not merely a human teacher but a direct manifestation of the divine consciousness of Shiva</note>.

> "He who is the **Guru** is said to be **Shiva**, 
> and He who is **Shiva** is remembered as the **Guru**. 
> There is no difference between the two, 
> between the Guru and Shiva."

---

<margin>Line 14: Manuscript "Kh" reads "relying upon and discussed" (*avalambya carcyate*) instead of "relying upon and perceiving."</margin>

<header>The Venerable Tantraloka</header>

The sense is that without receiving that command <note>original: *tada-desham*; refers to the divine permission or the Guru's instruction mentioned in the previous verse</note>, there would be no **authority** (*adhikara*) to compose this work at all. **Self-awareness** <note>original: *svasamvit*</note> refers to one's own direct experience. **Right reasoning** <note>original: *sattarka*</note> refers to logical proof. The **Scriptures of the Lord** <note>original: *patishastram*</note> refers to the Shaiva traditions that emphasize the distinction between the soul and God. The **Trika** <term>Trika; the "Triple" system of Kashmir Shaivism focusing on three primary energies: Supreme, Intermediate, and Lower</term> refers to the scriptures that name the three powers beginning with the **Supreme** (*Para*). **Krama** <term>Krama; the "Succession" or "Sequence" system which focuses on the cyclic nature of consciousness</term> refers to the fourfold stages of manifestation. Here, the term is used as a compound word joining these concepts. 

The author establishes that everything taught in this work is proven through **one's own experience**, **logic**, and both **general scriptures** and **specialized scriptures** (*Agama*). 

Regarding the word **Introduction** <note>original: *upodghata*</note>: the prefix *upa* implies "quickly" or "concisely." It is that in which the essence of the scripture is "struck" or "imprinted" at the very beginning, much like a **gold coin** (*dinara*) is struck with the name of a King. || 106 ||

<header>Verse 108 ] First Chapter</header>

The three powers beginning with the **Supreme** (*Para*) <note>The three powers are Para (Supreme), Parapara (Intermediate), and Apara (Lower)</note>, having internalized all other powers within themselves, are explained as being primary. They shine in **Creation**, **Maintenance**, **Reabsorption** <note>original: *samhara*; the withdrawal of the universe back into consciousness</note>, the **Fourth State** <note>original: *turiya*; the pure consciousness underlying waking, dreaming, and deep sleep</note>, and the **Ineffable** <note>original: *anakhya*; the state beyond all description</note>. That is to say, they manifest in a form that encompasses all things. 

The meaning of the sentence is this: because each one of these three powers possesses a fourfold nature—consisting of **Creation**, **Cycle** (*Kalpa*), and so on—there is a **twelvefold arising** <term>dvadasadhodaya; a key concept in the Krama system where the divine energy is realized through twelve distinct "Kalis" or functional stages of consciousness</term>. As it has been said:

> "For even these three domains, through the application of the sequence of creation and the rest,
> there occurs a fourfold state; thus he is manifest twelvefold.
> The Supreme Sun of one's own self-awareness is the inexhaustible city of light."

|| 107 ||

Now, an objection is raised: There is only one **Supreme Lord** (*Paramesvara*), whose nature is Supreme Light and who is designated by terms such as **Bhairava** <note>original: *bhairavadi*; a name for the Absolute that emphasizes its power to manifest, sustain, and withdraw the universe</note>. It has already been established that His power is also one and undivided, known as **Sovereignty** <term>Svatantrya; the absolute, independent freedom of divine consciousness</term>. If this is so, why is it said here that He has a "twelvefold arising"? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

-> **He who possesses such a full nature** <-
-> **is called Supreme Shiva.** <-
-> **Therefore, the practitioners here** <-
-> **are directly established in that very state.** 108 ॥ <-

<header>The Auspicious Light of the Tantras</header>

The phrase "That great" <note>original: *tavan*; referring to the scale of the Divine</note> means that his measure consists of the **twelve powers**; he is characterized in that way. For this reason, he is described as having a **Full Nature** <note>original: *purnasvabhavah*; the state of being complete, lacking nothing, and containing all possibilities</note>. In the state of Fullness, everything exists, and Fullness exists everywhere; otherwise, it would not truly be "Fullness" at all. 

Therefore, those practitioners who contemplate this **twelvefold wheel** of energies are established in **Supreme Shiva** <term>Paramasiva; the absolute reality or pure consciousness that transcends yet includes all of existence</term> himself—the meaning is that they share in his very essence. This is a topic that requires an extensive explanation, which will be discussed in detail in the chapter regarding the **Way of Power** <term>Shaktopaya; the second of the four methods of liberation in this system, which focuses on the purification of thoughts and the movement of divine energy</term>; for this reason, it is not elaborated upon here. || 108 ||

->The arrangement of these powers as having<-

->is defined in the scriptures solely<-
->by the force of His Absolute Freedom.<- || 109 || <term>svatantrya; the Divine's inherent power to act and manifest in any form without external cause</term>

->The Single Hero, the Couple,<-

Because they perform these specific functions, they are described as "following their own class" <note>original: *svavarganugama*</note>. It is for this reason that there is a "distinction within the wheels"; the scriptures describe an infinite number of such wheels. || 113 ||

<header>Shri Tantraloka</header>

# The Lordship over the six wheels
## of the Master, whose own form is diverse, has been stated. || 114 ||

By the doubling of four, there are eight; by doing so again, there are sixteen. By the doubling of six, there are twelve; by doing so again, there are twenty-four. This constitutes the "Lordship over the six wheels" <term>Shat-cakreshvarata; the sovereign mastery over six specific configurations of energy</term>. Because of the variety of the "limiting conditions" <term>Upadhi; external attributes that define or limit a thing</term> such as the wheels and other elements that He causes to manifest, His form is "diverse" <note>original: *citra*; meaning variegated, multi-formed, or colorful</note>—it possesses many shapes. Because nothing else is perceived apart from Him, this diversity is His "own form" <note>original: *nijakrtih*</note>. For this very reason, the Lordship of the Master—who is full of absolute freedom <term>Svatantrya; the sovereign, self-dependent power of the Divine</term> and who presides over those various wheels—is stated and proclaimed in the **Three-Headed Bhairava** <note>original: *Traishirase mate*; referring to the Triśirobhairava Tantra, an important scripture in the Trika system</note> doctrine. As it is said there:

> "The fourfold, the sixfold, the eightfold, the twelve-spoked, the sixteen-spoked,
> and the twenty-four-spoked [wheels], O Goddess, are well-established by division."

And so on. || 114 ||

The cause for the differentiation of the wheels into many types is also explained in the **Three-Headed Bhairava** itself; thus he [Abhinavagupta] says:

---

<margin>Line 11: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "the fourfold and sixfold chambers."</margin>
<margin>Line 12: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "likewise the eightfold by division."</margin>

It emphasizes that this diversity of form is not separate from the Lord's own nature but is a manifestation of His absolute freedom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the meditation for "nourishment" (puṣṭi) introduced on page 159. It explains the linguistic and phonetic theory behind why certain sounds (dentals and labiodentals) are used to "moisten" or "nourish" the practitioner's consciousness.</meta>

<header>The Venerable Tantrāloka</header>

...because it is characterized by the act of causing that which is dry to become like a lake. For water is that which nourishes <term>Āpyāyaka; the quality of making something swell or overflow with life-force</term>; it is the primary element and the cause of "nourishment" <term>Puṣṭi; prosperity, health, or spiritual fullness</term>, taking forms such as "fullness," and so forth.

<margin>Line 1: The manuscript variant "dry-lake" appears in some versions.</margin>

Now, he explains the "internal discourse" <term>Sañjalpa; the mental "speech" or inner dialogue used during meditation</term> as being of two types—worldly and transcendent—starting with the words "And those..." and so on.

The word "those" refers to phonemes <note>original: "varṇāḥ"</note> which are predominantly labiodental <term>Dantyoṣṭhya; sounds produced using both teeth and lips, such as "v"</term> and dental <term>Dantya; sounds produced with the tongue against the teeth, such as "t", "d", "n", or "s"</term>. "That consciousness" refers to the consciousness in the form of nourishment. "The status of a seed" refers to attaining the status of a mantra <term>Mantrabhāva; the state where a sound becomes a potent vessel of spiritual power</term>. 

It is for this reason that this specific internal discourse is considered transcendent <term>Alaukika; non-worldly or supernatural</term>. Labiodentals are sounds such as the letter *v*. Dentals are sounds such as the "nectar-seed" <term>Amṛta-bīja; a specific syllable, often "sa" or "vam", believed to release the nectar of immortality in the body</term>. The phrase "with certain phonemes" refers to those sounds that are not primarily labiodental or dental. As it has been said:

> "The syllable *Vaṣaṭ* is praised for the purpose of nourishment..."

And likewise:

> "In the act of prosperity and nourishment, with phonemes..."

In this way, retroflex <term>Mūrdhanya; sounds made with the tongue curled back toward the roof of the mouth</term> and other classes of sounds are also included. By using the phrase "conceptual in nature," the worldly aspect of this internal discourse is demonstrated. "That" refers to the consciousness of nourishment. 

<note>A manuscript variant suggests "form of creation" instead of "form of nourishment" here, though nourishment fits the context of the previous page better.</note>

Now, he begins to explain the external ritual <note>original: "bāhyam api"</note> which consists of fire-sacrifices <term>Homa; the ritual offering of substances into a consecrated fire</term> and other such rites—

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>The Splendor of the Tantras — Śrī Tantrāloka</header>

# They too, discerning the object of knowledge,
# regard it as non-different from consciousness.

Those sacrificers <term>yājaka; those who perform ritual offerings</term> who perceive various deities such as Indra—who possess specific, limited forms—as being distinct from consciousness (which is the singular nature of the Knower and one's own true Self), actually contemplate those deities very deeply through the power of intense faith. 

Even though these deities are viewed as objects of knowledge <term>vedya; that which is known or perceived</term> with fragmented and specific forms, the worshipers eventually come to understand them through the following logic:

> "The object of knowledge attains the state of the knower; the knower attains the nature of pure consciousness. If consciousness is indeed the essence of the Self, then truly this world is composed of You."
<note>original: *vedyo vedakatāmāpto...* — This famous verse describes the "ascent" of awareness where the external object is absorbed into the subject, and the subject is absorbed into universal consciousness.</note>

By this reasoning, they realize the deity as non-different from consciousness—meaning, they perceive the deity as being of the same essence as their own Self, the Supreme Knower <term>parapramātṛ; the ultimate, infinite subject of all experience</term>. This is the intended meaning.

***

An objection <term>pūrvapakṣa; a formal challenge in philosophical debate</term> is now raised: 

"It is said that a sacrifice <term>yāga</term> consists of the renunciation of a ritual substance for the sake of a deity. Therefore, the deity is simply the intended recipient for that renunciation. However, the true Self—which is pure consciousness—is not 'intended' or 'targeted' in that same external way. How then can the Self be considered the object of sacrifice <term>yājyatva</term>?"

Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 164, where Abhinavagupta addresses the philosophical objection regarding how ritual actions and deities relate to pure Consciousness. Having established that even limited worship eventually returns to the Self, he now explains why the Supreme "I" (the Self) is beyond the reach of religious commands or creative acts.</meta>

<page-num>165</page-num>
<header>Verse 127 ] First Chapter</header>

->**Therefore, for that whose nature is the expansion of "I-ness,"**<-
->**which consists of an uninterrupted self-reflection,**<-
->**there is no "injunction" that precedes it,**<-
->**as it is self-manifesting. Neither does a creative act**<-
->**precede this Reality. For the creation of deities**<-
->**is an object of knowledge, arising from a specific power.**<-
->**However, consciousness in the form of "I"**<-
->**is eternal, characterized by its own self-expansion. || 125-127 ||**<-

By that reason—meaning, because it is the very nature of awareness—there is no external "injunction" <term>vidhi; a Vedic command or religious rule that prompts one to act</term> or "creative act" <term>sṛṣṭi; the process of bringing something into being through ritual or will</term> that comes before this reality of one's own Self <term>svātma-tattva; the essential truth of the soul</term>.

This is because the Self follows the logic of the saying: "This Self is once-and-for-all illuminated." <note>original: "sakṛd-vibhāto'yam ātmā" — A classic philosophical maxim meaning that the light of the Self is always present and never flickers or turns off; it doesn't need to be "turned on" by a ritual.</note> It exists in a form that is continuous and never-ending, consisting of the light and self-recognition of the "Supreme I" <term>parāhamprakāśa-pamarśa; the ultimate subjective awareness that knows itself</term>. 

As such, it is self-proven <term>svataḥ siddha; inherently established without needing external evidence</term> and does not depend on means of knowledge like logic or perception. Therefore, an "injunction"—which is essentially a command intended to prompt someone to do something they haven't already started—cannot apply here. Nor can there be a "creative process" which serves as a means to achieve a specific result. 

In short, the reality of one's own Self, being the very nature of awareness, can never become the object of a command. Because—

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion on Verse 127 from the previous page. Abhinavagupta is refining the argument that the Self (Atman) cannot be an object of a religious command or injunction (vidhi) because the Self is the foundation of all awareness and is already "attained" by its very nature.</meta>

<page-num>166</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras (Tantrāloka)</header>

...due to the absence of reaching any injunction <term>vidhi; a religious rule or Vedic command</term>. For only that which is not already reached can be the object of an injunction; however, there is never a time when one's own Self is "not reached"—since it is established from the very beginning <term>ādi-siddha; a state of being inherently proven or existing prior to any effort</term> and is always shining forth <note>original: "sphuraṇāt" — The pulsing radiance of consciousness that makes all experience possible.</note>.

*Objection:* But it has been said that an injunction has many forms, such as a "mandate" <term>niyoga; the sense of obligation or "task" felt by a person</term> or a "productive urge" <term>bhāvanā; the inner impulse that leads to the completion of an action</term>. Why then should one's own Self not fall under the scope of some kind of injunction?

Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->**An injunction is a mandate, and the**<-
->**three-fold productive urge consists of an impelling force. || 127 ||**<-

An injunction is that which prompts someone to act who has not yet acted; it is not, however, that which simply makes known what was unknown. As the scholars say:

> "The definition of an injunction is strictly this: the prompting of action where there is no prior movement. Because of the fault of over-extension <term>atiprasaṅga; a logical error where a definition is too broad and applies to things it shouldn't</term>, an injunction is not defined as the making known of the unknown."

Regarding the relationship between the goal of Heaven and the means of Sacrifice, this same injunction functions as a prompter only insofar as it generates the knowledge in a person: "I am now prompted to act." This is what is called the "mandate" <term>niyoga</term>.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Verse 127 from the Tantrāloka. Having established on the previous page that the Self is already self-evident and thus cannot be the object of a Vedic command, Abhinavagupta now examines how the major schools of Vedic hermeneutics (Mīmāṃsā) define the nature of religious injunctions. He distinguishes between the "Mandate" (niyoga) theory of the Prābhākara school and the "Productive Urge" (bhāvanā) theory of the Bhāṭṭa school.</meta>

<page-num>167</page-num>
<header>Verse 127 ] Chapter One</header>

Thus it is described by the followers of Prabhākara <term>prābhākara; a school of Vedic interpretation emphasizing the duty or mandate of the command</term>, and as the **'Productive Urge'** <note>original: "bhāvanā" — the creative force or impulse toward action</note> by the followers of Bhaṭṭa <term>bhāṭṭa; the school of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa which focuses on the objective result of the action</term>. In that context, the **'Mandate'** <note>original: "niyoga" — a requirement or obligation</note> is the religious duty <term>dharma</term> to be performed; it is the essence of the action itself, characterized by an impelling force expressed as **"I am being prompted to act,"** and it is denoted by the verbal suffixes. And this [Mandate]—

->'He who desires heaven should sacrifice with the New-Moon and Full-Moon sacrifices.'<-

—is perceived in such instances as being delimited by two "attachments" <term>anubandha; essential connections or requirements that complete the meaning of a command</term>. Indeed, through the mention of the sacrifice and so forth, the "attachment to the object" is stated. And by the phrase **'he who desires heaven,'** the "attachment to the qualified person" <term>adhikāra; the person who has the right or eligibility to perform the ritual</term> is stated; for this very reason, the **'Mandate'** is proclaimed to be a friend to these two attachments. The very nature of a Mandate is that "it joins someone to something."

And the **'Productive Urge'** is the activity of the producer directed toward what is to be produced. That which is to be produced is the result, such as heaven; the activity of the person that resides within them and brings about that result is the Productive Urge. For a person "brings into being" <note>original: "bhāvayati" — makes happen or causes to be</note> an object such as heaven through their own activity; thus it is called a "Productive Urge." This urge is of two types: the Word-Urge <term>śabda-bhāvanā; the power of the Vedic word to inspire action</term> and the Object-Urge <term>artha-bhāvanā; the actual effort of the human agent</term>. This urge is said to have "three parts" because it requires three components: *what* should one produce, *by what means*, and *how*? As it has been said:

> "That Productive Urge, being understood from either the verbal root or the suffix, 
> requires a triad of components: what, by what means, and how."

Regarding these three parts: in the "Object-Urge," when the requirement of **'what'** arises, the answer is heaven; when the requirement of **'by what means'** arises, it is the sacrifice; when the requirement of **'how'**—

<summary>This page explores the technical definitions of Vedic injunctions, comparing the 'Mandate' (niyoga) of the Prābhākara school with the 'Productive Urge' (bhāvanā) of the Bhāṭṭa school. It details how a ritual command functions by connecting a specific person to a specific result through a three-fold process of intent and action.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Vedic hermeneutics (Mīmāṃsā) applied to the nature of the Self. On the previous page, the author began explaining the "Productive Urge" (bhāvanā) theory. Here, he completes that explanation and draws a sharp distinction: while ritual elements like deities are created or "enjoined" by the power of the Vedic word, the Self (Self-awareness) is already self-existent and cannot be treated as a mere object of a command.</meta>

<page-num>168</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

In the case of a requirement <note>original: "pekṣā" — the logical need for a sentence to be completed by specific details</note>, materials such as rice and so forth should be connected [to the action]. Similarly, regarding the **'Verbal Productive Urge'** <note>original: "śabda-bhāvanā" — the power inherent in a Vedic command that impels a person to act</note>, when the requirement **"What?"** is asked, the human activity to be produced is the answer. When **"By what means?"** is asked, the [power of the] word is the answer. When **"How?"** is asked, the function of the explanatory passages <term>arthavāda; portions of the Veda that praise a ritual or tell stories to encourage the performer</term> is the answer to be connected. An **'Injunction'** <note>original: "codanā"</note> is a Vedic mandatory sentence. As the authorities have said:

->"An injunction is a statement that impels one toward action."<-

This definition should be applied in both contexts <note>referring to both the "Mandate" theory and the "Productive Urge" theory mentioned on the previous page</note>. Furthermore, that [injunction] attains its status as a valid means of knowledge only when it expresses a meaning not established by other means, and it accomplishes that specific meaning.

->"One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni."<-

In such instances, just like the act of offering <note>original: "nirvapaṇa"</note>, even the deities like Indra and others who are mentioned are "to be enjoined" <note>original: "vidheyāḥ" — they are part of what is being commanded into existence for the ritual</note>. This is because the relationship between the ritual substance <term>dravya</term> and the deity <term>devatā</term> is the primary thing being directly communicated.

He says exactly this:

->Deities such as Indra and the rest are established solely by that [injunction];<-
->for deities are preceded by the mandate.<-
->However, **Self-awareness** is not like that;<-
->for they [the deities] possess the nature of being objects of cognition. || 128 ||<-

->Looking only at the emerged reality,<-

**"Preceded by an injunction"** <note>original: "vidhi-pūrvāḥ"</note> — An **Injunction** <term>vidhi; a scriptural command like "one should sacrifice"</term> is "preceding" or "prior" when it serves as the valid means of knowledge <term>pramāṇa</term> that reveals a meaning not previously understood. The position held is this: **Deities** <note>original: "devatā"</note> that are distinct from one's own Self are primarily objects to be known <note>original: "vedya"</note>. Since they are not perceived through other means of knowledge <note>such as the five senses</note>, they are established or "proven" by the Scripture. This is a logical stance for ritualists.

However, one’s own **Self** <note>original: "svātmā"</note> consists solely of the nature of **"I-consciousness"** <term>ahaṃ-bodha; the fundamental sense of being "I"</term>. Based on the reasoning stated previously, because the Self is always shining <note>self-evident</note>, it does not require any external means of knowledge to establish its own existence. Therefore, it is rightly said that the Self is **"not preceded by an injunction"** <note>original: "avidhi-pūrvakam"</note>. 

The author clarifies this by stating: **"I-consciousness."** The phrase "In the same way" implies the context of being "preceded by an injunction."

Now, a question is raised: If this is the case, why was it said that even those devoted to other deities perform sacrifice? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

### Light on the Tantras <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note>

->By the two words "Enjoyer" and "Lord,"<-
->He is expressed as both the object of worship and the worshipper. || 132 ||<-

In this context—meaning within the text of the *Gītā*—the intention is to explain **undivided pure awareness** <term>bodha-mātra</term> alone. For this reason, it is said that the "grasper" or the "subject who reflects" <note>original: "parāmraṣṭā"</note> is a designator for awareness in its absolute state. Indeed, there is no possibility of a second thing existing outside of **Light** <term>prakāśa</term> that could serve as a counter-correlate to be excluded. This is because any such thing would be subject to the dilemma of being either "manifest" or "unmanifest"—if it is manifest, it is already part of the Light; if it is unmanifest, it is nothing at all. 

However, the "I-awareness" <term>ahaṃ-vimarśa</term> that identifies with the body, such as in the thought "I am thin," is merely a **conceptual construct** <term>vikalpa</term>. This is because it relies on excluding other things; the "I" of the body is only defined in opposition to "others" or "objects" that are not the body. 

Now, a question is raised: If Awareness alone exists as a single reality without any opponent or "other," then how can the distinction between the **object of worship** <term>yājya</term> and the **worshipper** <term>yaṣṭṛ</term>—found in phrases like "they worship Me"—be considered ultimately real? 

Anticipating this doubt, the author says: *By the two words "Enjoyer" and "Lord"* and so on. The core idea is that **Awareness** <term>bodha</term> itself flashes forth or manifests in the form of both the subject and the object. As it is said in that very text <note>the Bhagavad Gītā, 9.24</note>:

> "I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices." 

|| 132 ||

### Light on the Tantras <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note>
<page-num>173</page-num>

->Only the Awareness belonging to the worshipper<-
->Is the object of worship, and no other; this has been declared.<-
->Indeed, no other form from any source whatsoever<-
->Is suitable to be the deity. || 133 ||<-

**Awareness** <term>saṃvit</term> alone is the **object of worship** <term>yājyā</term>; this is what has been stated—that is, it is the fundamental proposition. It is not, for any reason, some other external form such as the god Indra or others. Furthermore, that Awareness belongs specifically to the **worshipper** <term>yājamānī</term>, and is not "other"—meaning it is not separate. The sense is that the awareness of the worshipper is "composed of the pair" <note>original: "dvayamayī"; this implies it encompasses both the subject who performs the rite and the object toward which it is directed</note>. 

For a deity conceived as such a [separate] form, or even Awareness possessing such a separate form, would not be appropriate. This is because differentiation is impossible within pure Awareness, and anything that exists apart from Awareness is **inert** <term>jāḍya</term> <note>literally "frozen" or "dumb"; in this philosophy, anything outside of consciousness is considered "dead" or "insentient"</note>. 

The quality of being a "Deity" <term>devatā</term>—which consists of the singular nature of **luminosity** <term>dyotamānatva</term>—is not fitting for an inert object. Therefore, it is self-luminous Awareness alone which, being one, flashes forth in the form of these various identities. Thus, it was rightly said [in the previous verse], "He alone is declared as both the object of worship and the worshipper."

Precisely because Awareness is **primordially established** <term>ādi-siddhatva</term> <note>meaning it is self-evident and does not require external proof or a "command" to exist</note>, nothing such as a scriptural injunction or command is mentioned as the cause for its proof. <meta>This page continues the logical progression from page 173, where Abhinavagupta established that Awareness alone is the true deity. Here, he addresses why traditional ritual rules and mantras, which are central to Vedic religion, do not apply to the absolute state of pure Awareness, and begins to explain how diversity arises from a single, unified consciousness.</meta>

### Light on the Tantras <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note>
<page-num>174</page-num>
<header>The Light on the Tantras</header>

# No injunction is mentioned here,
## Nor are mantras and the like the locus of activity.

In this context, the sentences of the **Vedas** <term>veda-vākya</term> <note>the most ancient and authoritative scriptures of India</note> are of two types: those consisting of **mantras** <term>mantra</term> <note>sacred chants or formulas</note> and those consisting of **ritual instructions** <term>brāhmaṇa</term>. Furthermore, these ritual instructions are of three types, consisting of **injunctions** <term>vidhi</term> <note>commands to perform an action</note>, **explanatory praises** <term>arthavāda</term>, and **proper names** <term>nāmadheya</term> of the rites.

Regarding these, it has already been stated that "injunctions" have no function or operation within **pure Awareness** <term>saṃvit</term>. In the same way, mantras and other such elements also have no operation there. This is because a mantra is the "locus" or support for **activity** <term>vṛtti</term>—that is, for the ritual action which is the very nature of the operation of an injunction—for without the mantra, the ritual action cannot be accomplished. 

Furthermore, within pure Awareness, no distinction is possible, such as the relationship between the **expressed and the expressor** <note>original: "vācya-vācaka"; the object and the word that names it</note> or the **offering and the offerer** <note>original: "yājya-yājaka"</note>. It is thus established that there is only one, eternally-perfect **Consciousness** <term>bodha</term>.

->But if this is so, how then does this universal expansion,<-
->consisting of both the conscious and the inert, come to be?<-
->Raising this doubt, the author says:<-

> This very [Awareness], having veiled itself, 
> remains established in the state of the **inert** <term>jaḍa</term>. || 134 ||
> But possessing a nature both veiled and unveiled,
> it exists as everything from the gods down to stationary objects.

<margin>Line 3: The 'K' manuscript reads "as the nature of the Brāhmaṇas" <note>original: "brāhmaṇatvena"</note>.</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that because pure Awareness is a non-dual unity, the divisions of Vedic ritual (like commands and chants) do not apply to it. He introduces the concept of "veiling" to explain how one unified consciousness appears as a world of diverse, often insentient, objects.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of how pure Awareness (Samvit) is the ultimate reality, transcending ritual commands and mantras. Abhinavagupta now explains the transition from the "Original Creation," where everything is unified, to the diverse world of subjects and objects we experience through the power of limitation.</meta>

<page-num>175</page-num>
<header>Verse 135 ] Chapter One</header>

### This duality, consisting of both the inert and the sentient,
### possesses a marvelous diversity. [135]

The phrase "by covering" <note>original: "āvṛtya"</note> means causing the appearance of limitation <note>original: "saṃkocavattām"</note> through the **power of illusion** <term>māyā-śakti</term>, which consists of concealing one's own true nature. The term "inert" <note>original: "jaḍa-padam"</note> refers to the nature of the entire mass of objects which must be illuminated by something else <note>i.e., they cannot "shine" or be known without consciousness</note. 

Indeed, the **Supreme Lord** <term>parameśvara</term>, desiring to create the universe, first illuminates the universe as non-different from Himself. This very state is called the "Original Creation" <note>original: "ādi-sarga"</note> in various revealed scriptures <term>āgama</term>. 

Subsequently, when He wishes to create a world of diversity through the power of illusion <term>māyā</term>, He causes a continuous stream of infinite dual appearances—consisting of both the "perceiver" and the "perceived"—to shine forth upon the mirror of His own Self through His **absolute freedom** <term>svātantrya</term>. From within the mass of objects that are essentially His own "limbs" <note>meaning everything in existence is part of His being</note>, He transforms things like the physical body, the vital breath <term>prāṇa</term>, the intellect, and the "void" <note>the state of deep, dreamless sleep</note> into the state of a "perceiver" <term>grāhaka</term> by projecting onto them the sense of "I-ness" and agency <term>kartṛtā</term> that actually belongs to Him. 

Others, such as sound and other sensory objects, He makes into "perceived objects" <term>grāhyatā</term> by viewing them as "this" <note>original: "idantā"</note>, thereby overstepping their true nature as pure Consciousness. For this reason, the body and other such entities take on agency and the quality of being a "knower" <term>jñātṛtā</term> within themselves, while everything else takes on the quality of being an effect and an object to be known. 

This is why they are designated as "inert-and-sentient" <note>original: "jaḍājaḍa"</note>; thus the text says, "He is the Self that is both covered and uncovered" <note>original: "āvṛtānavṛtātmā"</note>. Even so, the diversity of these types...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion from page 175 regarding how the Supreme Lord, through His absolute freedom, manifests the appearance of duality. <page-num>176</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note></header>

Through the triad <note>referring to the three-fold power or the three bonds mentioned later</note>, infinity is established; thus the author says "inert," and so on, to explain this **diversity** <note>original: "citratā"</note>.
In that context, the **inert** <term>jaḍa</term> <note>the world of unconscious objects</note> possesses many varieties through the distinctions of sound and other sensory qualities, and even those are subdivided by variations such as high or low pitch. 
Even for the **sentient** <term>ajaḍa</term> <note>conscious subjects</note>, although there is infinity due to the different "streams" of individual souls, there is also a manifold nature caused by the varying degrees and intensities of the **three bonds** <term>bandha-traya</term> <note>The three impurities (malas) that limit the soul: āṇava (individualism), māyīya (illusion of duality), and kārma (binding action)</note>. 
Indeed, **limited perceivers** <term>pramātṛ</term>, wandering in accordance with the latent impressions of their respective past actions <term>karmāśaya</term>, experience themselves in various ways throughout their different states. They might perceive their own self as being devoid of the notions of virtue or vice, or as being fashioned by their specific desires. Thus, they perceive the **inert** object as having a manifold nature because it produces various effects like pleasure, pain, and so on. [134-135]

In response to the doubt, "What is the cause of this diversity?", he says:

->For His is the nature of Absolute Freedom;<-
->What is there that He might not imagine?<-

As it is stated in the **Scripture of the Three-Headed Bhairava** <term>Triśiraḥ-śāstra</term>:

->He who knows, "I am fully awakened." [136]<-

He confirms this very point by citing the source of the meaning, beginning with "As it is stated," and so on.

An objection may be raised: Even if the body and other such things are intended to be the **perceiver** <term>grāhaka</term> <note>the subjective grasper of experience</note>, they are actually **objects of knowledge** <term>jñeya</term> because they are **inert** <term>jaḍa</term>. Indeed, "being known" is a property of knowledge itself. When I say, "I know the object," there is no actual change or excellence added to the **object** <note>original: "artha"</note> itself; rather, it is the knowledge alone that takes on the form of that object. > "...the knowability of the object of knowledge is nothing but knowledge itself."

Thus, for those objects that exist—such as the body and other things—their "shadow" <note>The "shadow" refers to the perceived density or materiality of objects which seems to hide the spirit</note> cannot shroud or cover Consciousness <term>Chit</term> <note>original: "cit," the foundational, pure awareness that constitutes reality</note>, because it is impossible for something to be a veil for its own self. Because of this, even when one identifies the Self with the body, there is no actual loss of the Self's nature as pure consciousness. This is stated in that same text <note>The *Scripture of the Three Heads* mentioned on the previous page</note>:

> "The nature of the object of knowledge is itself the form of consciousness; therefore, its shadow does not cover [consciousness] at all." [136]

For this very reason, he says:

->Therefore, in the non-inert part<-
->named as the "individual soul" and so on,<-
->within that portion of the uncovered light,<-
->diversity is established in many ways. [137]<-

"Therefore" <note>original: "tena"</note> refers to the reason that consciousness is never actually shrouded. "In the uncovered" <note>original: "anāvaraṇe"</note> means within the Self, whose nature is pure Awareness <term>Samvid</term> <note>The light of consciousness that makes all experience possible</note>. For although the body and other objects are essentially forms of Awareness, because they appear at first glance as "objects of knowledge" <note>as things to be perceived rather than the perceiver</note>, the possibility of "impurity" <note>the illusion of being limited or separate</note> may arise. [137]

Now, one might ask: "If there is no possibility of division within pure Consciousness, how can the diversity of the world be explained?" Having raised this doubt, the author says:

->**Though no real division exists**<-
->**within the eternal form of Consciousness,**<-
->**it is nonetheless perceived as diverse**<-
->**due to the varying degrees of the waning of the veil. [138]**<-

"The veil" <note>original: "āvṛtteḥ"</note> refers to the primordial impurity <term>Anava Mala</term> <note>The "stain of smallness," or the foundational sense of being a limited, separate individual rather than the universal whole</note>. Its "waning" means its gradual destruction or wearing away. The "varying degrees" <note>original: "tāratamyam"</note> refer to the intensity of this process, which can be mild, middling, or intense. Because of this variation, diversity "is perceived" <note>original: "lakṣyate"</note>—meaning it does not actually exist in reality. This is precisely why the author previously used the specific qualifier "real" <note>original: "vāstavaḥ"</note> when saying no division exists. [138]

And what is that gradation of degrees? Raising this doubt, he says:

->**We shall explain that in detail**<-
->**in the "Decision on the Descent of Grace."**<-
->**Having concluded the discussion on the Supreme,**<-
->**it will be examined in the context of the Gross. [139]**<-

"We shall explain" refers to what he will say later <note>Abhinavagupta refers here to the 13th chapter of this work, where he discusses Shaktipata, the descent of divine energy that initiates spiritual liberation</note>.

Of all entities—such as the color "blue" (representing external objects) or "pleasure" (representing internal states)—there is one single underlying Essence. This is the primary Existence characterized by the Supreme Light, without which nothing could be manifest. The "revelation" of this nature—which is the very form of the Self—is a direct realization free from mental constructs <term>avikalpa-vṛtti</term> <note>A state of pure awareness that does not use words, labels, or logical distinctions</note>.

This is considered "lower"—meaning incomplete—because it lacks the full, direct manifestation of the nature of Consciousness. It is called "manifold" because it takes many forms, in the ways that will be explained later. [141]

He now demonstrates that very manifoldness:

->**And that knowledge is gained directly through a Means,**<-
->**or even through the lack of any Means...**<-

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines Supreme Knowledge as the direct, non-conceptual realization that the Self is the single essence of all reality. He contrasts this with lower, "manifold" forms of knowledge that rely on mental constructs and different spiritual methods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of the different "Means" (upāyas) to liberation. ### ...[it] shines forth, and is here 
### differentiated by manifold modes. [142]

"That" <note>original: *tat*</note> refers to either the Supreme or the lower knowledge. "Directly by the means" <note>original: *sākṣād-upāyena*</note> refers to the **Way of Shambhu** <term>śāmbhava-upāya</term> <note>The highest means, involving a direct transformation of consciousness without the need for mental effort or meditation</note>. This is because that [Shambhava] alone is the unmediated cause for attaining Supreme Knowledge; indeed, when it reaches its highest peak, it is called the **Beyond-Means** <term>anupāya</term> <note>literally "no-means." This refers to a state of realization so immediate that no technique is required</note>. 

For this reason, it will be stated later that "Beyond-Means" is not merely the negation of all means. The means to that Shambhava state is the **Way of Shakti** <term>śākta-upāya</term> <note>The path of pure thought or "wisdom," using the mind to transcend the mind</note>. From the use of the word "etc." [in the root text], the means to that [Shakta] is the **Way of the Individual** <term>āṇava-upāya</term> <note>The most basic level of practice involving breath, body, and external rituals</note>. 

The phrase "is differentiated" refers to a figurative <note>original: *aupacārikaṃ*</note> distinction <note>The distinction is called "figurative" because, in reality, all knowledge is one, but we categorize it into different paths for the sake of the student</note>. [142]

It is not only thus; rather, there is another cause for this variety, as he says:

### Even there, through the nature of being 
### the "door" and the "one at the door," 
### [divided] entirely and partially, 
### a great variety of distinctions proceeds 
### by way of mediation and non-mediation. [143]

"By one’s own"—for example, reaching the state of Shambhu through the Way of Shambhu. Thus, through the "door" <note>the means</note> characterized by either oneself or another, the "one at the door" <note>the goal</note> is that which possesses the means. "Entirely" means—

<page-num>१८३</page-num>
<header>Verse 144 ] Chapter One</header>

...as a **complete self** <note>original: *pūrṇātmanā*</note>. The phrase **"by parts"** <note>original: *aṃśaśaḥ*</note> means incompletely. The phrase **"by mediation"** <note>original: *vyavadhāne*</note> refers to cases where there is an absence of a direct means to the goal. 

Thus, in the first place, the **Means** <term>upāya</term> <note>The method or technique used to achieve spiritual realization</note> is threefold—based on the distinction between the **Way of Shambhu** <term>śāmbhava</term>, the **Way of Shakti** <term>śākta</term>, and the **Way of the Individual** <term>āṇava</term>. 

Because each of these can function as either a **gateway** <note>original: *dvāra*</note> or the **thing-at-the-gate** <note>original: *dvāri*—the goal being accessed</note>, they each become twofold, resulting in **six** variations. Furthermore, by being categorized as either **complete** or **incomplete**, they each become twofold again, resulting in **twelve**. Then, by being either **mediated** <note>indirect</note> or **unmediated** <note>direct</note>, they each become twofold once more, resulting in **twenty-four** variations. 

Since mediation can occur through many diverse, heterogeneous factors, the number of distinctions becomes vast. [143]

***

One might object: Knowledge has been established as the **Goal** <term>upeya</term> <note>the 'to-be-attained'</note>. Therefore, there must be some **Means** <term>upāya</term> to reach it. That means cannot be Knowledge itself—since Knowledge is the goal to be reached. Nor can it be ignorance—for ignorance is of no use in reaching the goal. What then is the actual nature of the Means? 

In response to this doubt, he says:

### And that which is the means to Knowledge 
### is not called "ignorance."
### Rather, it is Knowledge itself—subtle, 
### and considered to be of the nature of the Supreme Will. [144]

The connection here is that this "Means" is considered **subtle** <note>original: *sūkṣma*</note>, meaning it is distinct from the "gross" knowledge that consists of **conceptual thoughts** <term>vikalpa</term> <note>mental constructs or dualistic ideas</note> found in the Way of Shakti and elsewhere. For this reason, it is called **Supreme** <note>original: *para*</note>—the Way of Shambhu— <margin>Line 10: Manuscript K reads "because of its unconditioned nature" <note>original: *anaupādhikatvāt*</note> instead of "not conducive."</margin> <margin>Line 12: Manuscript K reads "and also the means"; Manuscript Kh reads "and the goal."</margin>

<summary>This page explains the mathematical sub-classification of the spiritual "Means" into twenty-four varieties and argues that the true means to liberation is not ignorance or gross thought, but a subtle form of Knowledge rooted in the Divine Will.</summary>
<keywords>upāya, upeya, Shambhava, Shakta, Anava, vikalpa, subtle knowledge, divine will, taxonomy of means</keywords>

<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

...is the meaning. This is why it was said to **"consist of Will"** <note>original: *icchatmakam*</note>. The implication is that the **Way of Shakti** and the **Way of the Individual** <note>original: *śākta* and *āṇava*</note> must consist of Knowledge and Action respectively. [144]

Now, an objection may be raised: even if this is so, how can the relationship between the **Means** <term>upāya</term> <note>The method or path</note> and the **Goal** <term>upeya</term> <note>The state to be attained</note> be applicable to one and the same reality? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->The relationship of Means and Goal<-
->is merely an illusion arising from the "thickness" of Knowledge.<-
->And this very Power of Action<-
->is the sole cause of both bondage and liberation. [145]<-

**"Thickness"** <note>original: *sthaulya*</note> refers to the submergence of the supreme, subtle nature—which is a single, solid **mass of Consciousness and Bliss** <note>original: *cidānandaikaghana*</note>—and its subsequent flaring up as differentiation through the infinite division of **perceiver and perceived** <note>the subject and the object</note>. This "thickness" creates the illusion that "this is the Goal" and "this is the Means." 

In reality, the Goal is **Shiva** <note>The Supreme Reality or absolute consciousness</note> himself, whose nature is the **Supreme Light** <note>original: *paraprakāśa*</note>. He shines everywhere and in all things, because He is never absent from any experience. Therefore, the various Means serve no real purpose here, as the function of a "means" is typically to make known something that is currently unknown <note>Since Shiva is always already "known" as our own consciousness, a "means" to find Him is technically redundant</note>. As it has been said:

> "Since Your reality is immediate, manifest everywhere, and ever-present, those who labor over spiritual Means surely do not know You."

<summary>This page explains that the distinction between the spiritual method (Means) and the ultimate realization (Goal) is a conceptual illusion caused by fragmented perception. Since the Divine (Shiva) is ever-present and self-evident, no external means is strictly necessary to reveal what is never hidden.</summary>

One might ask: If this is the case, how does this worldly convention <note>the distinction between a seeker and the goal</note> take root and flourish?

Anticipating this doubt, the author says: **"This very..."** and so forth. He refers to the **Power of Action** <term>kriyāśakti</term>—so called because it brings about the existence of various diverse forms and distinctions. The underlying thought is that all of this is simply the **Expansion of the Supreme Lord** <note>original: *parameśvara-sphāra*; the idea that the universe is not separate from God, but is God "spreading out"</note>. Therefore, when this Power is not recognized for what it truly is, it acts as a **Bonder** <term>bandhaka</term>; but when it is recognized, it is the **Liberator** <term>mocaka</term>. As it has been said: "It is the sole cause of both bondage and liberation."

->“This very Power, characterized by Action,<-
->belongs to Shiva but resides within the limited soul.<-

->but once recognized, it brings about spiritual perfection.”<-

**"In that"** <note>original: *tatra*</note>—meaning, in this situation. **"In the first"** <note>original: *ādye*</note>—referring to the nature of the primary, intuitive awareness <note>the flash of insight before the mind begins to categorize it</note>...

# The Venerable Tantrāloka

[Continued from the previous page]...even though the conceptual thought <term>vikalpa</term> involves two parts—what is called the Self and the non-Self—there is a recurring certainty <note>original: *niścaya*</note> regarding these parts, preceded by the denial of their opposites. This realization attains the nature of direct experience <note>original: *sākṣātkāram*</note> through reflecting on the nature of the Self even as it is being conceptualized. The wise know this to be the "Means of Knowledge"; that is, they should recognize it as the **Way of Power** <term>śākta-upāya</term>, which consists of the expansion of the Power of Knowledge. 

The word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> in the verse distinguishes this path from the previous one. For here, it is stated that conceptual thought itself gradually reaches the state of the **Non-conceptual** <term>nirvikalpatā</term>. In the previous path [the Way of Shambhu], however, the very form of the realization was non-conceptual from the start. Therefore, the relationship between these two paths is that of a doorway to the door; one serves as the entrance to the other. [147][148]

->produced by the activity of the imagination,<-
->is traditionally called the Way of Action;<-

# The Venerable Tantrāloka

[It was] stated <note>original: *uktam*; referring to the concluding portion of the previous verse</note> that by those imaginations—which consist of the expansion of difference—an object is "created." This means it is fashioned by the mind's own artistry. This object, such as the practice of **Recitation** <term>uccāra</term> and the like, is externalized and limited, yet it serves as the means of attainment. 

The word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> is used here to show a contrast. In the **Way of Power** <term>śākta-upāya</term>, the conceptual thought <term>vikalpa</term> itself is the object of focus; however, here [in the Way of the Individual], even external objects are included. For this very reason, practices like Recitation are not found in that higher path. 

Now, one might ask: "Since the means are different, shouldn't the goal—the 'thing to be reached'—also be different?" 

Anticipating this doubt, the text says: "**there is no difference in liberation here.**" The expansion of one's own true nature is indeed what we call liberation <term>apavarga</term>. This realization occurs through all these different paths via the relationship of the **doorway and the door** <note>original: *dvāra-dvāri-bhāva*; a metaphor where the lower path serves as the entrance (doorway) to the higher reality (the door/room)</note>. This is the underlying meaning. [149]

---

An objection is raised: It was previously asserted as a general rule that "Knowledge alone is the means." How then can it be said that **Action** <term>kriyā</term> is the means in the Way of the Individual? 

Anticipating this, the author says:

> Because there is no such thing as "Action"
> separate from Knowledge; rather, it is Knowledge itself
> that—through habituation and integration—has reached that state.
> Thus it is taught in the **Venerable Scriptures** <term>śrīmad-gamashāsana</term>. [150]

"Separate" means separate from Knowledge. Because that very Knowledge, through the "sprouting" of habituation, reaches the ultimate peak of integration <note>original: *yoga*</note>. Having attained that essential reality, it is everywhere designated by the term "Action." This is the meaning.

---

<margin>Line 4: Manuscript "K" reads "thought itself is the object" <note>original: *vikalpya evārtha*</note> as the variant reading.</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that while the "Way of the Individual" (Anava-upaya) uses external actions and rituals, these are not truly separate from Knowledge; rather, "Action" is simply Knowledge that has become solidified through practice. He emphasizes that despite different methods, the final goal of liberation—the expansion of the Self—remains identical across all paths.</summary>

### [ Verse 153 ] The First Daily Lesson

Now, one might ask: "What is the proof for this?" Anticipating this doubt, the text says: "**Thus [it is said] in the Venerable Scripture of the Tradition**" <note>original: *śrī-gama-śāsane*; likely referring to the Matanga Parameśvara Tantra</note>. This means: "it has been stated thus." [150]

He quotes the very passage from that scripture:

> **upon the pacification of the impressions of one's own mind,**
> **is what is designated as "Action."** [151]

> **In one's own mind, the impressions are**

> **Awareness, whose true nature is pure Consciousness,** <term>saṃvit</term>
