# The Venerable Tantrāloka

## Action is that same [awareness], and Yoga as well, 
## in the process of dissolving the principles of reality into consciousness. [153]

The commentary explains the grammar of the previous verse, noting that the word "cause" explains the relationship between the mind and its purification. By saying "of the nature of pure awareness," the author indicates that the word "intellect" or "mind" here actually refers to spiritual knowledge. That awareness is described as follows:

> "With the sacred syllable **Om** <note>original: *praṇava*</note>, O Goddess, one should ritually install all those categories that cause the origin of the body, thirty-one in number, in their proper order."

According to such scriptural passages, this awareness rests upon the specific categories that constitute the "pure body" <note>the subtle or divine body of the initiate</note>, as well as those external categories common to all. 

> "Leaving the lower path behind, O fair-faced one, one should transcend it, until the power of **Equispace** <term>samanā</term> <note>a high level of subtle energy reached in meditation before the state of Unmana or "beyond mind"</note> is reached..."

Through such teachings, when an initiate undergoes the "initiation into the principles" <term>tattva-dīkṣā</term>, their awareness rests upon these shared levels of reality. Because this process causes the "pacification" or quieting of the subconscious impressions within one's own mind, it is called **Action**. 

Similarly, that very same awareness is also called **Yoga**, as the scriptures say:

> "They define Yoga as the desired unity of one thing with another."

In this context, it is the "yoking" or joining of the various categories of existence into pure **Consciousness** <term>citi</term>. Therefore, it is correct to say that "Yoga is nothing else, and Action is nothing else," because neither of them is actually different from pure Knowledge. [152–153]

### [Verse 155] First Daily Lesson

But how can awareness alone be action? He explains this by demonstrating with an everyday example:

->Even in the world, that which flashes within as<-
->"I am going,"<-
->becomes the "action of movement" as it enters<-
->the body, the location, and the senses. [154]<-

The vibration <term>sphurā</term> <note>original: *sphurā* or *sphuraṇa*; the pulsing radiance of consciousness</note> occurring within the Self as "I am going" is consciousness <term>saṃvit</term> in the form of an initial "rising to act." That very same consciousness becomes the "action of going" by entering the body and other physical components, manifesting a state of being absorbed by them and making them one with itself. Thus, it is rightly said that "knowledge indeed is of that nature." For a traveler, when the vibration "I am going" exists, the accomplishment of the action of movement occurs through the animation of the body, the feet, and the physical surroundings, which are composed of the agent, the instrument, and the object of the action. [154]

He concludes this very point:

<margin>Line 16, Manuscript K: The reading is "Knowledge indeed leads to liberation."</margin>

->Therefore, even that which is called action<-
->is ultimately only awareness.<-
->Awareness alone leads to liberation;<-
->this has been rightly declared. [155]<-

<summary>Abhinavagupta uses the example of walking to show that physical action is merely an extension of an internal "spark" of intention, concluding that since action is awareness, awareness is the sole cause of spiritual liberation.</summary>

### [The Light of the Tantras]

**Therefore**, this is the case because action is fundamentally composed of awareness. It is for this reason that it has been stated that action is also a cause for final beatitude <term>apavarga</term> <note>original: *apavarga*; the ultimate completion or release from worldly existence</note>, in passages such as:
"Initiation alone liberates one upward; it even leads one to the state of Shiva." <note>original: *dīkṣaiva mocayatūrdhvaṃ śaivaṃ dhāma nayatyapi*</note>

In this way, it is rightly said that "knowledge is the sole cause of liberation." He [Abhinavagupta] expresses this by saying, "And this has been rightly declared." [155]

#### [The Nature of Liberation]

But an objection arises: previously, in verses such as "Apart from the independent Self...", it was stated that there is no such thing as "liberation" existing separately from the knowledge of the Self. If that is true, how can it be consistent to speak of a cause-and-effect relationship between the two—claiming that "knowledge leads to liberation"?

To address this doubt, he says:

->For what is called liberation is nothing else<-
->than the unfolding of one’s own true nature.<-
->The true nature of the Self is pure awareness,<-
->and nothing else. However, those various... [156]<-

->...powers, such as the power of action,<-
->are not something "extra" added to awareness.<-
->This is because they cannot exist as non-awareness,<-
->and the possessor of these powers could not<-
->otherwise be defined. [157]<-

# [Verse 157] First Chapter

Now, an objection might be raised: "What exactly is this so-called 'true nature' <term>svarūpa</term> whose unfolding <term>prathana</term> constitutes liberation?" In response to this, the author says "true nature," etc. By this, he means that the nature of one's own Self is pure awareness and consciousness <term>saṃvit-caitanya</term>. Its unfolding is knowledge as it truly is <note>original: *yathātattvaṃ jñānam*</note>, and that very thing is liberation. Thus, what was stated before is indeed correct. 

Furthermore, this "relationship of cause and effect" <term>hetu-phala-bhāva</term> that was previously mentioned is merely conceptual <note>original: *kālpanika*; a mental construct used for teaching purposes</note>, not ultimate <note>original: *tāttvika*</note>. As he will state later:

> "Since the relationship of cause and effect described 
> between knowledge and liberation 
> is not the primary truth..."

The word "other" in the text means "distinct from awareness." But one might ask: "If the Self has no nature other than awareness, how can it be associated with various different powers <term>śakti</term>?" <note>The questioner is confused how a single, simple awareness can possess multiple capacities like will, knowledge, and action.</note> Anticipating this, he says "therein," and so on. The word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> here is used in the sense of "and" <note>original: *ca*</note>. [156–157]

Now, another objection arises:

Since the possessor of attributes has not been defined independently of those attributes, isn't this logic unproven? To address this, he says:

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section where Abhinavagupta addressed the nature of the Self as pure awareness. Having established that liberation is the unfolding of this awareness, he now moves to distinguish the Shaiva view of "Power" (Shakti) from the viewpoints of other philosophical schools, specifically the Vaisheshika (Kanada) school, which sees qualities as separate from the substance they inhabit.</meta>

### [Verse 158] In the Scriptures of the Supreme Lord

### In the scriptures of the Supreme Lord,
### it is not like the view of the Kanadas.
### No separate substratum is mentioned
### for the powers that are in the form of attributes. [158]

<note>The "Kanadas" refers to the followers of the Vaisheshika school of philosophy, founded by the sage Kanada. They are known for their "pluralist" view, categorizing reality into distinct substances and qualities.</note>

Just as the followers of Kanada describe the Self as the possessor of attributes <term>dharmin</term> by saying things such as:
> "The Self is that which has a relationship with 'self-ness'."
<note>In Vaisheshika philosophy, a substance is defined by its relationship to a universal category; here, the soul is a substance because it possesses the quality of being a soul.</note>

And they accept a collection of separate attributes <term>dharma</term> that are united with that Self but are transient <note>original: *āgamāpāyi*; literally "arriving and departing." In their view, qualities like happiness or knowledge are not the essence of the soul, but things that happen to it.</note>, stating:
> "Its qualities are intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impressions, number, magnitude, distinctness, conjunction, and disjunction."

But here in our system, no such relationship of "attribute and possessor" is expressed between Power <term>śakti</term> and the Possessor of Power <term>śaktimat</term> <note>The Divine and His Power are considered inseparable, like fire and heat.</note>. For it is the Supreme, independent awareness <term>svatantro bodhaḥ</term> itself that is designated as various forms of power due to the influence of different limiting conditions <term>upādhi</term>. Therefore, in reality, there is no difference between the power and the one who holds it. As was stated previously...

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where the author contrasted the Shaiva non-dual perspective with the Vaisheshika school (the "Kanadas"). Having argued that attributes are not separate from their source, Abhinavagupta now uses the analogy of fire and its functions to conclude Verse 158 and moves into Verse 159 to warn against the logical collapse of non-duality if powers were seen as truly separate entities.</meta>

### [Verse 158] First Chapter

> "For the capacity of being the Subject <note>original: *mātṛ-kalpate*; referring to the conscious agency of the Self</note> is fully sufficient for the nature of every individual object. What difference is there in reality between them, any more than between the 'burning' and 'cooking' powers of fire?" <note>Just as fire is a single entity that can both burn and cook without being two different things, the divine Consciousness is one despite its various functions.</note>

**Thus ends Verse 158.**

Now, one might ask: "What would be the harm if we were to define the relationship between an attribute and its possessor <term>dharma-dharmi-bhāva</term> here in our system just as it is described in the school of Kanada and others?" <note>The Vaisheshika school, founded by Kanada, views qualities like 'knowledge' as separate things that 'attach' to the soul. The questioner asks why we cannot just use that model.</note>

Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->Therefore, if Knowledge, Action, Will,<-
->and the other powers were likewise distinct,<-
->then the statement "Shiva is One"<-
->would become entirely void of reality. [159]<-

For if there were a real, ontological difference between the Power <term>śakti</term> and the Possessor of Power <term>śaktimat</term> based on the logic of "attribute and possessor," then consider this scripture:

> "In this way, through diverse forms—both stationary and moving—the Lord Shiva alone, who is ever one, expands through his divine play."

In this and other passages, the statement **"Shiva is one alone,"** which is the fundamental declaration of the non-duality of the Lord <note>original: *īśvarādvaya-pratijñā*</note>, would be reduced to a mere word without meaning, because there would actually be many distinct entities in the form of various powers and the possessor of those powers.

<meta>This page continues the logical argument from the previous section (Verse 159), where Abhinavagupta argued that if the powers of Shiva were truly separate from Him, the concept of non-duality would collapse. ### [Verse 159 continued] First Chapter

...because of this possibility, [the statement that Shiva is One] would be void of reality—it would be devoid of its designated meaning. In other words, it would result in a refutation of the doctrine of non-duality <term>advaya-vāda</term>. [159] <margin>In manuscript 'K', the reading is "refutation of non-duality."</margin>

Now, an objection might be raised: "If in reality there is only Shiva, whose essence is pure Consciousness <term>saṃvit</term>, then why is our worldly experience <term>vyavahāra</term> conducted as if he were composed of various powers, such as consciousness and so on? Why is it treated otherwise?"

To settle this doubt by way of a concluding summary, the author says:

->Therefore, this very nature of Consciousness<-
->is also its absolute Freedom.<-
->When that Freedom is analyzed,<-
->it culminates in many distinct powers. [160]<-

This point has been determined previously, so it is not labored over again here. As it has been said in other scriptures:

> "Even His possession of many powers is nothing other than His inseparable connection to His own Power." <note>original: *bahu-śaktitvam apy asya tac-śaktyaivāviyuktatā*; this implies that 'powers' in the plural are just expressions of the one singular 'Power' of God.</note>

[160]

In this system, because of the principle that "knowledge of the Self alone is liberation" <term>ātma-jñānam eva mokṣaḥ</term>, there is actually no relationship of cause and effect <term>kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva</term> between knowledge and liberation. Thus, following the logical maxim that "it is not necessary that causes always produce [visible] effects," <note>This is a subtle point: if liberation were a 'result' caused by knowledge, it would be a temporary, created thing. Instead, liberation is the eternal state of the Self, merely revealed by knowledge.</note> for those who possess knowledge...

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that the "many powers" of Shiva are actually just the analytical breakdown of His single, absolute Freedom (Svatantrya). He also begins to argue that liberation is not a "product" caused by knowledge, but is identical to self-knowledge itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical argument from the previous section where Abhinavagupta established that the "powers" of Shiva are not separate entities but expressions of a single, free Consciousness. He now addresses a potential logical fallacy: if knowledge is the "cause" and liberation is the "effect," why do we not see the usual delays or failures associated with cause-and-effect in the physical world?</meta>

### [Verse 161] First Chapter . 187

"Even if the cause called 'knowledge' is present, liberation—viewed as its effect—might not occur." This kind of logic, which leads to an undesirable conclusion, should not be feared or even suspected here. To address this, the author says:

->Since liberation is the manifestation of the Self,<-
->such a doubt should not be raised here.<-
->[Otherwise,] the effect would not necessarily follow the cause,<-
->and thus the knower of the Self would not be liberated. [161]<-

The inner sense is that for the knower <term>jñānin</term>, liberation <term>mukti</term> is an absolute certainty. This is precisely why it is said in the *Bhagavad Gita*:

> "Of them, the man of knowledge, constantly disciplined and devoted to the One, is preeminent. For I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me." <note>original: Bhagavad Gita 7.17</note>

And likewise:

> "...but the man of knowledge, I consider him to be My very Self." <note>original: *jñānī tv ātmaiva me matam*; Bhagavad Gita 7.18</note>

This and other passages from the *Gita* support the point. [161]

Now, an objection might be raised:

"In passages such as 'Knowledge alone leads to liberation,' a relationship of cause and effect <term>kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva</term> has indeed been stated between knowledge and liberation. So how can you claim that this logical problem <note>The 'problem' being that effects don't always follow causes in the material world</note> does not apply here?"

In response, the author says:

->Since the relationship of cause and effect<-
->between knowledge and liberation that was mentioned...<-

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that liberation is not a distant 'effect' of knowledge, but rather the very manifestation of the Self; therefore, true knowledge and liberation are inseparable and instantaneous.</summary>

### The Light of the Tantras <note>original: Śrī Tantrālokaḥ</note>

->That is not the primary sense, therefore this<-
->logical consequence does not follow—this is certain. [162]<-

This point has already been settled previously, so we will not labor over it further here. [162]

Concluding this point, he introduces another topic:

->Thus, Action—whose very nature is Knowledge—<-
->bears a sense of "grossness" within itself.<-
->Because of this, one may indeed observe<-
->the diversity manifest within it. [163]<-

The author uses the phrase **"whose nature is Knowledge"** because action is inseparable from knowledge. <note>In this system, knowing and doing are two sides of the same coin of consciousness.</note> As it has been said:

> "...Action is never devoid of Knowledge."

**"Grossness"** <term>sthūlatva</term> refers to the way reality flashes forth through the division into the internal perceiver and the external perceived object. <note>While pure consciousness is "subtle," its manifestation as a world of distinct objects is called "gross."</note> **"Because of this"** means by reason of this bearing of grossness. **"Diversity"** <term>citratā</term> refers to the variety of distinctions found among those various perceived objects and so on. [163]

Therefore, he says:

->Among the various means within the "Path of Action,"<-
->which do not differ from external objects...<-

<vocab>
**Tantrāloka**: The "Light on the Tantras," Abhinavagupta’s masterwork on non-dual Shaivism.
**Jñānasvabhāva**: Having the nature of knowledge; the idea that even physical actions are rooted in awareness.
**Kriyā**: Action; the power of the Divine to manifest and act in the world.
**Sthūlatva**: "Grossness" or "solidity"; the state of being a physically manifest object.
**Citratā**: Multiplicity or variety; the colorful diversity of the universe.
**Kriyopāya**: The "Means of Action"; spiritual practices involving ritual, breath, or external objects.
</vocab>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that Action and Knowledge are inseparable; the diverse, "gross" physical world is simply a manifest form of divine consciousness. This introduces the "Path of Action," where external rituals are used as a means to realization.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Path of Action" (Kriyopāya), specifically detailing how the various ritual and meditative means are categorized. The previous page established that Action is essentially a "grosser" form of Knowledge and introduced the distinction between "perceived" and "external" objects. Here, Abhinavagupta explains why these means are considered infinite in number.</meta>

<page-num>१६६</page-num>
<header>Verse 164 ] First Chapter . 166</header>

## Due to the twofold nature of divisions and subdivisions,
## there is countlessness through intermediate variations. [164]

"Perceived objects" <note>original: *grāhya*</note> refer to things such as vocalizations <note>original: *uccāra*</note> and so on. "External things" <note>original: *bāhya*</note> refer to ritual pits <term>kuṇḍa</term>, sacred circles <term>maṇḍala</term>, and the like.

Vocalizations and similar internal processes, while belonging to the sphere of things perceived and even though they are determined to be "outside" the core self, are not strictly "external" in a physical sense. This is because they are not accessible to external senses like the eyes, nor are they common to other perceiving subjects. <note>In other words, your internal recitation of a mantra or the movement of your breath is an "object" of your awareness, but it is a private experience that others cannot see or share.</note>

On the other hand, ritual pits, mandalas, and such are considered external because they *are* accessible to the external senses and are common to all observers. Since they are external, they are "perceived objects." This is what was meant in the previous verse by the phrase "those divided into perceived and external objects."

In this way, even though there is a fixed classification, there is a "countlessness"—meaning a vast multiplicity of types—arising from their intermediate variations and the diversity of divisions and subdivisions.

To illustrate: regarding vocalization <term>uccāra</term>, there are first five divisions based on the different types of vital breath <note>original: *prāṇa*</note>. Even within those, there are many subdivisions such as the "point" <term>bindu</term> and the "resonance" <term>nāda</term>. <note>These terms refer to subtle stages of sound and light that a yogi experiences as consciousness moves upward.</note> Furthermore, because the mantras being recited are themselves infinite, the resulting divisions are truly countless. [164]

->And so:<-

> "Since there is no other action named..."

Line 11: The manuscript 'Ka' reads "firstly, five divisions."

<note>
**Divisions and subdivisions** (bhedopabheda): The layers of classification within ritual and meditative practice.
**Mantra**: Sacred sounds or syllables used in meditation and ritual.
**Point and Resonance** (bindu-nāda): Subtle levels of sound-consciousness; Bindu is the concentrated seed of light, and Nāda is the internal unstruck vibration.
**Divisions of breath** (prāṇādi-bheda): The categorization of the life force into five functions: inhaling, exhaling, pervasive breath, etc.
**Perceived** (grāhya): Anything that becomes an object of awareness, whether internal or external.
**Vocalization** (uccāra): The yogic process of directing awareness upward along with the breath or a sound.

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of the "Path of Action" (Kriyopāya). Having previously explained that there are countless varieties of ritual and meditative means, Abhinavagupta now addresses a potential misunderstanding: if the means are different, does that mean the final state of liberation is also different for everyone? He argues that because all action is fundamentally "Knowledge," the goal remains a single, unified reality.</meta>

<page-num>200</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Tantraloka</header>

The fact that "action is essentially of the nature of knowledge," which was introduced previously, has now been established through both logic and scripture. Therefore, Knowledge alone is the singular "means" <term>upāya</term> for attaining liberation; there is no true multiplicity of means. Consequently, regarding the result of that means—liberation <term>mokṣa</term>—there is no difference or hierarchy either. He states:

->**By this, that which some scholars suspected**<-
->**has been demolished:**<-
->**The idea that because there are different means,**<-
->**there might also be differences in liberation. [165]**<-

The connection in the text is to the phrase "which some scholars suspected." "Some scholars" refers to the dualists <note>original: *bhedavādin*; those who believe that the soul, the world, and God are eternally separate</note>. In their systems, there is a real, ontological difference between a cause and its effect. Thus, if the cause (the means) differs, the effect (the result) must also differ. 

But here, in this non-dual system:
> "Even a localized part of the Absolute <term>Brahman</term> does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptual division." <note>This is a famous philosophical principle suggesting that the totality of reality is present in every part of it.</note>

According to this principle, "Universal Consciousness <term>saṃvid</term> is everything." Given this, what could possibly be the difference between a cause and an effect? Even if we accept a conceptual or imaginary difference between cause and effect, it has already been admitted that the "means" consists solely of Knowledge. Thus, the very idea of a multiplicity of means...

---

Line 1, Manuscript Kh: reads "consisting of knowledge." <note>original: *jñānātmakatvam*</note>
Line 13, Manuscript Ka: reads "even a localized part" and "without conceptual division."
Line 15, Manuscript Ka: reads "in the conceptual cause," omitting the word "also."

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that since all spiritual practices (means) are ultimately forms of one Universal Consciousness, the resulting liberation is a single, unified state, contrary to dualist views that suggest different practices lead to different levels of salvation.</summary>

...en universal Consciousness? Therefore, since there is no difference in the underlying reality, what possible difference could there be in liberation <term>mokṣa; the final state of spiritual freedom</term>, which is the ultimate result?

An objection is raised:

Wait, since it has been stated in passages such as this that there is a "multiplicity of direct means," how can there *not* be a difference in the result based on the difference in those means? <note>The objector argues that if the "causes" (the methods) are diverse, the "effect" (the goal) must also be diverse.</note>

Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

Even in cases where a real relationship of cause and effect exists, there is no difference in the result—such as the destruction of impurity <term>mala; the spiritual "grime" or limitation that binds the soul</term> and its power—even if the cause, such as initiation <term>dīkṣā</term>, varies. This is because, although initiation may differ based on the specific power <term>kalā</term>, principle <term>tattva</term>, or cosmic realm <term>bhuvana</term> being addressed, the final result itself remains the same. 

To illustrate this: a pot can be smashed by a hammer, a hand, hitting a wall, or colliding with another pot. Despite these different "means" or causes of destruction, the resulting state—the "destruction" or "disappearance" of the pot—is exactly the same in every case. <note>This is a classic logical example in Indian philosophy to show that different actions can lead to an identical state of absence.</note> 

Therefore, it is by no means a universal rule that a difference in cause must necessitate a difference in the result. Where, however...

The relationship between the "means" <term>upāya; the method</term> and the "end" <term>upeya; the goal</term> is merely conceptual <note>original: "kālpanika"; suggesting that in the ultimate reality of non-dual consciousness, the distinction between the path and the destination is a mental construct used for teaching purposes</note>. Regarding the inverted order of this reading <note>referring to how the means are taught in relation to the goal</note>, the intention is this: through the relationship of "means and goal" or "door and doorway," the ultimate repose is found primarily in the Divine (Śāmbhava) means alone. The word "through that" means through the uselessness of mental constructs <term>vikalpa; the discursive thoughts or dualistic concepts that usually divide our experience</term>. For if mental constructs were still being utilized, then at that very moment:

> "One whose state of being is composed of the Object of Knowledge, steady and full on all sides..."
<note>This is a partial citation likely from the *Spanda Kārikā*, used to illustrate the state of someone who has moved beyond thought into direct realization.</note>

<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras [Śrītāloka]</header>

...from such a perspective, the attainment <term>samāpatti; the state of perfectly merging with or becoming one with the object of contemplation</term> of the ultimate nature of Consciousness <note>original: "cid-ātmanaḥ"</note>—which is the Object of Knowledge that must be known—would not occur. 

For a mental construct <term>vikalpa; a dualistic or discursive thought</term>, through the power of repeated practice, acts as a catalyst for the emergence of other mental constructs similar to itself. By gradually dissolving its own lack of clarity and following a sequence that generates increasingly refined thoughts, it eventually attains identity with pure Awareness, which is free from all constructs <note>original: "avikalpa-saṃvit-tādātmyam"</note>. 

As he [Abhinavagupta] will say later:

> "One who desires to enter should quickly refine the mental construct." 

And starting with such instructions, he concludes:

> "Awareness attains the pure state of non-conceptual reality." 

Therefore, it is precisely because of this [process of mental refinement] that this [the Divine means] is distinct from the Empowered Means <term>Śākta-upāya; the path where the mind is used to transcend the mind</term>. [171]

But one might ask: "How could this state [the Divine immersion] occur simply by the uselessness of mental constructs?" To address this doubt, he says:

->How does that occur? He explains:<-
->**Through a Guru who is immensely venerable,**<-
->**by an awakening directed toward the Object of Knowledge,**<-
->**which possesses the quality of being immediately and deeply rooted. [172]**<-

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the highest level of spiritual immersion, known as the "Divine Means" (Śāmbhava-upāya). On the previous page, Abhinavagupta explained that this state occurs instantly, bypassing the step-by-step mental refinements of the "Empowered Means" (Śākta-upāya). Here, he provides a linguistic and philosophical breakdown of how a disciple is "awakened" by an immensely venerable Guru.</meta>

<page-num>205</page-num>
<header>Verse 173 ] The First Chapter</header>

The prefix **"towards"** <note>original: "prati"</note> indicates a state of being "face-to-face" or directed toward something. This directedness requires another object to face; in this context, because it is the most appropriate subject, that object is said to be **pure consciousness alone**. This is why the phrase "facing the Object of Knowledge" was used. 

To explain the meaning of "immense venerability" <note>referring to the Guru's power mentioned in the previous verse</note>, the author used the phrase **"suddenly arising."** By using the word **"suddenly"** <term>drāk; instantly or without delay</term>, he indicates the total absence of the previously described "ascent through the sequence of mental constructs" <term>vikalpa-krama; the step-by-step process of refining one's thoughts to reach the truth</term>. [172]

But one might ask: "How can these two words, which have different grammatical case endings, be in agreement with one another?" <note>The objector is questioning the grammatical relationship between the "Guru" and the "Awakening" in the previous verse.</note> Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->**This is explained by the suffix *-tasi* acting as the third case,**<-
->**or by a lack of grammatical concord.**<-

The expression **"the suffix *-tasi* acting as the third case"** <note>The third case is the instrumental case, meaning "by means of"</note> refers to the usage of the suffix *-tasi* after dropping its silent marker. It is a grammatical rule that this suffix can be applied to a word stem to represent any case ending. 

The word **"or"** indicates an alternative explanation. The phrase **"by a lack of grammatical concord"** <term>vaiyadhikaraṇya; when two words in a sentence do not share the same case ending</term> means: "from that **awakening** which is performed **by the Guru**." <note>The meaning remains the same: the disciple's shift in consciousness is caused by the Guru's presence.</note>

->**Immersion is for one who is not independent,**<-
->**occurring when their non-independent nature sinks away.**<- [173]
->**It is the becoming of that Supreme Nature of Śambhu,**<-
->**attained from the Primordial One who is inseparable from Power.**<-

---

<margin>Line 10: In the Ka. manuscript, the reading is "tasi" twice.</margin>
<margin>Line 13: In the Ka. and Ga. manuscripts, the reading is "that awakening."</margin>
<margin>Line 16: In the Kh. manuscript, the reading "that nature" has been corrected.</margin>

<page-num>206</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

The connection known as **immersion** <term>āveśa; spiritual absorption</term> occurs when the unique, limited form of the dependent and inert **limited knower** <term>pramātṛ; the individual subject</term>—comprised of the intellect and other faculties—is submerged or made secondary. By relying on that submergence, one achieves **identity** <note>original: "tādrūpya" or "tādātmya"</note> with the supreme, independent Consciousness. As it has been stated:

> "The primary status belongs to the agency and consciousness of the Supreme Self, while the state of the void and others becomes subordinate; this knowledge is the defining characteristic of immersion."

One might ask: "From where does this immersion originate?" The author replies: **"From Shambhu"** <note>a name for Shiva, representing the supreme source of consciousness</note>. It does not come from the Power <term>Śakti</term> or the individual soul <term>aṇu</term>. He specifies it comes **"from the First"** because both the Power and the individual soul originate from Him alone. In this specific context, "Power" refers to **Will** <term>icchā</term>, rather than knowledge <term>jñāna</term> or action <term>kriyā</term>, as those two will be discussed later as part of other types of immersion. [173]

In this tradition, the meaning of a whole sentence is understood only after first grasping the meaning of its individual words. Therefore, after organizing the meanings of the words, the author speaks to explain the meaning of the sentence itself:

-> **Therefore, the meaning of the sentence here is this:** <-
-> **The object to be known reveals itself spontaneously,** [174] <-
-> **instantly reflected in the mirror of the Subject,** <-
-> **even without the need for a formal mental determination.** <-

---
Line 6: In manuscript "Ka," the phrase "knowledge of those qualities" <note>original: "tadguṇa-jñānam"</note> is read as a single compound.
Line 11: In manuscript "Ka," the text reads "because it will be explained" <note>original: "vyākhyāsyamānatvāt"</note> instead of "because it is being mentioned."

<summary>This page defines spiritual immersion (āveśa) as the process where the limited individual identity dissolves into the supreme consciousness of Shiva (Shambhu). It emphasizes that this state is driven by the divine Will and results in a spontaneous realization that bypasses normal intellectual processes.</summary>
<keywords>immersion (āveśa), Shambhu (Shiva), divine will (icchā), limited knower (pramātṛ), identity (tādātmya), mirror of the subject, spontaneous revelation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the "Divine Means" (Śāmbhava-upāya), the highest form of spiritual realization in the Trika system. <page-num>207</page-num>
<header>Verse 175 | Chapter One</header>

->**Subordinating the "mother,"**<-
->**Displaying its own glory, [175]**<-
->**It abides in the excellence**<-
->**of the heart’s purity, by degrees.**<-

"What is to be known" <note>original: "vijñeyam"</note> refers to the ultimate form, which is the essence of pure consciousness <term>cinmātra; consciousness alone, without objects</term>. The **"mother"** <note>original: "mātṛ"</note> is the **intellect** <term>buddhi</term>, so called because it is the cause for the production <note>or "giving birth"</note> of the entire assembly of the senses. This same intellect acts as a **mirror**, because it is capable of receiving the reflection <note>original: "saṅkrānti"</note> of the light of consciousness. In that mirror, the **limited knower** <term>pramātṛ; the individual subject</term>—who has falsely grasped a sense of self—is reflected. 

The verse says the realization **subordinates** <note>original: "adharī-kurvat"</note> this limited knower. This means it causes the false obsession of finding the "Self" in the intellect and other faculties to become secondary or subordinate. In this way, through varying degrees of intensity, it manifest's one’s own unique **glory** <term>vibhūti</term>—which consists of establishing the primacy of one's nature as pure awareness. 

By the logic just mentioned, this happens without the ascent of conceptual thought <term>vikalpa</term>. Because it is independent of any other means, it occurs instantly. 

As it is said:

> "This has been described as the essence; it is the **Heart** of the Supreme Lord."

Based on such authoritative sayings, the **Heart** <term>hṛdayam</term> is defined as **self-reflective awareness** <term>vimarśa; the capacity of consciousness to know itself</term>. Its **purity** <term>nairmalyam</term> is its unfading, pristine quality, which comes from not being directed toward anything else <note>i.e., it is entirely self-contained and not distracted by external objects</note>. Its **excellence** <term>atiśayaḥ</term> is the supreme...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of how the practitioner’s consciousness "immerses" into the divine state (Śāmbhava-upāya). Having established that the intellect acts as a mirror for this light, the text now addresses a potential contradiction: if consciousness is the only reality, how do we explain our experience of "inert" objects like colors or stones, and how can consciousness itself be an "object" of knowledge?</meta>

<page-num>208</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

...the limit <note>original: "kāṣṭhā"</note>. In that state, it remains self-manifesting—the meaning is that it shines by its own light. [174–175]

Now, a question arises: The object of knowledge <term>jñeyam; that which is perceived</term> can be of two types: inert <term>jaḍa; lacking consciousness, like a stone</term> or non-inert <term>ajaḍa; conscious</term>. In this context, even an inert object like the color blue can "enter" or occupy consciousness. Why then was it stated previously that "immersion <term>samāveśa; the merging of individual and divine consciousness</term> is of the nature of consciousness alone"? 

To answer this, he says:

->**The knowable is twofold: pure consciousness**<-
->**And the inert; the first is constructed. [176]**<-
->**The other is the Truth;**<-
->**The division between them is thus:**<-
->**Immersion with the inert**<-
->**Takes the form of a reflection. [177]**<-
->**But immersion with Consciousness**<-
->**Is identity, and nothing else.**<-

One might ask: How can self-luminous consciousness ever be "knowable" <note>original: "jñeyatvam"</note>? To be "knowable" usually means to be revealed by a light other than oneself, but consciousness is the light that reveals everything else. Anticipating this doubt, the text says: "the first is constructed" <note>original: "kalpitam"</note>. The particle "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> here is used to signal this very objection. 

For the Supreme Lord himself, through his absolute freedom <term>svātantrya</term>, makes himself appear as an "object" of knowledge during meditation or when receiving instructions—even though his nature as the eternal Knower <note>original: "vedaka-bhāva"</note> is never actually set aside.

<summary>This page explains that while we perceive both "inert" objects and "conscious" states, true spiritual immersion is a realization of identity with pure consciousness, whereas the perception of physical objects is merely a "reflection" within that consciousness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of "immersion" (samāveśa) in the Śāmbhava-upāya section. <page-num>209</page-num>
<header>Chapter 1, Verse 178 ] The First Daily Lesson</header>

With reflections such as "Lord Shiva alone is the agent <term>kartā; the doer or actor</term> of all actions," the text presents Consciousness as if it were a knowable object <note>original: "vedyatayā"</note> by setting aside <margin>Variant reading: "subordinating" (adharīkṛtya)</margin> the pure sense of subjectivity or "I-ness." 

This is indeed the Supreme Freedom <term>svātantrya; the absolute sovereignty of the Divine</term>—that the Divine causes its own nature, which is essentially the Subject (the Knower), to appear as if it were an object of knowledge. For this reason, it was stated previously that this objectified state is "constructed" and lacks absolute, independent reality.

The phrase "the other" refers to inert things <term>jaḍa; lacking awareness</term> such as the color blue. The term "thus" means they are presented as objects of knowledge. In those instances, such as in the "knowledge of blue," the meaning of "immersion" <term>samāveśa</term> is merely the reflection of the blue object within consciousness, following the **analogy of the face in the mirror** <note>original: "darpaṇa-mukha-nyāya"</note>. It is not an actual identity between the two. If there were true identity, then because the blue object would be one with the nature of the knowledge, only the knowledge would remain; the very arrangement of a "reflection" <margin>Variant reading: "the arrangement of objects" (pratikarma-vyavasthā)</margin> would no longer exist.

However, for the "contracted" <note>limited or individual</note> consciousness, "immersion" means realizing its absolute identity with the "uncontracted" <note>infinite or divine</note> Consciousness. This is because, in truth, the individual is nothing but that Infinite Reality. Therefore, it is rightly said that the meaning of "immersion" is the realization of identity with pure Awareness <term>bodha; the light of consciousness</term>. As the definition states: "Immersion is when that which is not independent takes on the nature of the Supreme." [176–177]

He concludes that very point:

->**Therefore, Pure Awareness is free from conceptual thought,**<-
->**And does not depend on practices like meditation. [178]**<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 209 regarding the nature of Shambhava-samāveśa (the Divine Immersion). It clarifies the role of thought and the distinction between the "Way of Shiva" (Śāmbhavopāya) and the "Way of Power" (Śāktopāya).</meta>

<header>The Illustrious Tantraloka</header>

### Having attained identity with Shiva,
### this is the Shambhava immersion.
### "Consciousness" here refers to its contracted form. || 178 ||

Now, a doubt is raised: In the arising of this state, let us grant that there is no requirement for conceptual thought <term>vikalpa; dualistic or discursive mental construction</term>. Indeed, if it were dependent on such thought, there would be no distinction between this and the "Way of Power" <term>śāktopāya; the spiritual path that utilizes the purified mind</term> <note>Variant reading: "dependence on conceptual thought" (vikalpāpekṣatvam)</note>. ->convictions occurring here<-
->may attain identity [with the Divine],<-

By the word "that," he refers to non-conceptual awareness <term>nirvikalpaka-parāmarśa; the direct, intuitive grasp of reality without labels</term>. The attainment of the nature of Shiva <note>original: "śivātmatā-adhigamaḥ"; variant reading: "attainment as the nature of Shiva" (śivātmanābhigamaḥ)</note> has been accomplished by non-conceptual consciousness alone. Since it is impossible to perform an action upon that which is already completed, the conceptual thoughts following in the wake of that immersion are irrelevant to the process. Thus he says, "but they do not serve as the means" <note>original: "na tu teṣām upāyatā"</note>. || 179 ||

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of the idea that non-conceptual spiritual experience requires subsequent conceptual validation to be considered "true" or "valid." It builds on the previous page's assertion that the Shambhava state is complete in itself.</meta>

<page-num>211</page-num>
<header>Verse 180 ] The First Daily Lesson</header>

For this very reason, those who assert that the validity of non-conceptual awareness depends upon conceptual thought <term>vikalpa; discursive or labeling thought</term> are refuted. Thus, the author says:

->By claiming that non-conceptual awareness<-
->is valid only in relation to conceptual thought,<-
->one is refuted; for that which is already established<-
->is merely followed by conceptual thought. || 180 ||<-

A valid means of knowledge <term>pramāṇa; a standard of truth or instrument of correct पहुँचा</term> must indeed have as its object something not yet known. As the authorities say:

> "A valid means of knowledge has an object not yet apprehended, or is the illumination of an unknown thing." <note>original: "anadhigata-viṣayaṃ pramāṇam ajñātārtha-prakāśo vā"</note>

A conceptual thought that follows in the wake of a non-conceptual experience merely defines the very object already grasped by that non-conceptual awareness. Because such thought is a "grasper of the already grasped" <term>gṛhīta-grāhaka; the act of re-cognizing something already known, which in many Indian schools of logic lacks primary validity</term>, it possesses no independent validity within itself. How then could it serve as the cause for the validity of something else? 

Therefore, the author says, "for that which is already established is merely followed by conceptual thought." "Established" <note>original: "siddham"</note> means already apprehended. "Followed" <note>original: "anugamyate"</note> means it is reached or apprehended afterward—that is the meaning. || 180 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: Let it be that conceptual thought operates upon an object already grasped. However, because its nature consists of determinative judgment <term>adhyavasāya; the mental faculty of decision or categorization</term>, its status as a "grasper" is not appropriate...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 211 regarding the relationship between non-conceptual awareness (nirvikalpaka) and the conceptual thought (vikalpa) that follows it. <page-num>212</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras</header>

How can one have the realization, "I am grasping what has already been grasped"? <note>This refers to the logical problem of "re-cognition" where a thought simply labels an experience that has already occurred.</note> Anticipating this question, the author says:

->Because the notion "it is grasped"<-
->is a very clear manifestation of certain judgment. || 181 ||<-
->But the sense "I am grasping" is realized<-
->through the power of unity with the non-conceptual.<-

The notion "it is grasped" is logically consistent because of the presence of conceptual thought <term>vikalpa; the discursive mind that labels things</term>, since its activity is directed only toward an object that has already been apprehended. However, the fact that one realizes "I am grasping" <note>the active, present-moment sense of awareness</note> is due to the power of resting in the oneness of non-conceptual awareness <term>nirvikalpaka; pure, pre-verbal experience</term>. This happens through the unification of the perceived object and the object as it is conceptualized. Therefore, it is rightly said that "what was already grasped is grasped [again] by conceptual thought." || 181 ||

Now, an objection is raised: Knowledge is indeed a revealer <term>jñāpaka; that which makes something known</term> and not a creator <term>kāraka; that which brings something into existence</term>. Therefore, through knowledge, there might be the "cognition" <note>original: "jñapti"</note> of a thing, but not its "perfection" or "establishment" <note>original: "siddhi"; referring to its ontological existence</note>. How then was it said earlier that "that which is established is followed by conceptual thought"? <note>The objector asks: if knowledge only reveals and doesn't create, how can we say the object is "already established" before the thought confirms it?</note> Anticipating this, the author says:

->That very radiance of the object<-
->within non-conceptual self-awareness... || 182 ||<-

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation into how objects are "established" or proven to exist. <page-num>213</page-num>
<header>Verse 183 ] The First Day </header>

->**That establishment does not come from conceptual thought,**<-
->**which is devoid of any dependence on the actual object.**<-

In the Theory of Manifestation <term>ābhāsavāda; the doctrine that all things are manifestations of universal consciousness</term>, it is stated that "to be manifested" is itself "to be established." The "shining forth" <note>original: "sphurattā"</note> of an object is its very proof of existence. 

Now, an objection might be raised: even conceptual thoughts <term>vikalpa; the discursive, labeling mind</term> are themselves non-conceptual in their own nature—meaning, when we have a thought, we experience the *fact* of that thought directly. Since thoughts have this quality of "shining forth," why shouldn't an object be established or made real through them? 

Anticipating this, the author says: "not from conceptual thought." Following the philosophical principle that "all conceptual thought is memory," the very nature of such thoughts is memory <term>smṛti</term>. Memory operates only on an object that was experienced previously and is not currently present. Therefore, conceptual thoughts are "devoid of dependence on the actual object" <note>meaning they do not require the physical object to be there to function</note>. 

Even in cases of "free conceptualization"—where the individual soul <term>kṣetrajña; literally "the knower of the field," referring here to the limited individual</term> constructs new ideas or mental images—those objects are still born from the impressions <term>saṃskāra</term> of previous experiences. This is why the text says they are "devoid of dependence on the actual object." The logic here is: if a thought does not depend on the object's immediate presence, how can it serve as the cause for that object's "establishment" or proof of reality? || 182 ||

If this is the case—if conceptual thought only operates on an object that has already been established by non-conceptual awareness and adds nothing new to its existence—then why is thought even necessary? To this, he says:

->**This is merely an appearance of clarity**<-
->**or its opposite within Consciousness. || 183 ||**<-

<vocab>Manifestation Theory (ābhāsavāda), Conceptual thought (vikalpa), Memory (smṛti), Consciousness (saṃvit), Non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka), Individual soul (kṣetrajña), Dependence on the object (vastvapeksā)</vocab>

<summary>The author argues that conceptual thought cannot establish the reality of an object because thought functions like memory, relying on past impressions rather than the object's immediate presence. Thought serves only to clarify or obscure the pure awareness that has already perceived the object.</summary>
<keywords>ābhāsavāda, vikalpa, smṛti, epistemology, establishment of objects, memory vs perception, Kashmiri Shaivism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the nature of consciousness and its relationship with conceptual thought (vikalpa). Having argued that conceptual thought is like memory and not the primary source of an object's reality, Abhinavagupta now uses the famous "jeweler's metaphor" to show how direct, non-conceptual awareness can perceive complex details instantly.</meta>

<page-num>214</page-num>
<header>The Auspicious Tantraloka</header>

->**Regarding its own nature, consciousness possesses**<-
->**both independence and dependence on conceptual thought.**<-

In everyday life and social transactions <term>vyavahāra</term>, it is a point accepted by all schools of thought that consciousness depends on conceptual frameworks <term>vikalpa; the mental process of labeling and categorizing</term>. However, setting that aside for a moment, the author provides an illustration to clarify how consciousness is fundamentally independent of such conceptualization:

->**Even at midnight, a gem expert—**<-
->**relying on what was shown in a flash of lightning—**<-
->**distinguishes the specific qualities**<-
->**of even a great many jewels. (184)**<-

A jeweler <term>vaikaṭika</term>, even in a flash of light that is momentary and limited, knows the extremely subtle differences between many different jewels. He achieves this not through a slow process of intellectual determination <note>original: "avasāya"; a step-by-step mental labeling</note>, but through the sheer intensity and excellence of his experience <term>anubhavātiśaya</term>. It is through this direct, non-conceptual awareness that he possesses the discernment <term>viveka</term> to say, "This one is small, this is large, and this one is even larger than the others."

What, then, is the cause of this "excellence of experience," which allows an object to be proven real and distinct even without the aid of conceptual thought? The author explains:

->**This is due to the purity of consciousness,**<-
->**and also the power of previous practice. (185)**<-

<summary>Abhinavagupta uses the analogy of a jeweler identifying gems in a lightning flash to prove that direct perception can be incredibly precise without needing slow, conceptual thought. This precision is attributed to the inherent purity of consciousness and the refinement gained through past experience.</summary>

<header>The Holy Tantrāloka</header>

Thus. The reason here is—**within the principles**. These thirty-six principles <term>tattvas; the building blocks of reality</term> contain within them the "Self" (*puman*) and the others. These categories, which fall in the middle of the thirty-six principles, will be explained separately. This section involves the consideration of their distinct divisions, which will be described in the following manner. (186)

->**He defines that very distinction:**<-

->**Since within these principles, the triad**<-
->**consisting of the Self, Pure Wisdom, and Power**<-
->**is divided by numbers corresponding to the**<-
->**oceans, the directions, and the fires, respectively. (187)**<-

The word "divided" is supplied from the context. Therefore, in that context, the **Self** (*puman*) is divided into four types, as stated by authorities such as:

> "This Self is indeed fourfold."

These are represented by the **oceans** <note>original: "ambhodhi"; in Sanskrit poetic code, there are four oceans, so this word signifies the number four</note>. These four are characterized as:
1. The Limited Subject <note>original: "sakala"; the ordinary soul bound by all limitations</note>
2. The Dissolution-Limited Subject <note>original: "pralayākala"; the soul in a state of deep, unconscious rest between world-cycles</note>
3. The Knowledge-Limited Subject <note>original: "vijñānākala"; the soul aware of its purity but not yet united with the Divine Power</note>
4. The Pure Self <note>original: "śuddha"; the liberated state</note>

Similarly, **Pure Wisdom** (*vidyā*) is divided into ten types by the **directions** <note>original: "kāṣṭhā"; the directions or "quarters" of the sky, which are traditionally counted as ten in Indian cosmology, representing the number ten</note>. These consist of the ten levels of subtle sound and consciousness:
1. Articulated Sound (*varṇa*)
2. The Point of concentrated energy (*bindu*)
3. The Half-moon (*ardhacandra*)
4. The Obstructress (*nirodhinī*)
5. Resonance (*nāda*)
6. The End of Resonance (*nādānta*)
7. Power (*śakti*)
8. The Pervasive (*vyāpinī*)
9. The Equalized (*samanā*)
10. The Beyond-Mind (*unmanā*)

Finally, **Power** (*śakti*) is divided into three types by the **fires** <note>original: "jvalana"; in Vedic tradition, there are three primary ritual fires, thus signifying the number three</note>. These consist of:
1. Will (*icchā*)
2. Knowledge (*jñāna*)
3. Action (*kriyā*). (187)

Now, one might ask: why is this triad of principles specified separately from the others?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->**Because the ones known as the Self, Wisdom, and Power**<-
->**are all-pervasive.**<-
->**Therefore, they are surely counted separately**<-
->**from those that are not pervasive. (188)**<-

The phrase "from those that are not pervasive" refers to the other principles that are "pervaded" <note>original: "vyāpyebhya"; meaning they are contained within or limited by the higher ones</note>. Indeed, the pervasion <term>vyāpti; the range or scope of influence</term> of the **Self-principle** extends up to the limit of Illusion <note>original: "Maya"; the boundary where unity appears as multiplicity</note>. The pervasion of the **Wisdom-principle** extends to the limit of the Benevolent Lord <note>original: "Sadāśiva"; the stage where the "I" and the "This" are balanced</note>. And the pervasion of the **Power-principle** extends to the limit of the Absolute <note>original: "Shiva"; the ultimate source</note>. As it has been said:

> "Indeed, they are pervasive up to the respective limits of Illusion, the Benevolent Lord, and the Absolute."

Thus is verse 188.

Not only is this triad distinct from the other principles, but the members are also distinct from each other. He says:

->**Even among themselves, they are distinct**<-
->**due to being impure, being in the process of purification,**<-
->**and being pure. (189)**<-

The **Self** <term>pumān; the individual soul</term> is "impure" because it is composed of duality and differentiation. **Wisdom** is "being purified"—

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) of reality. The previous page discussed the Self (Pumān) as "impure" and Wisdom (Vidyā) as "purifying." <page-num>218</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Tantrāloka</header>

...because it is composed of both difference and non-difference <note>referring to the state of "purifying" wisdom, which bridges the gap between the limited individual and the universal</note>; and **Pure Power** is so called because it is composed entirely of non-difference <note>original: "abhedamayatvāt"; a state of pure unity with the Divine</note>. (186)

Now, one might grant this, but ask: what is the reason for once again mentioning the **Gross Elements** <term>bhūtas; the five physical building blocks: earth, water, fire, air, and ether</term> separately? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->**The gross elements are established through direct perception,**<-
->**whereas the rest of the group of principles is inferred**<-
->**from those elements acting as the evidence of their cause.**<-
->**Therefore, they are indeed designated by a separate name. (190)**<-

To begin with, the gross elements are established through direct perception <term>pratyakṣa; immediate sensory experience</term>. This is the specific reason for taking them up as distinct from the other principles. For those other principles are "always to be inferred" <note>meaning they cannot be seen with the eyes, but their existence must be logically deduced</note>; as he said: "from the group of principles inferred from the elements as their effects."

The logical inference used here is as follows: The gross elements must be preceded by a cause, because, while being insentient, they are associated with a manifold number <note>meaning they are many and diverse rather than a single, simple unity</note>, just like a pot or other physical objects. 

And as for what their cause is: they are the **Subtle Elements** <term>tanmātras; the five subtle "essences" of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell</term>. This is based on the teaching: "And from the subtle elements, the gross elements arise," and so on. The existence of these subtle elements is inferred from their effects, which are the gross elements.

In this way, by this very same method of inference, the entire group of principles ending with **Illusion** <term>māyā; the principle that creates the appearance of limitation and separation</term> is to be inferred. This will be explained further in the section concerning the "Path of the Principles" <note>original: "tattvādhvani"</note>...

<summary>This page explains that while the five gross physical elements can be known through the senses, the higher metaphysical principles of reality must be proven through logical inference, using the physical world as evidence of its subtle causes.</summary>

The phrase "it will be" <note>original: *bhaviṣyati*</note> is not used with great effort here. "Therefore" is said because it is established through direct perception. (160)

Now, one might ask: granted that being established through direct perception is the reason for the **Gross Elements** <term>bhūtas</term> being separate from the group of principles that must be inferred; but why is that same reason used to define their very nature as "elements"? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Whether people are learned or unlearned, that which is the object of existence in a real and ultimate sense <note>original: *pāramārthikena sattāyā gocaram*</note> is what is called a **Gross Element** <term>bhūta</term>. For the word *bhūta* implies that which is "real" or "has become." That is considered "truth" about which there is never any disagreement by anyone at any time.

In contrast, regarding the **Inferred Principles** <note>the subtle levels of reality like the Intellect or the Ego</note>, the unlearned have no cognition of them at all. Even among the learned who do perceive them, there are many types of mutual disagreement. Therefore, in those cases, there remains the possibility of "untruth"—this is the underlying meaning. 

The particle "and" <note>original: *ca*</note> is used here to indicate the underlying reason. Therefore, in this context, "all this" is the "room" or "space" <note>original: *avakāśa*</note>; because it provides that space, it is the **Ether** <term>Ākāśa</term>. Within those four elements ending with Air, which are accompanied by that Ether...

Because the five gross elements, beginning with Earth, are the objects of existence for all types of perception <note>meaning they are accessible to everyone, unlike subtle principles</note>, the wise know the stable presence or status of those element-principles to be distinct. Thus, it was rightly stated that "the name 'element' <term>bhūta</term> comes from another reason entirely."

In this way, the **Immersion** <term>āveśa</term> <note>a state of spiritual absorption or "divine possession" where the seeker's consciousness merges with a higher reality</note> relating to the physical elements is five-fold. The immersion of the **Self** <term>ātman</term> is three-fold. Even though the principle of the individual soul <note>original: *pums-tattva*</note> is a single division of the Self, it must be established as a distinct category among the principles; otherwise, the immersion into the **Principles** <term>tattva</term> <note>the 36 levels of reality in Shaiva philosophy</note> would not be thirty-fold. 

Regarding **Pure Knowledge** <term>vidyā</term>, through the general form of the mantra mentioned just before, the immersion is ten-fold. However, it is also counted among the principles in its specific forms as Mantra, Lords of Mantras <note>original: *Mantreśvara*</note>, and Great Lords of Mantras <note>original: *Mantramaheśvara*</note>. 

Similarly, by establishing one division of **Power** <term>Śakti</term> within the principles, its immersion is two-fold. As for **Śiva**, He is the one into whom all are immersed; therefore, there is no "immersion" into Him—because His nature is supreme non-duality. From His perspective, the distinction between the "one who is immersed" and the "one who causes immersion" <note>the subject-object duality of spiritual practice</note> is impossible. Therefore, it was rightly said that "this immersion is of fifty types." (161)

But one might ask: "In the **Supreme Scripture** <note>original: *Śrī Pūrva Śāstra*, referring to the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra</note>, was it not promised that the worship of the immersion into Rudra's Power would be fivefold, and then the nature of the elements and other categories was described?" # The Immersion into Rudra’s Power

It is for this reason the objection was raised: "What room is there for describing the immersion into elements and so on?"

Furthermore, even though the promise was to describe the **Immersion into the Power of Rudra** <term>rudra-śakti-samāveśa</term> <note>Rudra is a name for Shiva in his fierce, transformative aspect; his "power" (Shakti) is the means by which a seeker reaches liberation. When a topic already under discussion is nearly concluded, and something else that is not the primary subject is mentioned because it is somewhat connected, the resolution <term>samādhi</term> <note>here meaning a logical solution or "justification" for a textual inconsistency</note> is to say: "This was mentioned in passing" <term>prasaṅga</term>. In this case, however, although the primary subject was introduced, without even stating its definitions or examinations, the author spoke of the immersion into elements and so on—

<meta>This page continues the logical defense of why "lower" spiritual immersions—such as those into the physical elements—are included in a text dedicated to the supreme non-dual realization. If it is argued that "this was mentioned by mere chance," what kind of reasoning is that? If that were the case, because irrelevant subjects of inquiry are infinite, one would then be faced with the impossible task of explaining an infinite number of secondary topics. It is for this reason it was said, "this does not win over our minds" <note>referring to the conclusion of verse 163 on the previous page</note>.

The reason for denying that separation is the very fact that this teaching is "free of duality." [164]

**"Whatever else"** refers to the various subdivisions of those principles, such as the various worlds <term>bhuvana</term> and so on. **"Unhindered"** <note>original: *anargalā*</note> means that because she is all-pervasive, she is unobstructed. As it has been said:

...and so on, continuing until the passage:

> "...... Shiva himself is not truly divided."

This will be explained further in the section on the "Differentiation of the Principles" <note>The *Tattva-bhedana* section later in the work.</note>; therefore, for fear of making this book too long, it is not labored over here. [166]

**Objection:** If this is the case, then let us only speak of "immersion" into the Power of Rudra. Why mention immersion into the physical elements <term>bhūta</term> and so on? Does this not bring back the same flaw we discussed? 

Suspecting this doubt...

<summary>Abhinavagupta cites the Shri Purva scripture to argue that even the densest element, Earth, is a fifteen-fold manifestation of divine Power. He concludes that Shiva remains undivided despite these many forms and prepares to address why the text still discusses "lower" forms of spiritual immersion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 223 regarding how the Earth element, though seemingly a "lower" or material reality, is actually a manifestation of the fifteen-fold Power of Rudra. It moves from the scriptural citation to a logical analogy explaining how we perceive a whole through its parts.</meta>

<page-num>224</page-num>
<header>The Shri Tantraloka</header>

Having internalised this, the author now establishes this very point by providing an analogy in the form of a concluding summary:

->**Therefore, just as with an object standing before one,**<-
->**through the medium of its parts, such as its qualities,**<-
->**the awareness of a partless state arises;**<-
->**so too should it be understood in this case. [186]**<-

Just as when an object such as a water-pot <note>original: *ghaṭādau*; a standard example in Indian philosophy to illustrate how we perceive physical objects.</note> is nearby, a correct awareness of its own unique character <term>svalakṣaṇya</term> <note>The specific, individual reality of an object as it exists in itself, rather than a general mental concept.</note>—which is partless and indivisible—arises through the appearance of parts like its redness <note>original: *lauhitya*; the color of the clay used as a specific quality to identify the pot.</note> and the synthesis of various common attributes; in the very same way, it should be understood that the manifestation of the entire Power of Rudra <term>rudra-śakti</term> <note>The divine energy of Shiva that performs the five cosmic acts of creation, maintenance, destruction, concealment, and grace.</note> occurs here through the medium of the elemental parts. [187]

One might ask: "Even if this is so, what is the result?" Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->**Therefore, through qualities such as non-conceptuality,**<-
->**permanence, mastery, and omnipresence,**<-
->**or through other inherent qualities**<-
->**because they are of the nature of Power, [188]**<-
->**either entirely or by way of a part,**<-
->**[one knows] that all-pervading Supreme Lord.**<-

---

<margin>Line 13, Manuscript ‘Ka’ reads: “Therefore, through conceptuality...”</margin> <note>original: *ata eva vikalpa...* This variant suggests a different philosophical emphasis where even conceptual thought can lead to the Divine, rather than the "non-conceptual" state usually preferred in this tradition.</note>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that just as we recognize a whole pot by seeing its specific qualities like color and shape, we can recognize the singular, all-pervading Supreme Lord through the "parts" of the physical elements and His inherent divine qualities.</summary>

->**Those who worship by relying on the**<-

The phrase **For this very reason** means that the understanding of the "Possessor of Qualities" <term>dharmin</term> <note>The underlying reality or Divine Substance that holds various attributes; in this context, the Supreme Lord.</note> occurs through the gateway of understanding the qualities <term>dharma</term> alone. **Firmness** refers to the state of being firm—which is to say, eternity. By **others**, he means qualities such as fullness and so on. By the phrase **inherent in themselves**, he means that these qualities are non-different from the Divine because they are of the nature of His Power <term>śakti</term>.

Whoever relies on the latent impression <term>saṃskāra</term> <note>The residual mental trace or memory left by previous experiences or studies.</note> of the flood of concepts <term>vikalpa</term> concerning specific, fixed qualities—attributes arising from scriptural study and reflection—and enters into the Supreme Lord <term>parameśvara</term> through all the powers just mentioned or even through a single power; they, having become absorbed, find those specific concepts flashing within them as their very own form. Relying on the intensity—that is, the awakening <note>original: *prabodha*</note>—of those qualities or powers (whether they be fixed or unfixed), they attain the full flood of qualities: a nature that is complete because it is inlaid with infinite powers...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 201, which argues that our specific, limited mental concepts actually serve as the necessary "entry points" to experiencing the infinite nature of the Divine. The text transitions from logical reasoning to scriptural authority.</meta>

<page-num>227</page-num>
<header>Verse 202 ] First Chapter . 227</header>

...if it [the conceptualization] were not to take [the Divine Nature] as its object by relying on differentiation through specific attributes <note>original: *tattaddharma*, referring to the specific qualities or characteristics we assign to God</note>, then these types of **experiences**—that is, perceptions—would not arise. These experiences are characterized by **consciousnesses** <term>saṃvid</term> that are diverse in their internal, secondary attributes, yet they reveal the nature of the "possessor of qualities" <term>dharmin</term> through the appearance of a specific, clearly defined attribute. Inwardly, however, these consciousnesses would remain indistinct in form.

This means that if all experiences were to occur within the "possessor of qualities" by encompassing *all* possible attributes at once, then in a case like the word "wandering ascetic" <note>original: *parivrāj*; a standard example in Indian logic where one term evokes a specific set of characteristics</note>, there would be three different simultaneous mental constructs for every single person. Therefore, it is logical that the manifestation within the "possessor of qualities" occurs only through the appearance of attributes specific to each individual perceiver—whether by the power of their own will, according to their specific needs, or through their spiritual proficiency—and not otherwise.

Thus, the manifestation of the **Supreme Lord** <term>parameśvara</term>, despite His having infinite powers, occurs through the manifestation of one specific power or another. [201]

And this is not only proven through logic, but also through scripture <term>āgama</term>. As it is said:

->**As stated in the venerable *Matanga Tantra*:**<-

> **Consisting of the rays of His own powers,**
> **and then "the ground of the Lord"—**
> **thus He is described by these and other specific attributes. [202]**

---

<margin>Line 11, Manuscript K: The reading is "through the manifestation of power in the One of infinite power."</margin>

<meta>This page continues the transition from logical proofs to scriptural evidence. <page-num>228</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras (Shri Tantraloka)</header>

->Within that luminous sky, the Self is radiantly shining,<-
->unshaking and possessing an immovable form.<-
->This is the supreme and subtle Goal,<-
->pervading all directions and consisting of the nectar of immortality. [203]<-

The reality that consists of the rays of His own power is what is meant by the **Station of the Lord** <term>patyuradhiṣṭhānam; the foundation or dwelling place of the Master</term>. This is the connection established by the adjectives used in the text. 

There is a divine scriptural reading that says: *"Now, the Station of the Lord consists of the instruments of His own power."* <note>original: *karaṇa* (instruments/organs)</note> However, the author <note>Abhinavagupta</note> has adjusted the reading in this way to demonstrate the relationship between the initial statement and its subsequent explanation. To reveal these specific attributes, the scripture from "Within that..." up to "is metaphorically described" has been cited. His "own" powers are unique and extraordinary; these very powers are called "rays" because of their non-differentiation from Him, their inherent luminosity, and their infinite nature.

<summary>Abhinavagupta quotes scripture to describe the "Station of the Lord" as a radiant, immovable state of consciousness where the Divine's infinite powers are visualized as rays of light. <meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 204 of the first chapter (Ahnikam). <page-num>226</page-num>
<header>Verse 204 ] The First Daily Lesson</header>

Consisting of that nature, the **Station** <term>adhiṣṭhānam; the base or place of manifestation</term> of the **Lord**—who is the **Possessor of Power** <term>śaktimataḥ</term>—means the "place of manifestation." This is the meaning. Power alone is the means for knowing Him, as it has been said:

> "Just as the directions and other such things are known 
> by the light of a lamp or the rays of the sun, 
> in the same way, O Dear One, Shiva is known through His Power." <note>original: "yathālokena dīpasya..." This is a famous verse from the Vijnana Bhairava Tantra, explaining that God is reached through His energy, just as light reveals the world.</note>

**Thus it is said.** For this very reason, when that Power is shining in the sky <note>The "sky" of pure consciousness</note>, He also appears with a perfectly luminous soul—possessing a **Body of Great Light** <term>mahāprakāśavapuḥ</term>. Because of this, He is **unshaking**—established firmly in His own true form. Indeed, if He, who is the very soul of Light, were to fall away from His own nature, this entire universe would become blind <note>That is, without the "light" of consciousness, nothing could be perceived or exist</note>. 

And for this reason, He is endowed with an **immovable**—that is, a praiseworthy—form consisting of Great Light. Since He exists in this way within the Power who is of such a nature, she is called the **Supreme Goal** <note>original: parā kāṣṭhā; the ultimate limit or pinnacle</note>, the extraordinary **Ground of Rest** <term>viśrāntibhūḥ</term>. 

Therefore, she is **subtle** and impossible to measure or define, because she has the single form of the **Supreme Knower** <note>The highest subject of all experience</note>. For this reason, she is **intensely devoted** to the pure and ultimate Reality; this means she is the very **Vibration** <term>sphurattā; the creative pulse of consciousness</term> of that reality. In this way, by the complete absence of mental impressions <note>saṃskāra; the subconscious traces that cause us to see things as separate</note>, she is the one by whom "external veils have been destroyed"—meaning that, for her, all sense of division has been profoundly stilled. 

Thus, she is **Peaceful**, which means her nature is **Pure Consciousness** <term>cinmātrarūpā</term>. Even so...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final parts of Verse 204 and introduces Verse 205. <page-num>230</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Light of the Tantras (Shri Tantraloka)</header>

"Existing in all directions" means she possesses a **manifold nature** <note>original: chitra-svabhāvā; having a diverse or "variegated" character</note> because she takes the form of the world, which consists of both stationary and moving things. Even so, she is **made of nectar** <term>amṛtātmikā; essentially immortal and blissful</term> and is eternal. For this reason, she is "beyond beginning and end." Indeed, only non-eternal things possess a beginning and an end. Consequently, she is **virtuous** <term>sādhvī</term>—meaning she is free from the impurity of defects like non-eternality. 

In this way, she is figuratively treated as the "body" or **manifest form** <term>mūrtitva</term> of the **Supreme Lord** <term>parameśvara</term>, who is the Possessor of Power. This means she is designated as being identical to Him through a **metaphorical function** <term>gauṇyā vṛttyā; a secondary or figurative application of language</term>.

**[Verses 202, 203, 204]**

Now, an objection might be raised: "In the use of a metaphor, a triad of conditions—such as the obstruction of the primary meaning—must necessarily be present. Does that exist here or not?" Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->**Thus, the cause for this metaphor here**<-
->**is accompanied by a specific purpose.**<-

"Cause" <term>nimittam</term> refers to the reason; for it is only by the force of such a reason that a metaphor can occur. In this context, regarding the designation of the Power as being the "form" of the Possessor of Power, the primary meaning is indeed "obstructed" <note>In Sanskrit logic, a metaphor requires "obstruction" (bādha), meaning the literal sense is set aside to reach a deeper truth. Here, Shakti and Shiva are technically distinct in speech but one in essence</note>. The connection between the two is that of **means** and **goal** <term>upāya-upeya-bhāva</term>.

He expresses this as follows:

->**Through her face, the clarity of the Bearer of Qualities**<-
->**quickly brings about the state of identity with Him.**<-
**[Verse 205]**

The main text here uses 'shaktimadrūpatvābhidhāne' (in the designation of the form...).</meta>
