For this very reason, those powers that draw in limited objects are considered "distant," because due to their lack of pervasiveness <term>avyāpakatva</term>, they are not present everywhere. <meta>This page concludes the discussion on why different deities yield different levels of spiritual results based on their pervasiveness. It then addresses a potential contradiction: why a text focusing on the direct, non-conceptual path (Shambhavopaya) is using logic and sequences that usually belong to the conceptual path (Shaktopaya).</meta>

<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>Verse 210 ] [ First Chapter</header>

The phrase **"those residing below"** refers to powers such as Ishvara and others. This distinction is made because of the difference between a nature that is "Full" and the state of Sadashiva <note>In this tradition, Sadashiva represents a high level of consciousness, but one where the 'subject' and 'object' are still slightly distinct, unlike the absolute unity of the Highest Reality</note>, based on whether that nature is pervasive or non-pervasive. 

Indeed, those who worship a form that possesses a **Full Nature** attain a result that is itself full, characterized by both **worldly enjoyment and spiritual liberation** <term>bhukti-mukti: the tantric ideal where one does not have to renounce the world to achieve spiritual freedom</term>. Conversely, if the nature of the deity is incomplete, the result is likewise incomplete. This is what was meant by the phrase "from the proximity or distance of worship." It is for this very reason that there are different philosophical systems <term>darśana: literally 'visions' or ways of seeing the truth</term>. [Verses 208–209]

*Objection:* But conceptual thought <term>vikalpa</term> is what allows a "universal quality" to appear through the power of our own imagination. Only through the lens of such concepts can the underlying Reality appear to have parts or sequences. Such a sequence belongs to the **Way of Energy** <term>śāktopāya: the spiritual path that uses the mind and pure ideas to reach the truth</term>. It should not apply to the **Way of Shambhu** <term>śāmbhavopāya: the highest, 'pathless' path of immediate, non-conceptual realization</term>, which is characterized by the appearance of an undivided reality. How can this sequence be described here in the context of the highest path?

In response to this doubt, the author says:

->**In this manner, there is a sequence**<-
->**of the conceptual path called the "Shakta" way.**<-
->**But because it is mentioned here, it serves as**<-
->**the non-conceptual counter-correlative.** [Verse 210]<-
<note>Abhinavagupta is explaining that even though he is describing a sequence (which seems conceptual), he does so only to highlight the non-conceptual state that transcends it.</note>

<page-num>234</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

The word **"here"** refers to this section on the **Way of Shambhu** <term>śāmbhavopāya: the highest spiritual path where realization occurs instantly without mental effort</term>. The phrase **"from that"** refers to **conceptual thought** <term>vikalpa: the mental process of dividing reality into distinct names and forms</term>. The author’s intention is this: when the opposing view is fully examined, the intended view is more effectively established. Therefore, nothing said here is irrelevant.

In the realm of conceptual thought, the appearance of the **Indivisible Reality** occurs through a sequence of steps. However, in the realm of **non-conceptual awareness** <term>avikalpa</term>, it occurs without any sequence at all. Thus, wherever a person attains this non-conceptual state, at that very moment and in that very place, they experience **attainment of the nature of Shiva** <term>śivatāpatti: the transformation of individual consciousness into divine consciousness</term>. [Verse 210]

The author says:

-> **Mounted upon the path beyond thought,** <-
-> **by whatever path one may enter—** <-
-> **from the Earth up to the level of Sadashiva—** <-
-> **by that very path, one becomes Shiva.** ॥२११॥ <-
<note>original: "dharā-sadāśivāntena". This refers to the 36 "tattvas" or levels of existence in Tantric philosophy, stretching from the densest material element (Earth) to the highest state of manifestation (Sadashiva). The verse suggests that for one who has transcended ordinary thought, any part of the universe can serve as a doorway to the Absolute.</note>

He provides an example of this:

-> **In the stainless heart, when one attains** <-
-> **that light which shines with expansive radiance,** <-
-> **through that very opening, consciousness reveals** <-
-> **its nature as the Supreme Shiva.** ॥२१२॥ <-

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that while conceptual thought is sequential, non-conceptual awareness (Avikalpa) is immediate. He asserts that once a practitioner reaches this state, any level of reality—from the material to the divine—becomes a direct path to realizing one's identity as Shiva.</summary>

<header>Verse 213 ] Chapter One</header>

Truly, here—within the stainless heart whose nature is the **full "I"-awareness** <term>pūrṇāhaṃvimarśa: the pulsating, self-reflective consciousness of the Absolute</term>—one finds the "foremost." This means that by making the reality pre-eminent through its indivisibility, the manifestation characterized as the **Earth** <term>pṛthivī: the 36th and densest level of existence</term>—which is the thirty-sixth part in relation to the other levels of reality—acts as the means. In this light, which consists of that very appearance, an absorption into the supreme consciousness of Shiva occurs through that very portion of the Earth. This is the meaning. [Verse 212]

-> He summarizes this very point: <-

> **Thus, the disciples of the wise Sumati**
> **know this to be the "Way of Shambhu"—**
> **a state of absorption that is a sublime means,**
> **consisting of a portion of the Supreme Will.** ॥ २१३ ॥

This **Supreme Will** <term>icchāśakti: the divine power of volition</term> is of the nature of the Supreme Goddess <note>original: "parā bhaṭṭārikā". This refers to the highest female principle of divinity in the Trika system.</note>. That portion consists of her. 

> "...but the supreme is considered to be of the nature of Will."

As stated in the passage above, because this is a direct means in comparison to the "Way of Shakti" and others, it is called a "sublime means." Regarding the phrase **"disciples of the wise Sumati"**—this refers to the followers of the venerable Somadeva... <note>Sumati was a teacher in the lineage of Abhinavagupta; Somadeva was his disciple.</note>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 213 of Chapter One, focusing on the lineage of Abhinavagupta’s teachers—specifically Sumatinatha, Somadeva, and Shambhunatha—before transitioning into the discussion of the "Way of Shakti" (śāktopāya).</meta>

<page-num>236</page-num>
<header>Light of the Sacred Tantras <note>original: "Śrītantrālokaḥ"</note></header>

...and others. The venerable **Somadeva** was the disciple of the venerable **Sumatinatha**; his disciple was the venerable **Shambhunatha**—this is indeed the tradition known by those who understand the succession of the lineage. As the author will state later:

> "From the venerable **Soma** <note>a shortened form of Somadeva</note>, Shambhunatha became all-knowing..."

However, it has been stated elsewhere:

> "There was a certain majestic Lord, a manifestation of the Divine Terror, who dwelt in the **Sacred Seat of the Southern Land** <term>dakṣiṇabhūmipīṭha: an important center of Tantric practice, likely in the Deccan region of India</term>. He was the author of scriptures belonging to the **Five Streams** <term>pañcasrota: the five major divisions of the Tantric revelations</term> and the **Sublime Path** <term>ātimārga: an early, highly disciplined path of Shaiva practice</term>. In the world, he was known as **Sumati**. From him arose his foremost disciple, the venerable **Shambhu**, who gained renown from the **Sacred Seat of Jalandhara** <term>jālandharapīṭha: a famous center of Tantric transmission located in North India</term>."

This should be understood as referring to the status of a "Grand-Teacher" <note>original: "paramaguru". Abhinavagupta is explaining why some texts skip Somadeva and link Shambhunatha directly to Sumatinatha.</note>. Alternatively, this explanation should be interpreted by relying on the principle that will be stated later:

> "To the extent that his lineage extends, that entire lineage is considered as one single Teacher."

This should also be understood in passages such as:

> "Thus the venerable Shambhunatha, whose inner darkness was dispelled by the moonlight of the wisdom of the venerable Sumati, described the **True Essential State** <term>sadbhāva: the fundamental reality of consciousness</term> at the beginning of the waking state and so on." ॥ 213 ॥

Now, having established the **Way of Shambhu** <term>śāmbhavopāya: the path of sudden realization through the Divine Will, requiring no mental effort</term>, he now speaks of the **Way of Shakti** <term>śāktopāya: the path of transformation through "pure thought" or correct mental orientation</term>:

## Now, the Way of Shakti is described:
## It is clearly the intellect, the 
## intuitive mind, the thought-mind, and the ego-sense.

<meta>This page transitions from the historical lineage of Abhinavagupta’s teachers to a philosophical analysis of how conceptual thought relates to divine power. It begins the commentary on Verse 214, which explains the relationship between the individual mind and the cosmic powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action.</meta>

<page-num>237</page-num>
<header>Verse 214 ] The First Chapter</header>

## Because of conceptualization, [it is]
## illusory; in reality, [it is] will, etc. || 214 ||

The author clarifies that this process does not involve the mind alone by stating **"intellect, mind, and ego."** For this reason, it is **distinctly** manifest—meaning its nature is directly perceived. Consequently, following the logic that:

> "All conceptualization is the cycle of suffering <term>saṃsāra: the continuous loop of birth, death, and rebirth driven by ignorance</term>..."

it is described as having the nature of the manifestation of duality <note>original: "bhedaprathārūpam"</note>. This is why the verse says it is "composed of illusion <term>māyāmayam: consisting of the limiting principle that makes the One appear as many</term> because of conceptualization." Even so, in the ultimate sense, this process is appropriately composed of the powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action; this is what is meant by the phrase "in reality, consisting of will, etc." 

The core idea is this: just as the Lord <term>Pati: the Supreme Consciousness or Shiva</term> creates the entire universe through His powers of Will and the rest, in the very same way, the limited soul <term>paśu: literally 'the tethered one,' referring to an individual bound by ignorance</term> creates conceptualizations and other mental constructs through the three-fold internal organ <note>original: "antaḥkaraṇa," consisting of intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas)</note>. In the act of conceptualization, the "Knower of the Field" <term>kṣetrajña: the conscious inhabitant of the body</term> possesses a degree of sovereign freedom <term>svātantrya: the innate autonomy of consciousness</term>, and the construction of those thoughts is dependent on this three-fold internal apparatus. This is the meaning of the verse. || 214 ||

Line 13: In the "Kha" manuscript, the reading is "For [of] the Knower of the Field..."
</margin>

<summary>This page explains that while human conceptualization is a product of "Illusion" (Maya) and creates a sense of separation, it is fundamentally a miniature version of the Divine's creative power. The individual soul uses the intellect, ego, and mind to exercise its inherent freedom, mirroring how the Supreme Being creates the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion from Verse 214 regarding how mental processes—usually considered part of the "illusory" world of duality—can be used as a spiritual path. It introduces Verse 215, which explains the transition from the "Means of Power" (Shaktopaya), which uses thought, to the "Means of Shiva" (Shambhavopaya), which is beyond thought.</meta>

<page-num>238</page-num>
<header>The Auspicious Tantrāloaka</header>

### Regarding this, the author says:

->**Through ego-identification, and through the sequence**<-
->**of imagination and intellectual determination,**<-
->**that which belongs to Power, though a means based in illusion,**<-
->**becomes non-conceptual at its conclusion. || 215 ||**<-

In this world, one assumes the role of an agent <note>one who acts or does something</note> by grasping at the "I-sense" <term>ahaṅkāra: the ego or the 'I-maker'</term> within one's own self. One then imagines external objects of desire and the like according to their various forms, and determines their specific nature by the "exclusion of others" <note>original: "anyāpohena," a logical process of defining something by what it is not</note>. 

From this, a conceptual cognition belonging to the "Means of Power" <term>Śākta: the spiritual path utilizing the power of refined thought</term> arises, taking the form of: "I alone am present everywhere," or "Everything is situated within me." 

Although this is technically a "means composed of illusion" <term>māyātmaka upāyaḥ</term>—because all concepts are inherently based on a sense of division—nevertheless, through the strength of practicing these specific concepts, one generates an increasingly refined and elevated state of thought. Consequently, at the very end, there occurs a non-conceptual "Immersion into Shiva" <term>Śāmbhava-samāveśa: a direct state of God-consciousness</term> which is a direct realization of the clearest possible reality. This is the meaning of the verse.

As the author will state later:

> "In this Supreme Nature of the Lord, which has been described in the subsequent chapters, one who desires to enter should quickly perform the refinement of conceptual thought." <note>This refers to the practice of 'Pratipakṣa Bhāvanā'—cultivating a counter-thought to dissolve limiting beliefs.</note>

<margin>Line 9, Manuscript K: Reads "situated, and thus in the middle."</margin>

<summary>This page explains how disciplined, monistic thought (Shaktopaya) serves as a bridge. By dwelling on the idea that "I am all," the seeker eventually transcends thought altogether to reach a direct, non-conceptual experience of the Divine (Shambhavopaya).</summary>

<page-num>239</page-num>
<header>Verse 216 ] First Chapter</header>

### Having begun with such words as:

> "Then, consciousness—nourished by its identity with that clearest and most exalted reality—arrives at its pure, non-conceptual nature." <note>original: "tataḥ sphuṭatamodāratādrūpyaparibṛṃhitā / saṃvidabhyeti vimalāmavikalpasvarūpatām"</note>

Thus, for this very reason, the "Means of Power" <term>Śākta-upāya: the path of using refined ideas to reach God-consciousness</term> is said to be the "Means to the Means" <term>upāya-upāyatva</term> <note>This means Shaktopaya acts as a bridge or a preparatory stage that leads into the higher, direct Shambhava path</note>. || 215 ||

But one might object: "For all of us, isn't a natural, effortless, and non-conceptual awareness <term>nirvikalpa-pratyaya</term> already present in daily life? Why then is that state described as an 'Immersion into Shiva' <term>Śāmbhava-āveśa</term>, and why is it taught as the ultimate goal to be attained?"

Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->**The non-conceptual ground of the limited soul**<-
->**is indeed the supreme state of Shiva.**<-
->**Yet it remains incomplete due to the "wickedness" of the knower;**<-
->**when that disappears, it becomes fully blossomed. || 216 ||**<-

"That" refers to the non-conceptual ground <note>the baseline of awareness before thoughts arise</note>. As it has been stated in other scriptures:

> "In that state <note>of non-conceptual awareness</note>, even the 'beast' <note>original: "paśu," the limited individual bound by the chains of ignorance</note> possesses the divine nature."

If this is the case, then what is the point of spiritual instruction and effort? To this he replies: **incomplete**. For the limited knower, whose perspective is contracted...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of why the "wickedness" or limitation of the ordinary subject prevents the natural non-conceptual state from being full enlightenment. <page-num>240</page-num>
<header>The Splendor of the Tantras (Shri Tantraloka)</header>

The powers of **knowledge and action** <note>original: "jñāna-kriyā"</note> are indeed **contracted** in the ordinary state. Therefore, the point is: how could this "wicked self" <note>original: "durātmanaḥ"; here referring to the soul hindered by the impurity of feeling limited and separate</note> directly possess the **state of Shiva** <term>śāmbhavatva: the unmediated, supreme state of God-consciousness</term>? 

Consequently, once that "wickedness of the knower" <note>original: "mātṛ-daurātmya," the fundamental limitation that makes us feel like tiny, separate individuals</note> is removed, and in a state of total expansion, that **Shambhava state** becomes **fully blossomed** <note>original: "vikasvarā"</note>, characterized by complete knowledge and complete agency. For this reason, it is established that the effort of spiritual instruction and practice is absolutely necessary to bring about the **recognition of one’s own Self** <term>pratyabhijñā: the realization that one is already and always identical to the Divine</term>. This process begins by setting aside the limitations of contracted knowledge and action. || 216 ||

He now applies this same logic to the current subject:

->**Thus, the ground of conceptual thought**<-
->**pertains to the realm of Power—to agency and knowing.**<-
->**Though these are clear, in this state there is still**<-
->**contraction, according to the principle established before. || 217 ||**<-

->**However, for one who is intent upon**<-
->**dissolving the entire mass of contraction,**<-
->**that radiant Power brings about internal manifestations**<-
->**exactly as desired. || 218 ||**<-

<page-num>241</page-num>
<header>Verse 216 ] The First Chapter</header>

In this context of the **Means of Power** <term>śāktopāya: the spiritual path that utilizes purified conceptual thought and the intellect to reach God-consciousness</term>, which is characterized by conceptual knowledge, the powers of knowledge and action are indeed clearly manifest when compared to the non-conceptual state. Nevertheless, due to the **wickedness of the knower** <note>original: "mātṛ-daurātmya"; this refers to the fundamental limitation or "stubbornness" of the ego-bound subject which prevents the realization of the Divine</note>, these powers remain in a **contracted** state. 

For this reason, even here, the effort of spiritual instruction and similar means is absolutely necessary. Through such effort, which is dedicated to the **dissolving of contraction** <note>original: "saṃkocha-vilāyana"; the process of melting away the boundaries of the limited self</note>, that **Ground of Power** <note>original: "śāktī bhūḥ"</note> becomes radiant and blossoming. This occurs because this ground manifests the desired goal: the essential nature of being one with the internal Knower. In other words, it shines forth as being solely focused on the Supreme Knower. || 217 || 218 ||

Now, a doubt is raised: The difference between the **Means of Power** and the **Means of Shiva** <term>śāmbhava: the highest, unmediated path</term> is already established, because one involves conceptual thought and the other is non-conceptual. But how is the Means of Power distinguished from the **Individual Means** <term>āṇavopāya: the path for the "small" or limited individual involving breath, mantras, and external rituals</term>, since that path is also entirely conceptual in nature? Having raised this doubt, the author explains the difference between those two.

->**Wait—is not conceptual thought**<-
->**present in the Individual Means as well?**<-
->**Indeed, it is present there.**<-
->**But here, the teacher has described it as being**<-
->**free from "utterance" and other such practices. || 219 ||**<-

The resolution to this doubt begins with the words "It is indeed there." The phrase "other such practices" refers to **utterance** <note>original: "uccāra"; a technical term for the yogic practice of directing the vital breath or sound upward through the subtle body</note> and the rest.

--- Page 252 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the "Means of Shiva" (the highest, non-conceptual path) to the "Means of Power" (Shaktopaya). The previous page ended mid-sentence, beginning to distinguish the Means of Power from the "Individual Means" (Anavopaya). This page clarifies that while the Individual path relies on external supports like breath and senses, the path of Power is purely mental and occupies a middle ground between unity and diversity.</meta>

<page-num>249</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantraloka</header>

In the **Individual Means** <term>āṇavopāya: the spiritual path for those who still perceive themselves as limited individuals, characterized by effort</term>, the conceptual intellect relies upon external supports such as **breath-movement** <term>uccāra: the practice of directing the vital breath or internal resonance</term> and the like. Here, in the **Means of Power** <term>śāktopāya: the path of purified thought and intellectual realization</term>, the distinction is that it is free from such external reliance. For this reason, it is specified that this path functions "by the mind alone," meaning it is described here as being strictly a matter of internal contemplation. || 219 ||

But a doubt is raised: Is this path free only from **breath-movement**, or is it also free from the use of the **sensory organs** <term>karana: the instruments of perception and action</term> and other such aids? To this, he says:

->By the word "breath-movement" here,<-
->others like it are implied by the plural.<-
->In the Means of Power, these do not exist,<-
->for the nature of Power is Unity-in-Diversity. || 220 ||<-

The phrase "ending in the plural" <note>original: "bahantena"; a grammatical reference to the plural suffix used in the verse</note> signifies that the word "and the rest" is understood. The sense of the phrase should be shown as "free from various forms of breath-movement." "These" refers to the breath-movements, the use of sensory organs, and so on. They "do not exist" in this path because such practices are rooted entirely in a sense of **separation** <term>bheda: the perception of the world as made of distinct, separate objects</term>. 

In this path, because there is an absence of external breath-movement, there is **non-difference** <term>abheda: the state of unity or oneness with the Divine</term>; however, because the path still operates through conceptual thought, the possibility of **difference** <term>bheda</term> also remains. Thus, this path possesses a dual nature. This is why the author says: "the nature of Power is both unity and diversity." In the Individual Means, however, the sense of difference is the primary characteristic. || 220 ||

<meta>This page resolves the objection raised on page 243. The previous page questioned how the intellect (a "lower" faculty) could possibly reach or "pervade" Shiva (the "highest" reality). Here, Abhinavagupta explains that this is possible because the intellect itself is actually Shiva in a concealed form.</meta>

<page-num>244</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

->It is said that, in reality, for us,<-
->Shiva Himself is of that nature.<-
->Having hidden His own essence,<-
->He likewise remains self-luminous. || 223 ||<-

In reality, according to the view of us Non-dualists <term>Advaitavādins: those who hold that the Creator and the creation are one</term>, "Shiva Himself is the one who has assumed the state of the bound soul" <note>original: "śiva eva gṛhīta-paśu-bhāvaḥ"</note>. By the reasoning established in such statements, through the greatness of His own absolute freedom <term>svātantrya</term>, He conceals His true nature and appears as a limited knower <term>pramātā</term> in the form of the intellect and other faculties. 

He Himself, again, by the logic of "unfolding" <note>original: "uddeṣṭana-yuktyā"; like unwrapping a hidden treasure</note>, through the gradual sequence of attaining the <gloss>intellect</gloss>-as-a-means, becomes self-luminous as Shiva. Therefore, regarding the question of whether the intellect and other faculties "pervade" Shiva or not, there is no logical flaw <note>because the intellect is not something separate from Shiva trying to reach Him; it is Shiva Himself "unwinding" His own concealment</note>. || 223 ||

This is stated not only in the non-dualist scriptures; it is also well-defined in the dualist scriptures <term>dvaita-śāstra: scriptures that teach a distinction between God and the soul</term>, as he says:

->In dualistic scriptures such as the *Matanga Tantra*,<-
->this point is also well-established:<-
->That light is determined to belong to Shiva alone,<-
->who pervades all that lies below. || 224 ||<-

---

<note>Line 17: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "the pervasion of the Lord" (prabhorvyāptiḥ).</note>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that the intellect can lead to liberation because it is actually Shiva Himself in a self-imposed state of limitation. He notes that even dualistic scriptures like the Matanga Tantra agree that all light and pervasion ultimately belong to Shiva.</summary>

<header>Verse 226] The First Chapter</header>

->By which the Supreme State shines even<-
->in the realms of the intellect and the mind. || 225 ||<-

As it is stated in that same scripture <note>the *Matanga Tantra*, a dualistic scripture cited to show that even those views support Abhinavagupta's point</note>:

> "Thus, from that virtuous Principle <term>Tattva</term>, the blameless Principle arises, filled with thousands of flashing rays, great and all-pervading below."

He concludes this very point with the phrase "of the one who pervades below," and so on. "He" refers to the one who takes the form of the intellect and other faculties. "By which" <note>original: "yena"</note> refers to the reason: because the intellect and other faculties possess the nature of Shiva’s light alone. || 224-225 ||

Having spoken thus on this incidental topic, he now returns to the main subject:

->Indeed, without being rooted in That,<-

The word "toward" <note>original: "prati"</note> signifies "facing" or "moving in the direction of." By this, he means that both of these <gloss>the Empowered and Individual immersions</gloss> find their final rest in the Immersion of Shiva <term>Śāmbhava-samāveśa: the highest state of absorption where the soul realizes its identity with the Divine</term>, which is the essence of the Supreme Light. 

The phrase "without being rooted in That, nothing at all exists" means that whatever does not rest in that Supreme State would be "nothing," because it would lack the light of consciousness to even be manifest.

<header>The Illustrious Light of the Tantras</header>

...Thus, in this way, it is stated that the Supreme Light <term>Prakāśa: the fundamental radiance of consciousness that allows everything to be known</term>, which is of the nature of the Concept-free <term>Nirvikalpa: a state of direct experience that precedes mental labels and language</term>, is the single spiritual means <term>Upāya</term> for all of these states. || 226 ||

And this is not merely our own invention; as he says:

->The fruit of Pure Consciousness here<-
->should not be conceptualized; therefore he spoke.<-
->The primacy of conceptualization<-
->is indeed indicated right here. || 227 ||<-

"Therefore" <note>original: "ataḥ"</note> refers to the fact that all paths ultimately enter into that one and only Concept-free Consciousness <term>Saṃvitti</term>. As it has been stated <note>in the *Matanga Tantra*</note>:

> "The wise should not conceptualize a distinction in the fruit of Pure Consciousness here."

In this context, because there are a variety of spiritual means, one might naturally arrive at the conceptualization of a "difference in fruits" (distinct results for different paths). Otherwise, if such a notion were not already likely to occur, a prohibition against it would not even be necessary <note>Abhinavagupta employs a logical rule here: a "prohibition" (negation) is only meaningful if the thing being prohibited is first perceived as a possibility</note>. By saying "should not be conceptualized," this possibility is acknowledged and then dismissed. This is what he means by the phrase "the primacy of conceptualization." "Primacy" <note>original: "mukhyatvam"</note> here refers to the status of being the primary subject under discussion. "Indicated" means it is hinted at rather than stated directly. || 227 ||

Furthermore, the reality of "resting" <term>viśrānti: the state of meditative repose or returning to one's source</term> in the Concept-free state is not found only in this system; it is found even in the views of those outside of it <note>referring to rival philosophical schools like the Buddhists or the Dualists</note>, as he says:

When he eventually reaches the arising of a natural, spontaneous <note>original: "svārasikasya"</note> Concept-free state that no longer requires these methods, he is then counted as a true "gem-knower" regarding that object... <meta>The sentence continues onto the next page</meta>

The meaning of the sentence is: "he is called one who knows the Reality as concept-free." -> **For action is nothing other than consciousness** <-
-> **assuming a sequential form...** <-

--- Page 260 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on how ritual action is fundamentally identical to consciousness (vijñāna). It addresses the logical problem of how a Guru's knowledge can liberate a disciple if knowledge is the sole cause of liberation.</meta>

<page-num>250</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras <note>original: Śrī Tantrālokaḥ</note></header>

->**That which is obtained through the force of means**<-
->**was previously stated to be "action." || 232 ||**<-

"That" <note>original: tat</note> refers to knowledge <term>vijñāna: specific discernment or spiritual realization</term>. "Previously" <note>original: purā</note> refers to the earlier discussion [starting with the verse] "Since there is no other thing named action," etc. || 232 ||

Now, an objection: It has been established through statements like "Knowledge is the sole cause of liberation" <note>original: jñānaṃ mokṣaika-kāraṇam</note> that "liberation comes from knowledge." But does this [liberating] knowledge reside in one’s own self <note>one's own locus</note>, or in another person? 

If it resides in one's own self, does it liberate whether or not initiation <term>dīkṣā: the ritual process of spiritual purification and transmission</term> has occurred? If you say it liberates even without initiation, then we must consider the rule:

> "Without initiation, there is no authority <term>adhikāritā: the formal spiritual eligibility or competence</term> in the Yoga of Shiva <note>original: Śāṅkare</note>."

According to such statements, if there is no initiation, there is no authority even to attain knowledge; so how could knowledge exist to liberate anyone? If you say knowledge only liberates when initiation is present, then there is a dependence on another, since it is logically impossible for one to perform initiation upon one's own self. 

On the other hand, if the knowledge resides in another person <note>such as the Guru</note>, then a major logical error arises: the cause <note>knowledge</note> would be in one place, while the effect <note>liberation</note> would be in another. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->**Perfect knowledge is the sole cause**<-
->**of liberation, whether residing in self or other.**<-
->**For indeed, the distinctions of self and other**<-
->**are nothing more than mental constructs. || 233 ||**<-

---

<margin>Line 17: Manuscripts G and GH read "situated within one's own self" <note>original: svaparisthitim</note> [instead of "self or other"].</margin>

<summary>This page clarifies that "action" is actually a form of knowledge and resolves a logical paradox regarding initiation: because the distinction between "self" and "other" is a mental construct, the Guru's knowledge can effectively liberate the disciple.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding whether knowledge resides in the Guru or the disciple. It resolves the paradox by explaining that from the perspective of ultimate reality, the distinction between "self" and "other" is a mental construct, and liberation occurs when this distinction dissolves into the unity of consciousness.</meta>

<page-num>251</page-num>
<header>Verse 234 ] First Chapter <note>original: prathamāhnikam</note>. 251</header>

The distinction is merely a construction <note>original: kalpanāmātram</note>. The intention is that in reality, only a single Consciousness <term>saṃvit: the pure, non-dual awareness that underlies all experience</term> shines forth, manifesting as the various levels of reality, starting from the Supreme and descending through the others. || 233 ||

For this very reason, the author says:

->**Even though the mental construction [of self and other] is the same,**<-
->**whenever there is a manifestation of oneness,**<-
->**the Guru is then considered a single Self,**<-
->**and is called "perfected" and "liberated." || 234 ||**<-

Even though the mental construction of "self" and "other" is equal in relation to the Guru, the non-guru, and others, when a disciple or a Guru achieves "oneness"—that is, unification—there is a "manifestation" <note>original: sphuraṇa</note>. This manifestation is a reflective awareness <term>vimarśana: the self-referential capacity of consciousness to "know" itself</term> in the form of a single, solid mass of consciousness <note>original: ekaghana-saṃvit</note>, without any division between the appearances of "self" and "other." 

At that moment, the Guru—who is defined by that limit of the manifestation of oneness—becomes a single Self. Being in such a state, he is called "perfected" <term>siddha: one who has attained supernatural powers or spiritual completion</term> and "liberated" <term>mukta</term>. This means he is described as being nothing but Supreme Sovereignty <term>pāramaiśvarya: the absolute power and freedom of the Divine</term>. 

The point being made is this: as long as there is a cognitive grasping <term>parāmarśa: the act of mentally "touching" or identifying with an object or state</term> of his own consciousness as the sole Self, he shines forth as one who has attained identity with the Supreme Light <term>paraprakāśa: the ultimate, self-shining illumination of Shiva</term>.

<page-num>252</page-num>
<header>The Tantraloka <note>The "Light on the Tantras," the masterwork of the philosopher-saint Abhinavagupta</note></header>

->“Thus, one who knows this pervasion <term>vyāpti: the way the supreme consciousness permeates all lower levels of reality</term><-
->through the division of the supreme and the non-supreme,<-
->becomes a liberator; he is manifestly Shiva, the ultimate cause.”<-

For this very reason, the author says:

->As far as his lineage <term>santāna: literally a "continuum" or "stretching out," referring to the succession of disciples and their students</term> extends,<-
->the Guru is said to be that vast.<-
->Being composed of perfect knowledge,<-
->he is liberated from that [continuum] through his own Self. || 235 ||<-

->Therefore, the wise one<-
->saves his own lineage; this<-
->is established through both logic and scripture,<-
->because the Sage is one with that [entirety]. || 236 ||<-

The "lineage" takes the form of disciples, grand-disciples, and so on; it is perceived as a single Self because of the manifestation <note>original: sphuraṇa</note> of this [Guru] alone. The phrase "from that" refers to that entire lineage. Indeed, by resting upon the extent of that lineage through the oneness of Consciousness <term>saṃvit: the fundamental, non-dual awareness</term>, the Guru is a single entity. Thus, when the members of the lineage are liberated, it is the Guru himself who is liberated through his own Self. Since the distinction between "self" and "other" is merely a mental construct <note>original: kālpanikatvāt</note>, there is no logical error in this view. This is why the author says, "Therefore," and so on, and "he saves." As it has been stated:

<page-num>253</page-num>
<header>Verse 238 ] Chapter One <note>original: prathamāhnikam; literally the "first daily lesson" or "session"</note></header>

> “The Teacher <term>ācārya: a master who understands the scriptures and establishes his students in good conduct</term>, through his complete realization of Knowledge and the Object of Knowledge, shall cause all his own people—even across thousands of millions of lineages—to cross over the ocean of worldly existence.”

This is the scriptural authority. The reasoning for this is: "Because the Sage <note>original: muni</note> is that singular and vast." In this context, "Sage" refers to the Guru. **|| 235 || 236 ||**

Since this is the case, the refutation of flaws <term>dūṣaṇoddhāra: the logical removal of objections or "faults" raised by opponents</term> raised by others is achieved without any extra effort. Thus, the author says:

->Therefore, those who raise objections here [saying]:<-
->“Surely, liberation comes only from Knowledge.<-
->But this ritual action, such as initiation <term>dīkṣā: the transformative ritual that bestows spiritual wisdom and severs worldly bonds</term> and the like,<-
->how could it possibly lead to liberation? || 237 ||<-
->If you argue that this ritual itself consists of Knowledge,<-
->then Knowledge should liberate only the person in whom it resides.<-
->If it were to liberate someone else,<-
->would that not be logically inconsistent?”<-
->In this way, those objections are cast aside at their very root,<-
->despite what others have attempted to argue here. || 238 ||<-

---

Line 11: Manuscript K reads "If it consists of Knowledge, then Knowledge..."; Manuscript Kh reads "If it is from Knowledge, then Knowledge..."
Line 14: Manuscript K reads "is it not consistent..." <note>original: nāma sāmañjasam</note>.

<summary>Abhinavagupta cites scripture to show that a Guru's realization saves his entire spiritual lineage and uses the concept of "unified consciousness" to dismiss the logical objection that ritual action or another's knowledge cannot liberate a disciple.</summary>
<keywords>Guru, lineage, initiation, dīkṣā, liberation, non-dualism, spiritual continuum, Tantraloka</keywords>

--- Page 264 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Chapter One of the Tantrāloka. Having previously addressed objections regarding how a Guru's ritual action can liberate a disciple, Abhinavagupta (via Jayaratha’s commentary) now focuses on the dualistic misconception that "impurity" is a physical substance that needs to be removed by a physical ritual.</meta>

<page-num>254</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Tantrāloka</header>

Those arguments which are of the nature of dualism <note>original: bhedavāda-prakārāḥ</note>, and which raise such objections, are cast aside—meaning they are rejected. This is because, at the very root of our system, the unity of Knowledge and Action <term>jñāna-kriyā: in Non-dual Shaivism, knowing and acting are two sides of the same divine consciousness</term> is accepted, and the distinction between "self" and "other" is recognized as being merely imaginary <note>original: kālpanikatvam</note>. This indeed is the only resolution here, and no other. Thus, the author says "But that which..." and so on. The connection to the text is: that which has been described by other Dualist Teachers <note>original: bhedeśvaravādibhiḥ; referring to the Shaiva Siddhānta school which views God, souls, and impurity as eternally distinct</note> will be refuted later on. **|| 237 || 238 ||**

Now, one might ask: if the dualistic view that "impurity" <term>mala: the spiritual "stain" or limitation that binds the soul</term> is a physical substance <note>original: dravya</note> is not accepted, then what is its nature? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->“Impurity, it is said, is a physical substance,<-
->Like a cataract <note>original: paṭala</note> in the eye and so forth.<-
->The ritual action of Initiation <term>dīkṣā</term> is its destroyer,<-
->Like the application of medicinal ointment.” || 239 ||<-

->“We shall refute that [view] later on,<-
->As it is condemned by both logic and scripture.<-
->And of Impurity, Illusion <term>māyā</term>, and Action <term>karma</term>,<-
->We shall demonstrate their true status.” || 240 ||<-

---

Line 3: Manuscript K reads "unity was accepted" <note>original: aikyamupagatam</note>.
Line 11: Manuscript K reads "destroyer" <note>original: vihantrī</note>; Manuscript G reads "like ointment and so forth" <note>original: tvāñjanādīti</note>.

<summary>Abhinavagupta begins to critique the dualistic view that spiritual impurity is a physical substance, comparing it to an eye disease that a ritual cures like medicine. He argues instead that impurity is a limitation of consciousness, promising a deeper explanation of Mala, Maya, and Karma.</summary>
<keywords>dualism, non-dualism, impurity, initiation, logic, scripture, consciousness, ritual action</keywords>

--- Page 265 ---
<meta>This page continues the first chapter of the Tantrāloka, where Abhinavagupta and his commentator Jayaratha are systematizing the different "means" (upāyas) of spiritual realization. Having dismissed the dualistic view of impurity as a physical substance, they now rank the three primary methods of practice—Individual, Empowered, and Supreme—before introducing the highest state: the "Means-less" way.</meta>

<page-num>255</page-num>
<header>Verse 241 ] Chapter One: The Daily Lesson on the Nature of Consciousness</header>

The author [Abhinavagupta] concludes this very topic by adding further detail:

->**Thus, regarding the knowledge that has three powers as its means,**<-
->**the last among them is the root;**<-
->**the one following it is the middle;**<-
->**and the first is the highest of all. || 241 ||**<-

The "last" refers to the Individual Means <term>āṇavopāya: the path of the limited soul using breath, ritual, and meditation</term>. The "root" refers to this same level as the starting point. Its state of coming to rest within the Supreme state <note>original: śāmbhava</note> by way of the Empowered path <note>original: śākta</note> is what he means by the phrase "the one following it." Therefore, the Empowered means is "following" (or higher than) the Individual means because it serves as its place of repose <note>original: viśrānti-sthānatvād</note>. Even higher than the Empowered is the Supreme means. As it has been said:

> "Immersion <term>samāveśa: the state of being 'possessed' by or fully absorbed into Divine Consciousness</term> is considered threefold, arising from the connection with the All-Pervasive Lord, His Power, and the Individual Soul. Linked to the powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action, each is progressively more complete than the last."

**|| 241 ||**

Not only is the Supreme means <note>original: śāmbhava</note> excellent as the ultimate resting place for the Individual and Empowered paths; there is another state even beyond this, called the "Means-less" path <term>anupāya: the highest realization where no effort or practice is required because the self is recognized as already identical to God</term>. Thus he says:

->**Beyond even that is the supreme knowledge,**<-
->**which is entirely devoid of means and the like.**<-

---

</margin>

--- Page 266 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of page 255 regarding the "Means-less" way (anupāya). Having established the hierarchy of the three primary paths—Individual, Empowered, and Supreme—Abhinavagupta now introduces the "Ultimate" state, which transcends all methods and rests in pure Bliss.</meta>

<page-num>256</page-num>
<header>The Light of the Tantras</header>

### This state is described here as the Ultimate,
### resting within the Power of Bliss. || 242 ||

This state is called "Supreme" <note>original: paramam</note> because its nature consists exclusively of the goal to be attained <term>upeya: the final destination of spiritual practice, as opposed to the methods used to get there</term>. For this very reason, it has been described previously as being "entirely devoid of any practical means." 

And this is also why it is said to "rest within the Power of Bliss" <note>original: āṇanda-śakti</note>. Regarding the other powers, such as the power of Will <note>original: icchā-śakti</note>, they are directed toward external objects and are limited by the specific things to be desired or known. Because of this outward focus, there is still the possibility of a sense of duality or division. The Power of Bliss, however, is different. As it is said in the sacred texts:

->**"Bliss is the very nature of the Absolute."**<-

By such statements, it is understood that Bliss is the essential nature of Consciousness itself. Therefore, the underlying point is that in this state, there is not even a trace <note>original: gandha, literally "scent"</note> of a "means" <term>upāya: a technique, ritual, or disciplined practice used to achieve liberation</term>. || 242 ||

Lest one think this is merely his own invention, the author explains that this is taught everywhere in the Traditions <term>āgama: the divinely revealed scriptures of the Tantric tradition</term>:

### This self-luminous realization,
### the existence of which is difficult to attain 
### even for the Lords and Ladies of Wisdom,
### is described in the venerable Siddha Tantra. || 243 ||

### This was also clearly indicated 
### in the eighteenth chapter of the Mālinī scripture.

This self-luminous realization is described in the venerable *Siddha Tantra* as a state of being that is rare and difficult to achieve even for the Lords of Wisdom <term>vidyeśvara: high-level spiritual beings who govern the pure regions of the universe</term> and the Ladies of Wisdom <note>original: vidyā-vidyeśvara</note>. Furthermore, this same teaching was clearly pointed out in the eighteenth chapter of the *Mālinī* <note>referring to the *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*, the most authoritative scripture for the Trika school of Shaivism</note>.

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines the Ultimate state (Anupāya) as resting in pure Bliss, a state so high it transcends all techniques and is rare even for celestial beings. He cites the Siddha Tantra and Mālinīvijayottara Tantra to authorize this "Means-less" path.</summary>

<keywords>Power of Bliss, Ultimate state, Means-less path, Siddha Tantra, Mālinīvijayottara Tantra, Lords of Wisdom, Absolute, Consciousness</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 256, where Abhinavagupta is explaining that the supreme realization of the "means-less" way (anupāya) is not something that can be seized by personal effort alone. It concludes the thought that this realization is difficult to attain without divine grace.</meta>

<page-num>257</page-num>
<header>Verse 244 ] The First Lesson</header>

->**"...and this is not [taught] by an ungracious**<-
->**Shankara," according to this very statement || 244 ||**<-
->**found in the text of the**<-
->***Supreme Mālinīvijaya*.**<-

In that scripture <note>original: Mālinīvijayottara-tantra, the primary authority for the Trika school of Shaivism</note>, it is said:

> "O Lord of Yoga, best among the knowers of Yoga! I wish to hear of that Yoga which is effortless <note>original: anāyāsam</note>, without need for preparation, entirely without ritual means <term>anupāya: the highest stage of practice where no external or internal technique is required because one rests in pure consciousness</term>, and yet yields the greatest fruit."

When the Goddess <note>Devi, the consort and student of Shiva</note> asked this, the Lord replied:

> "Listen, O Goddess, I shall describe this unsurpassed nectar of Yoga, by attaining which mortals reach the state of Shiva <note>original: śivatām</note> while being freed from all strenuous effort.
> 
> And this is not taught by Shankara <note>a name for Shiva, meaning "The Beneficent"</note> unless he is gracious <note>original: aprasannena, referring to the lack of divine grace or 'shaktipata'</term>. Even if one somehow obtains this through deception, the true inner resonance <term>vāsanā: a latent impression or spiritual 'perfume' that transforms one's character</term> does not take root."

Continuing the passage:

> "Therefore, one should practice this constantly with a mind that is never weary. That, O Great Goddess, is the 'Emission' <term>visarga: the creative outpouring of divine consciousness where the practitioner finds final rest</term> where one deserves to find peace.
> 
> That alone is called the 'Mouth of the Teacher' <note>original: guru-vaktram</note>; it is called the 'Circle of Powers' <term>śakticakra: the assembly of divine energies that govern the senses and the universe</term>. That is the supreme place of origin for all sacred mantras."

Thus it has been stated. || 243 || 244 ||

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the Mālinīvijaya Tantra, concluding the introductory section on the "means-less" way (anupāya) and transitioning into the formal declaration of the purpose of this entire treatise, the Tantrāloka.</meta>

<page-num>258</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>The Light of the Tantras</header>

And this is indeed the intended meaning of the scripture; as he states:

->**Thus, this fourfold knowledge,**<-
->**which is the great dawn of power and liberation,**<-
->**is now being expounded by me in this teaching**<-
->**known as the "Light of the Tantras" || 245 ||**<-

Regarding the word "Thus" in the title *Tantrāloka*: it is like a light <note>original: āloka</note> for the Tantras <note>the revealed scriptures of the Supreme Lord</note>, or rather, it is that which "beholds" <note>original: ālokayati</note> or illuminates them. "Thus" refers to the fourfold knowledge <term>jñāna-catuṣka: the four levels of spiritual practice in the Trika system—the means-less (anupāya), the divine (śāmbhava), the empowered (śākta), and the individual (āṇava)</term> whose nature has been described.

Of what nature is this? It is described as "the great dawn" <note>original: mahodaya</note> because within it occurs the great rising of both supernatural power <term>siddhi: worldly success or miraculous powers attained through yoga</term> and spiritual liberation <term>mukti: the final release from the cycle of rebirth</term>. This knowledge is "expounded" <note>original: tanyate</note>—meaning it is illuminated in great detail—here in this teaching, the *Tantrāloka*. || 245 ||

Now, it is often said:

> "Reasoning does not operate upon matters that are unperceived, nor upon those already fully decided. Rather, reasoning <term>nyāya: logic or the systematic method of inquiry</term> applies to that which is doubted; therefore, doubt is an essential limb of reasoning."

Following this principle, it is understood that the composition of a scripture intended to provide definitive realization is generally undertaken only when a subject is a matter of doubt. Since doubt is an essential component <note>original: tadamgatvāt, a "limb" or necessary precursor</note> of this process, the author begins by first determining the actual nature of doubt itself.

---

<margin>Line 14: In manuscript ‘Ka’, the reading is: "Logic is a limb of logic, therefore..."</margin>

<vocab>Tantrāloka (The Light of the Tantras), Shāstrārtha (meaning of the scripture), Jñāna-catuṣka (fourfold knowledge), Siddhi (spiritual power), Mukti (liberation), Nyāya (logic/reasoning), Saṃśaya (doubt)</vocab>

<summary>Abhinavagupta formally introduces his work, the Tantrāloka, as an illumination of the four types of spiritual means and transitions into a philosophical inquiry into the nature of "doubt" as the starting point for all systematic teaching.</summary>
<keywords>Tantraloka, fourfold knowledge, siddhi, liberation, logic, doubt, epistemology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the end of the previous page regarding the role of reasoning and doubt. Abhinavagupta is now defining the psychological and epistemological nature of "doubt" as the starting point for inquiry in the Tantrāloka.</meta>

<page-num>259</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>[Verse 247] The First Daily Lesson</header>

->**In this world, whatever is perceived,**<-
->**whether it be internal or external,**<-
->**first shines forth in a form**<-
->**that is "unopened." || 246 ||**<-

"Internal" refers to states such as mental consciousness <term>mānasa-vijñāna: the internal sense-mind that processes thoughts and feelings</term>. Regarding the phrase "unopened form" <note>original: anudghāṭita-rūpam</note>: it means a state consisting of a general characteristic <term>sāmānya-dharma: a universal quality, such as "object-ness," before specific details are noticed</term> where specific distinctions have not yet been delineated. This is the meaning. || 246 ||

And he explains that it is primarily this state that is called "doubt":

->**Thus, a manifestation that has**<-
->**an unopened form and an indefinable nature**<-
->**is "doubt." Once a specific form**<-
->**is determined, it is no longer so. || 247 ||**<-

"Thus" refers to the primary state where the form is "unopened"—it is "unsealed" because specific distinguishing features, such as hands or feet <note>the specific parts that would identify a shape as a human being</note>, have not yet been perceived. Rather, there is only a general characteristic, such as "height" or "uprightness." Because of this, it is "indefinable" <note>original: anirvācyena</note>; since there is no certainty regarding the specific property of one possibility or the other, the awareness hangs between two alternative aspects.

---

<margin>Line 15: In Manuscript 'K', the reading is "a specific property of either side" <note>original: anyatara-dharme-viśeṣa</note>.</margin>

<note>The vocabulary listed at the bottom of the original page includes: doubt, unopened form, general characteristic, indefinable, shines forth, and mental consciousness.</note>

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines "doubt" as the initial, indeterminate stage of perception where an object's general qualities are visible but its specific identity remains "unopened" or undecided.</summary>
<keywords>doubt, saṃśaya, perception, general characteristic, sāmānya-dharma, epistemology, Abhinavagupta, Tantrāloka</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical definition of "doubt" (saṃśaya) according to Abhinavagupta’s epistemology. The previous page established that doubt begins with an "unopened" perception where only general features are visible. Page 260 now clarifies the relationship between the general substrate and the specific, hidden qualities.</meta>

<page-num>260</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>The Light of the Tantras <note>original: Śrītantrālokaḥ</note></header>

A manifestation—meaning a perception—that is characterized by an essence or nature that is impossible to describe in a fixed, definite way is called **doubt**. This doubt arises when a general characteristic <term>sāmānya-dharma: a universal quality shared by many things, such as "uprightness"</term> is understood, but specific characteristics <term>viśeṣa-dharma: unique traits that distinguish one object from another</term>, such as the crookedness or hollows of a tree trunk, are not yet understood. 

The author states "somewhere" <note>referring to the previous verse</note> to mean: within some substrate <term>dharmin: the "thing" or object that possesses qualities</term> which is defined by those general characteristics. The phrase "not otherwise" means that doubt does not occur when a substrate is either completely determined or completely unknown. || 247 ||

He explains this further by breaking it down:

->**In this primary state of "What is this?",**<-
->**the "this" part is well-ascertained.**<-
->**Doubt is that whose nature consists of**<-
->**unopened attributes like "existence" or "non-existence." || 248 ||**<-

"What is this?"—this is the reflective awareness <term>parāmarśa: the mind's internal "grasping" or naming of an experience</term> that constitutes doubt. It is "primary" <note>original: mukhya</note> because all specific characteristics remain unopened, unlike in subsequent reflections such as "Is it a fence-post or a human being?" In that state, compared to the "what?" part, the "this" part is perfectly certain <note>original: suniścita</note> because the observer has successfully grasped the bare substrate <note>the observer knows "something" is there, even if they don't know "what" it is</note>. But—

---

<note>Line 3: Manuscript 'K' reads "the comprehension of the pervasion of attributes, and the crookedness/hollows..." <note>original: dharma-vyāpty-adhigame vakra-koṭaratva</note>.</note>

<vocab>doubt, Tantrāloka, substrate, specific attribute, general nature, comprehension, well-ascertained, existence, non-existence</vocab>

<summary>This page defines doubt as a specific mental state where the object (the "this") is certain, but its specific qualities (the "what") remain "unopened" or hidden. It explains that doubt requires seeing a general shape without seeing the details that would identify it definitively.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of the definition of doubt (saṃśaya) from Verse 248. The previous page introduced the concept of an "unopened" perception where the "this" (the object) is known generally, but its specific nature remains hidden. This page explains why this state is considered the "primary" or purest form of doubt.</meta>

<page-num>261</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>Verse 248 ] First Chapter <note>original: prathamāhnikam</note></header>

->**"Doubt is a reflective awareness that does not lean on either of two fixed alternatives."**<-
<note>original: niyato-bhayāṃśā-navalambī vimarśaḥ saṃśayaḥ</note>

This is the formal definition of doubt. Regarding this, if any one part or alternative were certain, the doubt would be resolved by it; thus the author says, "Doubt," and so on. The phrase **"existence and non-existence"** refers to the specific characteristics <term>viśeṣa-dharma: unique traits that identify what an object is</term> starting with whether a thing exists or not. An **"unopened nature"** means the essential form <term>ātman/svarūpa: the core identity of the object</term> has not yet been "unsealed" by these specific characteristics. 

Indeed, where even the basic qualities of "being" and "non-being" remain uncertain and have not been "unsealed," what can be said of other, more specific qualities? Therefore, because the forms of all specific qualities are not yet clearly outlined, and because the mind does not lean on any fixed characteristic, this is considered **primary doubt**. The sense is that the "What?" portion of the thought "What is this?" indicates a form whose objective meaning has not yet been etched out or determined. || 248 ||

He explains this:

->**In this word "What?",**<-
->**no additional meaning shines forth.**<-
->**"Additional" means anything beyond the meaning of the word "this."**<-

If that is the case, why is "this" even used as a condition? Raising this doubt, he says:

---

<note>Line 2, Manuscripts K. and Pu.: the reading is "if this part."</note>
<note>Line 4, Manuscripts K. and Pu.: the reading is "existence, non-existence, etc."</note>
<note>Line 7, Manuscripts K. and Pu.: the reading is "unsealing has not occurred due to uncertainty."</note>
<note>Line 10, Manuscripts K. and Pu.: the reading is "referring to a form that is not yet etched out."</note>

<summary>This page defines the purest form of doubt as a state where the mind cannot settle on any specific attribute—even basic existence or non-existence—of a perceived object. It distinguishes between the general awareness of an object ("this") and the unresolved inquiry into its nature ("what?").</summary>
<keywords>doubt, reflective awareness, vimarśa, existence, non-existence, specific characteristics, primary doubt, epistemology, Abhinavagupta</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of doubt (saṃśaya). Having defined primary doubt as the vague "What is this?"—where the object's specific nature is entirely "unsealed"—the text now contrasts this with more specific forms of doubt, like "Is that a post or a man?"</meta>

<page-num>262</page-num>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<header>The Illustrious Tantraloka</header>

->**Rather, this [word "What?"] signifies**<-
->**the object itself in its unopened form.** || 249 ||<-

The word "this" in the verse refers to the interrogative word "What?" <note>original: kim-śabdaḥ</note>. || 249 ||

Since the "primary" status of a doubt is only logical if a "secondary" or non-primary form of doubt also exists, the author now speaks to demonstrate that secondary nature:

->**The doubt "Is it a post or a man?"**<-
->**is not the primary form of doubt.**<-
->**For in such cases, there is actually an emergence**<-
->**of certainty regarding many existing qualities.** || 250 ||<-

**"Not primary"** means that, unlike the previous case, it is not a situation where the forms of all qualities are "unopened" <note>original: anudghāṭita-rūpa</note>. Because the specific mental grasp <term>parāmarśa: the way the mind "touches" or identifies an object</term> of things like a "post" would be impossible otherwise, this cognition is actually an awareness characterized by certainty <note>original: niścayātmā pratyayaḥ</note> regarding the many qualities that exist within the object—excluding the specific identities of "post" or "man" themselves. || 250 ||

<note>Abhinavagupta's point here is subtle: when you ask "Is that a post or a man?", you are already certain about many things. You know it is a tall, vertical object at a certain distance. Therefore, it is not "pure" or "primary" doubt, which is a total lack of specific information.</note>

But if that is the case—if there is a mixing of possible meanings here and yet a lack of certainty regarding one fixed alternative—would this not simply be a **conceptual division** <term>vikalpa: a mental construct that oscillates between two choices</term>? This would follow the **Logic of the Risen and Unrisen Offerings** <term>uditānudita-homa-nyāya: a traditional rule of logic based on Vedic rituals where one must choose between performing an offering either before or after sunrise, but not both</term>.

Anticipating this objection, he says:

---

<margin>Line 7, Manuscript Ka: "Doubt is indeed primary."</margin>
<margin>Line 8, Manuscript Ka: "Regarding many good qualities..."</margin>
<margin>Line 13, Manuscript Ka: "...certainty of the qualities themselves."</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta distinguishes between "primary doubt" (vague) and "secondary doubt" (specific alternatives like post vs. man). He argues that secondary doubt contains a high degree of certainty about the object's general attributes, leading to a discussion on whether doubt is merely a form of conceptual oscillation (vikalpa).</summary>

<header>Verse 251 ] Chapter One</header>

## Because the two forms to be grasped
## have not yet "unopened,"
## this remains a doubt in the aspect of "What?"
## An "option," however, is clearly different. || 251 ||

The "two forms" <note>original: dvairūpya</note> to be mentally grasped <term>āmarśanīya: the object as it is being processed by the mind</term> are the characteristics of a post or a man. Their "non-opening" <note>original: anudghāṭana</note> refers to the fact that their specific identifying features—such as the crookedness or hollows of a wooden post—have not yet been revealed. Because of this, the resulting cognition is still a **doubt** <note>original: saṃśaya</note>, as it is mixed with the questioning aspect of "What is it?"

In the thought, "Is it a post or a man?", the actual underlying sense of the doubt is "Is it a post? Is it a man?" The distinction is this: in a "pure" doubt (the simple question "What?"), it is considered **primary** because the specific qualities of *all* possibilities remain "unopened." In the case of the post or the man, it is considered **secondary** (non-primary) because the mind has already grasped some general qualities, even if the **fixed** specific qualities <note>original: niyata-viśeṣa-dharma</note> are not yet understood.

In the case of a ritual **option** <term>vikalpa: a situation where one has a choice between two known alternatives</term>, however, the situation is different. When one considers using either rice or barley <note>original: vrīhi, yava</note> for a sacrifice, both items are already certain and known; their forms are not "unopened." This is why the verse states: **"An 'option,' however, is clearly different."**

"Different" <note>original: anyathā</note> means that both the rice and the barley are already grasped with certainty through their own specific qualities. Such a state [of ritual choice] is...

<margin>Line 13: Manuscript Kh reads "of both moons" <note>original: ubhayorindos</note>—likely a scribal error.</margin>
<margin>Line 14: Manuscript K contains a variant reading regarding the "form."</margin>

<meta>This page continues the logical justification for why "doubt" is the starting point of spiritual and philosophical inquiry. <header>The Light of the Tantras <note>original: Śrī Tantrālokaḥ</note></header>

It has already been established that **doubt** <note>original: saṃśaya</note> acts as the catalyst for the movement toward scripture. A scripture, indeed, is definitive in nature; it is a **determination** <term>nirṇaya: a final decision or settling of a matter</term>. Such a determination usually applies only to a subject that is currently in doubt. An object that is already fully perceived does not become a subject of doubt, nor does an object that is entirely unperceived. 

Because doubt is an **attribute of the knower** <term>pramātṛ-dharma: a condition belonging to the conscious subject rather than the object itself</term>, even if someone in a state of doubt perceives a doubtful object, that perception is what occurs to them. The verbal expression of that state is called a **question** <note>original: praśna</note>. Therefore, the question—much like the doubt that caused it—should be considered a catalyst for the scripture’s activity. 

To reach a determination, a scripture that is being composed employs a threefold methodology: **Enunciation**, **Definition**, and **Scrutiny** <note>original: uddeśa, lakṣaṇa, parīkṣā</note>. 

1. **Enunciation** <note>original: uddeśa</note> is simply the naming of the categories or objects of study. 
2. This naming must necessarily be done first. Without enunciation, both definition and scrutiny are impossible. 
3. Therefore, without enunciation, the very composition of a scripture—which consists of definitions and examinations—cannot function. Thus, naming is an essential limb <note>original: aṅgatva</note> of the process. || 251 ||

Now, one might ask: "If the purpose of the scripture can be accomplished by just one of these methods, why are all three required?" 

To this we respond: that is not the case. It is only through their mutual interconnection that these...

<header>Verse 252 ] First Chapter <note>original: prathamāhnikam</note></header>

...because it has been stated that these are the causal factors. Indeed, when an object is in a state of **doubt**, it is then identified by some scripture through the means of **Enunciation** <note>original: uddeśa</note> and so on, and thus it is **determined** <term>nirṇīyate: settled or resolved through logic</term>.

->Therefore, the first manifestation of<-
->an object as having an unrevealed nature<-
->is what is meant here by "Enunciation,"<-
->as well as "Question" and "Doubt." || 252 ||<-

**By that**—meaning, by the logic previously mentioned—the first manifestation of a **state** <note>original: bhāva</note>, or a mere object, as having an **unrevealed nature** <term>anudghāṭitātmatva: the quality of being named but not yet explained or "opened up"</term>, is what is defined here as **Enunciation**. This also applies to the **Question** and to **Doubt**. 

Among these, the fact that **Doubt** takes this form has just been explained. In **Enunciation**, the manifestation of the object is also of an "unrevealed" nature, because the categories are expressed **by name alone**. The same must be said for the **Question**; otherwise, if a question already possessed the nature of a **determination** <term>nirṇaya</term>, there would be no distinction between the question and the final answer. || 252 ||

Because a question arises only regarding a matter that is in doubt, the nature of the "Question" must be determined immediately after the nature of doubt has been settled. Having reached the appropriate moment to explain its true essence, the author says:

->Thus, through the path of the expansion of states,<-

In this **Non-dualist system** <term>advaya-naya: the philosophy that all of reality is a single, undivided consciousness</term>, the principle is that "Consciousness alone, which is the ultimate reality, is everything." Therefore, it is logically impossible to maintain a fundamental distinction between the questioner and the answerer, or the roles of the **Teacher** and the **Disciple**. 

"Thus"—meaning, in the manner previously described—there is an **unrevealed form**. Because it is filled with every possible object and state, this is the single nature of Consciousness. This "State" is the ultimate, full nature of reality. Its "Expansion" <note>original: prasara</note> refers to its descent through the stages of speech, beginning with **Paśyantī** <term>paśyantī: the "seeing" or intuitive stage of language where thought and word are one</term> and so on. This is the "Path." 

Flowing along this path—reaching the stage of **Vaikharī** <term>vaikharī: the final stage of speech, where it is articulated out loud</term>—one’s own **Self-awareness** <note>original: sva-saṃvitti</note> becomes contracted. It manifests the role of a limited **Subject** <term>pramātṛ: an individual knower or perceiver</term> taking on the persona of a disciple. In this state, it is called the "Questioner."

<header>The Venerable Tantrāloka</header>

->**The creation of an attribute is a general**<-
->**creation; it is of the nature of doubt. || 258 ||**<-

Regarding the phrase "about to be created": this refers to the specific parts or details that are about to be manifested in their own unique characteristics. In that context, there is an "expectation"—an orientation toward those details—because of the logic stated in verses such as:

> "A generality without particulars would be like a rabbit's horn." <note>original: "nirviśeṣaṃ hi sāmānyaṃ bhavecchaśaviṣāṇavat"; this is a traditional logical maxim meaning that a universal category cannot exist if there are no specific examples of it.</note>

Because the two are inseparable, even when there is no explicit orientation toward the details, the generality remains all-pervading and does not lose its essential nature. Thus, the external manifestation of a specific, fixed attribute <term>dharma: a quality or characteristic</term>—such as "cow-ness" <note>gotva</note>—is called **"General Creation."** This is referred to as **"doubt"** because it represents a stage where the full expansion of the self has not yet been opened or revealed. The meaning is that the perception of a generality, which carries with it the expectation of further details, is identical to the experience of doubt. || 258 ||

He explains that, likewise, "Specific Creation" takes the form of a perception of certainty:

->**But when the specific part that was to be created**<-
->**comes to its fulfillment, then there is**<-
->**a certainty agreeable to the Subject.**<-
->**It cannot be otherwise, even in millions of ages. || 259 ||**<-

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mechanics of perception and certainty within the Trika system. <page-num>271</page-num>
<header>Verse 260 ] Chapter One</header>

When, however, the process of "Specific Creation" reaches its fulfillment—meaning that all the particular details required for firm conviction have been created—then the specific portion yet to be created comes to a rest. At that moment, because the expansion of the Self’s own light is fully revealed, a certainty arises in the form of a cognition: "This is indeed a wooden post" <note>original: "sthāṇurevayam"; this refers to a classic Indian philosophical example where a person in the dark doubts if an object is a man or a post, eventually achieving certainty that it is a post</note>. 

The basis for the emergence of this certainty is simply the will of the **Conscious Subject** <term>pramātṛ: the perceiving individual or the "Knower"</term>, as previously expressed by the phrase "suitable to the Knower." The essence of the matter is that a thing is considered "determined" only as long as the Knower is satisfied, thinking "I have known this." Otherwise, certainty would never occur at any time, because there would be no point of repose within the Knower's will. As it is said: "It cannot be otherwise even in ten million eons." || 256 || <note>The prose here cites a verse numbered 256 in the manuscript's internal sequence.</note>

Not only does this process take the form of certainty, but it also manifests as the defining of characteristics and similar functions. He says:

->**Then, because the vigor of one’s own Self**<-
->**has the intensity to pervade that object,**<-
->**an "unsealing" occurs. Through that form,**<-
->**there is definition, subsequent inquiry, and determination. || 260 ||**<- <note>original: "unmudraṇam"; literally "unsealing," referring to the moment an object's true nature is revealed by the power of consciousness</note>

--- Page 282 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of how the Conscious Subject moves from doubt to certainty. The previous page introduced the concepts of "unsealing" and "determination" as functions of the Knower's will. This page defines specific logical terms—Definition (lakṣaṇa), Answer (uttara), and Determination (nirṇaya)—within the framework of the Trika system's theory of perception.</meta>

<page-num>272</page-num>
<header>The Sri Tantraloka</header>

Of that—meaning, of the object that possesses a specific nature—the "vigor of one’s own Self" refers to its state of being excluded from all other things <note>This refers to the logical principle of "apoha," where an object is defined by what it is not</note>. Its "pervasion" is the act of making that object a part of one's own consciousness. In that state, there is "skill" or "intensity," which arises because there is no longer any "expectancy" <note>original: nairākāṅkṣya; a state where the mind no longer seeks further information to identify the object</note>. From that intensity, an "unsealing" <note>original: unmudraṇa; the metaphorical opening of the object's true nature to the observer</note> occurs in that very form. 

This unsealing manifests the object’s specific, individual nature. Because this process is essentially the expanded light of the Self becoming manifest, it is called—without distinction—the "Definition," the "Answer," and the "Determination." 

Within this: 
The **Definition** <term>lakṣaṇa: a unique characteristic that distinguishes an object from others</term> is the unique quality that allows for the understanding of reality. 
The **Answer** <term>uttara: here, the resolution of an inquiry</term> is the removal of objections, which serves as a tool for that understanding. 
The **Determination** <term>nirṇaya</term> is the understanding of reality itself. || 260 ||

Now, one might ask: "Since the essence of all these is the understanding of reality, why isn't 'Examination' <term>parīkṣā: a critical investigation or trial</term> also grouped under Definition, just as Determination is?" Fearing this doubt, he says:

> **Because it follows upon those**
> **aspects of properties already determined,**
> **"Examination" is the repeated application**
> **of the "Initial Mention" and the "Definition."** || 261 ||

<margin>Line 5: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "the nature of the expanded light of the Self."</margin>

**Determined** means made the object of a final decision. **That much** refers to an object targeted by specific, fixed characteristics. That which is the **aspect of the property** is the subject of repeated **Indication** <term>samuddeśa: the initial naming or pointing out of a topic</term>. Furthermore, **Definition** <term>lakṣaṇa</term> consists of the description of both common and unique attributes. Finally, **Examination** <term>parīkṣā</term> is the act of **looking** <note>original: īkṣaṇa</note> **all around**—that is, from every side—by means of rejecting all opposing views without exception. This is the meaning of the sentence. || 261 ||

He states that this triad, beginning with Indication, exists in every instance of knowledge:

->**In perception, inference, analogy,**<-
->**authoritative testimony, and so on,**<-
->**the triad of Indication, Definition, and Examination**<-
->**shines forth within all living beings everywhere.** || 262 ||<-

He demonstrates this very thing in sequence:

->**Indication is the non-conceptual state,**<-
->**Definition, however, is the conceptualization.**<-
->**Likewise, in direct perception, Examination**<-
->**is the continuous sequence of such concepts.** || 263 ||<-

->**is the Examination that resides in the remaining details.** || 266 ||<-
<note>Authoritative Testimony (Agama/Scripture) follows the same pattern: it identifies the seeker, defines the necessary action (sacrifice), and examines the specific procedures (the Agniṣṭoma rite).</note>
