And the production of the certainty of the object as it is—this is the nature of the **Examination** of these. **Indication** refers to the statement "this is a mountain," because it presents the mere subject <term>dharmin: the "property-bearer" or the thing being discussed</term> in a state where its nature as possessing the property to be proven <note>original: sādhya-dharma</note> has not yet been revealed. **Definition** refers to the state where the nature of the subject is revealed as being characterized by the property to be proven. **Pervasion** <term>vyāpti: the logical "web" or "inseparable connection" where the presence of the sign (smoke) necessitates the presence of the target (fire)</term> refers to positive and negative concomitance <note>original: anvaya-vyatireka; the rule that "where there is smoke, there is fire" and "where there is no fire, there is no smoke"</note>. Because of those relationships, the certainty of the inseparable connection between the proof <note>original: sādhana</note> and the proven <note>original: sādhya</note> is produced—this is why it is called the **Examination**. [Verse 268] Chapter 1. 277

## At that very moment, consciousness collects
## as much as is yet to be created.

By means of conceptualization <term>vikalpa: the mental process of creating distinctions, labels, and mental constructs</term>—because the general category has been created by the Knower <term>pramātā: the conscious subject or the "I" who experiences</term> who is primarily focused on that conceptualization—those specifics are "yet to be created" <note>original: srakṣyamāṇāḥ</note> with respect to that general category. This means they are to be brought into manifestation through "Definition" <term>lakṣaṇa: the second stage of inquiry, where the unique characteristics of a thing are defined</term>. 

For this very reason, these specific details are "others"—meaning they are distinct from the general category—and because they bring satisfaction to the Knower, they are "delighted in" <note>original: rucitāḥ</note>, or desired. The nature of a general object is such that it "tolerates" or contains these parts within itself as things to be pervaded by it. In this way—through the capacity to contain the specifics that are yet to be created—"Creation" occurs, which is "Indication" <term>uddeśa: the first stage of inquiry, simply naming or pointing out a topic</term>. In that context, as many desired specifics as are yet to be created, just so many does consciousness "collect" <note>original: saṃvic-cinute</note>—meaning it synthesizes or connects them—at that very time, at the moment of Indication. This is the meaning. [Verse 267]

### The reason for this:

->**For, because Consciousness is not limited by time,**<-
->**it connects that which belongs to all times.**<-

->The word "for" <note>original: hi</note> is used here as a sentence ornament. [Verse 268]<-

---

Line 3, Manuscript ‘Ka’: the reading is "in the conceptualization, being focused on that."

# The Light of the Tantras
# Chapter 1. 278

Now, an objection is raised: If "Definition" consists of the manifestation of the soul's own expansion, and if both the general category and the specific details are manifested together, then which is the "defined" <term>lakṣya: the object or concept being described</term> and which is the "definition" <term>lakṣaṇa: the identifying mark or characteristic</term>? Because there is a lack of clear distinction here, wouldn't the relationship between the two become unregulated? In response to this doubt, the author says:

->**The creation of that which is to be created,**<-
->**and the withdrawal of the part previously created—**<-
->**it is this that is called the "Definition" of consciousness**<-
->**regarding the attribute being referred back to. [Verse 269]**<-

In this context, consciousness—which consists of both the "creation" and "withdrawal" of the general and specific objects—is the "Definition." It is the very seed of our practical interaction with the world. In this process, there is indeed a clear distinction: the specific part currently being "created" <note>original: srakṣyamāṇasya; meaning the details being brought into focus</note> is the "Definition" because it is the new information being predicated. Meanwhile, the general part, which is being "withdrawn" <note>original: saṃhṛta; meaning it is receding into the background as a known factor</note>, is the "defined" object, as it is the subject being referred back to <term>anūdyamāna: that which is mentioned again or given as the subject of a sentence</term>. [Verse 269]

But, it has been said:

> "Examination consists of repeated naming, defining, and then testing." <note>This is a standard sequence in Indian logic (Nyāya) used here to challenge Abhinavagupta’s metaphysical interpretation.</note>

---

<note>Footnotes and variants at the bottom of the page</note>

*If there is a general state where specifics were previously unmentioned, and later the specific details arise, then—because the general and specific are manifested distinctly—the relationship between the "defined" and the "definition" is well-established. However, if the specific details already resided within the general state previously, then there would be no fixed rule here. The thought is that a single state would be tainted by the flaw of "confusion" <term>saṃkara: a logical fallacy where two distinct categories overlap or mix inordinately</term>.

Line 10: In manuscripts K and G, the text reads: "...is the seed of the practice of definition."

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that "Definition" is a dynamic movement of consciousness where specific details are brought forward (Creation) while the general category recedes into the background (Withdrawal) to serve as the subject.</summary>

> "That which is unperceived, without attributes,

By such passages, it is shown that the Supreme Power <term>parā śakti: the highest creative energy of consciousness</term> of the Lord alone has expanded in the form of these various connections. > according to the nature of divine immersion." 
<note>original: "āveśa-svarūpataḥ." "Immersion" (āveśa) refers to a state where the individual's limited identity is overwhelmed or permeated by divine consciousness.</note>

The term "Mixed" refers to the "Divine-and-Non-Divine." The term "Mutual" means: that which is other than the Divine is the Mixed, and that which is other than that is the Non-Divine. Indeed, there are only three possible categories: Divine, Divine-and-Non-Divine, and Non-Divine. This is why it is referred to here by the word "Mutual" <note>original: "itaretara," literally "one with the other" or "reciprocal."</note>. As it is said:

> "The Great, the Intermediate, the Divine, 
> and the Mixed is the fourth. 
> Through the 'Mutual' path, the definitions 
> are divided into five types."

These five connections proceed from the level of Shiva to that of Sadashiva... <note>original: "śivāt sadāśivasya." This refers to the highest levels of the metaphysical hierarchy in this system.</note>

---

<margin>Line 1: Manuscript K reads "grasped" <note>original: "āmṛṣṭam"</note> instead of "unperceived."</margin>

[ Verse 274 ] # First Chapter | 283

Therefore, it should be understood as proceeding in order: from Lord Ananta <note>Anantanātha: the lord of the infinite, a high-ranking deity in the pure hierarchy who initiates the descent of knowledge</note> to the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha, Nandi, Kumāra, and others; from them to the sages such as Sanatkumāra; and from them to human beings. As it is said in that same work:

> "For Shiva, who is complete, supreme, and of immeasurable light, 
> His Power is called 'Sādākhyā' <note>original: 'sādākhyā'; the state of 'Always-Being,' representing the first manifestation of the divine through its own will</note>, acting within the sphere of His own free will. 
> The first connection is known as that state of existence attained through this initial relationship. 
> The second connection is proclaimed as the 'Intermediate,' attained through union sequentially from the Sādākhyā state by the god Ananteśa. 
> The third, O Goddess, is called the 'Divine' connection, transmitted by the god [Ananteśa] to Śrīkaṇṭha along with Nandi. 
> The fourth is proclaimed by the Blessed Lord as the 'Divine-and-Non-Divine' <note>Mixed</note>, communicated by Nandi to the sages in a concise manner. 
> Through the practice of the sequence of explanation, in the worship of the seat of knowledge <term>vidyā-pīṭha: a specific tradition, assembly, or mystical collection of wisdom</term>, the fifth is the 'Mutual' connection, existing in the form of teacher and student. 
> Thus, this connection is proclaimed to be of five types."

Thus ends verse 274.

He now explains the nature of being the Supreme Energy <term>parakalātmatva: the essence of the highest creative power or 'digit' of consciousness that underlies all communication</term>:

### That unity which exists
### between two distinct individuals—
### the questioner and the speaker—is called [the Supreme Connection].

# The Illustrious Light of the Tantras
### Page 284

When the questioner is Sadāśiva <note>Sadāśiva: the 'Ever-Beneficent' form of the divine, representing the stage of manifestation where the 'I' and the 'This' (the universe) are held in perfect balance</note> and the speaker is Śiva, the word "that" refers back to the act of questioning. Even though these two appear to be distinct, a connection exists because of the firm identity of consciousness <term>aikātmya: the state of being one single self</term> regarding that specific meaning—since that connection is composed of both difference and non-difference <note>bhedābheda: a philosophical concept where two entities are simultaneously distinct and identical</note>. When, in the state of identity, even the slightest scent of difference dissolves and a state of "Fullness" characterized by being the "Self of All" arises, that is known as the Supreme Connection.

As he says:

-> The connection and the supremacy of this <-
-> consist of the expansion of full identity. [275] <-

Supremacy is indeed defined as the expansion of full identity. For within the "Full," everything exists, and the "Full" exists everywhere. Since this principle is present in all five types of connections <note>The five levels of transmission: Great, Intermediate, Divine, Mixed, and Human</note>, it is rightly said that "Everything is of the nature of the Supreme Energy."

As it was stated:

> "O Supreme Goddess, every connection is composed of the Supreme Energy <term>parakalā: the highest creative power or 'digit' of the divine consciousness</term>. They are: the Great, the Intermediate, the Divine, the Mixed, the Human, and that which is beyond."

[275]

# First Daily Lesson
### Page 287

<meta>Referring to Verse 284</meta>

-> Secret conduct <note>rahasyacaryā: specialized esoteric practices</note>, the multitude of mantras, <-
-> the sacred circle <term>maṇḍala: a geometric diagram representing the cosmos and the deity's retinue</term>, and the ritual of gestures <term>mudrā: symbolic hand positions used in ritual and meditation</term>. <-
-> Unification within one's own true nature, <-
-> entry into the self, and the convergence of the scriptures. [283] <-
-> The account of the lineage and the demonstration of <-
-> the scriptural authority. <-

The act of naming through a general term is called the "Primary Enumeration" <note>original: pūrvaja-uddeśa</note>, while naming through a specific term is the "Secondary Enumeration" <note>original: anuja-uddeśa</note>; this is also referred to as "Classification" <note>vibhāga</note> in other contexts. In this passage, he provides the Primary Enumeration, beginning with the phrase **"The distinctions of pure awareness"** [Verse 278] and ending with **"determination"** [Verse 284]. The phrase "the distinctions of pure awareness" refers to the point where the various cognitions, such as those belonging to the Method of Śiva <note>Śāmbhavopāya</note> and others, are differentiated. **"The transcended method"** refers to the "No-method" <note>anupāya: the highest state where no effort is required</note>. The phrase **"in the rite for the spiritual son"** indicates that one relies on the procedure for the *pautrika* <note>a specific grade of initiate</note>. The term **"initiation"** should be connected with the preceding verses. The phrase **"The procedure for the objects of knowledge"** <note>prameya-prakriyā</note> should be understood as applying to the context of **"the rite for the spiritual son."** As he will later state:
> "That was stated in the Secondary Enumeration of that chapter, regarding the rite for the spiritual son."
[Verses 278-283]

Line 7: MS Ka reads "The account of the lineage."

And so forth—not only is it such, but even more of its greatness is declared, ending with the phrase "surpassing existence... in the illumination." Here, the author has fundamentally composed thirty-seven chapters <term>āhnika: literally a "day-session," the name for the divisions of the Tantrāloka</term> in both collective and individual forms. Just as in the element of **Earth** duality/differentiation predominates and everything exists in a gross form, so too what is about to be said here is described as the "sequential enumeration of everything."

Regarding the **Supreme Means**—that is, the **Way of Shambhu** <term>śāmbhavopāya: the highest path in Trika Shaivism where realization is achieved through a sudden, thought-free immersion in divine Will</term>—it has already been stated that its nature is **non-conceptual** <term>avikalpaka: a state of awareness free from the mental constructions and dualistic labels of the mind</term>. In that state, since the "expressed" universe is a **reflection of Consciousness** <term>cit-pratibimba: the philosophical doctrine that the world is not an external object but a reflection appearing within the "mirror" of divine awareness</term>, manifesting through its nature as both universal and particular...

<meta>This page continues the systematic overview of the Tantrāloka’s chapters. Abhinavagupta is transitioning from the "Way of Shambhu" (the highest, non-conceptual path) into the "Way of Energy" (Shaktopaya), detailing how conceptual thought is used to transcend itself.</meta>

# The Light of the Tantras
### First Chapter
#### Page 266

->Verse 326<-

Since the universe, in its dual form of the "signifier" <note>original: vācaka; the word or sound that points to a concept</note> and the "signified" <note>original: vācya; the object or concept itself</note>, is non-different from Consciousness, it is said to share a single nature. This unity exists because the universe follows the same sequence of emergence as the **Mantras** and the movement of awareness. Here, the three central **Objects of Knowledge** <term>prameya: the topics or categories of spiritual reality to be understood</term> are introduced.

Because the nature of the **Way of Energy** <term>śāktopāya: the spiritual path centered on the purification of the mind and the use of conceptual thought to transcend concepts</term> is inherently rooted in **thought-constructs** <term>vikalpa: the dualistic mental activity that divides reality into "this" and "that"</term>, the "refinement" of these constructs is addressed first. This refinement is achieved through **Spiritual Reasoning** <term>tarka: not mere academic logic, but the intuitive ability to distinguish the Reality of the Self from the illusions of the world</term>, which operates by investigating what should be abandoned. This is the principle that follows.

Furthermore, the "brilliance" or expansion of this reasoning—which is the very essence of **Pure Knowledge** <term>śuddhavidyā: the level of awareness where one realizes "I am All"</term>—is what leads to finding a **True Guru** <term>sadguru: an enlightened teacher capable of transmitting the grace of liberation</term>. Thus, the necessity of the teacher's presence is established.

Indeed, **Reasoning** is the only direct "limb" of Yoga. This implies that the other traditional limbs of yoga <note>referring to the classical eightfold limbs like physical posture or breath control</note> are secondary or even unnecessary in this context. Because this Reasoning is of the nature of Pure Knowledge, it strikes down the dualistic mental constructs born of **Maya** <term>māyā: the power of illusion that creates the appearance of separation</term>. Consequently, there is a disregard for external, "constructed" rituals such as **image worship** <note>original: arccā; the ritual adoration of physical icons</note>.

Through the strengthening of this non-conceptual refinement, the **Wheel of Consciousness** <term>saṃviccakra: the dynamic, radiating power of awareness</term> emerges. It is in this emergence that the **Mantras** find their supreme potency. Such internal awareness is the only true form of **recitation** <term>japa: usually the repetition of a mantra, here defined as the constant vibration of self-awareness</term> and other rituals. Because there is no division within Consciousness itself, prohibitions and injunctions <note>religious "dos and don'ts"</note> are seen as equal. These nine principles are thus introduced.

Similarly, in the **Way of the Individual** <term>āṇavopāya: the path for those still bound by a sense of limited selfhood, involving techniques like meditation</term>, the direct utility of the intellect and meditation is explained by us—this is done briefly, as it is quite clear.

### First Chapter
#### Page 300

Due to the fear of making the book excessively long, and because these matters will be determined in detail later in the text, they have not been explained here; the reader should understand this for themselves.
|| 284-326 ||

One might ask: Why was a **subsequent enumeration** <term>anujoddeśa: a detailed list of sub-topics or a secondary table of contents provided after the main headings</term> not provided for the **Chapter on Unification** <term>ekīkārāhnika: the 33rd chapter of the Tantrāloka dealing with the integration of all paths into one</term> and the chapters following it? In response to this doubt, the author says:

->From the thirty-second principle onwards, and from the one<-
->named after the Lord, it is manifest that<-
->there is no primary difference; therefore, no<-
->further enumeration of topics was stated here. || 327 ||<-

The **Chapter on Mudrās** <term>mudrā: ritual hand gestures or "seals" that reflect the internal state of consciousness</term> is the thirty-second in this sequence. From that point, following the thirty-second chapter, begins the thirty-third known as "The Lord's" <note>original: īśākhya</note>—which is the **Chapter on Unification**. Because the sense of **difference** <note>original: bheda; the perception of reality as consisting of separate, distinct objects</note> is no longer the primary focus in these advanced stages of consciousness, a secondary list of topics was not created. This is the meaning.

A question arises: If from that point onward there is no distinction or difference, why was the work divided into separate chapters at all? In response to this, the author says:

->Because they must be understood as primary subjects,<-
->there is a sequence of distinct sections. || 328 ||<-

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that he has omitted detailed sub-topic lists for the final chapters because they deal with states of consciousness where dualistic distinctions fade, though separate chapters remain necessary to highlight the primary importance of each subject.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verse of the first chapter of the Tantrāloka (Verse 330). Having established the Self as the "light of consciousness" on the previous page, the commentator Jayaratha now explains how this singular consciousness becomes "bound" and how its "liberation" is simply the recognition of its own inherent power.</meta>

# The Light of the Tantras
### Page 302

Consciousness alone is the nature of the **Light** <term>prakāśa: the fundamental radiance of awareness that allows anything to be known</term>; it is its very form. And because consciousness is partless, it exists as a single, undivided form of Light. This is the meaning.

Therefore, by the logic stated in passages such as:
> "Power is indeed the very nature of an entity, though [conceptually] constructed by the Knower." <note>original: śaktiśca nāma bhāvasya svaṃ rūpaṃ mātṛkalpitam</note>

The essential nature of the Self encompasses infinite **powers** <term>śakti</term>. Even though the Self is non-dual <note>advaya: without a second; a single reality</note>, by virtue of its **sovereign autonomy** <term>svātantrya: the absolute freedom of the divine to act</term>—which is characterized by the capacity to perform the most difficult of feats—it hides its own unique **splendor** <term>mahas: the radiant power of the soul</term> <margin>Line 8: Manuscript 'Ga' reads "from the hiding of his greatness" <note>original: mahimno gopanāt</note> instead of "hiding of his splendor."</margin> consisting of the capacity to know and to act. By hiding this, it causes the duality of the "perceived" and the "perceiver" to appear. As it is said:

> "...it is **Shiva** himself who has assumed the state of the **bound soul** <term>paśu: literally 'beast' or 'tethered one'; the individual limited by ignorance</term>."

By this logic, the Self is called "bound." Even so, through the "turning back" toward that Self:

> "Liberation is surely nothing other than the unfolding of one's own nature; and the nature of the Self is Consciousness..."

Following this logic, **liberation** <term>mokṣa</term> is the unfolding of that very splendor which consists of being the Knower and the Agent. It is for this purpose alone that this vast apparatus of various infinite **scriptures** <term>śāstra</term> exists. This is what the author means by the phrase "And this..." and so on. This liberation belongs to the seeker who has occupied the various stages of the "lower" systems of philosophy...

<summary>This page explains that the Self is a singular, partless Light of Consciousness which, through its own absolute freedom, hides its power to appear as a limited individual. Liberation is defined not as a new achievement, but as the "unfolding" or recognition of one's own true nature as the infinite Subject.</summary>
<keywords>Samvit, Prakasha, Svatantrya, Shiva, Pashu, Moksha, consciousness, liberation, sovereign autonomy, agency</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 330 of the first chapter of the Tantrāloka. On the previous page, the author established that consciousness is essentially a single, undivided light. Here, Jayaratha explains how this singular light appears in "varied" ways and addresses the potential contradiction between the unity of the Self and the diversity of spiritual experiences.</meta>

# The Light of the Tantras
### Page 303

**Verse 330 ] First Chapter**

> "Untainted by passion and the like, internal, empty, I am devoid of agency." <note>original: rāgādyakaluṣo'syantaḥ śūnyo'haṃ kartṛtāojjhitaḥ. This quote likely refers to a state of void-like meditation or a specific philosophical view of the self as a passive observer.</note>

By the reasoning stated in passages such as this, the soul is of a **varied nature; or rather**,

> "Therefore, in that conscious portion designated as a 'person' <term>pudgala: a term for the individual soul, often used in Buddhist and Jaina contexts</term> or an 'atom' <term>aṇu: the limited individual soul, 'atomic' because it is fragmented from the whole</term> and so on, diversity exists in many ways within the portion that is free from veils."

By this principle, the soul possesses a **varied form**.

> "Thus, toward some perceivers <term>pramātṛ: the subject who knows or experiences</term>, the Lord reveals his own form in its fullness; toward others, he reveals it through a gradual sequence, part by part."

By this statement, a **varied immersion** <term>āveśa: a state of spiritual absorption or 'possession' by the divine</term> **characterized by the Shāmbhava state <note>The highest of the three primary paths in Kashmir Shaivism, where the seeker realizes identity with Shiva through a direct flash of intuition.</note> and others is revealed.**

**"Here"** in this context means—in this first chapter. This relates to the fact that **this meaning has been revealed through a concise summary of both bondage and liberation.** ||330||

**Now, one might object: it has been stated that "liberation" <term>mokṣa</term> is nothing more than the manifestation of the Self's true nature. Since the Self is one and indivisible, how can there be any variety in liberation, which is simply the manifestation of that Self? Having raised this doubt, he says:**

->False knowledge, like a cataract of the eye,<-
->produces unequal defects of vision.<-

---

Line 3: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "the division of the conscious" <note>original: ajadavibhāgasya</note> and "designated" <note>original: saṃjñita</note>.
Line 5: Manuscript 'Kha' reads "of a varied nature" <note>original: citrasvabhāvasya</note>.
Line 8: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "by the reasoning stated in passages such as..." <note>original: ityādyuktayuktyā</note>.

<vocab>prathama-āhnikam (first chapter), mokṣa (liberation), śāmbhava-ādi-āveśa-ātmā (immersion starting with the Shāmbhava state), pudgala-aṇu (the individual soul/spiritual atom), mithyā-jñāna (false knowledge), vaicitrya (variety/diversity)</vocab>

<summary>This page explains that while the Self is a single unity, it appears as a "varied" reality (citra) depending on the level of spiritual immersion (āveśa) and the gradual removal of "veils." It concludes by introducing the idea that diversity in spiritual experience arises from "false knowledge," which acts like a medical defect in the eye.</summary>
<keywords>variety, immersion, Shāmbhava path, individual soul, false knowledge, liberation, Jayaratha, Abhinavagupta</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of how the singular, pure consciousness appears to be fragmented or "stained" by limitations. Following the previous page's discussion on the varied nature of the soul and spiritual immersion (āveśa), Jayaratha now provides a detailed commentary on Verse 331, which uses the medical metaphor of "blindness" or "cataracts" to explain the origin of spiritual impurity.</meta>

# The Light of the Tantras
### Page 304

-> Because of its presence, even that which is pure <-
-> appears as the abode of impurity. <-
-> But once that which is to be seen enters the vision, <-
-> it drives far away the seal of the defect of blindness; <-
-> how then could a suspicion of impurity <-
-> arise in that state? [331] <-

**Blindness** <term>timira: literally a medical condition like cataracts or darkness that obscures sight</term> refers to the **stain of finitude** <term>āṇavamala: the "impurity of the atom," which is the primal limitation that makes the infinite soul feel like a small, separate entity</term> itself. This is **false knowledge**, which consists of the **expansion of difference**—an **incomplete cognition**.

From the perspective of **vision**—referring to the full meaning of **consciousness** <term>saṃvitti</term>—this blindness generates "uneven" defects, such as the **conceit of the "non-self" within the Self** <note>the mistaken belief that the body, mind, or ego is the true Self</note>. Thus, due to the presence of this false knowledge, even though that knowledge is inherently pure and full, it **appears as the abode of impurity**. 

In other words, through its own absolute freedom, the **Self** <term>ātman</term> manifests as if it were incomplete. This is the extent of the meaning traditionally used in this context. However, that which is to be viewed as the ultimate goal—that which must be known—is the **full knowledge** whose essence is the single **Supreme Knower**:

> “I am not the life-breath, nor the body, nor the mind;
> I am not the intellect, nor the sense of ego, nor the thoughts.
> That portion of consciousness which is here—that indeed I am...”

---

<margin>Line 13: In Manuscript K, the reading is “as a comparison” <note>original: punar-upameyatvena</note> rather than “as the goal.”</margin>

<summary>Verse 331 and its commentary explain that spiritual impurity is not a permanent stain but a "blindness" or incomplete knowledge that makes the pure Self appear limited. This state is driven by the āṇavamala, but it is ultimately a manifestation of the Self's own freedom.</summary>

<keywords>āṇavamala, false knowledge, consciousness, Self, blindness, impurity, Supreme Knower, Tantrāloka</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 331. Jayaratha now explains how the realization of the true Self dissolves the very concepts of bondage and liberation.</meta>

# Page 305

### [ Verse 331 ] First Chapter

In this manner, through the process of **unwinding** <note>udveṣṭana: the "unfolding" or opening up of consciousness from its contracted, limited state</note>, once one has ascended to the **path of reflection** <term>vimarśa-padavī: the stage where consciousness recognizes its own dynamic nature and power</term>, one should drive far away the **seal of defect** <note>doṣa-mudrā: the "stamp" or "imprint" of limitation</note>. This defect arises from **false knowledge** <term>mithyā-jñāna</term> and consists of the conceit of the "Self" in that which is actually the "non-self" <note>anātmani ātmābhimāna: the mistaken belief that the physical body, the mind, or the ego is our true essence</note>.

One should cast this defect aside by maintaining the conceit of the "Self" only within the true Self. In such a state, what possible **suspicion of impurity** could there be? Indeed, in that state, even the mere possibility of impurity cannot exist. The reality of the situation is that there is actually no such thing as **bondage** <term>bandha</term> or **liberation** <term>mokṣa</term> at all. Therefore, what possibility could there be for the variety of states one imagines themselves to be in? 

It is with this intention that the following has been stated elsewhere:

> “In reality, there is no such thing as the cycle of rebirth for embodied beings; what talk can there even be of ‘bondage’? For one who was never bound in the first place, the ‘act of liberation’ for a supposedly liberated soul is a pointless endeavor. This is merely a delusion created by **false infatuation** <term>mithyā-moha</term>, like the error of seeing a **snake in a rope** <note>rajju-bhujaga: a classic Indian philosophical metaphor for seeing something that isn't there due to poor light or ignorance</note> or the phantom of a shadow. Do not discard anything; do not grasp anything. Cease your striving and remain at ease, exactly as you are.” <note>Original Sanskrit: *saṃsāro'sti na tattvatas...* This famous verse by Abhinavagupta emphasizes that enlightenment is not a change in state, but a realization of what has always been true.</note>

Furthermore, a comparison is implied here: just as a specific eye disease called **blindness** <term>timira: referring to cataracts or darkness of vision</term> produces a collection of defects consisting of distorted perception, which is then neutralized by an ointment or similar remedy, so too, in this state of realization, even the suspicion of "stain" or impurity does not arise. [331]

---

Now, the author, considering the **supreme depth** <term>gāmbhīrya</term> of this scripture, [notes that] even by others who do not understand the true essence of this matter, [it is often interpreted] otherwise—

<summary>Jayaratha explains that once a seeker realizes their true nature through the "path of reflection," the false identification with the body vanishes. He argues that bondage and liberation are ultimately illusions, concluding with a famous verse urging the seeker to simply "remain as they are."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary following the declaration that bondage and liberation are ultimately illusory. # Light of the Tantras
## [ Verse 332 ] First Chapter

Regarding those who, due to their limited awakening, describe reality in a superficial or contrary way, the author speaks the following to mock them through **indirect praise** <term>aprastuta-praśamsā: a literary figure where one praises or describes something other than the immediate subject to make a point</term>:

->**O Multitude of Objects!**<-
->You forcibly seize the hearts of men and make them dance,<-
->hiding your own heart behind various disguises as you play your game.<-
->The dullard—misled by the conceit that he is wise—<-
->who calls you "inert" is someone I consider truly "dull";<-
->indeed, his dullness is a form of praise,<-
->for it suggests he might actually be equal to you!<-

<note>Verse 332. The "Multitude of Objects" (bhāvavrāta) refers to the entire physical and mental world. Abhinavagupta is personifying the world to show that it is not "dead matter" but a playful expression of conscious power.</note>

O **Multitude of Objects** <note>original: "bhāvavrāta"</note>—referring to things such as the color blue and all other perceived entities—you hide your own "heart," which is your true, essential nature <note>ātma-tathya-rūpa</note>. Having done so, you forcibly seize the hearts—the inner intentions—of all disputants <note>vādinaḥ: philosophers or theologians who argue about the nature of reality</note> and make them dance.

As it has been said elsewhere:

> "Will this object now make the non-existent existent, or will it make the existent non-existent? Or will it somehow be both? Is it something enduring, or is it fleeting? Are things fundamentally different from one another, or are they non-different? Thus, those whose hearts are suppressed by the silence of contemplating the true nature of things—the very forms of the world—remain in a state of distress."

---
<margin>Line 7: In the Gaṇapati manuscript, the reading is "one who considers himself wise is ill-taught."</margin>
<margin>Line 17: In the Gaṇapati manuscript, the reading is "therefore they remain in distress."</margin>

<vocab>bhāvavrāta: multitude of objects, Tantrāloka: Light of the Tantras, aprastuta-praśamsā: indirect praise/allegory, jaḍātmatā: dullness or being composed of inert matter</vocab>

<summary>This page features Verse 332, where Abhinavagupta uses irony to mock philosophers who view the material world as "inert" (jaḍa). He suggests that the world is actually a playful manifestation of consciousness that "tricks" the ignorant into seeing it as dead matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 332. The previous page introduced a poetic address to the "Multitude of Objects," mocking the materialist view that the world is "dead" or "inert." Abhinavagupta now explains the irony in this verse: that if a dull-witted person is compared to the world, it is actually a compliment to the person, because the world is secretly alive with consciousness.</meta>

# Light of the Tantras
## [ Verse 332 ] First Chapter

...and so on. By such a state, as you play while making others dance with various turns—appearing like an actor in a form that is not your ultimate reality—the philosopher who considers himself a "connoisseur" <term>sahṛdaya: literally "one with a heart," referring to someone with the aesthetic and spiritual sensitivity to perceive the truth</term>, but who is actually unrefined, ill-taught, and full of false pride, knows nothing. He calls you, the **multitude of objects**, "inert"—meaning unconscious.

Therefore, we suggest <note>utprekṣyate: a poetic or metaphorical inference</note> that since you are essentially consciousness, if one says this philosopher is "equal to you" in being "inert," then that which was intended as an insult to him is actually praise! 

For the true nature of objects is consciousness itself; if they were not being perceived <note>original: "aceityamānatve," literally "if they were not being conscious-ed"</note>, they would have no form or existence at all. Thus, those who do not understand this truth are "more inert than the inert"—they are duller than the very objects they claim are dead. How then could there be any real comparison between them and these objects, which are actually conscious in nature? Such a comparison would only end in a failed attempt at insult. 

This logic applies to the present work as well: if someone does not understand the truth of this book, let him remain ignorant. If he speaks nonsense against it, it is he who is "inert" <note>jaḍa: a double meaning implying both "unconscious matter" and "a stupid person"</note>, and it is not a flaw of the scripture itself. ॥332॥

->**But if this is so, then for the understanding of this scripture, for some**<-

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the concluding verses of Chapter 1. Previously, Abhinavagupta addressed the "inert" nature of objects and the ignorance of those who fail to see consciousness within them. Here, he shifts to the intended audience of his work, explaining why he does not seek the approval of those who are spiritually unprepared.</meta>

# Light of the Tantras

Someone might raise an objection: "Should you not make a formal request to other scholars, asking them to first understand the subject matter as it truly is, so that they do not view this work with malice or hatred?" To answer this doubt, the author says:

->In this world, those whose impurities have faded, who know the highest and lowest truths,<-
->and who are filled with the true being of Shiva, are the ones authorized to study this.<-
->Since they are the masters of spiritual investigation,<-
->any plea for others to set aside the stain of hatred is useless. 333<-

In this world, there are two kinds of people: those upon whom the **descent of power** <term>śaktipāta: the touch of divine grace that initiates spiritual awakening</term> has not yet occurred, and those upon whom it has. 

Regarding the former group, even if they are begged a hundred times to grasp this teaching, their minds will not even move toward understanding it. Therefore, one should realize that a request such as "please do not be hateful toward this work" is completely ineffective. 

The second group, on the other hand, will naturally and of their own accord apply themselves to understanding this work, even without being asked. Thus, for them as well, such a request is unnecessary. 

This is what he means by "the plea to set aside the stain of hatred is useless." 

What are those people like upon whom the descent of grace has occurred? He describes them as those whose **impurities have faded** <note>original: galita-malāḥ</note>. "Faded impurities" refers to those whose ignorance has been dissolved. Because of this, they know the **highest**—the primordial, the "Beyond-the-Beyond" <term>Anuttara: the ultimate reality, symbolized by the first letter of the alphabet</term>—and the **lowest**—the final "Emission" <term>Visarga: the outward manifestation of the universe, symbolized by the last sign of the alphabet</term>. They are those who understand the seed of the Mantra, which consists of the **Supreme "I" Awareness**...

---

<margin>In manuscript "Ga," the text reads "their intellects" <note>original: dhiyastad</note> instead of "since they are" <note>original: yatastad</note>.</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that his work is intended only for those who have received divine grace (shaktipata), as they will naturally appreciate it, while those without grace will remain hateful regardless of any plea for fair judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the final verse of Chapter 1 of the Tantraloka. The previous page established that the text is intended for those who have received divine grace and whose ignorance has faded. Here, Jayaratha explains why these individuals are the true "authorities" on the subject and introduces Abhinavagupta's characteristic style of transitioning between chapters.</meta>

They are the **knowers** <note>original: jñāḥ; the OCR reads yajñāḥ, likely a scribal error for the plural of 'knower'</note>. This means they are filled with the **true being of Shiva** — in other words, they possess the knowledge of being one with the **Supreme Subject** <term>parapramātṛ: the ultimate consciousness that experiences all of reality</term>. 

For this reason, they are the **Gurus**—those who teach the essential, ultimate meaning. It is said that they alone are the supreme authorized readers for the comprehension of this work, because they are the ones called upon to perform deep investigation. As the author will state later:

> "The definition of a Guru is simply this: he should know the beginning and the end <note>The 'beginning and end' refers to the entire process of manifestation and withdrawal of consciousness</note>. Such a knower is to be worshipped as if he were Me—for he is **Bhairava** <term>Bhairava: the terrifyingly vast and inclusive form of Supreme Consciousness</term> himself, the very essence of the deity." 

— Verse 133

In this work, the author uses the **logic of accumulation** <term>sañcayana-nyāya: a method where each part is woven into the next like a continuous string of pearls</term> to demonstrate the interconnectedness between one chapter and the next. Following the "author's style," he uses a single verse to both conclude the current chapter and introduce the next. With the first half of the following verse, he concludes the meaning of this chapter:

->In this *Light of the Tantras*, newly composed by Abhinava,<-
->this chapter reaches its conclusion;<-
->it has been skillful in revealing the various<-
->manifestations of the reality of consciousness.<-

## Second Daily Lesson
<note>original: dvitīyam āhnikam; the text is divided into 'daily lessons,' suggesting a curriculum to be studied day by day.</note>

---

> *May the victorious **Rudra** <note>a name for Shiva in his fierce, transformative aspect</note> be triumphant—he who grants victory to those who bow before him. Acting as the **Lord of Desire** <note>original: Kāmeśvara</note>, who is there whose desires he does not fully satisfy, even without the use of external means?* <note>Verse 1: This is an introductory prayer (maṅgala) by the commentator Jayaratha.</note>

Now:

> "He who is superior in qualities to another is described as being 'above' that person."

According to this established principle, and because there is a hierarchy of excellence among the individual <term>āṇava: the 'limited' or individual means of spiritual practice</term> and the other methods, it is intended that they be discussed here in their respective order of superiority. Because the ultimate goal <note>the 'upeya' or the state of Shiva-consciousness</note> is essentially of a single, unified nature, the divine method <term>śāmbhava: the 'divine' means of sudden immersion in consciousness, the highest of the three methods</term>—

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the hierarchy of spiritual means. The first chapter ended by identifying the divine method (śāmbhava-upāya) as the highest of the traditional methods, but now introduces 'Anupāya'—the "No-Means" or "Immediate" approach—which transcends even the highest graded methods.</meta>

# The Illustrious Tantrāloka

...of even the **No-Means** approach <term>anupāya: literally "without means"; the highest state of realization where spiritual liberation occurs instantly upon hearing the truth once, without the need for progressive techniques</term> and its excellence. To describe its essential nature first, the author pledges to begin another daily lesson with the second half of the verse:

->That first state, which is the nature of uninterrupted, supreme consciousness,<-
->to define that, I begin this second chapter. [1]<-

The author describes that very definition:

->For that nature which is without means,<-
->what indeed is the purpose of instruction here?<-
->Instruction may occur once; thereafter,<-
->it is called the "No-Means" approach. [2]<-

The word "indeed" <note>original: vai</note> is used for emphasis; by this, it means there is absolutely no purpose [for gradual instruction in this state]. He resolves this very point with the phrase "Instruction may occur once." The word "instruction" is an illustration <note>an 'upalakṣaṇa' or inclusive term</note>—it also encompasses the beholding of a Perfected One and so on, as it has been said:

> "The beholding of the **Perfected Ones** <term>Siddhas: semi-divine enlightened beings</term> and the **Yoginis** <term>Yoginis: female deities or advanced practitioners embodying divine power</term>, the partaking of the **sacrificial food** <term>caru-bhojanam: a ritual meal of cooked grain or oblations that transmits grace</term>,
> Discourse, the transmission within the scripture, the practice, and the **service of the Guru** <term>guru-sevanam</term>—
> This is the summary of the "No-Means" approach, O Beautiful-faced One."

The word "once" <note>original: sakṛt</note> means that there is no repeated experience of spiritual methods. Thus he says, "thereafter, it is called the No-Means approach."

<summary>This page introduces the second chapter of the Tantraloka, focusing on Anupāya (the No-Means approach). It argues that for the most advanced seekers, a single encounter with the truth—through a teacher, a text, or a ritual meal—is sufficient for instant enlightenment without further practice.</summary>

## Verse 3 ] The Second Daily Chapter

In the **Individual Means** <term>āṇava-upāya: the lowest level of practice involving breath, body, and ritual</term> and other methods, instruction and similar aids are practiced repeatedly <note>original: asakṛd-bhāvyamānaḥ</note> to bring about the attainment of the goal. Therefore, the nature of "means" was described in that context. Here, however, it is not so; hence it is called "No-Means." This term is a **relative negation** <term>paryudāsa: a type of negation that implies a small degree or a specific alternative, rather than a total absence</term>. Much like the phrase "a girl without a belly" <note>original: anudarā kanyā; a Sanskrit idiom referring to a girl with an exceptionally slender waist</note> refers to someone with a very small waist, the term "No-Means" refers to a state where the means used are minimal. The idea is: once the goal is reached, what is the point of those useless and exhausting efforts such as meditation and the like? As it has been said:

> "Shiva does not shine by means; the means shine only by His grace. 
> It is I, the self-luminous one, who shines as the nature of the universe. 
> Hearing this word from the Guru, some become certain once and for all. 
> Without further contemplation, they remain as the nature of pure consciousness."

Indeed, if one has achieved this certainty, what use is further practice? [2]

But then, why shouldn't we interpret "No-Means" in its primary sense as the **absolute absence of means** <term>prasajya-pratiṣedha: an absolute negation where the existence of a thing is completely denied</term>? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->This reality is "No-Means"—<-
->how can it be so without any means?<-
->For those [great souls], it is self-evident;<-
->what indeed can we say to them? [3]<-

---

<margin>Line 12: Manuscript K reads "the state of having means" <note>original: vidyamānopāyam</note> instead of "the state of having no means."</margin>

<vocab>Anupaya, Shiva, Prasajyapratishedha, Paryudasa, Samvid, Bhāvanā, Deshanā, Anava</vocab>

<summary>This page explains that "No-Means" (Anupāya) does not mean a total absence of method, but rather a method so instantaneous and minimal that it is effectively non-existent. It emphasizes that for highly advanced seekers, a single word from a teacher is enough to trigger full enlightenment without further meditation.</summary>

# Page 4

## The Illustrious Tantrāloka

Regarding the statement, "This reality is No-Means"—there must necessarily be some sort of means, such as a single instruction <term>upadeśa: the formal transmission of knowledge from a teacher to a student</term>. Otherwise, how could the definition [of this state] be established without a means? As it was said: "Without a means, how can it [realization] occur?" Thus, there must be some means, like a single instruction; otherwise, there would simply be no realization of the supreme reality called "No-Means."

But one might object: "Some are seen to have reached the goal through the power of their own self-reflection <term>vimarśa: the active, self-reflective capacity of consciousness</term>. What is the point of even a slight, informal instruction for someone who is not [formally] trained?" To address this doubt, the author says, "By oneself," and so on. This "No-Means" state is the nature of the Supreme Light. The intention is that the scripture itself does not apply to those who have already attained this state.

As it has been said:

> "To the knower of truth, scripture is but a blade of grass..."

It is with this intention that it is said:

> "An excellent person who wishes to cross the ocean of worldly existence <note>original: saṃsāra-ambunidhi; the turbulent sea of birth and death</note>, who is neither an absolute knower of that [truth] nor a fool, is the one authorized <term>adhikāra: the spiritual qualification or 'right' to engage with a particular practice</term> to study this scripture."

In these matters, it is stated that the "absolute knower" has no need for the scripture. Therefore, we who are "limited-seers" <note>original: arvāg-darśinaḥ; those whose perception is turned toward the external world rather than the divine</note>, even though we cannot see the unseen truth, have the scripture as our only divine eye...

# The Sacred Tantraloka

A means <term>upaya: a spiritual method or technique</term> indeed exists when an instrument is active. Therefore, there must be a state of fullness <note>original: "pūrṇa"</note>; this is something no one disputes. However, that is not the case here. Actions and other such things, because they are objects of perception <note>original: "samvedyamānatvāt"</note>, actually reside within consciousness itself. Without the power of consciousness <term>samvit-shakti: the innate energy of pure awareness</term>, they would not even be established. How, then, could they attain the status of being a "means" toward it? On the contrary, it is more logical to say that consciousness is the "means" for the outward appearance of action and the rest. Therefore, the author says:

-> **For it [action] is born from That [Consciousness],** <-
-> **and is instead clearly manifested by it.** <- || 8 ||

-> **"From That" means from the reality of Consciousness, which is "without means" [anupāya].** <- || 8 ||

Now, if it is argued that action and other such factors are not the *producer* <term>karaka: a causal factor that brings about an effect</term> of consciousness, but rather the *indicator* <term>jnapaka: an informative factor that makes something known, like a lamp revealing a jar</term>, even that is not logical. The author explains:

-> **If it is argued that there must be a means for "knowing,"** <-
-> **then we must ask: what is this "knowing"?** <-
-> **If it is "the quality of being light," then how can that** <-
-> **be brought to what is Self-Luminous by something else?** <- || 9 ||

In this world, an insentient object <term>jada: something lacking consciousness or agency, like a stone</term> is, by its very nature, without light. It does not [possess light] of its own...

---

<margin>Line 3: Manuscript K reads: "Since consciousness is already well-known, how can..."</margin>

<gloss>consciousness, means, action, knowing, light, Tantraloka, Abhinavagupta</gloss>

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that external rituals and actions cannot produce or reveal Consciousness, because Consciousness is the self-luminous source that allows those very actions to be perceived in the first place.</summary>
<keywords>consciousness, upaya, self-luminosity, jnapaka, karaka, Abhinavagupta, Kashmir Shaivism, non-duality</keywords>

--- Page 331 ---
<meta>Page 9 continues the argument from Page 8, which questioned how external "means" or "indicators" could possibly reveal Consciousness. ### Verse 10 ] The Second Chapter

[An insentient object] shines, but it does so only for another—meaning its light belongs entirely to someone else. However, that which is not insentient <term>ajada: sentient or conscious</term> is self-luminous by its very nature; it shines for itself and not for another. Thus, its light is not derived from another, but is its own inherent light. Indeed, if it were to be illuminated by another, it would lack the nature of light and would therefore be characterized by insentience <term>jadya: inertness, like a stone or a jar</term>. 

For this reason, the author states: "Since it is self-luminous in essence, how could that [light] come from elsewhere?" This defines the very nature of light <term>prakashatvam: the state of being manifest or conscious</term>. Furthermore, any "other" factor would either have to be self-luminous or not. If it were self-luminous, then that same quality should be attributed to the first consciousness itself—what then is the purpose of positing another? 

If that "other" were not self-luminous, it too would fall into insentience. Consequently, if one requires a different perceiver <term>pramatr: a subject or knower</term> to manifest the nature of light, it leads to the fallacy of infinite regress <term>anavasthapatti: a logical "endless loop" where no final proof is ever reached</term>. In such a case, because everything would lack the nature of light, nothing at all would be manifest. Therefore, this entire universe would be blind <note>original: "sarvam idam andhaṃ syāt." A famous philosophical warning: without the "sun" of consciousness, the world would be effectively non-existent because it could never be perceived.</note>. || 6 ||

The author summarizes this:

-> **Regarding the fact that the reality of consciousness** <-
-> **is self-luminous—what is the use of logical proofs?** <-

---

### The Splendor of the Tantras <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note>

->In its absence, the universe would be<-
->unilluminated due to its insentience. [10]<-

What is the use of many arguments? He states that there is no need for numerous proofs, for this single argument is supreme: if the self-luminosity <term>svaprakāśatvam: the inherent capacity of awareness to shine by itself without needing an external light</term> of Consciousness <term>saṃvit: pure awareness or the faculty of perception</term> did not exist, then nothing at all would be manifest. [10]

One might object: "If it is true that external actions <term>kriyā: ritual or physical acts</term> and similar things have no power here, then perhaps the knowledge of the Guru <term>guru-jñāna: the wisdom or instruction transmitted by a spiritual teacher</term> and other such factors might serve as the means of realization?" Raising this doubt, the author says:

->Whatever means there may be, whether external<-
->or internal,<-
->all of them gaze toward Its face;<-
->how then can they be considered the "means" to reach It? [11]<-

"Whatever" refers to the various methods taught in the many scriptures. "All" includes those that are external or internal. "Gaze toward Its face" means that their very proof and existence depend entirely on Consciousness <note>original: "saṃvidadhīna-siddhiḥ." Just as a flashlight's beam is only "proven" to exist because your eyes see it, all spiritual tools are only "proven" because Consciousness is already there to perceive them.</note>. The underlying sentiment is this: if a thing depends entirely on something else for its very existence to be established, how can it then be the "means" to bring that very thing into being? [11]

In that regard, if the nature of the Self is Full, then attention <term>avadhāna: the mental act of focusing or directing awareness toward a specific point</term> is not appropriate. <note>original: "Śrī-Tantrālokaḥ." This is the "Light of the Tantras," the masterwork of the 10th-century philosopher Abhinavagupta, which synthesizes the non-dual traditions of Kashmir Shaivism.</note>

### [Verse 17 ] Chapter Two

Indeed, in this context, whatever is sought after as a **means** <term>upāya: a method, technique, or tool used to achieve spiritual realization</term>—is it unmanifest or manifest? 

If it is **unmanifest** <note>original: "aprakāśamānaṁ," meaning it does not "shine" or is not present to consciousness</note>, it would have no form at all. If it has no form, how could it possibly function as a means? 

If it is **manifest**, then it is established as **Shiva** himself, whose very essence is **Light** <term>prakāśa: the foundational, self-shining consciousness that allows all things to be known</term>. Nothing else apart from that Light can be logically established. Therefore, what is the status of a "means"? A means, by definition, must be something distinct from the **goal** <term>upeya: the object to be reached or the result to be achieved</term>. But in this case, such a distinction is not logical. Thus, what could the relationship between "means" and "goal" possibly mean? [15]

It is not only **contemplation** <term>bhāvanā: the practice of creative visualization or cultivating a specific spiritual state</term> and similar practices that are sought as a means; the same logic applies to everything else. As he says:

->**Blue, yellow, or pleasure—**<-
->**all is purely Light, which is Shiva.**<-
->**In this Supreme Non-duality,**<-
->**whose essence is Light, what else exists? [16]**<-

->**How could there be a relationship**<-
->**between a "means" and a "goal,"**<-
->**for He is solely and simply Light? [17]**<-

Even though the status of contemplation and other practices as a means is well-known in the world, once it is refuted, for another...

---

<margin>Line 17: Manuscript 'K' reads "rejected as a means elsewhere" instead of "rejected as a means, [for] another."</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that since everything—including our thoughts and the tools of meditation—is made of the same divine Consciousness (Light), there can be no real distinction between the "method" and the "goal." All things, from colors to feelings, are simply manifestations of Shiva.</summary>

# The Illustrious Tantraloka
### Page 14

...so that not even the slightest possibility of doubt should remain for anyone, the phrase "who else" was spoken in Verse 17—referring to any instance where the possibility of something acting as a **means** <term>upāya: a method or tool for spiritual realization</term> might exist. [17]

Now, an objection is raised: "If this is so, then how can the universally recognized practice of **duality** <term>dvaita-vyavahāra: the everyday experience of subjects and objects as separate</term> be denied?" Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

->**"This is duality; this is difference;**<-
->**and this, too, is non-duality."**<-
->**The Supreme Lord, whose very body is Light,**<-
->**appears in all these forms. [18]**<-

The intention here is that even the experience of duality is essentially composed of **Light** <term>prakāśa: the foundational, self-shining consciousness</term>, precisely because it is being manifest or perceived. The author repeats the phrase "this is difference" <note>original: "ayaṃ bhedaḥ"</note> to indicate that this is the established view of many different philosophical schools. 

Just as in the appearance of **non-duality** <term>advaita: the state of oneness or non-differentiation</term> it is the one Supreme Lord, as the essence of Light, who shines forth, so too does He shine in the appearance of duality. To highlight this comparison, the phrase "and this, too, is non-duality" was included. [18]

But then, another objection arises: "Let us grant that an external object is identical to Light because it is being manifest. However, what about the **mutual difference** <note>original: "anyonya-bheda," the distinction between one object and another</note> between objects? Does this not mean that duality has inevitably forced its way back in?" Anticipating this concern, he says:

---

<margin>Line 13: Manuscript K reads "the analogy was thus stated."</margin>
<margin>Line 16: Manuscript K reads "how has this [duality] arrived?"</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that both duality and non-duality are simply different ways the Supreme Lord—who is pure Light—manifests Himself. He argues that even our perception of "difference" is ultimately an expression of a single, underlying consciousness.</summary>

Regarding the phrase **"on this ground"**: this means in the state of supreme non-duality <term>paramādvaya-daśā: the ultimate level of reality where all distinctions dissolve into one</term>.

**"Share a single meaning"** indicates that the one **Light** <term>prakāśa: the foundational, self-shining consciousness</term> is the only true object being named by all these terms. The underlying thought is this: if pleasure, pain, and other such things possessed some fixed, individual nature of their own separate from Light, then the possibility of them being truly different might exist.

Because of this, it has been said by other masters:

> "The pot knows through my own essence, and I know through the essence of the pot."
<note>original: "ghaṭo madātmanā vetti vedmyahaṃ ca ghaṭātmanā"</note>

Now, an objection might be raised: "If this is so, then wouldn't **duality** <term>dvaita: the state of seeing things as separate</term> still persist because of the different words used to name these experiences?"
In response, the author states: **"and they themselves are but one."**
The word **"one"** here means that since these words and their meanings are being perceived, they are essentially nothing but **Consciousness** <term>saṃvedana: the act of pure sensing or awareness</term> itself. [16]

But then, another question arises: if objects like a blue color or a feeling of pleasure are identical to Light because they are being manifest, then in what specific form do they appear? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

Regarding the phrase **"non-luminous part"** <term>aprakāśāṃśa: an aspect of reality that appears inert or separate from awareness</term>: this refers to inert objects such as pleasure and other experiences. **"How indeed"** means: "in what possible form?"

In that regard, if an object shines solely through the nature of **Light** <term>prakāśa: the foundational, self-shining consciousness</term> itself, then the specific nature of that object—such as "blueness" or "pleasure"—would be compromised <note>original: "doṣaḥ," implying its individual characteristics would be negated or seen as a flaw in the unity</note>. To be precise, it would not appear in its defined, external form as "blue"; only the Light itself would remain.

Conversely, if it is said to shine as something **non-luminous** <term>aprakāśātmanā: having a nature that is not consciousness</term> in its own fixed form, then its very existence could not be ascertained. Indeed, the nature of things like "blue" is never perceived at any time without Light. To say "it shines in a non-luminous form" is a hollow contradiction in terms <note>original: "vāco-yuktiśca riktā syāt," literally "the joining of words would be empty"</note>. This is what the author means by the phrase beginning with **"Or if it does not shine..."**

Moreover, the **Light** <term>prakāśa: the foundational, self-shining consciousness</term> shines even in the "non-blue" and other states by setting aside "blue" and similar objects. Indeed, "blue" and so forth are merely **limiting adjuncts** <term>upādhi: a conditional property that appears to limit or color a thing, like a red flower held near a clear crystal</term>. Because such an adjunct is nothing more than the expansion of the Light's own sovereign freedom, it is not ultimately real. Thus, it is the one, undivided Light alone that manifests.

It is by the **glory** <term>mahimnā: the innate power or grandeur of consciousness</term> of this Light alone that the entire universe—which consists of appearances such as "blue" and so on—is able to flash forth. For this very reason, the author states: **"Therefore, it cannot be proven as a specific attribute of Light."** The word **"therefore"** indicates that because it is the one, undivided Light that shines forth in the form of these various appearances, no division actually exists.

One might object: "But the 'light of blue' is one thing, and the 'light of yellow' is another. Surely there is a difference between them? Why then say that 'no specific attribute is possible'?"

This is not so. This difference is merely **conditional** <term>aupādhika: dependent on external factors or superimpositions</term>, and it is not real—this has been demonstrated many times. Since blue and other objects are essentially Light itself (because they are being perceived), what is there to be differentiated from what? Indeed, a thing cannot be divided from its own self. This is why it has been said: **"Within Consciousness, which consists of the singular form of Light, there is no other consciousness."** <note>original: "na ca prakāśaikarūpāyāṃ saṃvidi saṃvidantaramasti"</note> 

Therefore, when the everyday usage of "difference" is applied to the very nature of things, one single difference—

# The Illustrious Light of the Tantras #

Only the **nature of the Light** <term>prakāśa: the foundational, self-shining consciousness</term> would be expressed. Thus, the argument would be **like an elephant’s bath** <term>gajasnāna-tulya: a traditional metaphor for a futile action where an elephant washes itself and then immediately throws dust over its body; here, it refers to establishing a distinction only to have it immediately dissolve</term>. Consequently, we would arrive once more at the conclusion that "it is only one undivided consciousness." 

Furthermore, even **space and time** <term>deśa and kāla: the primary dimensions of physical reality</term> reside within the state of the Light. Because they are "things to be illumined," they are absorbed into the essential identity of the Light. How, then, could they possibly impose a division upon that Light? Even if one were to assume that space and time existed beyond the Light, they would still be unable to create division because of their own **eternality and pervasiveness** <note>original: "nityatva-vyāpakatvābhyām." Things that are everywhere and always cannot mark the boundaries where one thing ends and another begins</note>. 

Therefore, the Light is one and undivided. In this way, those other thinkers who wish to establish an alternative view <note>referring to dualists or certain Buddhist schools who argue for a stream of separate moments of consciousness</note> are completely refuted. [21]

->Therefore, he says:<-

> Because this doctrine of a **single Light**
> is now firmly established here,
> those who argue for **multiple cognitions** 
> are truly excluded from a distance. [22]

One might ask: "If different cognitions are impossible, why is the word 'one' used here at all? What is it meant to exclude?" <note>In Sanskrit logic, if only one thing exists, the word "one" is redundant unless it is specifically denying the possibility of "many."</note> Suspecting this doubt, the author says:

---

<note>Line 6, Manuscript Ka: "incapability of division due to eternity and pervasiveness."</note>

# The Illustrious Light of the Tantras #

### [Verse 24] Second Chapter. 16 ###

->Only the **nature of the Light** is expressed,<-
->by the negation of what is **non-light**.<-
->The meaning of the word "**one**" is not numerical,<-
->for that would imply a division of consciousness. [23]<-

**Non-light**—referring to external objects such as "blue" and so on that are meant to be illumined—is hereby denied. Therefore, in the statement "the Light alone exists," the word "**one**" (eka) functions in the sense of being **unaccompanied** <term>asāhātya: solitary or without a second</term>. Thus it was stated: "The meaning of the word 'one' is declared as only the nature of the Light." 

It does **not** mean a **numerical value** <term>saṃkhyārtha: the concept of "one" as a number in a sequence</term> characterized by "one, two, three," and so on. If it were numerical, it would imply a **division of Light** <note>original: "prakāśa-bheda-bhāk"</note>, which would suggest that alternative views <note>referring to other philosophical schools that posit multiple souls or separate streams of awareness</note> could potentially be valid as things to be refuted. [23]

For this reason, not even a **mere conventional usage** <term>vyavahāra-mātra: everyday linguistic habit</term> that suggests a sense of division is recognized here. 

Thus, he says:

->This is not the **Great Goddess Power**,<-
->for it does not depend on another.<-

### Verse 27 ] The Second Chapter ###

<page-num>21</page-num>

...[the word "Power"] would not reach its referent. Therefore, this Supreme Light is not **Power** <term>śakti: the creative or kinetic aspect of God</term>, for power exists only by depending upon a **Possessor of Power** <term>śaktimān: the foundational or masculine aspect</term>. Because the Light is entirely independent, if any appearance of division were allowed to emerge, the fundamental premise—that "Light alone is one"—would be lost. 

In the same way, the conventional use of the term **Possessor of Power** does not apply here either. That term also functions only by accepting a meaning defined by its relationship to Power. If we used such terms, we would fall back into **division** <term>bheda: the perception of reality as consisting of separate parts</term>. 

The same logic should be understood regarding the "Object of Meditation" and other such categories. The term **Mantra** refers to the deity being addressed by a sacred sound, such as the syllable *Om* <note>original: "praṇavādi"</note>. The **Reciter** is the one who chants these mantras. There is no **Initiation** <term>dīkṣā: the ritual process of spiritual awakening</term> here because initiation requires the interaction of an agent <gloss>the initiator</gloss> and an object <gloss>the person being initiated</gloss>. In this state of **Supreme Sovereignty** <term>māhaiśvarya: the absolute, unrestricted freedom of God</term>, the only "cause" is the Lord’s own mastery.
[24-25-26]

For this very reason, anything that introduces even the slightest hint of division has no place here. As the text states:

->**Ritual postures, seating, and breath restraint;**<-
->**unification, invocation, and the rest,**<-
->**ending with the dismissal—none of these exist here,**<-
->**as this state is devoid of agent, object, and action.** [27]<-

# The Tantrāloka #

<page-num>22</page-num>

**Placement** <term>sthāna: the ritual act of establishing the deity in a specific location</term> is the resting of the Lord by means of the **Gesture of Establishment** <term>sthāpana-mudrā: a symbolic hand gesture used to "fix" or stabilize a divine presence during ritual</term>. 

**Seat** <term>āsana: the formal positioning of the deity</term> is the turning toward the worship <margin>Manuscript variant: "toward the object of worship"</margin> by means of the **Gesture of Presence** <term>sannidhāna-mudrā: a gesture used to invite the deity to be intimately present before the practitioner</term>. 

**Restraint** <term>nirodha: the ritual act of "locking" the deity into the space</term> is remaining in that very state in an immovable way. 

The **Honorific Offering** <term>argha: a traditional welcoming libation</term> consists of eight parts. 

**Uniting** <term>sandhāna: the spiritual joining of different elements</term> concerns the **mantra** <gloss>the sacred sound-syllables</gloss> and other ritual objects. 

**Invocation** <term>āvāhana</term> is the act of bringing something that was not facing you to be face-to-face. 

**Dismissal** <term>visarjana</term> is the act of making something that was face-to-face no longer face-to-face. 

The reason why these acts—from Invocation to Dismissal—do not truly exist <gloss>in the ultimate reality</gloss> is found in the qualifier "the agent, etc." <note>This refers to the previous verse, which argued that the roles of the one performing the ritual and the ritual itself are dualistic</note>. Because the "agent" and the other ritual categories are ultimately nothing more than **mental constructs** <term>vikalpa: the dualistic way the human mind labels and divides the seamless reality of consciousness</term>, and because the **Light** <term>prakāśa: the fundamental, self-shining awareness</term> is identical with the **Supreme Knower** <term>parapramātṛ: the ultimate Subject of all experience</term> and is thus beyond all constructs, it cannot be described by any designation whatsoever. For this reason, it was stated previously that "This is not Power," and so on. [27]

Nor is this conclusion based solely on logical reasoning; it is also established by **Scripture** <term>āgama: the revealed tantric traditions</term>. To demonstrate this, he quotes the *Śrī Bhargaśikhā* <note>original: "bhargaśikhā"; an ancient, now-lost scriptural text often cited in this tradition</note>:

->It is not existent, nor is it non-existent,<-
->nor is it both existent and non-existent,<-
->nor is it a state free from both.<-
->Indeed, that state is difficult to know;<-
->this is the indescribable **Supreme** <term>anuttara: the "Absolute" or "Unsurpassable," representing the heart of reality beyond all categories</term>. [28]<-

In the world, any object that appears as "this" <gloss>original: ayam</gloss>, standing before a person and distinguished from other things of its own kind <note>The Sanskrit term *sajātiya-vyāvṛtti* refers to the logical process of defining a thing by what it is not—for example, a pot is defined by not being a cloth or another object.</note>, is designated as "existent" <term>sat: that which has being or reality in a conventional sense</term>. For example, a pot. 

However, **Light** <term>Prakāśa: the primordial, self-shining consciousness</term>—the nature of which was explained immediately prior—is filled with infinite entities. It is not like a pot, because it is not limited; its nature is the **Great Existence** <term>Mahāsattā: the universal, unlimited Being that underlies all specific forms of existence</term>. Since it is not of a limited form, it cannot be designated by the word "existent" <gloss>sat</gloss> in the worldly sense. This is the intended meaning. || 28-29 ||

One might then ask: "In that case, should it be designated by the word 'non-existent'?" To address this doubt, he says:

->Non-existence is the absence of Light;<-
->it possesses no utility anywhere.<-

This is exemplified by such things as the **horns of a hare** <note>A classic Indian philosophical metaphor for something that is purely imaginary and has no basis in reality.</note>...

<summary>Abhinavagupta defines the Absolute (Bhairava) as "Great Existence," which transcends worldly definitions of "existent" (limited objects) and "non-existent" (that which does not manifest). He argues that reality is defined by Light (Prakāśa), the self-manifesting consciousness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 23 regarding the nature of the Absolute (Bhairava) as "Light" (Prakāśa). On the previous page, the author began defining why the Absolute cannot be called "non-existent" (asat) just because it lacks the limited existence of a physical object like a pot. This page completes that thought and moves into the Absolute's role as the animating force of all reality.</meta>

# The Holy Tantrāloka #

<page-num>24</page-num>

...[nature like that] of stones and so forth; and for that very reason, it is not useful for any **causal efficacy** <term>arthakriyā: the ability of a thing to produce a result or perform a function, which is the standard of reality in many Indian philosophical schools</term> in any way. In other words, it performs no causal action at all.

->However, Light is not like that; he says:<-

->It is the true life of the universe,<-
->and its essence is Light alone. || 30 ||<-

"Of the universe"—meaning everything, whether conscious or unconscious—it is the ultimate **Life**. It is the animating principle by virtue of its **creative vibration** <term>sphurattā: the pulse of divine consciousness that brings the world into appearance</term>. Indeed, it has been said that without this Light, nothing at all could shine or be perceived. Thus, it is described as "its essence is Light alone." The inner meaning is that because it manifests as many forms, it cannot be designated by the word "non-existent" <gloss>original: asat</gloss>. || 30 ||

->For this very reason, he says it is also not of a nature that is both existence and non-existence:<-

->For these two reasons alone,<-
->it is neither of a dual nature, nor is it devoid of both.<-
->Since this Light shines as the self of everything,<-
->in what specific form could it be discussed? || 31 ||<-

"For these two"—referring to the two reasons just mentioned: the lack of limitation <note>original: anavacchinnatva</note> and the nature of Light...

<summary>This page defines the Absolute (Light) as the animating life-force (sphurattā) of the universe, arguing that it transcends human categories of existence, non-existence, or a combination of both.</summary>
<keywords>Light (Prakāśa), Causal Efficacy (Arthakriyā), Creative Vibration (Sphurattā), Existence (Sat), Non-existence (Asat), Abhinavagupta</keywords>
