<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 31 of Chapter 2. The previous page established that the Absolute (Light) is the life of the universe. This page addresses the philosophical paradox of how the Absolute can be both beyond the categories of "existence" and "non-existence" while simultaneously being the source of both.</meta>

# The Holy Tantrāloka #

<page-num>25</page-num>
<header>Verse 31 ] Chapter Two</header>

...by the characteristics [of being unlimited and being the source of Light]. Now, an objection is raised: "If this is so, then surely the Absolute would be transcendent of the two states consisting of existence and non-existence?" Anticipating this doubt, he says: **"not of a dual nature, etc."** Even at the time when existence and non-existence are being perceived, it is He alone who shines supremely; so how could He be considered divested of both existence and non-existence? To this he replies: **"For this Light shines as the self of everything."**

The essential meaning is this: The Light becomes one with the Supreme Subject <term>parapramātṛ: the ultimate, undivided consciousness that experiences all of reality</term>. Otherwise, because it is of an unlimited nature, it would never fall into the realm of conceptual thought <term>vikalpa: the dualistic mental process of naming, categorizing, and separating things into "this" and "not-that"</term>. As it has been said:

> “From the existent, the supreme non-existence and existence are certainly beyond that, O All-pervasive Lord. You are other than the non-existent and the existent; therefore, you are composed of both existence and non-existence.” <note>original: "sato'vaśyaṃ paramasat sacca tasmāt paraṃ vibho..."</note>

->And likewise:<-

> “Your form is neither quieted, nor arisen, nor is it in the middle. Your form, O Lord, is that which is spoken of by no one.” <note>original: "na śāntam uditaṃ vāpi..."</note>

Therefore, we do not know by what imagined form this Light is being described. For this state is difficult to understand for those "subjects of Illusion" <term>māyā-pramātṛ: a person whose perception is limited by the physical world and who sees themselves as separate from the Divine</term>, whose intellects are impaired by dualistic thinking. This means that, according to the reasoning just stated, it is impossible to know this state through ordinary logic. For those who have directly realized the truth of the Supreme Self—

<summary>This page argues that the Absolute cannot be limited by the categories of "existence" or "non-existence" because it is the very Light that allows both to be perceived. <meta>This page continues the commentary on the nature of the Absolute as the "Light of Consciousness." Having established in the previous verse that the Absolute shines as the self of all things, Abhinavagupta now describes the internal experience of this state and cites the Triśirobhairava Tantra to support the idea that the Absolute is always "pregnant" with its own creative Power.</meta>

# The Holy Tantrāloka #

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>The Holy Tantrāloka</header>

...ed. However, for those whose mental fluctuations have settled into a state of pure stillness <term>kalpavṛtti: the state where the churning of conceptual thought has ceased</term>, this reality shines as something that surpasses everything else. It is perceived as a dense, concentrated mass of supreme bliss and aesthetic wonder <term>camatkāra: the "aha!" moment of consciousness recognizing its own infinite nature</term> that arises from one's own direct experience. This is why it was said in the previous verse that "this state is the incomparable Beyond." <note>original: "kimapyetadanuttaram"</note> ॥ 31 ॥

This truth has not only been stated here in this text, but has been declared elsewhere in the scriptures as well. Thus, the author says:

->In the venerable *Triśirobhairava Tantra*,<-
->the nature of supreme knowledge is declared:<-
->"The supreme state is 'pregnant with Power'<-
->through that Power which resides within its very womb."<- ॥ 32 ॥

The intention here is that the Blessed Lord spoke of this "nature of supreme knowledge" in order to resolve the question asked by the Goddess: "O Lord, how is supreme knowledge attained?" He then quotes the passage beginning with "through that Power." This "supreme state" is "pregnant with Power" <term>śaktigarbham: literally 'having Power in the womb,' meaning the Absolute contains all potential within itself</term>. Here, "Power" refers to that which is called by such names as "Absolute Freedom" <term>svātantrya</term> and "Reflective Awareness" <term>vimarśa</term>. This Power is the "womb" or the "essence" of the supreme state.

Furthermore, this Power is not something separate or external to the Absolute. This is why the verse says "through that Power which resides within its very womb." Because of that very Power called Freedom, the "womb"—which refers to the inner reality or the state of being one with the Subject <term>pramātṛ-aikātmya: the state where the individual experiencer realizes they are identical with the universal Knower</term>—exists in its highest possible limit. It is characterized by this Power, which is the Absolute's own true nature. If it were otherwise, the Absolute would not possess the quality of being "supreme" at all. As it has been said:

<summary>This page explains that the Absolute is experienced as concentrated bliss (camatkāra) and cites the Triśirobhairava Tantra to define the supreme state as being "pregnant with Power" (śaktigarbha).</summary>

--- Page 349 ---
<meta>This page continues the explanation of the "supreme state" mentioned in Verse 32. It completes the discussion on how the Light of Consciousness (prakāśa) must possess Reflective Awareness (vimarśa) to be sentient, and then moves to Verse 33, which describes the Absolute as being beyond all categories of existence and non-existence.</meta>

<page-num>27</page-num>
<header>Verse 33 ] Second Chapter</header>

...ness <term>vimarśa: the capacity of consciousness to be aware of itself</term>." As it is said:

> "The wise know that the essential nature of the Light's manifestation is Reflective Awareness; otherwise, the Light, even when 'colored' by objects, would be like an inert crystal."
> <note>original: "svabhāvamavabhāsasya vimarśaṃ viduranyathā | prakāśo’rthoparacto’pi sphaṭikādijaḍopamaḥ ||" — This famous verse explains that without self-awareness, consciousness would be like a mirror or crystal: it might reflect things, but it wouldn't "know" it was reflecting them.</note>

Therefore, the Absolute resides in its own essential nature within that Power which is the Self of Absolute Freedom <term>svātantrya</term>. This means that the Absolute always exists in that specific form. For this reason, it is "pregnant with Power" <term>śaktigarbham</term>. The meaning is that without this Power of Freedom, no other powers of the Absolute could exist. It is this very Power that is spoken of as "manifold" or "diverse" only because of the limiting conditions of the various objects that we desire or perceive. As it has been stated:

> "Therefore, it is a direct rule that He is joined only by the Power of Freedom. Even His possession of 'many powers' is simply His non-separation from that one Power."
> <note>original: "tena svātantryaśaktyaiva yukta ityāñjaso vidhiḥ | bahuśaktitvampyasya tacchaktyaivāviyuktata ||"</note>

Consequently, following the established principle that "Independent Consciousness is the Ultimate Reality," the supreme truth is nothing other than pure Light <term>prakāśa</term>. This Light is undivided in nature, possesses Absolute Freedom, and is free from the limitations of conceptual thought <term>avikalpaka</term>. This is the intended meaning of verse 32. ॥ 32 ॥

Furthermore, because this reality cannot tolerate being restricted by specific definitions or boundaries, it does not fall within the realm of conceptual thought. Thus, the author says:

> ->It is not being, nor is it non-being,<-
> ->nor is it both; for it is beyond the reach of words.<-
> ->Having ascended to the path of the inexpressible,<-
> ->it resides in Power, yet is devoid of Power.<- ॥ 33 ॥

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that the Light of Consciousness is inherently self-aware (vimarśa) and that all divine powers are actually just expressions of a single Absolute Freedom. He concludes that the ultimate reality is "inexpressible," transcending categories like existence and non-existence.</summary>

<keywords>Reflective Awareness, Light of Consciousness, Absolute Freedom, svātantrya, vimarśa, prakāśa, śaktigarbham, inexpressible, non-dualism, Triśirobhairava Tantra</keywords>

--- Page 350 ---
<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Verse 33, which emphasizes that the Absolute is "inexpressible." It then transitions into Verse 34, which marks a significant shift in the text: it describes the state of those who have already attained "established awareness." For these advanced practitioners, the various "means" or methods (upāyas) of spiritual practice are no longer necessary because they already reside in the "Path of the Absolute."</meta>

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>The Light on the Tantras</header>

The phrase "beyond the reach [of speech]" is used here as an abstract noun. By this, the author means that the Absolute has "attained the path of the inexpressible" because it cannot be grasped by words. Since all of this has been explained multiple times already, we shall not exert ourselves by repeating it here. [33]

Now, he explains that those who are attentive to this reality are indeed the most successful:

-> Thus, those who are purified by the supreme reality <-
-> of established consciousness, <-
-> having ascended the path of the Absolute, <-
-> are no longer constrained by any means. [34] <-

**Thus**—by the aforementioned teachings of the Guru and other factors.
**Established**—this refers to those in whom a "blossoming" has been brought about through the attainment of oneness with that reality. 
**Consciousness... Supreme Reality**—this refers to the "vibration" or manifestation of the Self as the essence of all things in all things. 
**Purified by [this]**—this means those who have been made fit for the state of supreme non-duality by the removal of the turbidity <note>original: "kaluṣya"—referring to the "muddiness" or spiritual impurity caused by the false belief in separation.</note> caused by the modifications of duality.
For this very reason, they are **not constrained** by any external or internal "means" <term>abhyupāya: the spiritual methods or disciplines, such as ritual or meditation, used to reach God-consciousness</term>. They are independent of such methods. 
**On the path of the Absolute** <term>Anuttara-pathe: the "unsurpassable" or "highest" path</term>—on that path which surpasses all because it is a solid mass of the wonder of full bliss, a flowering of consciousness...

---

<margin>Line 12: Manuscript K reads "removal of the turbidity caused by the agents of modification."</margin>
<margin>Line 13: Manuscript K reads "by that which is not separate."</margin>

<summary>This page concludes the discussion on the ineffability of the Absolute and introduces the concept that for highly realized beings, spiritual methods (upāyas) are no longer required. It defines "purification" as the removal of the mental "turbidity" that makes us see the world as separate from ourselves.</summary>

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>Verse 35 ] Second Chapter</header>

They are **resting in the path of their own self-nature**—this means they have attained a state of **essential identity** <note>original: "sāmarasya"—literally "equal flavor," referring to the state where the individual soul and the Divine have become one, like salt dissolved in water.</note> simply by abiding in the natural flow of their own essence. As it has been said:

> "Remain exactly as you are; go neither to the external nor the internal. Destroy the multitude of mental fluctuations solely through the **blossoming of consciousness**."

And likewise:

> "The yogi who rests in the **Power of Bliss** <note>original: "ānanda-śakti"</note> becomes integrated in that **equal flavor**."

And also:

> "There is no other means of liberation than the realization of one's own existence. Following that reality alone, the yogi who is established in himself becomes happy." [34]

What follows from this? The author says:

-> For them, this entire <-
-> circle of existence appears, <-
-> standing right before them, <-
-> yet dissolved in the fire of Bhairava-Consciousness. [35] <-

**For them**—meaning for those who possess the "immersion without means" <term>anupāya-samāveśa: a state of sudden enlightenment where no specific technique or ritual is required because the practitioner is already one with the Absolute</term>. Even though this entire **circle of existence** <term>bhāva-maṇḍala: the totality of all objects and experiences in the world</term> appears as if it is "in front" of them in relation to the body and senses, they perceive it as:

> "All this has arisen from me alone; it is reflected within me alone; and it is non-different from me..."

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the transformation of the external world into pure consciousness. It specifically addresses how, for an enlightened being, the distinctions between mundane emotions and even spiritual hierarchies dissolve into the singular experience of the Absolute.</meta>

<page-num>30</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantraloka</header>

In this manner, the meaning is that everything appears as consisting of **Full Consciousness** <term>pūrṇa-saṃvid: the state of absolute, non-dual awareness that lacks nothing</term>. As it has been said:

> "Just as wood, leaves, stones, and other objects that have fallen into the salt mines of Rumā <note>Rumā refers to a famous salt lake or region (likely Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan) used in classical Indian philosophy as a metaphor: just as the intense salinity transforms any object into salt, the "fire" of pure consciousness transforms all objective experiences into its own essence.</note> are transformed into salt, so too do all objective things become one with the **Self of Consciousness**."

[35]

For this very reason, the author says:

-> For such individuals, the divided thoughts <-
-> of pleasure and pain, and the anxieties and <-
-> fears associated with them, have come to a <-
-> state where only the supreme, <-
-> thought-free immersion remains. [36] <-

-> For them, there is no mantra, no meditation, <-
-> no ritual worship, nor any mental construction. <-
-> There is no resting point in any stage, <-
-> from the level of an initiate to that of a master. [37] <-

It is not only that their worldly mental constructions become nothing because they have attained the **state of immersion beyond thought** <term>avikalpaka-āveśa: a direct, non-conceptual experience of the Divine</term>; even their spiritual constructions—such as specific techniques or stages—are transcended. This is what the author means by "For them," referring to things like the mental constructs of practice-locations and so on. [36-37]

---

<margin>Line 7, Manuscript Ka: The reading is "the fear of pleasure and pain."</margin>
<margin>Line 9, Manuscript Ka: The reading is "merely the awareness" <note>original: "parāmarśa-mātra"</note>.</margin>

<summary>This page describes how the enlightened practitioner views the world as being entirely absorbed into pure consciousness, much like objects turning into salt in a salt mine. Consequently, all worldly anxieties and even formal spiritual requirements—like mantras, rituals, and the hierarchy from student to teacher—are rendered unnecessary and dissolved into a state of direct, thought-free immersion.</summary>

--- Page 353 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the state of the liberated being. Having established on the previous page that such a person transcends all religious rituals and mental constructs, the text now addresses why such a person continues to live and act in the world.</meta>

<page-num>31</page-num>
<header>Verse 38 ] Second Chapter</header>

Now, one might ask: if this is the case—that the enlightened soul has no need for rituals—how then does his **remaining activity** <term>śeṣa-vṛtti: the continued life and conduct of a liberated soul while still in the physical body</term> proceed? Anticipating this doubt, the author says:

-> For one who possesses the nature of an axe <-
-> in severing the web of all constraints, <-
-> there is no purpose in his remaining life <-
-> other than the bestowing of grace. [38] <-

**All** refers to the entirety of the **constraints** <term>yantraṇā: restrictive rules or bondages</term> prescribed by the **scriptures** <term>śāstra: sacred law and teaching</term>—rules such as "this must be done" and "this must not be done." Because these rules are woven or spread out, they are called a **web** <term>tantra: here used in its etymological sense of a loom or a woven system of threads; <note>original: "tantram"</note></term>, much like the network of threads that forms the beginning of a cloth or similar object. 

In the **severing** or cutting of that web, the phrase **nature of an axe** <note>original: "ṭaṅka-dharmiṇaḥ"</note> means he acts like a weapon. Just as an axe cuts through a web, so too does this individual—having entered the **Non-Way** <term>anupāya: the highest state of realization which requires no specific technique or "way"</term>—sever scriptural constraints. The inner meaning is that for one who has ascended to this height, there is no longer any sense of **limitation** <term>saṃkoca: the "contraction" of infinite consciousness into a small, bound ego</term> arising from those rules. 

For the **scriptures** act as a regulator only for those who desire to ascend and are still fit for instruction, as was stated just moments ago. Therefore, because he has already accomplished everything that needed to be done for his own self, his continued existence is solely for the purpose of bestowing **grace** <term>anugraha: the divine power of liberation or favor</term> upon others. This is what the author is saying.

---

Line 8: In manuscript 'Kh', the reading is: "The 'web' refers to cloth etc.; there, 'severing' means cutting; 'possessing the nature of an axe' means having the quality of splitting like a chisel or a weapon." This is the interpretation of the text.

<summary>This page explains that a liberated master, having severed the "web" of scriptural rules like an axe, continues to live and act only to bestow grace upon others, as they have no remaining personal goals.</summary>
<keywords>grace (anugraha), scriptural constraints (yantraṇā), the Non-Way (anupāya), remaining life (śeṣa-vṛtti), liberation, teacher's purpose</keywords>

--- Page 354 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the liberated soul’s role in the world. Having established that the enlightened person acts only out of grace, Abhinavagupta now contrasts the self-centered actions of ordinary people with the selfless, divine-focused activity of the master who has realized his identity with Bhairava.</meta>

<page-num>32</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Tantrāloka</header>

The phrase **"than the bestowing of grace"** <note>original: "nānugrahād-iti"</note> refers to any remaining actions, such as **observing spiritual commitments** <term>samaya-paripālana: the keeping of vows or rules of conduct within a tantric lineage</term> and so forth. [38]

To explain this, he says:

-> This world, striving to fulfill some duty of its own, <-
-> does not engage in any activity for the sake of others. <-
-> But for one who has destroyed every stain of worldly existence <-
-> and is filled with the nature of Bhairava, <-
-> his only clear task is simply this: the welfare of the world. [39] <-

**This world** <note>original: "eṣa lokaḥ"</note> refers to the **class of contracted subjects** <term>saṃkocita-pramātṛ-varga: ordinary individuals whose consciousness is limited and separated from the whole</term>. According to the principle that:
> "...desire is the stain here [in the soul]..."

and other such teachings, because they are joined with the **primordial stain of individuality** <term>āṇava-mala: the "stain of smallness" or the basic ignorance that makes one feel incomplete</term> and the stains of the world, they perceive themselves as **incomplete** <term>apūrṇa-manyatā: the sense of "I am not enough" or "I am lacking"</term>. 

Because of this perceived lack, they are constantly **striving**—expressed generally here as "some duty"—to fulfill all their **own** needs, as these are seen as desirable goals. Following the logical maxim:
> "That which is itself unproven cannot accomplish what is to be proven."
<note>original: "tad-asiddhaṃ yad-asiddhena sādhyate"</note>

The inner meaning is this: how can someone who has not even achieved their own goal <term>svārtha: self-interest or one's own liberation</term> engage in even the slightest activity for the **sake of others**? <margin>In manuscript 'Kha', the reading is "belonging to others" <note>original: "pārakya"</note> instead of "for the sake of others."</margin> Even if such a person were to engage in such activity, it would produce no real result. 

However, for the master who has entered the **Non-Way** <term>anupāya: the immediate realization of reality without needing progressive techniques</term> and has thereby **destroyed** <term>khilīkṛta: literally "turned into a wasteland," meaning neutralized or rendered powerless</term> the stains...

<summary>This page explains that ordinary people are too hindered by their own sense of incompleteness (Aṇavamala) to act truly for others. In contrast, the liberated soul, being "full" of the divine nature of Bhairava, has no personal needs and thus exists solely to benefit the world.</summary>

<keywords>Bhairava, Aṇavamala (Stain of Individuality), Self-interest vs. Altruism, Contracted Subject, Anupāya (Non-Way), Spiritual Completeness</keywords>

--- Page 355 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Verse 36 of the second chapter of the Tantrāloka. It elaborates on the nature of a liberated soul (jīvanmukta) who, having identified with the divine nature of Bhairava, acts in the world solely for the benefit of others rather than out of personal need or lack.</meta>

<page-num>33</page-num>
<header>Verse 36 ] Second Chapter</header>

...all bonds are destroyed. Therefore, through the **state of Bhairava** <term>bhairavī-bhāva: the internal realization of being one with the absolute reality, Bhairava</term>, and by attaining the **non-dual knowledge of the Lord** <note>original: "bhagavad-advaya-jñāna"</note>, such a person has **accomplished all that was to be done** <term>kṛta-kṛtyatva: the state of having fulfilled all spiritual obligations and needs</term> within his own Self. Because there is nothing left for him to desire, he is **Full**—resting in his own Self without looking toward anything else. 

For him, the only task remaining toward the entire world—an absolute necessity—is simply this: **making the world recognize its own true Self** <term>svātma-pratyabhijñāpana: the process of leading others to the "recognition" (pratyabhijñā) of their own inherent divinity</term>. This alone is his clear and undiminished duty. In other words, his only remaining obligation is **grace toward the world** <term>lokānugraha: the compassionate act of a liberated being to help others achieve spiritual freedom</term>. The idea is that there is nothing left for him to do for his own sake, as he has already attained everything that could possibly be attained. As was sung by the Blessed Lord [Krishna]:

> "But for the human being whose delight is in the Self alone, who is satisfied with the Self, and who is content only in the Self, there is no duty to be performed." <note>Bhagavad Gītā 3.17</note>

And also:

> "O Partha, there is nothing in the three worlds that I must do; there is nothing unattained that I must attain, yet I remain engaged in action." <note>Bhagavad Gītā 3.22</note>

There are two kinds of grace bestowed upon others: those intended for seekers with **pure consciousness** <term>nirmala-saṃvit: awareness that is already refined and free from the densest veils of ignorance</term> and those for seekers with **impure consciousness**. Regarding those with pure consciousness, his ability to bestow grace requires no external rituals or instruments. Thus, he [Abhinavagupta] says:

---

<note>Footnote referring to line 1 of the page: Manuscript 'K' reads "by the attainment of knowledge of the objects of knowledge" (jñeya-jñānopapattyā) instead of "attaining non-dual knowledge of the Lord."</note>

<sig>5</sig>

<summary>Abhinavagupta explains that a person who has realized their identity with Bhairava is "full" and has no personal duties left; their only activity is the selfless act of helping the world recognize its own divine nature. He cites the Bhagavad Gita to support the idea that the enlightened act without personal necessity.</summary>
<keywords>Bhairava, non-dual knowledge, self-recognition, grace, pure consciousness, Bhagavad Gita, fullness, liberation</keywords>

--- Page 356 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the liberated soul who acts only for the grace of others. Having established that the liberated being is "Full" and motivated solely by compassion, Abhinavagupta now explains how this grace is transmitted to others simply through the act of being seen.</meta>

<page-num>34</page-num>
<header>The Śrī Tantrāloka</header>

->Those of pure consciousness who behold Him<-
->through the process of becoming one with Him—<-
->they too take on His form; such is<-
->the nature of His grace. [40]<-

Those who possess **pure consciousness** <term>nirmala-saṃvid: awareness that is free from the limitations of the ego and mental constructs</term>—whether through the momentum of **previous spiritual practice** <note>original: "pūrvābhyāsa"</note> or because they are recipients of an **extremely intense descent of power** <term>tīvra-tīvra-śaktipāta: the most powerful form of divine grace which results in immediate realization without effort</term>—they "behold" Him. This "He" refers to the perfected being whose nature was described in the preceding verse. 

They realize Him through the process of **identification** <term>tādrūpya: literally "becoming that nature"; the state where the subject and object of meditation become one</term>. They experience this directly through knowledge, recognizing it as the **fortune of the means-less immersion** <term>nirupāya-samāveśa-bhāgya: the highest state of spiritual absorption that happens spontaneously, without requiring specific techniques or rituals</term>. 

Consequently, merely by beholding such a perfected soul, their own consciousness is transformed through a "contagion" or transmission of that state. As it will be said later in this text:

> "...arisen like one lamp lit from another." <note>A classic metaphor for the transmission of spiritual awakening from a master to a student.</note>

According to this logic, by sharing in that "means-less" immersion, they become exactly like Him. Furthermore, it has been previously established that the very act of seeing a **Siddha** <term>siddha: a perfected master who has attained supernatural powers and liberation</term> or similar beings acts as the catalyst for this immersion. As stated in the scriptures:

> "The sight of the Siddhas and the Yoginis..." <note>original: "siddhānāṃ yoginīnāṃ ca darśanam"; refers to the transformative power of meeting enlightened beings or deities.</note>

Therefore, the nature of His **grace** <term>anugrahātmatā: the essence of divine favor</term> is found in this very act of seeing. It does not require the support of the various **spiritual means** <term>upāya: the structured methods of practice, such as meditation or ritual, categorized in this system into three levels</term> that will be described in the chapters to come. This is the meaning of the verse.

<summary>This page explains that a highly advanced seeker can achieve liberation simply by beholding a perfected master. This "means-less" transmission of grace happens like one lamp lighting another, transforming the witness into the likeness of the divine being they perceive.</summary>

<keywords>Tantraloka, Nirupaya-samavesha, Shaktipata, Grace, Siddha, Transmission of Consciousness, Identification</keywords>

--- Page 357 ---
<meta>This page addresses a potential contradiction: if traditional initiation (diksha) is usually required for liberation, how can the "means-less" path (anupaya) described on the previous page—where one is liberated simply by beholding a Master—be valid? Abhinavagupta argues that internal realization is the true, "primary" form of all rituals.</meta>

<page-num>३५</page-num>
<header>Verse 41 ] Second Chapter</header>

### But is it not true of all initiation?

> "...and liberation [comes] through **Shiva-initiation** <note>original: "shiva-dikshaya"</note>."

By such statements, [the scriptures] declare that initiation is the means to liberation. How then can it be said here that liberation is attained just by "seeing" <note>the Master</note>, even without initiation? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

->This thorough knowledge of reality<-
->is said to be the primary sacrifice and so on,<-
->culminating in initiation, by the All-pervading Lord<-
->in the venerable **Siddhayogīśvarīmata**. [41]<-

The "thorough knowledge" <note>original: "parijñānam"</note> of this reality—which was just described as being "means-less" <note>the state of *anupāya* where no techniques are needed</note>—is itself, in the primary sense, "sacrifice, fire-oblation, and the rest." This is the connection to the phrase "is said by the All-pervading Lord" in the **Venerable Siddhayogīśvarīmata** <term>Śrī Siddhayogīśvarīmata: an essential Tantric scripture of the Trika school focusing on the power of the goddesses</term>—and indeed, in all the scriptures <term>āgamas</term>. 

From this, the meaning is established: external **sacrifice and ritual** <term>yāgādi: refers to the formal offerings and ceremonies performed with physical materials</term> are secondary or symbolic. If they were not secondary, then this internal knowledge could not be called the "primary" sacrifice. It is with this very intention that such external acts are forbidden even in the **path of conduct** <term>caryākrama: the stage of practice involving daily rituals, discipline, and behavioral rules</term>. As it has been said:

> "For this, neither mandalas <note>sacred geometric diagrams</note> nor sacrificial pits <note>kunda</note> and so on are of any use. Nor are preliminary rituals like the 'placing' of mantras on the body <term>nyāsa: the ritual sanctification of the body by touching various points while reciting mantras</term>, nor even ritual baths and so on, which may be done or not according to one's will."

---

<margin>Line 14: Manuscript 'Ka' reads "disciplinary conduct and sacrificial altars are also forbidden."</margin>

<summary>Abhinavagupta argues that the spontaneous internal realization of reality is the highest form of ritual, superseding the need for external ceremonies like formal initiation or physical sacrifices. He cites the Siddhayogīśvarīmata to prove that internal knowledge is the "primary" sacrifice, while physical rituals are merely secondary.</summary>
<keywords>initiation (diksha), internal knowledge (parijñāna), sacrifice (yāga), Siddhayogīśvarīmata, ritual conduct (caryā), means-less path (anupāya)</keywords>

--- Page 358 ---
<meta>On the previous page, Abhinavagupta established that internal realization is the "primary sacrifice." Page 36 expands on this by presenting a hierarchy of ritual and mental states, moving from the most external physical objects to the highest internal state of Knowledge (jñāna).</meta>

<page-num>३६</page-num>
<header>The Venerable Light of the Tantras <note>original: "Śrī Tantrāloka"</note></header>

->Higher than the **sacrificial ground**<-
->is the **vessel-carving**;<-
->higher than the vessel-carving is the **image on cloth**;<-
->higher than the image is **meditation**, and then the **object of meditation**;<-
->beyond that, **concentration** is superior. [42]<-

->Higher even than that is the **form born of yoga**;<-
->and higher still than that is **Knowledge**.<-
->For through Knowledge, one indeed becomes<-
->a **Great Adept** and a **Lord of Yogis**. [43]<-

The **sacrificial ground** <term>sthaṇḍila: a patch of earth leveled, purified, and prepared for ritual offerings</term> is a plot of land taken for the purpose of sacrifice. The **vessel-carving** <term>tūra: a specific ritual design or geometric shape engraved upon a pot or vessel</term> is a particular form carved into a vessel or similar ritual object. 

He explains the reason for the absolute supremacy of **Knowledge** <note>original: "jñāna"</note> with the phrase "through Knowledge." This means that through Knowledge, one becomes a master even over other yogis. Precisely for this reason—to emphasize this point—the terms "Great" <note>original: "mahat"</note> and "Lord" <note>original: "īśvara"</note> are used [in the titles "Great Adept" and "Lord of Yogis"]. [42-43]

However, for those whose **consciousness is not yet pure** <term>anirmala-saṃvid: individuals who still possess spiritual obscurations and cannot yet grasp reality without the help of external tools</term>, this [Master's] act of grace still operates through external means. Thus, he says:

->If He, by the power of His own **sovereign Freedom**,<-
->even for those of **impure consciousness**...<-

<summary>This page outlines a hierarchy of spiritual practices, ranking external rituals (like altars and icons) below internal mental states (like meditation and concentration), and placing Knowledge at the very top. It explains that while Knowledge is the highest path, external aids are still necessary for those whose consciousness is not yet fully purified.</summary>

<keywords>ritual hierarchy, sthaṇḍila, tūra, meditation, Knowledge, Great Adept, consciousness, grace, Abhinavagupta</keywords>

--- Page 359 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 36 regarding the Master who has attained the highest state of Knowledge. Having established the Master's internal realization, the text now shifts to how that Master acts in the world to help others through the "descent of grace."</meta>

<page-num>३७</page-num>
<header>Verse 46] The Second Chapter</header>

->**Desiring to bestow grace,**<-
->**he should adopt the ritual procedure that follows. [44]**<-

This adoption of ritual is done through the **power of absolute freedom** <term>svātantrya: the innate, sovereign power of consciousness to act spontaneously without external cause</term>, and not because of scriptural constraints. This is because the "breaking" <note>original: "troṭana"</note> of such constraints was explained just before this. [44]

What is this "following ritual procedure" like? He says:

->**That procedure is described as varied,**<-
->**according to the person who is to be graced;**<-
->**due to the different ways the various means—**<-
->**Supreme, Lower, and so on—are mingled. [45]**<-

The term "**Supreme-and-Lower**" <note>original: "parāpara," used here as a linguistic shorthand known as ekaśeṣa</note> implies three categories: the **Supreme** <note>original: "para"</note> refers to the Path of Śiva (Śāmbhava); the **Lower** <note>original: "apara"</note> refers to the Path of the Individual (Āṇava); and the **Supreme-and-Lower** <note>original: "parāpara"</note> refers to the Path of Energy (Śākta). Their "**mingled nature**" refers to their association with other various spiritual means. [45]

Resorting to these upcoming ritual procedures is useful not only for his ability to bestow grace upon others, but also for the scriptures and other tools that describe these procedures. Thus, he says:

->**And for that very purpose, for this one**<-
->**who takes the form of the Supreme Lord... [46]**<-

<margin>Line 3: Manuscript 'K' reads "the breaking of the constraint" instead of "of the constraint, because of the breaking."</margin>

<summary>This page explains how a liberated Master uses his sovereign freedom to adapt ritual procedures—the paths of Śiva, Energy, and the Individual—to best serve the spiritual needs of his students. It marks the transition from the Master’s internal realization to his external role as a channel for divine grace.</summary>
<keywords>grace (anugraha), ritual procedure (vidhi), freedom (svātantrya), Supreme Path (Śāmbhava), Path of Energy (Śākta), Path of the Individual (Āṇava), Supreme Lord (Parameśvara)</keywords>

--- Page 360 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from the internal state of the liberated Master to his external actions. It explains why a Master who has already attained the goal still engages with scriptures and rituals: not for his own sake, but as a "Supreme Command" to provide a path for others whose minds are not yet purified.</meta>

<page-num>३८</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

### ...there is regard for the hearing 
### and study of the scriptures and 
### other means. [46]

The scripture is to be accepted not only by those **desiring to ascend** <term>ārurukṣu: a seeker who is still climbing the ladder of spiritual practice</term> the path, but even by this person (the Master). This is the significance of the word "**also**" <note>original: "api"</note> in the verse. As it has been said:

> "Even if he is free from doubt and a knower of Reality, for the sake of the path of those seeking liberation, he should not abandon the boundaries of scripture; such is the Supreme Command of the Lord."

[46]

One might ask: "If he must look toward these means and methods, does this not imply a loss of his absolute freedom?" Anticipating this doubt, he says:

### For him, who is autonomous, 
### there is no restriction 
### anywhere or at any time. 
### Yet, for a person whose mind is not pure, 
### grace cannot occur without a means. [47]

Unlike the seeker who is still ascending, he has no need for a **means** <term>upāya: a spiritual method or discipline</term> for his own sake; if he did, it would indeed be a restriction <note>original: "khaṇḍanā," literally a breaking or limitation</note> of his **absolute freedom** <term>svātantrya: the sovereign, independent power of consciousness</term>. 

Rather, because he has already accomplished everything he needed to do for himself, his acceptance of these methods is entirely for the sake of others. This is because, since the minds of others are not yet purified, **grace** <term>anugraha: the divine descent of power that initiates liberation</term> will not be successfully established for them without the use of a formal method. This is stated by adopting a rule for future conduct, as "sung" <note>original: "yadgītam," referring to the Bhagavad Gītā, which is often cited as "The Song" to validate the behavior of a liberated soul in the world</note>:

<vocab>Tantrāloka, Upāya-śāstra, Ārurukṣu, Svātantrya, Anugraha, Pārameśvarī Ājñā</vocab>

<summary>This page explains that a liberated Master continues to study and follow scriptures not for his own benefit, but to maintain a path for seekers. It clarifies that this adherence to ritual does not limit the Master's absolute freedom, as it is a voluntary act of compassion for those who require structured means to receive grace.</summary>
<keywords>scriptural authority, spiritual means, absolute freedom, compassion of the master, descent of grace, purification of the mind</keywords>

--- Page 361 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on why an enlightened Master, who has achieved absolute freedom, still adheres to scriptural injunctions. The previous page established that the Master acts not for his own sake—since his mind is already pure—but to provide a path for others (grace) and to maintain the world's order, a principle known as "the Supreme Command."</meta>

<page-num>३६</page-num>
<header>Verse 48] The Second Chapter [Tantrāloka] 36</header>

> "Just as the ignorant act out of attachment to their work, O descendant of Bharata, so should the wise act without attachment, desiring **the welfare of the world** <term>loka-saṃgraha: the maintenance and cohesion of the social and spiritual order</term>."

[Quote from the Bhagavad Gītā 3.25]

**Thus concludes verse 47.**

Furthermore, what I have stated is not my own invention <note>original: "svopajñam," meaning something discovered by oneself or a new doctrine</note>. Rather, it has been expressed everywhere by the Lord and by the ancient masters. To demonstrate that the meaning of this entire chapter is undisputed and consistent with tradition, the author says:

->In the glorious **Great Scripture of the Wave**<-
-><term>Ūrmi Mahāśāstra: A foundational, highly secret Tantric text of the Kaula tradition</term>,<-
->which takes the form of the **Lineage of the Perfected Ones**<-
-><term>Siddha-santāna: The historical and spiritual transmission of the masters</term>,<-
->this has been stated; and likewise it was said by<-
->the glorious **Somānanda** and other teachers. [48]<-

<note>Somānanda (c. 900–950 CE) was the grand-teacher of Abhinavagupta and the founder of the Pratyabhijñā or "Recognition" school of Shaivism.</note>

Regarding the "Great Scripture of the Wave"—this refers to the glorious *Ūrmi-kaula-siddha-santāna-rūpaka*. By using this title, the author shows that the lineage remains pure and "unfading" even within the specific branch of the tradition known as the *Pādovahlyā*. Within that text, the following dialogue occurs:

> "The **Void** <term>śūnya: a state of consciousness free from mental constructs and objective limitations</term> is nothing, yet that Void is actually 'non-void' (full); it is not mere emptiness. If it were truly nothing, how could it be, and how could it be impossible to 'cut' <note>Meaning it is indestructible and indivisible</note>?"

**When questioned in this way by the Goddess (Bhagavatī), the Lord (Bhagavān) replied:**

> "In this system, the Self should be known as the Void when it is stripped of **the qualities of Shiva** <term>śivadharma: the specific attributes or powers associated with the state of liberation</term>. Shiva is to be understood as the Void—stainless and formless in essence."

**Starting with these and subsequent words...**

<summary>Abhinavagupta validates his teaching by citing the Bhagavad Gītā and the Ūrmi Mahāśāstra, a key Kaula scripture. He argues that the concept of the enlightened acting for the world is a universal truth held by the ancient masters like Somānanda.</summary>

<keywords>Loka-saṃgraha, Ūrmi Mahāśāstra, Somānanda, Śūnya (Void), Siddha-santāna, Kaula tradition, lineage authority</keywords>

--- Page 362 ---
<meta>This page continues the citations from authoritative scriptures to support the claim that the enlightened state is beyond ritual necessity. It transitions from quoting the "Great Scripture of the Wave" to the works of Somānanda, specifically his foundational text "The Vision of Shiva" (Śivadṛṣṭi), culminating in Verse 49 which emphasizes the role of the Guru and reasoning in dispelling doubt.</meta>

<page-num>४०</page-num>
<header>The Illustrious Tantrāloka</header>

> "The four logical positions—'it is not,' 'it is,' 'it both is and is not,' and 'it neither is nor is not'—do not touch it. Because it is beyond the reach of words, that Reality <term>tattva: the fundamental essence or "that-ness" of existence</term> is described here in this way.
> 
> What is not destined to happen will not happen; what is destined to happen cannot be otherwise. Reflecting thus, the wise person should not rely on dualistic mental constructs <term>vikalpa: the conceptual "either/or" thoughts that fragment pure awareness</term>.
> 
> Reality is all-pervading, subtle, and free from all limiting conditions <term>upādhi: external attributes or "colorings" that seem to limit the infinite</term>."

Thus, and in other such passages, much has been said. It has also been stated by the venerable **Somānanda** and other great teachers in the **Vision of Shiva** <note>original: "Śivadṛṣṭi"; a seminal 10th-century text of the Pratyabhijñā school</note> and similar works, as follows:

> "What is the use of meditative cultivation <term>bhāvanā: the process of repeatedly bringing a realization to mind</term> or ritual action for Shiva, who is eternally manifest?"

And also:

> "Once gold is recognized as gold, does one continue with the process of 'cultivating' that knowledge or performing a ritual to make it so?
> 
> Once the state of being Shiva <term>śivatva: the inherent divinity or "Shiva-ness" within all things</term>, which resides in everything, is realized through a valid means of knowledge <term>pramāṇa: an instrument of correct perception, such as direct experience or logic</term>—whether from the scriptures or the words of the Guru—and is held with a firm conviction, there is no further need for ritual action or meditative cultivation anywhere." [48]

The author now states that this same principle should be carefully observed in all circumstances:

> When the clouds of doubt have dissolved through the words of the Guru, through the refining power of a collection of sound reasonings, or through the confidence gained from the scriptures—whether studied or heard—then one should touch the feet of the Lord. He is like the sun, the conqueror of darkness, shining brilliantly in the sky of the heart. [49]

<summary>This page concludes verse 48 and introduces verse 49, citing Somānanda to argue that once one's identity as Shiva is realized through a Guru or scripture, ritual efforts become unnecessary. It compares the Lord to a sun that dissolves the "clouds" of conceptual doubt in the heart.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the role of the Guru and logic in achieving liberation. It explains how intellectual ignorance is removed through a combination of the Guru's instruction, scriptural study, and internal realization, specifically for those who have received the descent of divine grace.</meta>

<page-num>४१</page-num>
<header>Verse 46] The Second Chapter</header>
<sig>६</sig>

From the statement beginning with "From the Guru" and so forth, through a single instruction on the nature of the Self—such as "the Self alone is the Lord, all-knowing and the author of all"—a systematic arrangement of logical arguments is constructed. This scriptural methodology, which serves to refute opposing views and establish one’s own position, brings about a "cleansing." This refers to the uprooting of **intellectual ignorance** <term>bauddhājñāna: ignorance that exists as a conceptual misunderstanding in the mind</term>. The meaning is that through the dawning of intellectual knowledge, one attains a firmness in **Self-recognition** <term>svaparāmarśa: the direct, reflective awareness of one's own divine identity</term>.

"Scripture" refers to the **non-dual revelation** <term>advaitāgama</term>, which possesses an authority equal to the Lord Himself. Through conviction in this, realization may come to those who possess the "intense-intense" **descent of grace** <term>śaktipāta: the transformative touch of divine energy</term> through these sources individually: from the Guru, from the scripture, or from within oneself. Alternatively, it may come from the combination of all three for those who possess the "intense-medium" and other degrees of grace.

**Doubt and conceptual constructs** <term>vikalpa: the dualistic 'either/or' thoughts that fragment awareness</term> are like "clouds" because they act as a veil. When these dissolve, the **Heart**—which is **reflective awareness** <term>vimarśa</term> itself—is like the "sky" because it is unconfined and boundless. In that sky shines a great **Radiance** <term>mahas</term> or light, characterized by the powers of knowing and acting. 

Therefore, you should touch the **Feet** of the Lord—the Supreme Self who manifests as the very essence of the universe and who conquers the "darkness" of ignorance, which consists of the appearance of duality that hides one’s own true Self. Regarding the "Feet": since the verbal root *car* (to move) also implies "to know," the feet represent forms of knowledge such as **individualized knowledge** <term>āṇava-jñāna: the limited knowledge associated with the finite ego</term>. You—those mentioned previously who have received the various intensities of the descent of grace—should "touch" these; that is, you should realize them as being essentially identical with your own Self, following the progressive stages of realization.

# The Illustrious Tantraloka

The meaning is: you should contemplate in this way. For this very reason, a comparison with the **sun** has been stated. Indeed, when the clouds have melted away, the sun shines in the sky and dispels the darkness; in the same way, the "touch of its rays" <note>original: *pāda-sparśaḥ*; the word *pāda* is a clever pun in Sanskrit meaning both the "rays of the sun" and "the feet of the teacher," implying that the teacher's grace acts like sunlight to dissolve ignorance</note> is appropriate. (49)

Now, the author concludes the chapter with the first half of the following verse:

> This **Daily Session** <term>āhnika: literally a "daily lesson," used here to denote a chapter of the text</term> has been composed as a discernment of the **Supreme Abode** <term>anuttara-dhāma: the "Beyond-the-Highest" state of consciousness that is the goal of the Tantric path</term>, in which all **prescribed means** <term>aupayika: the various yogic methods, breathing exercises, or rituals usually required for spiritual progress</term> have dissolved. (50)

The word "prescribed means" refers to the yogic methods themselves. May there be peace.

->Through the process of searching for hundreds of<-
->ways to understand these various scriptures,<-
->this Chapter on the **Methodless Way** <term>anupāyāhnika: the section of the text describing liberation that occurs spontaneously without the need for techniques</term><-
->has been rapidly explained by Jayaratha.<-

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Methodless Way" <term>Anupāya-prakāśana</term>, in the *Illustrious Tantraloka* <note>meaning "The Light of the Tantras"</note> composed by the venerable Master Abhinavagupta, accompanied by the commentary named "The Light" <note>original: *Prakāśa*; the name of the scholarly commentary by Jayaratha</note> by the teacher Jayaratha. (2)

->May this work, published by the virtuous Mukunda Rama,<-
->who is under the protection of the King of Kashmir,<-
->be offered to Shiva for the joy of the righteous.<-
